Data: confounder-in vs confounder-out states in flip cases (reused) to recover the direction. Model: frozen TabPFN/baseline; only the direction is fitted, recovered as a supervised probe direction and as a confounder-in-minus-out delta, steered at matched L2 norm. Systems compared: (i) adjustment direction; (ii) 20 matched-norm random directions; (iii) an observational-association direction. Decisive metric first: mechanism-selectivity = |predicted X->Y effect shift toward the do-calculus answer under adjustment steering| / |mean shift under random directions|. Convincing: selectivity >= 3, movement toward the correct adjusted sign, and the observational-association direction failing to reproduce it, across probe and delta recovery. Refute: selectivity <= 1.5. Indeterminate band 1.5-3 (declared up front): partial causal traction, reported without a strong claim. A negative result means the adjustment axis is not causally wired to the predicted effect, contradicting clause (c).

Experiment 5 (H1-H3 -- layer emergence, cross-model convergence, and adjustment brackets): Tests robustness of clauses (a)-(c) and whether adjustment structure is specific to SCM-pretrained models. Data: synthetic and semi-realistic tables (reused). Model: TabPFN and the general tabular baseline, frozen; probes/directions as above. Systems compared: (i) per-layer Adjustment-Beyond-Observational Index and steering selectivity (testing the prior expectation that TabPFN's mid layers carry it); (ii) CKA between recovered adjustment subspaces across TabPFN and the baseline; (iii) upper bracket = an explicit backdoor-adjustment estimator computing P(Y|do(X)) by construction, lower bracket = an observational-association regressor with no confounder access. Decisive metric first: fraction of the observational-to-adjustment bracket each model closes. Convincing: >=50% closure for TabPFN AND either cross-model CKA >= 0.5 (convergent) or a clear TabPFN-vs-baseline gap (SCM-pretraining-specific) -- both are informative. Refute: all models within noise of the observational lower bracket. Indeterminate band: 20-50% closure or CKA 0.3-0.5 (declared up front) -- partial/model-specific. A negative result means no model exceeds observational association. All runs are inference-only on public models plus small probes and synthetic/semi-realistic tabular data, feasible on a single GPU.
Risk Factors and Limitations: Observational association and adjusted effect coincide except in confounded cases, making the adjustment-beyond-observational separation statistically demanding; we mitigate with observational-residualization, the confounder-in-vs-out counterfactual (which holds the data-generating process fixed and varies only confounder availability), the Simpson's-flip diagnostic subset, and the dose-response sign-crossing test that an association-only model cannot reproduce.

Withholding the confounder column changes the input dimensionality/schema, which for some tabular models is a structural edit that could confound the comparison with generic distribution shift; we mitigate by using confounder-free datasets (where withholding an equally-informative non-confounding column should NOT flip the effect) as a matched control, so any generic schema-change effect is shared, and report sensitivity.

TabPFN and tabular transformers may implicitly perform some adjustment when all variables are supplied simply by conditioning, blurring 'representing the mechanism' from 'conditioning gives the right answer'; we distinguish these by requiring the correct SIGN FLIP specifically in Simpson's-flip cases, the distinct-axis probe, and the dose-response sign-crossing, none of which a naive conditioner passes without representing adjustment.

Synthetic SCM data gives exact ground truth but may not reflect real confounding structure; we cross-validate on semi-realistic tables (confounding-by-indication, batch confounding) where the true adjusted effect is known or estimable, and report synthetic-vs-real agreement, treating synthetic as the decisive-counterfactual testbed and real as the transfer check.

Linear probes recovering an adjustment direction do not guarantee causal use; we address this with steering plus random/observational-direction controls, though distributed/superposed encodings may blur single-direction interventions - we use both probe directions and delta-representations.

A negative result (models encode observational association and fail to flip under confounder presence in Simpson's-flip cases) is scientifically decisive and directly safety-relevant - it would warn against trusting tabular/scientific foundation models for causal-effect estimation in confounded domains (drug outcomes, clinical, omics) where confounding by indication or batch dominates; we frame either outcome as the first mechanism-defining, representational test of whether foundation models represent the backdoor confounder-adjustment mechanism.
All experiments are inference-only on public pretrained models (TabPFN, a tabular baseline) plus small probes and synthetic/semi-realistic tabular datasets, keeping compute at academic scale.

Name: geostrophic_balance_manifold_probe
Title: Wind Follows Pressure, Inside the Model Too? Probing Whether Weather Foundation Models Internally Encode Geostrophic and Thermal-Wind Balance, Including Its Latitude-Dependent Breakdown
Short Hypothesis: Atmospheric dynamics is governed not by independent fields but by diagnostic balance relationships that couple them: geostrophic balance ties the horizontal wind to the pressure-gradient force via the Coriolis parameter f, thermal wind ties vertical wind shear to horizontal temperature gradients, and hydrostatic balance ties vertical pressure structure to density. We hypothesize that if data-driven weather foundation models represent atmospheric mechanism rather than field-wise pattern matching, their internal representations will (a) encode these balance relationships as coupled directions (wind and pressure-gradient live on a shared balance manifold, not as independently decodable features), (b) causally enforce them (perturbing internal pressure-gradient structure induces the geostrophically-consistent wind change and vice versa), and, most decisively, (c) reproduce the physically-mandated latitude-dependent breakdown of geostrophic balance near the equator where f -> 0. The equatorial breakdown is an exact, physics-predicted signature that a mere pattern matcher would not reproduce internally. Geostrophic balance and its equatorial breakdown are the core, first-class claim; thermal-wind and hydrostatic balance are supporting generalizations, not co-equal contributions.
Related Work: Two lines bracket the gap. (1) Interpretability of weather models: SAE studies on GraphCast (2025) recover single physical features (tropical cyclones, atmospheric rivers, sea-ice) and steer them; GraphDOP work (2025) shows unified world-model representations and applies data-assimilation diagnostics (FSOI). These recover and manipulate individual quantities/objects, not the diagnostic BALANCE RELATIONSHIPS that couple fields. (2) Dynamical/physics tests: 'Dynamical Tests of a Deep Learning Weather Prediction Model' (2024) and the Matsuno-Gill/ASL studies subject Pangu-Weather to classical perturbation experiments and find geostrophic adjustment and wave responses AT THE INPUT-OUTPUT LEVEL; the hydrostatic-balance-constraint (2025) and neural background-error-covariance (2026) papers impose or exploit balance in outputs/latents by construction. None tests whether the model's INTERNAL REPRESENTATION encodes the balance constraints as coupled structure, whether that coupling is causally load-bearing, or whether it reproduces the latitude-dependent (f -> 0) breakdown of geostrophy that formally distinguishes mechanism from pattern matching. Our relational, causal, and physics-predicted-breakdown test is the novel contribution. Output-level geostrophic-adjustment studies (e.g., Pangu perturbation experiments) cannot rule out that balance holds only in the predicted fields while the internal representation encodes wind and pressure independently; only an internal, relational probe with the latitude-dependent (f -> 0) breakdown can discriminate relational encoding from generic correlation.
Abstract: Data-driven weather foundation models now rival physics-based forecasts, and interpretability studies have shown they encode recognizable physical objects such as cyclones and atmospheric rivers. But atmospheric dynamics is defined by diagnostic balances that couple fields: geostrophic balance links horizontal wind to the pressure-gradient force through the Coriolis parameter, thermal wind links vertical wind shear to horizontal temperature gradients, and hydrostatic balance links vertical pressure structure to density. We ask whether weather foundation models internally represent these coupling relationships rather than storing fields as independently decodable features. Using pretrained models (GraphCast and Pangu-Weather) evaluated on ERA5, we first train probes to test whether the wind field and the pressure-gradient force share a common internal balance subspace, quantifying coupling beyond what independent field decoding predicts. Second, we run causal balance-consistency interventions: perturbing internal pressure-gradient structure should induce the geostrophically-correct wind change (parallel to isobars, magnitude scaling as 1/f) while a matched non-balance perturbation should not, and the analogous test for thermal wind. Third, and most discriminatively, we test the physics-mandated latitude dependence: geostrophic coupling in the representation should be strong in midlatitudes and break down near the equator where the Coriolis parameter vanishes, exactly as theory dictates; a pattern matcher would lack this internal latitude-structured breakdown. Metrics quantify a balance-coupling-beyond-independence index, a causal balance-consistency asymmetry, and the correlation between internal coupling strength and the true Coriolis parameter across latitude. Either outcome sharpens what these operationally deployed models actually represent. Practically, the latitude-structured coupling score is a physics-specific diagnostic for comparing models, selecting checkpoints, and detecting extrapolation risk in operational forecasting and climate emulation, complementing accuracy-only evaluation.
Experiments: Experiment 1 (H1 — Balance coupling beyond independent field encoding): Tests the H1(a) claim that weather foundation models encode balance relationships as coupled directions — wind and pressure-gradient share a balance subspace rather than being independently decodable. Data: ERA5 reanalysis snapshots (hourly global fields, decades available); we use 500 snapshots stratified across seasons and latitude bands — 500 gives stable per-band statistics while keeping inference-only extraction to a few GPU-hours; from ERA5 we compute ground-truth geostrophic wind v_g = (1/(f·rho)) k×∇p, the ageostrophic residual, thermal-wind shear, and hydrostatic residual per grid point. Model: pretrained GraphCast and Pangu-Weather (public weights), frozen; trainable = per-layer linear probes for wind, pressure-gradient, temperature-gradient; canonical correlation analysis / PLS between the wind and pressure-gradient subspaces; 3 seeds. Systems compared: shared balance-subspace prediction vs independent per-field encoding, with a shuffled-probe control; repeated for thermal-wind and hydrostatic relations. Decisive metric first: Balance-Coupling Index BCI = shared-subspace predictive R² − what independent per-field encoding predicts. Convincing result: BCI > 0.1 for geostrophic (and ideally thermal-wind/hydrostatic), significant over seeds — a single low-dimensional direction predicts both the pressure gradient and the geostrophically-implied wind. Undecidable band: BCI in [0.0, 0.05] — coupling attributable to fields being separately encoded, reported as no shared manifold; band fixed before data. Negative result: BCI ≤ 0 means fields are encoded independently, H1 fails and the latitude/causal tests targeting the balance subspace are moot.

Experiment 2 (H3 — Latitude-dependent breakdown of geostrophic coupling, decisive test): Tests the decisive H3(c) claim that internal coupling strength follows the physics-mandated latitude dependence, vanishing near the equator where f→0. Data: the 500 ERA5 snapshots binned into latitude bands (e.g., 10° bins from equator to pole). Model: frozen GraphCast/Pangu, fixed Experiment-1 subspaces; BCI recomputed per band; 3 seeds. Systems compared: per-band geostrophic BCI vs the true Coriolis parameter f = 2·Omega·sin(latitude); controls = humidity and a second unconstrained variable (e.g., total column water) decodability (not geostrophically constrained), plus a latitude-shuffled-label null and grid-position controls, none of which should show |f|-structured coupling. Decisive metric first: Spearman/partial correlation between per-band coupling strength and |f|, controlling for data density and field magnitude. Convincing result: coupling strength scales with |f| (correlation ≥ 0.6), strong in midlatitudes and vanishing near the equator, while the humidity control shows no such structure. Undecidable band: correlation in [0.3, 0.45] — a latitude trend too weak to attribute to f, reported as inconclusive; band fixed before data. Negative result: no correlation with |f| (or the humidity control shows the same latitude structure) means the model does not reproduce the physics-predicted equatorial breakdown, the decisive H3 test fails. As pre-specified, the equatorial region is treated as the predicted breakdown zone, not a region where geostrophic coupling is expected.

Experiment 3 (H2 — Causal geostrophic-consistency intervention): Tests the H2(b) claim that the model causally enforces balance — perturbing internal pressure-gradient structure induces the geostrophically-consistent wind change (and the thermal-wind analogue). Data: 200 ERA5 snapshots with target midlatitude regions where f is well away from 0. Model: frozen models; at a chosen layer, perturb the decoded pressure-gradient direction and measure the induced change in decoded wind and next-step wind forecast; run the analogous temperature-gradient→vertical-shear intervention; controls = matched-norm random directions and a non-balance (divergent) perturbation; 3 seeds. Systems compared: balance perturbation vs random / non-balance controls. Decisive metric first: Balance-Consistency Selectivity = |geostrophic-aligned response to balance perturbation| / |response to matched control|, with the induced wind expected parallel to isobars and scaling as 1/f. Convincing result: selectivity ≥ 3 with the induced wind change parallel to isobars and 1/f magnitude scaling. Undecidable band: selectivity in [1.2, 2.0] or no isobar alignment — reported as inconclusive causal enforcement; band fixed before data. Negative result: selectivity ≈ 1 means balance is decodable but not causally enforced, H2 fails.

Experiment 4 (H2 — Geostrophic-adjustment timescale test): Tests the dynamical half of H2(b) — that a deliberately unbalanced internal state relaxes toward balance on the physically-expected latitude-dependent timescale. Data: 150 ERA5 snapshots across latitude bands. Model: frozen models; perturb the internal state into a wind–pressure-inconsistent configuration and roll forward; 3 seeds. Systems compared: restoration rate vs the true inertial timescale 2·pi/f across latitude bands. Decisive metric first: rate and latitude-dependence of balance restoration in representation and outputs, compared to 2·pi/f. Convincing result: the model relaxes toward balance with a restoration timescale that tracks the latitude-dependent inertial period (correlation with 2·pi/f ≥ 0.5). Undecidable band: restoration observed but its latitude dependence correlates with 2·pi/f only in [0.2, 0.35] — reported as weak/inconclusive; band fixed before data. Negative result: no relaxation toward balance, or a timescale unrelated to f, means the model does not implement geostrophic adjustment, bounding H2.

Experiment 5 (H1 — Cross-model convergence and pattern-matching-to-mechanism brackets): Tests whether balance structure is convergent and brackets it, without enlarging the claim. Data: the Experiment-1 ERA5 set. Model: frozen GraphCast and Pangu; brackets = a constraint-imposed model (hydrostatic/geostrophic by construction, e.g. a hydrostatic-constrained DLWP variant, upper) and a randomly-initialized same-architecture model (lower), probed identically; CKA between GraphCast and Pangu balance subspaces; grid/mesh artifacts controlled by latitude-band aggregation and grid-position controls. Systems compared: BCI and latitude-|f| correlation across models and brackets; CKA of balance subspaces. Decisive metric first: mean pairwise CKA of balance subspaces and where the operational models' BCI falls between the random lower and constrained upper brackets. Convincing result: CKA ≥ 0.6 (convergent) and operational-model BCI clearly above the random lower bracket. Undecidable band: CKA in [0.3, 0.45] or BCI within noise of the random bracket — reported as weakly convergent / no learned balance advantage; band fixed before data. Negative result: operational-model balance structure at the random-init bracket means balance is not learned during pretraining, bounding H1.
Risk Factors and Limitations: Wind and pressure-gradient fields are strongly correlated in real data, so shared-subspace coupling could partly reflect data statistics rather than encoded constraint; we mitigate with independent-encoding baselines, the latitude-dependent breakdown test (a signature data correlation alone would not structure by f), and causal interventions.
Linear probes and CCA may miss nonlinear coupling; we report nonlinear (kernel-CCA) variants and rely on causal interventions as primary evidence.

Interventions in a nonlinear GNN/transformer may push activations off-manifold and produce unphysical outputs; we bound perturbation magnitude, report sensitivity, and use matched-norm and non-balance controls.
GraphCast operates on an icosahedral mesh with grid-locked features reported in prior work; we account for mesh artifacts by controlling for grid position and using latitude-band aggregation.

Near the equator, additional balances (e.g., equatorial wave dynamics) replace geostrophy; we treat the equatorial region as the predicted breakdown zone rather than expecting geostrophic coupling, and cross-check with expected equatorial balance signatures.

A negative result (fields encoded independently, no latitude-structured balance coupling) is scientifically decisive and directly relevant to trusting these operationally deployed models beyond their training distribution, though it may be perceived as confirmatory of skepticism; we frame either outcome as the first internal, relational, physics-predicted test of atmospheric balance in weather foundation models.
All experiments are inference-only on public pretrained models plus small probes/CCA and public ERA5 data, keeping compute at academic scale.

Name: conditional_independence_scfm_probe
Title: Do Single-Cell Foundation Models Represent the Conditional-Independence Structure of Gene Regulation, or Just Marginal Co-Expression? A d-Separation Test
Short Hypothesis: The defining feature of a genuine regulatory mechanism, versus raw co-expression, is its conditional-independence (d-separation) structure: a directly-regulated target should remain associated with its regulator after conditioning on mediators, whereas a purely-mediated (indirect) target should become independent. We hypothesize that if single-cell foundation models (scFMs) internally represent mechanism rather than marginal correlation, then their internal gene representations will encode this conditional-independence structure — direct edges will survive representational conditioning on mediators while indirect edges will vanish — and that this internal structure will causally govern how the model propagates in-silico perturbations. This is a stronger, mechanism-defining test than the marginal edge-recovery (AUROC) studies that dominate the literature and that have found only co-expression-level signal. We frame a positive result as evidence *consistent with* mechanistic (conditional-independence) structure rather than proof of causal identification, and a negative result as decisive for the co-expression view.
Related Work: A 2026 benchmark (Ye et al.) and Qi et al. (2026) evaluate GRN edge recovery from scFMs and find transferable but limited regulatory signal; a 2026 systematic evaluation (paper 1) shows scGPT/Geneformer attention captures co-expression, not causal regulatory signal, and adds no incremental predictive value over gene-level baselines. SAE/transcoder interpretability work (InterPLM-style, transcoder circuits, scFeatureLens) recovers concept features but validates against marginal annotations. Causal single-cell VAEs (sVAE+, SAMS-VAE) learn causal latent structure by construction from perturbation data — but they are bespoke models, not tests of what large pretrained scFMs already encode. Crucially, no prior work tests whether pretrained scFMs internally represent the *conditional-independence / d-separation* structure that formally distinguishes direct from mediated (indirect) regulation. Since marginal co-expression cannot separate these, showing internal conditional-independence structure would be the first mechanism-defining (rather than correlation-consistent) evidence, directly addressing the 'co-expression not causation' verdict of recent work. The closest prior family is marginal GRN edge-recovery benchmarks (Ye et al. 2026; Qi et al. 2026): because marginal AUROC scores an edge in isolation, it is formally blind to whether that edge survives conditioning on a mediator - exactly the direct-vs-indirect distinction we test. Our contribution is the d-separation-based evaluation protocol, not a new model or dataset.
Abstract: Recent studies conclude that single-cell foundation models (scFMs) capture gene co-expression rather than causal regulation, based on marginal edge-recovery benchmarks. But marginal correlation is fundamentally incapable of distinguishing a direct regulatory edge from an indirect, mediated one — that distinction requires conditional independence, the formal signature (d-separation) of a causal mechanism. We propose the first test of whether pretrained scFMs internally represent this conditional-independence structure. Using known regulatory cascades (regulator R -> mediator M -> target T) curated from validated pathways and perturbation-derived ground truth, we compare, in the model's internal gene representation space, the association between R and its direct target versus R and a purely-mediated target, before and after representationally conditioning on M. A mechanistic representation should retain R-direct association after conditioning while eliminating R-mediated association; a co-expression representation should show both surviving or both vanishing equally. We further run a causal in-silico perturbation test: perturbing M should block propagation of an R-perturbation to a mediated target but not to a direct target, if the internal structure is load-bearing. We test scGPT, Geneformer, and scFoundation across immune and fibroblast cell types, using Perturb-seq data (K562, RPE1) for ground-truth cascades. Metrics quantify a conditional-independence selectivity index, mediation-blocking asymmetry, and agreement with perturbation-derived causal structure. We define the Conditional-Independence Selectivity Index (CISI) as the ratio of the mediator-conditioned representational association of direct pairs to that of indirect pairs, where conditioning is estimated both by linear partialling-out and by a nonparametric kernel conditional-independence test. If CISI is consistently null, researchers should stop interpreting scFM representations as causal and treat them as co-expression encoders useful for hypothesis screening; if positive, scFMs gain support as mechanistic priors for perturbation-guided discovery. Either outcome moves benchmarking beyond marginal AUROC toward conditional criteria.
Experiments: Experiment 1 (H1 — Cascade ground truth and marginal-association baseline): Establishes the labeled direct-vs-mediated edges H1 needs and confirms the starting point that both edge types are marginally associated (the co-expression finding). Data: ground-truth regulatory triples (R→M→T_indirect and R→T_direct) from (a) Replogle et al. genome-scale Perturb-seq in K562 and RPE1 (~2,000 perturbations, ~2.5M cells exist), (b) linear cascades from Reactome/KEGG, (c) STRING/ChIP-seq for TF binding; we curate 300 high-confidence triples (each with a designated mediator M and perturbation-established causal ordering) — 300 balances statistical power for the paired index against the scarcity of clean linear cascades; provenance and confidence tier recorded per triple. Model: scGPT, Geneformer, scFoundation, all frozen, inference only; per-gene contextual representations (token embeddings and final hidden states) extracted for each cell. Systems compared: representational R–T association for direct vs mediated pairs. Decisive metric first: marginal association (cosine / co-activation) of R and T representations, per pair type. Convincing (expected) result: both direct and mediated pairs show high marginal association (median cosine > 0.5), replicating co-expression and setting up the conditioning test. Undecidable/If-here note: if even marginal association is absent (< 0.2 for direct pairs), the models do not represent these relationships at all and Experiments 2–3 cannot separate direct from mediated; this floor is fixed before data. Negative interpretation: no marginal signal would make the conditional test uninterpretable and is reported as such.

Experiment 2 (H1 — Conditional-independence selectivity after conditioning on the mediator): Tests the core H1 claim that direct edges survive representational conditioning on the mediator while indirect edges vanish. Data: the 300 triples from Experiment 1 across their native cell types. Model: frozen scGPT/Geneformer/scFoundation representations; conditioning done two ways — (a) linear partialling-out of mediator M's representation, (b) a nonparametric kernel conditional-independence test (KCIT) conditioned on M; no model training, only the CI estimators; 3 seeds over cell subsampling. Systems compared: partial association of direct vs mediated pairs, plus three controls — condition on a random gene R′ of matched marginal correlation, a reverse-cascade control, matched non-cascade (co-member) pairs of equal marginal correlation, a pathway-shuffled baseline, and a raw-log-expression baseline run through identical CI tests, isolating the effect from expression level, pathway co-membership, and batch/cell-state confounds. Decisive metric first: Conditional-Independence Selectivity Index CISI = (partial association of direct pairs) / (partial association of mediated pairs). Convincing result: CISI significantly ≫ 1 (mediated pairs drop toward independence, direct pairs retained) AND the model's CISI exceeds the raw-expression baseline's, with the random-gene control near 1. Undecidable band: CISI in [0.9, 1.4] — no reliable direct-vs-mediated separation, read as pure co-expression (H1 unsupported); band fixed before data. Negative result: CISI ≈ 1 or not above the raw-expression baseline means the representation encodes marginal correlation, not conditional-independence structure, and H1 fails.

Experiment 3 (H2 — Causal mediation-blocking under in-silico perturbation): Tests the H2 claim that the internal conditional-independence structure causally governs perturbation propagation — clamping the mediator cuts the indirect path but not the direct one. Data: the 300 triples; perturbations delivered through each model's masked-prediction / perturbation head. Model: frozen models with their native perturbation heads; simulate perturbation of R, measure induced change at T_direct and T_indirect, then clamp M and re-measure; 3 seeds. Systems compared: effect reduction at T_indirect vs T_direct when M is clamped. Decisive metric first: Mediation-Blocking Asymmetry MBA = (reduction in R→T_indirect effect when M clamped) − (reduction in R→T_direct effect when M clamped). Convincing result: MBA large and positive (indirect path collapses, direct path preserved), significant across models. Undecidable band: MBA within its 3-seed CI of 0 — no differential blocking, reported as no causal mediation structure; band fixed before data. Negative-result caveat stated in advance: scFM perturbation heads are known to be weak predictors, so a null MBA is interpreted conservatively — the representational CISI of Experiment 2 remains the primary H1 evidence, and a null here is reported as head-limited rather than refuting H1.

Experiment 4 (H1 — Layer localization and cross-cell-type invariance): Sharpens H1 by locating where conditional-independence structure lives and whether it is context-invariant. Data: the subset of Experiment-1 cascades active in ≥2 cell types (e.g., immune vs fibroblast), ~100 triples. Model: frozen models; CISI recomputed per layer and per component (token embeddings vs contextual hidden states vs attention); 3 seeds. Systems compared: CISI across layers/components and across cell types. Decisive metric first: layer/component of peak CISI and the cross-cell-type correlation of per-triple CISI. Convincing result: a reproducible layer where CISI peaks and cross-cell-type CISI correlation ≥ 0.5, indicating context-invariant mechanistic structure. Undecidable band: cross-type correlation in [0.2, 0.35] — reported as partially context-specific; band fixed before data. Negative result: CISI present in one cell type but uncorrelated across types means the model encodes cell-state-specific co-expression, bounding H1's generality.

Experiment 5 (H1 — Brackets against purpose-built causal and marginal GRN models): Places the scFMs on a correlation-to-mechanism spectrum without enlarging the claim. Data: the 300 triples, plus the same perturbation data used to train a causal single-cell VAE (sVAE+) as an upper reference. Model: frozen scFMs; brackets are sVAE+ (upper, trained on matched perturbation data) and classical GRN inference GENIE3 and PIDC (marginal lower bounds), each producing a comparable direct-vs-mediated selectivity. Systems compared: scFM CISI vs sVAE+ CISI (upper) vs GENIE3/PIDC selectivity (lower). Decisive metric first: where scFM CISI falls between the marginal lower bracket and the causal upper bracket. Convincing result: scFM CISI clearly above the GENIE3/PIDC lower bracket, indicating structure beyond marginal inference. Undecidable band: scFM CISI within noise of the marginal lower bracket — reported as no advantage over co-expression methods; band fixed before data. Negative result: scFMs at or below the marginal bracket means they add no conditional-independence structure over classical marginal GRN inference, a decisive bound on H1.
Risk Factors and Limitations: Conditioning in a nonlinear representation via linear partialling may be incomplete; we mitigate with nonparametric kernel CI tests, but residual nonlinear dependence could inflate or deflate the selectivity index.

Ground-truth mediator assignment from Perturb-seq epistasis is noisy and some 'direct' edges may themselves be mediated by unmeasured genes; we restrict to well-supported cascades and report sensitivity to cascade confidence thresholds.
Distributed/superposed gene representations may make single-mediator conditioning imprecise; we address this with subspace-level conditioning and report aggregate directions.

The in-silico perturbation heads of scFMs are known to be weak predictors; a null mediation-blocking result may reflect head quality rather than representation structure, so we emphasize the representational CI test as the primary evidence.

A negative result (no conditional-independence structure beyond co-expression) is scientifically decisive and consistent with recent findings, but may be perceived as confirmatory; we frame it as the first mechanism-defining test that closes the 'correlation vs. mechanism' question rather than re-litigating edge AUROC.
All experiments are inference-only on pretrained public models plus small probes and CI tests, keeping compute at academic scale.
We pre-register the mediator-selection rule, cascade-confidence thresholds, and sensitivity analyses before touching representations, so CISI cannot be tuned post hoc.

Name: orphan_feature_triage
Title: Signal or Artifact? A Prospective, Externally-Grounded Protocol for Triaging Unannotated Discovery Features in Scientific Foundation Models
Short Hypothesis: Sparse-autoencoder features of scientific foundation models that do NOT map onto any existing annotation ('orphan features') fall into two separable classes: (a) genuine latent scientific signals that predict independent, held-out external measurements the model never saw, and (b) technical/dataset artifacts. We hypothesize these two classes are distinguishable in advance by a small set of cheap, model-internal and cross-modal criteria - external-modality predictivity, cross-dataset stability, and causal ablation specificity - yielding a reusable triage protocol that turns interpretability from post-hoc confirmation into prospective, validated discovery.
Related Work: A wave of dictionary-learning work extracts SAE features from scientific FMs and validates them against KNOWN annotations: InterPLM (2024) and Adams et al. (2025) on protein LMs, Discovering Interpretable Biological Concepts in scRNA-seq FMs (2025), SAEs Reveal Interpretable Features in Single-Cell FMs (2025), ICFL on microscopy FMs (2024), and Open-Ended Visual Scientific Discovery with SAEs (2025). All of these note that MANY features do NOT map to existing annotations, and InterPLM/ICFL propose auto-interpretation to label them - but auto-interpretation still hallucinates and cannot distinguish a real undiscovered signal from an artifact. The Pleiades Alzheimer's biomarker study (2026) shows interpretability CAN surface a genuinely novel biomarker class (fragmentomics), but it is a single bespoke success validated by heavy downstream work, not a general triage rule. 'On the definition and importance of interpretability in SciML' (2025) argues that without prior knowledge one cannot tell whether a discovered structure is meaningful. The critical, unaddressed gap is a GENERAL, PROSPECTIVE decision procedure that, for an arbitrary orphan (unannotated) feature, predicts whether it is a real latent signal or an artifact BEFORE expensive follow-up. Our protocol - using cross-modal external ground truth the model never ingested plus cross-dataset stability and causal ablation as a triage classifier - is that missing piece, and is distinct from all prior annotation-matching and single-case discovery work.
Abstract: Sparse autoencoders now routinely extract thousands of interpretable features from scientific foundation models of proteins, cells, and images, and the field has begun to celebrate features that align with known biological concepts. But every such study reports a large fraction of 'orphan' features that map onto no existing annotation, and interpretability's promise for discovery hinges precisely on these: some are undiscovered scientific signals, others are dataset artifacts (batch effects, sequencing depth, staining, plate position), and current practice - auto-interpretation by a stronger LLM - cannot reliably tell them apart. We propose the first general, prospective triage protocol that decides, for an arbitrary unannotated feature, whether it is a genuine latent signal or an artifact, and validates the decision against independent evidence the model never saw. Working with public single-cell RNA-seq foundation models (scGPT, Geneformer) and protein language models (ESM-2), we train SAEs, remove features matching known annotations, and score the remaining orphans on three cheap criteria: (1) external-modality predictivity - does the feature predict a held-out measurement from a DIFFERENT modality/assay the model was never trained on (e.g., a scRNA feature predicting matched CITE-seq surface-protein levels, or an ESM-2 feature predicting an experimental deep-mutational-scanning quantity)? (2) cross-dataset stability - does an equivalent feature reappear across independent datasets/labs? (3) causal ablation specificity - does ablating it selectively change model outputs for a coherent biological subset, not diffusely? We test whether these three criteria jointly separate a curated set of known-signal orphans from planted-artifact orphans, calibrate a triage classifier, and then apply it prospectively to surface and externally confirm candidate novel signals. The result is a reusable instrument that converts interpretability from confirmation into validated discovery. The contribution is a decision protocol, not a new SAE method: its novelty is the prospective triage rule and the cross-modal external ground truth it is validated against, distinct from prior annotation-recovery and LLM auto-labeling that can only confirm known concepts or hallucinate labels. The user story is concrete, an interpretability practitioner runs it on their own SAE features, on any scientific FM, before committing wet-lab or downstream-enrichment follow-up, and the payoff is quantified as discovery precision at K over a random-orphan baseline and the cost of chasing artifacts avoided. If it only partially works, the calibrated classifier is still usable as a ranked prioritizer with reported precision and recall rather than a hard filter, and the three-criterion design is intended to transfer beyond the showcased modalities.
Experiments: Experiment 1 (H1 -- feature extraction, orphan set, and a two-class development set of known-signal vs planted-artifact orphans): Establishes the substrate and the ground-truth labels that clauses (a)/(b) and the triage claim are tested on -- namely that orphan SAE features split into genuine latent scientific signals and technical/dataset artifacts. Data: two scRNA-seq FMs (scGPT ~51M and Geneformer ~10-40M or scFoundation) and a protein LM (ESM-2 650M), public weights, frozen (inference-only); SAEs are the only trainable objects. We train TopK SAEs (dictionary width 16x hidden dim, k=32, Adam lr 1e-4, up to ~1e8 token-activations, 3 SAE seeds) on one hidden layer of each model, following InterPLM/single-cell SAE recipes. Each feature is matched to known annotations (cell type, tissue, cell-cycle phase, GO terms, secondary structure, binding sites) by activation-vs-label alignment; features with F1 or AUROC >= 0.7 are 'annotated', the remainder are ORPHANS. From the orphans we build a labeled development set: KNOWN-SIGNAL orphans = features correlating (Spearman >= 0.5) with an independently-validated signature deliberately held out of the annotation set; PLANTED-ARTIFACT orphans = features aligning (AUROC >= 0.8) with technical covariates (sequencing depth, batch/lab ID, plate/well position, staining intensity, mitochondrial fraction). Target >= 100 orphans per class per model. Decisive metric first: development-set class balance and label-confidence (fraction with covariate/signature alignment above threshold). Convincing: >= 100 orphans per class per model with confident labels. If fewer than ~40 per class are recoverable for a given model, that model is reported as underpowered and excluded from the decisive triage test rather than analyzed at low power. A negative finding here (orphans do not resolve into the two labeled classes at all) would itself contradict the premise that the classes exist and are identifiable.

Experiment 2 (H1 -- Criterion 1, external-modality predictivity separates the two classes): Tests whether external-modality predictivity distinguishes genuine-signal from artifact orphans. Data: the development-set orphans from Experiment 1 (reused). scRNA case: paired CITE-seq (matched cells with ~130-200 surface-protein readouts) and multiome ATAC (existing public sets used as is); protein case: an experimental deep-mutational-scanning fitness set and a mega-scale stability ddG set (existing, used as is). Model: frozen FMs and fixed SAE features; only a ridge/logistic read-out from a feature's activation to the held-out external measurement is fitted (5 seeds, cell/protein-grouped splits). Systems compared: each orphan's cross-modal predictive R^2/AUROC residualized against the matched ANNOTATED features, known-signal vs planted-artifact. Decisive metric first: AUROC of Criterion-1 score for separating known-signal from planted-artifact orphans. Convincing: separation AUROC >= 0.75 with 95% bootstrap CI (over features) excluding 0.5. Refute: AUROC <= 0.6. Indeterminate band 0.6-0.75 (stated before the data): Criterion 1 is a weak-but-usable signal, retained only as one of three inputs, not a sole arbiter. A negative result means external-modality predictivity does not separate the classes, weakening the triage protocol.

Experiment 3 (H1 -- Criterion 2, cross-dataset stability separates the two classes): Tests whether cross-dataset stability distinguishes the classes. Data: independent datasets from different labs/protocols for each modality (existing public sets); we train independent SAEs (same recipe) on each and match features across dictionaries by activation-correlation and matched top-activating examples. Model: frozen FMs; SAEs trainable. Systems compared: cross-dataset stability score of known-signal vs planted-artifact orphans (genuine signals expected stable; artifacts dataset-specific, or, if stable, covariate-aligned and caught by Criterion 3). Decisive metric first: AUROC of Criterion-2 score for class separation. Convincing: AUROC >= 0.75 (bootstrap CI over features excluding 0.5). Refute: AUROC <= 0.6. Indeterminate band 0.6-0.75 (declared up front): weak-but-usable, kept as one of three inputs. We report robustness to SAE width/k because feature splitting/merging can blur matching. A negative result means stability does not separate the classes, weakening the protocol.

Experiment 4 (H1 -- Criterion 3, causal ablation specificity separates the two classes): Tests whether ablation specificity distinguishes the classes. Data: development-set orphans (reused). Model: frozen FMs; we ablate each orphan feature in the SAE reconstruction and measure the induced change in downstream outputs, bounding edits and comparing to matched random-feature ablations. Systems compared: specificity index = concentration of the ablation effect on a coherent biological subset (cell type / protein family) vs diffuse or technical-covariate-aligned change, known-signal vs planted-artifact. Decisive metric first: AUROC of Criterion-3 score for class separation. Convincing: AUROC >= 0.75 (bootstrap CI over features excluding 0.5). Refute: AUROC <= 0.6. Indeterminate band 0.6-0.75 (declared before the data): weak-but-usable, one of three inputs. A negative result means ablation specificity does not separate the classes, weakening the protocol.

Experiment 5 (H1 -- triage classifier calibrates and beats the LLM auto-interpretation default): Tests the core claim that the three cheap criteria JOINTLY yield a reusable triage instrument, and that it beats the current default. Data: development-set orphans with the three criterion scores (reused). Model: a logistic-regression triage classifier on the three scores (the only fitted model), with leave-one-model-family-out and leave-one-modality-out cross-validation to test generality; per-criterion ablations to see which carries the signal. Baseline system: LLM auto-interpretation (labeling top-activating examples) confidence used as a predictor of genuine-vs-artifact status. Decisive metric first: cross-validated AUROC of the triage classifier separating known-signal from planted-artifact orphans. Convincing: triage AUROC >= 0.8 that generalizes across held-out model families/modalities (drop <= 0.1) AND exceeds the LLM-auto-interpretation baseline AUROC by >= 0.15. Refute: triage AUROC <= 0.6 or no improvement over the LLM baseline. Indeterminate band 0.6-0.8 (declared up front): a partial instrument -- reported with its precision/recall and error analysis, not advanced as a validated triage rule. A negative result means the cheap criteria do not jointly separate the classes better than the current default, contradicting the central hypothesis.

Experiment 6 (H2 -- prospective, externally-confirmed discovery): Tests the claim that the calibrated triage turns interpretability into prospective, validated discovery -- that top-ranked unlabeled orphans confirm against external evidence not used in triage. Data: the remaining UNLABELED orphans (held out of Experiments 2-5); external confirmation sources not used in triage -- a newer/independent database for enrichment, a matched-cell external assay, and a held-out DMS set. Model: the frozen triage classifier from Experiment 5 applied to unlabeled orphans; no further fitting. Systems compared: confirmation rate of the top-ranked predicted 'genuine signals' vs a random-orphan baseline. Decisive metric first: discovery precision = fraction of top-K predicted-genuine orphans that externally confirm, relative to the random-orphan baseline rate. Convincing: top-K confirmation rate >= 2x the random-orphan baseline with a 95% CI excluding parity, plus 2-3 externally-confirmed novel-signal case studies. Refute: confirmation rate within noise of the random baseline. Indeterminate band: 1.2x-2x baseline (declared before the data) -- suggestive prospective value that does not yet establish the triage as a discovery instrument; reported as such. A negative result means the triage does not prospectively surface genuine signals, contradicting the discovery claim. All work is inference-only on public FMs plus academic-scale SAE training and public paired datasets, feasible on a single GPU.
Risk Factors and Limitations: The 'known-signal vs planted-artifact' development labels may be imperfect; some presumed artifacts could carry biology and vice versa. We mitigate by using clearly technical covariates (depth, batch, plate) for artifacts and independently-validated signatures for signals, and report sensitivity to label noise.

Paired cross-modal data (CITE-seq/multi-omic matched cells, DMS with sequence) is limited in quantity and coverage, which constrains Criterion 1; we use the best available public paired datasets and treat cross-modal predictivity as one of three criteria rather than the sole arbiter.

Some genuine signals may be dataset-specific (cross-dataset stability fails) and some artifacts may be stable across labs; the three criteria are designed to be complementary so no single failure is decisive, but the triage classifier may still misclassify edge cases - we report calibration and error analysis rather than claim perfect separation.

SAE features can be split/merged across dictionaries, complicating cross-dataset matching; we use matched-top-example and activation-correlation matching and report robustness to SAE hyperparameters and width.
Ablation in SAE reconstruction may push activations off-manifold; we bound edits and report specificity relative to matched random-feature ablations.

External confirmation of prospectively-surfaced novel signals is inherently harder to guarantee within one paper; we frame the contribution primarily as a validated TRIAGE INSTRUMENT (evaluated on the development set with ground truth) plus a small number of externally-confirmed case studies, so the paper stands even if only a few novel signals confirm.
All experiments are inference-only on public pretrained models plus academic-scale SAE training and public paired datasets, keeping compute feasible for an academic lab.

Name: selection_rule_forbidden_transition_probe
Title: Bright or Dark? Testing Whether Molecular/Materials Foundation Models Represent Symmetry-Based Optical Selection Rules, Not Just the Energy Gap
Short Hypothesis: Whether an electronic transition absorbs light is set by an exactly-known symmetry mechanism—optical selection rules (Laporte/parity, spin, and orbital-symmetry rules)—that determines the oscillator strength (bright vs dark) largely independently of the energy-gap size: two molecules can have nearly identical HOMO-LUMO gaps yet one is intensely absorbing and the other symmetry-forbidden (dark). We hypothesize that if a molecular/materials foundation model represents this selection-rule mechanism rather than treating optical activity as a monotone function of the energy gap, then (a) transition brightness (oscillator strength) is decodable from internal representations along an axis distinct from the gap, (b) a symmetry-breaking counterfactual—a small distortion that lowers molecular symmetry and turns a forbidden (dark) transition allowed (bright) at nearly-fixed gap—shifts the internal brightness signal accordingly, whereas a symmetry-preserving perturbation of matched magnitude does not, and (c) steering a recovered 'allowedness' direction causally reshapes predicted absorption without changing the gap. The forbidden-vs-allowed symmetry counterfactual is an exact, mechanism-defining test that gap correlation cannot pass.
Related Work: Two lines bracket the gap. (1) ML for optical/excited-state properties—TD-DFT surrogate models, oscillator-strength and UV-Vis spectrum predictors (e.g., message-passing and transformer models on QM8/QM9-spectra, Oled/optical datasets), and excited-state foundation models—are trained to predict excitation energies and intensities but are judged by regression error, not by whether they internalize the selection-rule mechanism. (2) Interpretability of chemistry/atomistic foundation models—SAE studies on chemistry FMs, 'Circuits, Features, and Heuristics in Molecular Transformers' (2025), MoleX (2024), and periodic-law/spin-state probes—recover substructure/element/valence features validated against ground/scalar annotations, none of which concern excited-state symmetry. Physics/interpretability work recovers and steers single scalar quantities (energy, vorticity) but never the parity/spin symmetry that decides whether a transition is bright or dark. Crucially, no work tests whether a foundation model internally represents optical selection rules—the symmetry mechanism separating oscillator strength from the energy gap—whether that representation is causally load-bearing, or uses a symmetry-breaking counterfactual to arbitrate mechanism vs gap correlation. Because bright transitions also tend to have accessible gaps in typical data, correlation-based benchmarks cannot separate the two. Our brightness-beyond-gap probe, forbidden-vs-allowed symmetry counterfactual, and causal allowedness steering are the novel, mechanism-defining contribution, distinct from the chirality (pseudoscalar) and spin-state probes in also targeting the parity/orbital-symmetry selection mechanism of excited states. Positioned against three method families: intensity-regression benchmarks judge output error, SAE and feature cataloguing on chemistry FMs recover static substructure, and geometric sensitivity analysis varies distortion magnitude, none holding the gap fixed while flipping only symmetry as our counterfactual does.
Abstract: Whether a molecule absorbs light at a given color is governed not by the size of its energy gap alone but by an exactly-known symmetry mechanism: optical selection rules. Parity (Laporte), spin, and orbital-symmetry rules decide whether an electronic transition is allowed (bright, large oscillator strength) or forbidden (dark, vanishing intensity), and this can flip a transition from dark to bright with a tiny symmetry-lowering distortion that barely changes the gap. This makes selection rules an ideal, mechanism-defining probe for whether molecular/materials foundation models learn excited-state symmetry or merely a gap-to-intensity correlate. We probe pretrained molecular foundation models and optical-property predictors on datasets with computed oscillator strengths and excitation energies (e.g., QM8, QM9-spectra, and curated symmetric/near-symmetric molecule sets). First, a brightness-beyond-gap probe: is transition oscillator strength decodable from internal representations beyond what the energy gap predicts, along a distinct axis? Second, and most decisively, a symmetry-breaking counterfactual: we apply a small distortion that lowers molecular symmetry and turns a forbidden transition allowed at nearly-fixed gap, versus a matched symmetry-preserving distortion that keeps it dark, and test whether the internal brightness signal responds to the symmetry change, not the gap; a gap-correlate model responds identically. Third, causal allowedness steering reshapes predicted absorption without shifting the gap. Metrics quantify a brightness-beyond-gap index, a symmetry-break-vs-preserve causal asymmetry, and an intensity-error failure predictor. Either outcome sharpens whether deployed optical-property models represent selection rules or are blind to them—critical for photochemistry and materials discovery. The novelty is twofold and explicitly separated: a representation finding (brightness on an axis distinct from the gap) and a causal mechanism test (the symmetry-breaking counterfactual), in an excited-state selection-rule setting no prior probe has entered. Beyond scientific insight into what optical-property models learn, this is a practical model audit: excited-state-ML, photochemistry, and mechanistic-interpretability researchers would run it before deploying a model for dark/bright-state design, e.g. OLED-emitter and forbidden-transition screening, where a model that treats intensity as a gap correlate will mis-rank symmetry-forbidden dark states. A positive result licenses such screening; a negative result flags a specific, correctable blind spot.
Experiments: Experiment 1 (H1 -- transition brightness is decodable along an axis distinct from the energy gap): Tests clause (a): oscillator strength (brightness) is decodable from internal representations on an axis distinct from the HOMO-LUMO gap. Data: QM8 (an existing set used as is; 21,786 molecules with TD-DFT excitation energies and oscillator strengths for the lowest transitions) plus QM9-spectra; from these we curate a diagnostic subset of ~500 high-symmetry / near-symmetric molecules (centrosymmetric species, symmetric aromatics) that host Laporte/parity-forbidden transitions, chosen because forbidden-vs-allowed pairs at matched gap are the decisive cases. For each low-lying transition we record excitation energy (gap), oscillator strength f, spin/symmetry-forbidden class, and point group. Model: a 3D atomistic FM (Uni-Mol or MACE latents, ~few-x10M parameters) and a SMILES/graph FM (ChemBERTa-2, ~46-125M parameters), public weights, frozen; only linear probes trained. Probes: ridge (f, gap) and logistic (forbidden vs allowed), L2 via 5-fold CV, standardized features, 5 seeds with scaffold-grouped splits (no molecular scaffold shared across splits); report mean +/- SD. Systems compared: (i) a gap-only baseline predicting f from excitation energy; (ii) Brightness-Beyond-Gap Index = probe R^2 for f from the representation minus the gap-only R^2, after residualizing the gap-predictable component; (iii) the angle between the recovered gap direction and the recovered brightness direction. Decisive metric first: Brightness-Beyond-Gap Index. Convincing: Index >= 0.10 R^2 (95% bootstrap CI over held-out scaffolds excluding 0, >=4/5 seeds) AND gap-vs-brightness axis angle >= 60 degrees (distinct axes), holding on the matched-gap forbidden/allowed subset. Refute: Index <= 0.02 and angle <= 20 degrees (brightness collapses onto the gap). Indeterminate band 0.02-0.10 R^2 or angle 20-60 degrees (stated before the data): unresolved -- some gap-independent brightness signal but not a cleanly separate axis; we report it and do not treat clause (a) as established. A negative result means the model encodes intensity as a gap correlate, contradicting clause (a).

Experiment 2 (H2 -- a symmetry-breaking edit brightens a forbidden transition while a matched symmetry-preserving edit does not): Tests clause (b), the decisive counterfactual. Data: ~150 centrosymmetric/high-symmetry molecules from the Experiment-1 diagnostic subset each hosting a parity-forbidden dark transition; for every molecule we construct one symmetry-breaking distortion (lowers the point group; by selection rules turns the transition allowed at nearly-fixed gap) and one symmetry-preserving control distortion at matched RMSD (transition stays dark). Both edits are constructed and verified by recomputing TD-DFT oscillator strengths and confirming the gap moves <5%. Model: the same frozen FMs, plus (where available) an excited-state/optical head for a direct brightness readout; inference-only, probe from Experiment 1 reused. Systems compared: symmetry-breaking edit vs matched symmetry-preserving edit, per molecule. Decisive metric first: Symmetry-Break-vs-Preserve Causal Asymmetry = |change in the internal brightness signal under the symmetry-breaking edit| / |change under the matched symmetry-preserving edit|. Convincing: median asymmetry >= 3 across the ~150 molecules with the brightness signal rising under symmetry breaking in >=70% of cases and bootstrap-CI lower bound > 1.5. Refute: asymmetry in [0.7, 1.5] (both edits move the signal similarly -- a gap correlate). Indeterminate band 1.5-3 (declared up front): partial support, reported as a qualified positive. Matched RMSD and verified near-fixed gap make any generic off-distribution effect shared. A negative result means brightness does not respond to the symmetry change that the selection rule requires, contradicting clause (b).

Experiment 3 (H2 -- parity/spin double dissociation): Strengthens clause (b) by checking the model reproduces the correct qualitative selection-rule structure, distinguishing two mechanisms an intensity-from-gap model cannot. Data: from the diagnostic subset, ~150 parity-forbidden (Laporte) transitions in centrosymmetric molecules and ~100 spin-forbidden (singlet-triplet) transitions, each with the symmetry-breaking edit from Experiment 2 (reused); reference TD-DFT confirms parity-forbidden transitions brighten under symmetry lowering while spin-forbidden ones stay dark. Model: frozen FMs with the brightness probe/head. Systems compared: parity-forbidden vs spin-forbidden classes under identical geometric symmetry breaking; shuffled-symmetry-label control. Decisive metric first: double-dissociation score = fraction of parity-forbidden transitions correctly predicted to brighten minus the fraction of spin-forbidden transitions incorrectly predicted to brighten. Convincing: score >= 0.5 (parity brightens, spin does not) with the shuffled-label control near 0. Refute: score <= 0.1 (the model cannot separate the two rules). Indeterminate band 0.1-0.5 (declared in advance): partial dissociation, reported without claiming a mechanistic separation. A negative result means the model does not distinguish parity from spin selection rules, weakening clause (b).

Experiment 4 (H3 -- steering an allowedness direction changes predicted absorption without moving the gap): Tests clause (c). Data: bright-vs-dark transition pairs and symmetric/symmetry-broken molecule pairs (from the sets above) used to recover the direction. Model: frozen FMs with excited-state/optical head; only the direction is fitted. We recover an 'allowedness/brightness' direction three ways -- supervised probe, SAE feature separating bright from dark, and a symmetry-broken-minus-symmetric delta -- and steer at matched L2 norm. Systems compared: (i) allowedness direction; (ii) 20 matched-norm random directions; (iii) a matched gap direction. Decisive metric first: mechanism-selectivity = |predicted-absorption change under allowedness steering| / |mean change under random steering|; cross-talk = |gap shift under allowedness steering| / |gap shift under the gap direction|. Convincing: selectivity >= 3, cross-talk <= 0.2 (brightness moves, gap barely does), and the gap direction moving the gap but not brightness -- a disentangled double dissociation replicated across the three recovery methods. Refute: selectivity <= 1.5 or cross-talk >= 0.6. Indeterminate band: selectivity 1.5-3 or cross-talk 0.2-0.6 (declared before the data): entangled/partial control, reported without a clean causal claim. A negative result means allowedness is not an independently steerable axis, contradicting clause (c).

Experiment 5 (H1-H3 -- layer emergence, cross-model convergence, and selection-rule brackets): Tests robustness of clauses (a)-(c) across depth and models and places them on a spectrum. Data: QM8/QM9-spectra and the diagnostic subset (reused). Model: Uni-Mol/MACE and ChemBERTa-2, frozen; probes/directions as above. Systems compared: (i) per-layer Brightness-Beyond-Gap Index and steering selectivity; (ii) CKA between recovered allowedness subspaces across models; (iii) upper bracket = a symmetry-aware transition-dipole model computing f from symmetry by construction, lower bracket = a gap-to-intensity regressor with no symmetry access. Decisive metric first: fraction of the gap-to-mechanism bracket each model closes. Convincing: >=50% bracket closure for at least one model AND cross-model CKA >= 0.5. Refute: all models within noise of the gap-regressor lower bracket. Indeterminate band: 20-50% closure or CKA 0.3-0.5 (declared up front) -- partial/model-specific, reported without a universality claim. A negative result means no model exceeds a gap shortcut. All runs are inference-only on public FMs plus small probes/SAEs and public excited-state data, with reference TD-DFT only for the counterfactual geometries, feasible on a single GPU.
Risk Factors and Limitations: Oscillator strength and energy gap are correlated in typical datasets (accessible bright transitions dominate), making the brightness-beyond-gap separation statistically demanding; we mitigate with gap-residualization, the symmetry-breaking double-dissociation counterfactual (which holds the gap nearly fixed while varying symmetry), and the parity-vs-spin dissociation that a gap-correlate model cannot reproduce.

Constructing symmetry-breaking vs symmetry-preserving distortions with matched magnitude but different selection-rule consequences requires care with point-group assignment and verifying the intended brightness flip via reference TD-DFT; we compute reference oscillator strengths for the distorted geometries and report sensitivity to distortion magnitude and to point-group-assignment confidence.

Small geometric distortions may push conformers off the model's training distribution, confounding the symmetry-breaking response with generic out-of-distribution failure; we bound distortion RMSD, verify the gap stays nearly fixed, and compare against the matched symmetry-preserving distortion so any generic OOD effect is shared.

Many molecular FMs predict ground-state/scalar properties and may not natively output excited-state brightness; for these we probe whether the representation encodes brightness/selection-rule structure at all and prioritize models with excited-state or optical heads for the causal-steering readout, reporting per-model scope and treating scalar-only models as an informative lower bracket.

Excited-state reference data (TD-DFT oscillator strengths) is functional- and basis-set-dependent and noisy for weak transitions; we use curated consensus datasets (QM8, QM9-spectra), restrict decisive tests to well-characterized symmetric molecules, and emphasize the qualitative bright/dark flip over exact intensity magnitude.

Linear probes recovering an allowedness direction do not guarantee causal use; we address this with steering, cross-talk controls, and random-direction controls, though distributed/superposed encodings may blur single-direction interventions—we use both probe directions and SAE features.

A negative result (models predict intensity as a gap correlate and fail the symmetry-breaking counterfactual) is scientifically decisive and directly relevant to trusting molecular/materials FMs for photochemistry, OLED/dye, and optical-materials discovery, where symmetry-forbidden dark states are a central design consideration; we frame either outcome as the first mechanism-defining test of whether foundation models represent optical selection rules.

All experiments are inference-only on public pretrained models plus small probes/SAEs and public excited-state datasets (QM8, QM9-spectra), with reference TD-DFT for counterfactual geometries, keeping compute at academic scale.

Name: teleconnection_remote_forcing_probe
Title: Weather Here Because of the Ocean There: Testing Whether Weather/Climate Foundation Models Represent the Non-Local ENSO Teleconnection Mechanism, Not Just Local Persistence
Short Hypothesis: A defining, causally-directional, non-local mechanism of climate is the teleconnection: a remote tropical Pacific SST anomaly (ENSO) forces a Rossby-wave train that reorganizes distant mid-latitude weather (e.g., the Pacific-North American pattern) with a characteristic lag and phase, whereas local persistence carries no such distant, directional signal. We hypothesize that if data-driven weather/climate foundation models represent this teleconnection mechanism rather than local autocorrelation, then (a) the remote-forcing state (ENSO phase) is decodable from internal representations and linked to distant mid-latitude circulation beyond what local antecedents predict, (b) a remote-forcing counterfactual that perturbs ONLY the tropical Pacific state propagates the physically-correct downstream teleconnection pattern (correct sign, region, and lag), while a distance-matched control perturbation elsewhere does not, and (c) steering a recovered 'ENSO-forcing' direction causally shifts distant weather in the teleconnection-consistent direction. The tropical-Pacific-vs-elsewhere perturbation is an exact, mechanism-defining test that local-statistics correlation cannot pass.
Related Work: Interpretability of weather foundation models recovers single physical OBJECTS/features: SAE studies on GraphCast (2025) find tropical cyclones, atmospheric rivers, and sea-ice and steer them; GraphDOP work (2025) shows a unified observation-driven world model that infers non-local structures (jet streams) and applies FSOI/DA diagnostics; Physics Steering (2025) steers vorticity/diffusion directions. Separately, an ocean-role study (2026) correlates GraphCast OUTPUT errors with SST (an input-output diagnostic, not an internal test), and a coupled DL emulator study (2025) finds AMPLIFIED ENSO teleconnections at the OUTPUT level. Climate science establishes the mechanism precisely: ENSO remotely forces mid-latitude circulation via Rossby-wave teleconnections, distinct from local air-sea coupling (QTCM 2006; tropical-Atlantic remote-vs-local studies 2001-2021). Crucially, no work tests whether a weather/climate foundation model's INTERNAL representation encodes the non-local, causally-directional teleconnection mechanism (remote cause -> distant effect with correct lag/phase), whether it is causally load-bearing, or uses a remote-forcing counterfactual to separate teleconnection from local persistence. Because ENSO state and local antecedents are correlated, output-level benchmarks and error-SST correlations cannot arbitrate this. Our teleconnection-beyond-local probe, tropical-Pacific-vs-elsewhere counterfactual, and causal ENSO-forcing steering are the novel, mechanism-defining contribution. In comparison-table terms across method families: SAE cataloguing localizes static objects, output-level causal-RL and error-SST diagnostics test inputs-to-outputs without internal access, and sensitivity/ablation varies magnitude rather than remote-vs-local location; only our internal counterfactual isolates non-local causation.
Abstract: Data-driven weather and climate foundation models now rival physical models and have been shown to encode recognizable physical objects such as cyclones and atmospheric rivers. But one of the deepest organizing mechanisms of the climate system is non-local and causally directional: teleconnections, in which a remote tropical Pacific sea-surface-temperature anomaly (El Nino/La Nina) forces a Rossby-wave train that reorganizes weather thousands of kilometers away, with a characteristic lag and phase. A model can forecast well by exploiting local persistence without ever internalizing that distant weather is caused by the ocean elsewhere, making teleconnections an ideal, mechanism-defining probe. We test whether pretrained weather/climate foundation models (GraphCast, Pangu-Weather, and a coupled ocean-atmosphere emulator such as DLESyM where available) internally represent the ENSO teleconnection, using ERA5 and coupled-emulator states. First, a teleconnection-beyond-local probe: is the remote-forcing state (ENSO phase) decodable from internal representations and predictive of distant mid-latitude circulation beyond what local antecedents allow? Second, and most decisively, a remote-forcing counterfactual: we perturb ONLY the tropical Pacific state (imposing an ENSO anomaly) and measure whether the model's internal representation and rollout produce the physically-correct downstream teleconnection (e.g., the Pacific-North American pattern) with the right sign, region, and lag, compared to a distance-matched control perturbation elsewhere that should not trigger it. Third, causal steering along a recovered ENSO-forcing direction. Metrics quantify a teleconnection-beyond-local index, a remote-vs-control propagation asymmetry, and a lag/phase fidelity score. Either outcome sharpens whether these operationally-deployed models represent the non-local causality behind seasonal climate. Our contribution is not the ENSO teleconnection itself but a new internal, causal test of whether a deployed model represents it, separating the novelty of the setting (foundation-model emulators) from the novelty of the mechanism test (a remote-forcing counterfactual that isolates non-local causation from local persistence). Unlike SAE feature cataloguing, which names static objects, output-level causal or error-SST diagnostics, which never inspect internal representation, and standard sensitivity or ablation analysis, which cannot hold perturbation magnitude fixed while varying only remote location, the tropical-Pacific-vs-matched-control counterfactual is decisive, and the probe template generalizes to auditing any non-local physical mechanism. Weather-service modelers, climate-AI researchers, and forecast-verification practitioners would use the result for model selection and trust calibration on subseasonal-to-seasonal and ENSO-year forecasts: a model that fails should not be trusted to propagate teleconnection skill, and we report an application-facing teleconnection-forecast-degradation metric alongside the internal indices.
Experiments: Experiment 1 (H1 -- ENSO-forcing is decodable and carries distant circulation beyond local persistence): Tests hypothesis clause (a): that the remote-forcing state (ENSO phase) is decodable from internal representations and predicts distant mid-latitude circulation beyond what local antecedents predict. Data: ERA5 reanalysis (Copernicus CDS; hourly 1940-present, ~83 years). We use monthly-mean SST, 500 hPa geopotential (Z500), 850/250 hPa winds, and 2 m temperature on a 1.5-degree grid for 1940-2022 (996 monthly fields, an existing set used as is); ground-truth Nino3.4 index and the Pacific-North American (PNA) index come from NOAA CPC. We composite over the ~40 El Nino/La Nina events since 1950 (NOAA ONI list) for event-level statistics. Model: GraphCast (~37M parameters) and Pangu-Weather (~256M parameters), both public pretrained weights, entirely frozen; only linear probes are trained. We extract per-grid activations at every block and pool to the North-Pacific/North-American PNA region. Probes: ridge regression (continuous targets: Nino3.4, Z500) and logistic regression (El Nino vs La Nina), L2 strength chosen by 5-fold CV on the train split, features standardized; 5 seeds for year-blocked train/val/test splits (leave-whole-years-out to bar temporal leakage); report mean +/- SD. Systems compared: (i) decoding of Nino3.4 from representations; (ii) a local-persistence baseline predicting the PNA-region Z500 from its own and neighboring recent antecedents; (iii) the Teleconnection-Beyond-Local Index = distant-Z500 decoding R^2 from the model representation minus the R^2 of the local-persistence baseline, after regressing the local-antecedent-predictable component out of the representation. Decisive metric first: Teleconnection-Beyond-Local Index. Convincing: Index >= 0.10 R^2 with a 95% bootstrap CI (1000 resamples over held-out years) excluding 0, in >=4 of 5 seeds, and the residual distant signal correlating |r|>=0.4 with the ENSO-forcing direction rather than local features. Refute: Index <= 0.02 with CI including 0 (the representation adds nothing beyond local persistence). Indeterminate band 0.02-0.10 R^2 (stated before the data): treated as unresolved -- some non-local signal is present but too weak to claim the teleconnection is robustly encoded, and we do not advance to the causal tests as if H1 held. A negative result means the model's distant-circulation information is explained by local autocorrelation, contradicting clause (a).

Experiment 2 (H2 -- a tropical-Pacific-only perturbation propagates the correct downstream teleconnection while a matched control does not): Tests clause (b): a remote-forcing counterfactual perturbing ONLY the tropical Pacific produces the physically-correct downstream teleconnection (correct sign, region, lag), whereas a distance-matched control perturbation elsewhere does not. Data: 30 initialization dates drawn from ERA5 neutral-ENSO winters (1979-2022, existing set used as is) so the injected anomaly is the dominant remote forcing; canonical PNA response pattern and its 2-6 week onset lag from NOAA CPC composites as ground truth. Model: for the decisive coupled test we prioritize an SST-aware/coupled DL emulator (DLESyM-class, public weights) that ingests evolving SST, frozen; for atmosphere-only GraphCast/Pangu (which do not ingest SST) we instead impose the ENSO-associated atmospheric anomaly and report per-model exactly what is manipulable. No training; inference-only rollouts. Systems compared: (i) tropical-Pacific El-Nino-like warm anomaly (and La-Nina-like cold) imposed on the initial state, rest held fixed, rolled forward to the model's horizon; (ii) a distance-matched, equal-magnitude control anomaly placed in a basin with no relevant remote link; (iii) the true canonical PNA pattern. Decisive metric first: Remote-vs-Control Propagation Asymmetry = |projection of the distant response onto the canonical PNA pattern under the tropical-Pacific perturbation| / |same projection under the matched control|, with 30 initializations per condition. Convincing: median asymmetry >= 3 with the correct PNA sign in >=70% of cases and a bootstrap-CI lower bound > 1.5. Refute: asymmetry in [0.7, 1.5] (both perturbations act only locally; no non-local propagation). Indeterminate band 1.5-3 (stated up front): weak/partial support -- the model shows some preferential propagation but not the clean mechanism-defining asymmetry; reported as such, not as confirmation. Because both perturbations are equal-magnitude, any generic off-distribution effect is shared and cancels. A negative result means the model treats the tropical-Pacific forcing like any local perturbation, contradicting clause (b).

Experiment 3 (H2 -- sign reversal and lag fidelity of the teleconnection response): Further tests clause (b) by checking that the propagated response has the physically-correct sign and lag, the parts of (b) a location-only asymmetry does not by itself establish. Data: the same 30 neutral-winter initializations as Experiment 2 (reused), each run under an El-Nino-like and an opposite La-Nina-like tropical-Pacific anomaly; canonical PNA sign and 2-6 week onset lag from NOAA CPC. Model: the coupled/SST-aware emulator (primary) and atmosphere-only models (reported separately), all frozen, inference-only. Systems compared: warm vs cold tropical-Pacific perturbation, plus a shuffled-region control that scrambles where the anomaly is placed. Decisive metric first: sign-reversal consistency = fraction of cases whose distant PNA-pattern response flips sign when the perturbation sign flips. Secondary: correlation between the model's response-onset lag and the canonical lag. Convincing: sign-reversal consistency >= 0.80 AND lag correlation >= 0.5 across cases, with the shuffled-region control near 0.5 consistency. Refute: sign-reversal consistency <= 0.6 (no reliable anti-symmetry) OR lag correlation <= 0.1. Indeterminate band: sign-reversal 0.6-0.8 or lag correlation 0.1-0.5 (stated in advance) -- partial fidelity, logged as a qualified positive that does not on its own settle clause (b). A negative result means the response lacks the sign/lag structure the teleconnection mechanism dictates.

Experiment 4 (H3 -- steering a recovered ENSO-forcing direction causally shifts distant weather in the teleconnection-consistent sense): Tests clause (c). Data: representation pairs from El-Nino vs La-Nina composites (ERA5, existing) used to recover the forcing direction; the same 30 neutral-winter states as steering targets. Model: frozen GraphCast/Pangu and the coupled emulator; the only fitted object is the probe/delta direction. We recover an 'ENSO-forcing' direction two ways -- a supervised logistic-probe direction and an El-Nino-minus-La-Nina delta-representation -- and add it at matched L2 norm to the chosen block's activations during rollout. Systems compared: (i) ENSO-forcing direction; (ii) 20 matched-norm random directions; (iii) a local-feature direction. Decisive metric first: mechanism-selectivity = |shift of the distant PNA-region readout along the teleconnection-consistent axis under ENSO-forcing steering| / |mean shift under random directions|. Convincing: selectivity >= 3, correct PNA sign, and the local-feature direction producing no teleconnection-consistent shift, consistent across the two direction-recovery methods. Refute: selectivity <= 1.5 (indistinguishable from random). Indeterminate band 1.5-3 (declared before the data): the direction has some causal traction but not the clean selectivity needed to claim causal use; superposed/distributed encoding is the leading alternative, so we report both recovery methods and withhold a strong causal claim. A negative result means the recovered direction is not causally wired to distant circulation, contradicting clause (c).

Experiment 5 (H1-H3 -- layer emergence, cross-model convergence, and mechanism brackets): Tests whether the clause-(a)-(c) findings are robust properties rather than single-model artifacts, and locates them on an interpretable spectrum. Data: all ERA5 fields and ENSO events above (reused). Model: GraphCast, Pangu, and the coupled emulator, all frozen; probes/directions as in Experiments 1 and 4.
