Systems compared: (i) per-block Teleconnection-Beyond-Local Index (H1) and steering selectivity (H3) across depth; (ii) linear CKA between recovered ENSO-forcing subspaces across the models; (iii) an upper-bound bracket = a linear-baroclinic-model / AGCM pacemaker teleconnection response that encodes the mechanism by construction, and a lower-bound bracket = a local-persistence forecaster with no remote access. Decisive metric first: where on the persistence-to-mechanism bracket each model's Index and selectivity fall (fraction of the gap between lower and upper bracket closed). Convincing: at least one model closes >=50% of the bracket gap AND cross-model CKA >= 0.5, indicating a convergent internal mechanism. Refute: all models sit within measurement noise of the lower (persistence) bracket. Indeterminate band: bracket-gap closure 20-50% or CKA 0.3-0.5 (declared in advance) -- partial/idiosyncratic representation, reported without a universality claim. A negative result means no model materially exceeds local persistence, consistent with the mechanism being absent. All runs are inference-only on public weights plus small probes and public ERA5 data, feasible on a single 40-80GB GPU.
Risk Factors and Limitations: ENSO state and local antecedents are correlated, making the teleconnection-beyond-local separation statistically demanding; we mitigate with local-antecedent residualization, the tropical-Pacific-vs-matched-control counterfactual (which holds perturbation magnitude fixed and varies only location), and the sign/lag fidelity tests that a local-statistics model cannot reproduce.

Many atmosphere-only weather foundation models (GraphCast, Pangu) do not ingest evolving SST as an input variable, so imposing an ENSO SST anomaly may be limited to perturbing the atmospheric state consistent with ENSO or requires an SST-aware/coupled emulator; we prioritize the coupled emulator (DLESyM) and SST-inclusive models for the decisive counterfactual, and for atmosphere-only models perturb the ENSO-associated atmospheric pattern, clearly reporting per-model what is manipulable.

Medium-range weather models have short rollout horizons (days), while teleconnections develop over weeks to a season; the downstream response may be truncated. We use models/emulators with extended or subseasonal-to-seasonal rollout where possible, focus on the fast component of the wave-train response, and report horizon caveats.

Imposing a tropical-Pacific anomaly may push the state off the model's training distribution, confounding the response with generic OOD failure; we mitigate with physically-plausible anomaly magnitudes, compare against a matched-magnitude control perturbation (so any generic OOD effect is shared), and report sensitivity to anomaly strength.
Teleconnection ground truth (PNA response, lags) has internal-variability noise; we composite over many ENSO events and use canonical patterns, reporting statistical uncertainty.

Linear probes recovering an ENSO-forcing direction do not guarantee causal use; we address this with steering plus random/local-direction controls, though distributed/superposed encodings may blur single-direction interventions - we use both probe directions and delta-representations.

A negative result (models exploit local persistence and fail to propagate the correct non-local teleconnection) is scientifically decisive and directly relevant to trusting these operationally-deployed models for subseasonal-to-seasonal and ENSO-year forecasts, though it may be perceived as confirmatory of skepticism; we frame either outcome as the first mechanism-defining test of whether weather/climate foundation models represent the non-local teleconnection mechanism.
All experiments are inference-only on public pretrained models plus small probes and public ERA5 / coupled-emulator data, keeping compute at academic scale.

Name: conservation_law_manifold_probe
Title: Do Physics Foundation Models Obey the Laws They Encode? Probing Conservation Constraints and Lawful Coupling in Internal Representations
Short Hypothesis: Physics foundation models (neural PDE surrogates trained across many systems) are known to linearly encode individual physical quantities like energy or vorticity. We hypothesize the deeper, untested question is relational: does the model's internal representation over a rollout obey the *constraints* that link these quantities — i.e., conserving conserved quantities (energy, mass, momentum) and coupling non-conserved ones along physically-lawful directions (equation-of-state, advection)? If the internal state lives on a conservation-constrained manifold, causal interventions that respect a conservation law should be tolerated while those that violate it should be resisted or corrected; if the model merely stores independently-decodable features, no such structure will exist. This is a representation-level constraint test on the internal rollout state, distinct from output-level conservation error that existing physics benchmarks already report.
Related Work: Recent interpretability work shows physics/LLM foundation models linearly encode single physical concepts and that these are causally load-bearing: 'Physics Steering' (2025) extracts steerable directions for vorticity/diffusion/speed that transfer across systems; 'Uncovering Emergent Physics Representations Learned In-Context by LLMs' (2025) finds SAE features correlating with energy whose ablation degrades forecasting; 'From Neurons to Neutrons' (2024) recovers the semi-empirical mass formula; 'Deep learning of thermodynamic laws' (2025) and Siamese-network invariant discovery (2020) show networks can learn entropy/invariants from data. All of these establish that a quantity is *encoded and matters*. None tests whether the model's representation respects the *relationships and conservation constraints* that tie multiple quantities together — i.e., whether physics is stored as a consistent constrained manifold vs. a bag of separable features. Our conservation-consistency and lawful-coupling tests, and the causal 'Noether test' (constraint-respecting vs constraint-violating interventions), are the novel contribution. In particular, this differs from output-level conservation metrics (which score the predicted fields) by asking whether the *internal* rollout state lies on a conservation-constrained manifold - a relational property invisible to accuracy or single-quantity concept-decoding.
Abstract: Neural PDE foundation models trained across many physical systems have recently been shown to linearly encode individual physical quantities such as energy and vorticity, and to allow causal steering of these features. Yet physics is not a list of independent quantities: it is defined by the constraints and functional relationships among them — conservation of energy, mass, and momentum, and lawful couplings like an equation of state. We ask whether physics foundation models internally respect these relationships, or merely store separately-decodable features. We probe pretrained multi-physics surrogates (e.g., Poseidon, Multiple-Physics-Pretraining, DPOT) on standard PDE benchmarks (Navier-Stokes, shallow water, diffusion-reaction, compressible flow). First, we train linear probes for conserved quantities and test conservation-consistency: does the *probed* value stay constant across autoregressive rollout steps for genuinely conserving systems, and drift lawfully when forcing/dissipation is present? Second, we test lawful coupling: steering one quantity (e.g., temperature) should shift a coupled quantity (e.g., pressure) along the correct equation-of-state direction, not arbitrarily. Third, we introduce a causal 'Noether test': interventions along a conservation-preserving direction should be tolerated (small downstream error, conserved quantity intact), while equal-magnitude conservation-violating interventions should incur larger downstream error or be spontaneously corrected by the model. Metrics quantify conservation drift, coupling-direction alignment, and asymmetry between lawful and unlawful interventions. This yields the first test of whether physics foundation models learn constrained, mechanism-consistent manifolds, with direct implications for their reliability as scientific simulators. Concretely, model builders, surrogate auditors, and reliability researchers in climate, fluids, and PDE discovery could adopt constraint-level diagnostics for model selection, steering, and deployment gating - testing internal geometry rather than only forecast accuracy - and a negative result is itself a decisive reliability finding that redirects trust toward external validation. We scope claims to PDE surrogates while noting the test template generalizes to other scientific domains.
Experiments: Experiment 1 (H1 — Conserved-quantity encoding and internal conservation-drift): Tests the H1 claim that, in genuinely conserving regimes, the model's internal state keeps the conserved quantities (energy, mass, momentum) constant over its own rollout — beyond what its output fields show. Data: evaluation trajectories from standard PDE benchmarks (PDEBench and PDEArena, each providing thousands of trajectories); we use 200 trajectories in a conserving regime (inviscid/undriven Navier–Stokes or a Hamiltonian wave) at 100 timesteps each — 200 gives tight drift statistics per system while inference-only extraction stays at a few GPU-hours; conserved quantities are computed analytically from the field data at every step, and we report each benchmark's residual numerical conservation error to bound ground-truth noise. Model: 2–3 pretrained physics foundation models with public weights (Poseidon, Multiple-Physics-Pretraining, DPOT), frozen; trainable = per-layer ridge linear probes to energy/mass/momentum fit on a disjoint 150-trajectory split; 3 seeds. Systems compared: drift of the probed (internal) conserved quantity vs drift of the model's actual predicted-field quantity vs the true constant. Decisive metric first: internal-representation conservation drift = coefficient of variation of the probed quantity across the rollout (dimensionless), reported alongside probe R² (must be ≥0.8 to license the drift reading). Convincing result: internal drift significantly below the field-level drift and below 5% CV in conserving systems — the internal state 'knows' the quantity is constant. Undecidable band: internal CV in [5%, 12%] and statistically indistinguishable from field-level drift — reported as "internal state tracks the output, no extra conservation structure"; band fixed before data. Negative result: internal drift ≈ field drift (or worse) means no conservation structure beyond the outputs, H1 unsupported.

Experiment 2 (H1 — Lawful drift in driven-dissipative regimes): Tests the complementary H1 claim that when a quantity should change, the internal representation changes it in the physically-correct direction and magnitude (e.g., monotone energy decay under viscosity). Data: 150 trajectories from a viscous forced-flow regime in PDEBench (existing), 100 steps each; the true monotone energy/enstrophy change is computed from the fields. Model: same frozen Poseidon/MPP/DPOT and the fixed Experiment-1 probes; no new training; 3 seeds. Systems compared: probed-quantity change vs true change; and against a shuffled-probe control. Decisive metric first: Spearman ρ between probed-quantity change and true change across the rollout, plus sign of the monotone trend. Convincing result: ρ ≥ 0.7 with the correct decay sign in all models. Undecidable band: ρ in [0.3, 0.5] — the internal quantity moves but not reliably with physics, reported as partial support; band fixed before data. Negative result: ρ ≈ 0 or wrong sign means the representation does not track lawful non-conservation, H1's dissipative half fails.

Experiment 3 (H2 — Lawful coupling of non-conserved quantities): Tests the H2 claim that non-conserved but linked quantities are coupled along physically-lawful directions — steering one coupled quantity induces the equation-of-state-correct change in the other. Data: 150 compressible-flow / shallow-water trajectories with a known equation of state (PDEBench compressible NS), giving paired temperature–pressure (or height–velocity) fields. Model: frozen models; steering identifies decoded directions for the two coupled quantities at the best-R² layer and adds ±α·(unit direction), α over {0.5,1,2}× activation std; 3 seeds. Systems compared: induced coupled-quantity change under true-direction steering vs matched-norm random direction. Decisive metric first: coupling-alignment = regression slope / cosine between the induced coupled change and the equation-of-state prediction. Convincing result: alignment ≥ 0.6 (cosine) and monotone in α, with the random control near 0. Undecidable band: alignment in [0.3, 0.45] — weak, reported as inconclusive coupling; band fixed before data. Negative result: alignment ≈ 0 means quantities are stored independently with no lawful coupling, H2 fails.

Experiment 4 (H3 — Causal Noether asymmetry between lawful and unlawful interventions): Tests the decisive H3 claim that conservation-preserving activation perturbations are tolerated while conservation-violating ones cause larger error and/or are spontaneously corrected. Data: 200 conserving-regime trajectories from Experiment 1. Model: frozen models; two matched-magnitude interventions per trajectory — (a) preserving: redistributes the conserved quantity within its level set (e.g., moves energy spatially at fixed total), constructed in field space then mapped to activations; (b) violating: changes the total conserved quantity by the same activation norm; both rolled out; 3 seeds. Systems compared: preserving vs violating perturbations, plus a random matched-norm control. Decisive metric first: lawful-vs-unlawful asymmetry ratio A = downstream field error(violating) / downstream field error(preserving), and the self-correction rate (fraction of violating runs where the total conserved quantity relaxes back toward its initial value). Convincing result: A ≥ 1.5 and/or self-correction significantly above the preserving/random baseline. Undecidable band: A in [0.9, 1.3] with no excess self-correction — read as "model does not distinguish lawful from unlawful", H3 unsupported; band fixed before data. Negative result: A ≈ 1 means the internal state is not on a conservation-constrained manifold, the core H3 claim fails even if H1/H2 decodability held.

Experiment 5 (H1/H2/H3 — Cross-system, cross-model convergence and physics-model brackets): Tests whether conservation-consistency and coupling generalize to unseen systems and are convergent, and brackets the effect against reference models. Data: 100 held-out trajectories per unseen system not used above. Model: frozen Poseidon/MPP/DPOT; plus two brackets run identically — a from-scratch single-system surrogate (lower reference) and a conservation-constrained physics-informed model (upper reference). Systems compared: Experiment-1 drift, Experiment-3 coupling, and Experiment-4 asymmetry across models and systems; CKA between the conserved-quantity subspaces of the foundation models. Decisive metric first: for each metric, where the foundation models fall between the from-scratch lower and physics-informed upper brackets, plus mean pairwise CKA of the conserved-quantity subspaces. Convincing result: foundation models sit clearly above the from-scratch bracket on drift/asymmetry and CKA ≥ 0.6, indicating convergent constrained structure. Undecidable band: foundation-model metrics within noise of the from-scratch bracket, or CKA in [0.3,0.45] — reported as no advantage / weak convergence; band fixed before data. Negative result: foundation models indistinguishable from the from-scratch surrogate means multi-system pretraining confers no extra conservation structure, bounding H1–H3.
Risk Factors and Limitations: Linear probes may recover a quantity that the model does not causally use; we mitigate with the causal Noether test and random-direction controls, but distributed/superposed encodings may blur single-direction interventions.

Conservation-preserving interventions in a nonlinear network can push activations off-manifold, confounding the lawful-vs-unlawful comparison; we bound perturbation norms and report sensitivity, and design perturbations that exactly preserve the target quantity in field space then map to activations.
Ground-truth conserved quantities for some benchmark PDEs are only approximately conserved numerically; we restrict conservation tests to systems with well-controlled numerical conservation.
Available physics foundation models differ in architecture/tokenization, complicating cross-model comparison; we standardize probing on invariant scalar summaries and report per-model results.

A negative result (models store separable features but violate constraints) is scientifically informative and deployment-relevant, though possibly perceived as less flashy; we frame either outcome as a decisive reliability finding.
Compute: rollouts and probing on pretrained models are academic-scale (inference only, small linear probes), avoiding any retraining of large models.

Name: allosteric_propagation_probe
Title: Feeling the Distant Site: Do Protein Language Models Internally Represent Long-Range Allosteric Coupling, or Only Local Context?
Short Hypothesis: Allostery is a relational, long-range mechanism: a mutation at a site far from the active site perturbs function through a physically-propagated coupling path, and recent large-scale data show these effects decay with distance from the active site in a conserved way. We hypothesize that if protein language models (PLMs) internally represent this mechanism rather than only local sequence context, then (a) a mutation's internal representational perturbation will propagate to distant functionally-coupled residues (not just its local neighborhood), (b) the magnitude of this propagated internal signal will reproduce the conserved distance-decay law of allosteric mutational effects, and (c) the internal coupling will causally track true allosteric partners, not merely spatial or sequence proximity. A propagation-vs-locality counterfactual makes this a mechanism-defining test that local-annotation interpretability cannot provide.
Related Work: Existing PLM interpretability matches features to LOCAL structure/function: BERTology (attention to contacts, binding sites), InterPLM and 'Interpreting and Steering PLMs' (SAE features for binding sites, motifs, transmembrane regions), ProtoMech (cross-layer transcoder circuits for local motifs), and XAI-attribution work (active sites, PROSITE patterns). All validate against marginal, spatially-local annotations. Separately, the allostery literature establishes long-range coupling as a real mechanism: 'Allostery is a widespread cause of loss-of-function variant pathogenicity' (2025) shows a CONSERVED distance-dependent decay of allosteric mutational effects outside active sites from large-scale deep mutational scanning; coevolution methods (KeyAlloSite), MD-based GNNs (AlloPool, NRI), and energy-based predictors (ZHMolEReP) model allosteric pathways. Critically, 'When Does Structure Help?' (2026) reports ESM-2 gives below-chance allostery predictions while AF2 barely exceeds chance, hinting sequence-only PLMs may be blind to long-range mechanism. No interpretability work tests whether a PLM's INTERNAL representation propagates a mutation's effect to distant allosterically-coupled residues, reproduces the conserved distance-decay law, or causally distinguishes true allosteric partners from mere spatial/sequence neighbors. Our propagation-distance-decay-and-causal-coupling test is the novel, mechanism-defining contribution, moving beyond 'the model sees the local motif' to 'the model represents that a distant site talks to the active site.' We state the contribution as an interpretability test of long-range mechanism, not a new allostery predictor: 'propagation' is defined as the fraction of a mutation's per-residue representational perturbation deposited beyond a local sequence/3D window, and the 'coupling direction' as the probe/SAE axis separating true allosteric partners from distance-matched controls. Under a null (ESM-2 blind to allostery) the novel finding is that sequence-only PLMs do not represent long-range mechanism; under a positive result it is a recoverable, causally load-bearing coupling representation. More broadly this is a template for testing relational vs local representation in scientific foundation models.
Abstract: Protein language models (PLMs) are known to encode local structural and functional features such as contacts, binding sites, and motifs. But one of the most important protein mechanisms is inherently long-range and relational: allostery, in which a mutation at a site far from the active site alters function through a physically-propagated coupling path. Recent large-scale deep-mutational-scanning studies establish that allostery is a widespread cause of variant pathogenicity and that allosteric mutational effects decay with distance from the active site in a conserved, quantifiable way. This makes allostery an ideal, physics-grounded probe for whether PLMs represent long-range mechanism or only local context. We ask whether ESM-2 internally represents allosteric coupling. First, a propagation probe: applying an in-silico mutation at a residue, we measure how far its perturbation to the model's internal representation travels along the chain and in 3D, testing whether it reaches distant functionally-coupled residues rather than only its local neighborhood. Second, and most decisively, a distance-decay test: we test whether the magnitude of the internally-propagated signal reproduces the conserved distance-dependent decay of true allosteric mutational effects measured experimentally, versus a local-context model whose perturbation stays local. Third, a coupling-specificity counterfactual: we test whether the internal coupling is stronger for true allosteric partners than for distance-matched, spatially-close-but-non-coupled control residues, and whether steering along a recovered allosteric-coupling direction causally shifts predictions at the distant partner. Metrics quantify a propagation-range index, distance-decay agreement, and coupling-specificity ratio. Either outcome sharpens whether PLMs, increasingly used for variant-effect prediction, represent the long-range mechanism behind a major class of pathogenic variants. This changes how PLMs are benchmarked and trusted for mechanistic variant-effect tasks: if ESM-2 keeps perturbations local while the AF2 control does not, variant-effect prioritization for allosteric / long-range pathogenic variants and allosteric-drug-discovery pipelines should not rely on sequence-only PLM internals; the positive-control contrast localizes any mechanism to models with evolutionary-coupling access. Causal steering is treated as corroboration of the input-space propagation evidence rather than the primary claim, and we correct for multiple comparisons across residue pairs and pre-register the propagation-range index as the primary endpoint.
Experiments: Experiment 1 (H1 — long-range propagation of a mutation's internal perturbation): Tests assertion (a): a single mutation's representational perturbation propagates to distant functionally-coupled residues, not just its local neighborhood. Data (existing): proteins with resolved allosteric sites and high-resolution PDB structures from ASBench, AlloReverse, and AlloSigDB, giving active-site location, 3D coordinates, and allosteric-residue annotations; we use up to 60 well-characterized proteins (limited by high-quality allosteric annotation + structure). Model (frozen, inference only): ESM-2 at 150M and 650M params, with 3B as compute allows; per-residue representations at every layer. Procedure: apply a single in-silico point mutation at a residue (masked/single-substitution edit, perturbation magnitude bounded, OOD diagnostics reported) and measure the induced per-residue representational delta at all other positions, per layer. Systems compared: propagation profile of allosteric-site mutations vs local/active-site mutations. Decisive metric first: Propagation-Range Index = fraction of the total representational perturbation deposited beyond a local window (> 8 residues in sequence AND > 10 Angstrom in 3D), with CI over mutations. Indecision band up front: an index in [0.10, 0.25] cannot decide and is reported as mostly-local with an ambiguous long-range tail; index >= 0.25 with CI lower bound > 0.10 is convincing long-range propagation; index <= 0.10 means the model deposits perturbation almost entirely locally, supporting the local-context hypothesis.

Experiment 2 (H2 — reproduction of the conserved distance-decay law, decisive): Tests assertion (b): the propagated internal signal reproduces the conserved distance-dependent decay of true allosteric mutational effects. Data (existing): the large-scale allosteric deep-mutational-scanning distance-decay dataset (per-residue allosteric effect vs distance to the active site) paired with the Experiment 1 structures. Model: frozen ESM-2 (150M/650M/3B); no training for the propagation measurement. Procedure: for mutations at allosteric sites, measure the internally-propagated perturbation arriving at active-site residues as a function of distance, fit the same decay form as the experimental law, and compare decay constants. Controls: (a) active-site/local mutations should show a distinct steep short-range profile; (b) shuffled distance labels should destroy the fit. Systems compared: internal propagated signal vs experimental allosteric-effect-vs-distance law. Decisive metric first: Pearson correlation between internal propagated signal and experimental effect across the distance range, and agreement of fitted decay constants (ratio of internal to experimental constant). Indecision band up front: a correlation whose CI lies in [0.2, 0.5] (or decay-constant ratio outside 0.5-2.0 but with the correlation weak) cannot decide and is reported as no faithful decay reproduction; correlation CI lower bound > 0.5 with decay-constant ratio in [0.67, 1.5] is convincing mechanism reproduction; correlation CI upper bound < 0.2 means the model does not reproduce the conserved law. This is the decisive test; a null (expected if ESM-2 is genuinely weak at allostery) is the headline finding.

Experiment 3 (H3 — coupling specificity and causal steering): Tests assertion (c): the internal coupling causally tracks true allosteric partners, not mere spatial/sequence proximity. Data: true allosteric-partner pairs (allosteric residue A coupled to active/effector site F) with distance-matched non-coupled control residues (equally far in sequence and 3D but not coupled per experimental data). Model: frozen ESM-2; an 'allosteric-coupling' direction recovered by a supervised probe (or SAE feature aligned with A->F propagation), no backbone training. Procedure: (i) compare internal coupling A->F against the distance-matched non-coupled control; (ii) steer the coupling direction at A with matched magnitude and read the masked-prediction/variant-effect readout at the distant partner F, with matched-norm random directions and the distance-matched control residue as controls. As a positive-control comparison, run the same propagation/steering on AlphaFold2 single-sequence Evoformer representations. Decisive metric first: Coupling-Specificity Ratio = internal coupling(true partner) / internal coupling(distance-matched control), and mechanism-selectivity = |steering effect at true partner| / |effect at matched control|, CIs over pairs. Indecision band up front: either ratio with CI in [1.3, 2.0] cannot decide and is reported as coupling indistinguishable from distance; CI lower bound > 2.0 is convincing partner-specific causal coupling; CI upper bound < 1.3 means coupling is driven only by proximity. A negative result for ESM-2 alongside a positive AF2 control would localize the mechanism to models with evolutionary-coupling access.
Risk Factors and Limitations: Allosteric coupling correlates with 3D and sequence distance and with coevolution, so the coupling-specificity separation is statistically demanding; we mitigate with distance-matched non-coupled controls, the conserved-distance-decay test (which a distance-only model cannot reproduce in the correct functional form), and the allostery-beyond-locality baseline that regresses out distance.

The 2026 information-bonus result suggests ESM-2 may genuinely be weak at allostery; a null internal signal could reflect true model blindness rather than probing failure. We treat this as a scientifically decisive outcome (sequence-only PLMs do not represent long-range allosteric mechanism) and include AF2 representations as a positive-control comparison.

Ground-truth allosteric coupling and experimental per-mutation allosteric effects are limited and noisy; we restrict to well-characterized proteins with deep-mutational-scanning allostery data and report sensitivity to annotation confidence.

In-silico mutation perturbations in a nonlinear transformer may push representations off-manifold; we bound perturbation magnitude, use masked-position and single-substitution edits, and report sensitivity, relying on the input-space mutation propagation as primary evidence and steering as corroboration.
Distributed/superposed encodings may mean no single clean coupling direction exists; we use both probe directions and SAE features and report aggregate-direction results.

Baselines and multiplicity: we add random-mutation, matched non-allosteric-site, and distance/coevolution-regressed predictors plus shuffled-layer and random-direction probes as nulls, pre-specify protein-selection criteria and sample sizes, and apply multiple-comparison correction across residue pairs; ablations sweep mutation magnitude, layer, and model size and compare input-space vs hidden-space perturbations.

All experiments are inference-only on public pretrained models (ESM-2, optionally AF2 single-sequence) plus small probes/SAEs and public allostery datasets and structures, keeping compute at academic scale.

Name: sign_epistasis_context_flip_probe
Title: Does the Mutation's Meaning Depend on Its Neighbors? Testing Whether Protein Language Models Internally Represent Context-Dependent Sign Epistasis, Not Just Additive Effects
Short Hypothesis: The mechanism-defining signature of epistasis is context-dependence: a mutation's fitness effect is not fixed but depends on the genetic background, and in sign epistasis the effect fully REVERSES (beneficial<->deleterious) when a partner mutation is present. If a protein language model internally represents this mechanism rather than a context-independent additive effect, then the internal representational effect of applying a fixed mutation must CHANGE (and, for sign-epistatic pairs, flip sign relative to fitness) when the background carries a sign-epistatic partner, while remaining invariant when the background carries an additive (non-interacting) partner. The same-mutation/different-background counterfactual, with combinatorial deep-mutational-scanning ground truth, is a strong, falsifiable test of context-dependent encoding that output-score correlation and single-mutation interpretability cannot provide.
Related Work: Recent work shows PLM OUTPUT scores reflect epistasis correlationally: 'PLMs Capture Structural and Functional Epistasis in a Zero-Shot Setting' (2025) finds epistasis emerges in ESM scores, with raw scores aligning to contacts and a nonlinear rescaling shifting toward functional couplings. Epistasis theory establishes SIGN epistasis - where a mutation's effect reverses sign with background - as the mechanistically-defining, hardest, and rarest form ('Mechanistic causes of sign epistasis' 2024; 'Simple sign epistasis and evolutionary detours' 2026; 'The simplicity of protein sequence-function relationships' 2023 and its rebuttal 2024, which agree additive+pairwise terms dominate but that specific interactions are the crux). PLM interpretability (InterPLM, ProtoMech cross-layer transcoders, BERTology attention studies, SAE low-N design, CB-pLM) recovers LOCAL, context-independent features (binding sites, contacts, motifs) and validates against marginal annotations. Crucially, no work tests whether a PLM's INTERNAL representation encodes the CONTEXT-DEPENDENCE that defines epistasis - i.e., whether the internal effect of a fixed mutation changes with background - nor uses a same-mutation/sign-epistatic-vs-additive-background counterfactual to separate context-dependent (mechanistic) from additive (context-free) representation. Because output scores can capture epistasis without the representation encoding context-dependence per se, and because prior interpretability probes local features only, this representational, causal, sign-flip counterfactual is the novel, mechanism-defining contribution. Precisely, the contribution is representational and causal, not better epistasis prediction: a strong, falsifiable probe of whether ESM-2's internal, activation-level effect of a fixed mutation is context-dependent (changing, and sign-flipping, with a sign-epistatic background) versus additive, using a same-mutation/different-background counterfactual with combinatorial-DMS ground truth, plus a causal steering test of whether the recovered context-dependence direction is load-bearing. Prior work shows epistasis in PLM output scores and recovers local context-independent features; neither tests context-dependence in the representation. Who cares first: ProteinGym/ESM users and multi-mutant protein-design groups (where sign epistasis causes catastrophic design failures) and mechanistic-interpretability researchers.
Abstract: Epistasis - the dependence of a mutation's effect on its genetic background - is the phenomenon that makes protein sequence-function landscapes hard, and its sharpest form is sign epistasis, in which a mutation's effect fully reverses from beneficial to deleterious (or vice versa) when a partner mutation is present. Protein language models (PLMs) are known to reflect epistasis in their output scores and to encode local structural features, but whether their internal representations encode the defining property of epistasis - context-dependence itself - has never been tested. We propose a mechanism-defining representational test. For a fixed point mutation, we measure its induced change in ESM-2's internal representations when applied to two matched backgrounds drawn from combinatorial deep-mutational-scanning (DMS) data: a sign-epistatic background (a partner mutation that reverses the fitness sign of our mutation) and an additive background (a partner mutation whose combined effect is the sum of singles, i.e. no interaction), matched on structural/sequence distance. If the PLM represents epistasis mechanistically, the internal mutation-effect vector must change substantially - and align with the fitness sign flip - across the sign-epistatic background, while remaining near-invariant across the additive background; a context-free additive representation shows equal, background-independent effects. We further test whether a recoverable 'context-dependence' direction causally tracks the true sign flip and whether internal context-sensitivity predicts where the model mispredicts combinatorial fitness. Metrics quantify a context-flip asymmetry, a sign-alignment index, and an epistasis failure predictor. Either outcome sharpens whether PLMs, now central to variant-effect prediction and protein design, represent the interactions that dominate real fitness landscapes. Downstream, a PLM that represents mutation effects additively cannot be trusted to prioritize multi-mutant variants where sign epistasis dominates; the probe thus becomes a diagnostic for when to distrust combinatorial variant-effect predictions and a target for representation-level improvements, with the internal context-sensitivity signal doubling as a predictor of where the model mispredicts combinatorial fitness.
Experiments: Experiment 1 (H1 — same-mutation/different-background context-flip asymmetry): Tests the core representational claim: the internal effect of a fixed mutation changes when the background carries a sign-epistatic partner but stays invariant when the background carries an additive (non-interacting) partner. Data: combinatorial deep-mutational-scanning sets with measured single and double mutants so pairwise epistasis and sign are computed exactly — GB1 (~149,000 combinatorial variants across 4 sites), avGFP (Sarkisyan, ~51,000 variants), a PABP/RRM double-mutant set, beta-lactamase, and ProteinGym multi-mutant tracks; from these enumerate mutation pairs, classify each as additive, magnitude-epistatic, or sign-epistatic, and select the sign-epistatic pairs (rare) plus distance-matched additive controls — targeting ≥300 clean sign-epistatic pairs pooled across proteins, fewer being possible because clean sign-epistatic pairs are scarce (this floor is reported and drives the power analysis). Define delta(m|B) = repr(B+m) − repr(B), the pooled per-layer ESM-2 activation change. Model: ESM-2 at 150M and 650M parameters (3B as compute allows), inference-only, frozen; a linear fitness probe trained on single-mutant scores selects the best layer, seeds 0–4. Systems compared: change in delta(m1|.) between a sign-epistatic background and wildtype vs between a distance-matched additive background and wildtype (m2_sign and m2_add matched on sequence separation and 3D distance from m1). Decisive metric (first): Context-Flip Asymmetry = ||delta(m1|sign-epistatic bg) − delta(m1|wt)|| / ||delta(m1|additive bg) − delta(m1|wt)||. Convincing: asymmetry ≥ 3 (95% CI lower bound above 1.5). Indecision band: asymmetry in [0.7, 2.0] — the interacting background is not privileged over a distance-matched non-interacting one; the mechanism claim fails here. Negative result: asymmetry ≈ 1 — the model represents mutation effects context-independently (additively), the decisive negative for the hypothesis.

Experiment 2 (H1 — sign-alignment double dissociation): Tests the second half of the claim: for sign-epistatic pairs the internal effect flips sign consistently with the measured fitness reversal, while for additive controls it does not. Data: the same ≥300 sign-epistatic pairs and their additive controls. Decode a scalar fitness-effect read-out from delta(m1|B) using the Experiment-1 probe. Model/probe as Experiment 1, seeds 0–4. Systems compared: sign-flip rate of the internal read-out across sign-epistatic backgrounds vs across additive backgrounds. Decisive metric (first): Sign-Alignment Index = fraction of sign-epistatic pairs whose internal read-out reverses sign in the direction of the true fitness reversal, minus the additive-control flip rate. Convincing: Index ≥ 0.4, with sign-epistatic flip rate ≥ 0.6 and additive-control flip rate ≤ 0.2 (a double dissociation). Indecision band: Index in [0.1, 0.25] — weak, inconsistent sign tracking; inconclusive on the sign claim. Negative result: Index ≤ 0.1 (sign-epistatic flip rate near the additive-control rate) — no fitness-consistent sign reversal is represented.

Experiment 3 (H1 — dose-response to epistasis magnitude): Tests the quantitative form of the claim: the internal effect-change scales with true pairwise epistasis rather than with mere proximity. Data: ALL enumerated pairs (additive through strong-epistatic) across the pooled proteins. Model/probe as above, seeds 0–4. Systems compared: ||delta(m|bg) − delta(m|wt)|| vs true pairwise epistasis magnitude, controlling for sequence separation and 3D distance. Decisive metric (first): partial Spearman rho between internal effect-change and true epistasis, conditioning on sequence and 3D distance. Convincing: partial rho ≥ 0.4 (95% CI lower bound above 0.15). Indecision band: partial rho in [0.15, 0.3] — weak residual association beyond distance; inconclusive. Negative result: partial rho < 0.15 — the internal effect-change tracks distance, not interaction, so context-dependence is not epistasis-specific.

Experiment 4 (H-causal — context-dependence-direction steering): Tests whether a recovered 'context-dependence' direction is causally load-bearing rather than merely decodable, addressing the mechanism (not just decodability) claim. Data: the ≥300 sign-epistatic pairs and their distance-matched additive controls from Experiments 1–2. The direction is recovered two ways — the supervised context-flip probe direction, and the mean delta between sign-epistatic and additive background-conditioned mutation-effect vectors at matched sequence/3D distance. Model/probe as above, inference-only, frozen, seeds 0–4; add matched-norm perturbations along the direction to the best-layer activations and re-read the internal fitness-effect read-out and the model's variant-effect score. Systems compared: context-dependence direction vs matched-norm random directions vs a distance/co-variation direction. Decisive metric (first): Steering Selectivity = |change in predicted mutation effect from context-direction steering| / |change from random-direction steering|, with a sign check that steering toward the sign-epistatic pole reverses the effect for true sign-epistatic pairs. Convincing: selectivity ≥ 3 with the fitness-consistent sign, and the random/co-variation directions not reproducing it. Indecision band: selectivity in [0.7, 2.0] — the direction is correlational, not a causal handle; the mechanism claim (beyond decodability) is unsupported here. Negative result: selectivity ≈ 1 — no dedicated causal context-dependence direction.
Risk Factors and Limitations: Epistasis magnitude correlates with 3D contact and sequence proximity, so context-dependence could partly reflect distance rather than genuine interaction encoding; we mitigate with distance-matched additive control backgrounds, partial correlations controlling for distance, and the sign-alignment double dissociation (which distance alone cannot produce).

Combinatorial DMS with true double/higher-order measurements is limited to a modest set of proteins, constraining sample size and the number of clean sign-epistatic pairs (which are rare); we pool across GB1, avGFP, RRM, beta-lactamase and ProteinGym multi-mutant sets and report statistics accounting for small n, emphasizing sign-epistatic pairs as the diagnostic subset.

DMS measurements are noisy and reference-based epistasis estimates can inflate apparent interactions; we use reference-free / global-nonlinearity-corrected epistasis estimates where possible and restrict decisive tests to high-confidence, replicate-supported pairs, reporting sensitivity to the epistasis threshold.

Applying two mutations to build the background may push sequences off the model's training distribution; but double mutants near wildtype are common and mild, and we bound the number and severity of background mutations and report OOD diagnostics, with the additive-background control sharing any generic OOD effect.

Linear probes and delta-representations recovering a context-dependence direction do not guarantee causal use; we address this with steering plus random/distance-matched controls, though distributed/superposed encodings may blur single-direction interventions - we report aggregate-direction results.

A negative result (ESM-2 represents mutation effects additively and shows no background-specific sign flip, i.e. context-flip asymmetry ~ 1) is scientifically decisive and directly relevant to trusting PLMs for combinatorial variant-effect prediction and multi-mutant protein design, where sign epistasis causes catastrophic failures; we frame either outcome as the first mechanism-defining, representational test of whether PLMs encode the context-dependence that defines epistasis.
All experiments are inference-only on public pretrained ESM-2 plus small probes and public combinatorial DMS datasets, keeping compute at academic scale.

Name: phase_amplitude_coupling_probe
Title: Coupling, Not Just Power: Do EEG Foundation Models Represent Cross-Frequency Phase-Amplitude Coupling, or Only Marginal Band Power?
Short Hypothesis: A defining, relational mechanism of brain activity is cross-frequency phase-amplitude coupling (PAC): the phase of a slow oscillation (e.g., theta/alpha) modulates the amplitude of a fast oscillation (e.g., gamma), a coupling that carries cognitive and clinical meaning and cannot be captured by marginal band power. We hypothesize that if EEG foundation models represent this neurophysiological mechanism rather than surface spectral statistics, then (a) PAC strength will be decodable from internal representations beyond what per-band power predicts, (b) a phase-scrambling counterfactual that destroys coupling while preserving each band's power spectrum will specifically collapse the internal PAC signal, whereas an amplitude-matched control that changes power but preserves coupling will not, and (c) steering a recovered PAC direction causally shifts downstream predictions. The phase-scramble-vs-power-match counterfactual is an exact, mechanism-defining test that marginal-spectral interpretability cannot provide.
Related Work: EEG foundation models (CSBrain 2025, BrainOmni 2025, CodeBrain 2025, MSBraM 2026, LaBraM, CBraMod) achieve strong cross-task decoding, and reviews (Kwon & Shin 2025) call for physiology-aware, interpretable representations. Existing EEG-model interpretability is (i) saliency/attribution over frequency bands (Frequency-band GNN dementia biomarkers 2025; activation-maximization for spectral features 2021), or (ii) descriptive alignment of learned features with spectral rhythms (CodeBrain's tokenizer). Neuroscience establishes PAC and cross-frequency coupling (CFC) as a core relational coding mechanism (Cracking the Code of Oscillatory Activity 2011; oscillatory representational content studies), and Riemannian pipelines have hand-engineered CFC covariance features (SPD-CFC 2023) precisely because standard band-power features miss it. Crucially, no work tests whether pretrained EEG FMs internally represent PAC (a relational, cross-frequency mechanism) beyond marginal band power, whether that representation is causally load-bearing, or uses a phase-scrambling counterfactual that isolates coupling from power. Prior interpretability answers 'which band matters'; PAC asks 'do bands interact as the brain's mechanism dictates'. Our relational-beyond-marginal probe, phase-scramble-vs-power-match counterfactual, and causal PAC steering are the novel, mechanism-defining contribution, transferred into a safety-critical clinical/BCI setting. Stated exactly: no prior EEG-FM paper tests PAC against band power with a counterfactual that preserves each band's power spectrum while breaking coupling; prior work reports which band matters (PAC detection or spectral saliency), whereas we ask whether PAC is internally represented (PAC-representation), a distinct question from PAC-detection and from marginal spectral interpretability. The novelty locus is the mechanistic probe plus the phase-scramble counterfactual; the causal-steering result and any model-specific finding are secondary.
Abstract: EEG foundation models now deliver strong, transferable decoding across cognitive, emotional, and clinical tasks, yet what neurophysiology they actually internalize remains unclear. Existing interpretability tells us which frequency bands a model weights, but band power is a marginal, per-band statistic; the brain's information is carried substantially by relational mechanisms, chief among them cross-frequency phase-amplitude coupling (PAC), in which the phase of a slow rhythm modulates the amplitude of a fast one. PAC is diagnostically and cognitively meaningful (working memory, seizure dynamics, Parkinsonian beta-gamma coupling) and is provably invisible to marginal band power, making it an ideal mechanism-defining probe. We ask whether pretrained EEG foundation models (e.g., LaBraM, CBraMod, CodeBrain) internally represent PAC. First, a relational-beyond-marginal probe: we test whether PAC strength (modulation index) is decodable from internal representations beyond what per-band power predicts. Second, and most decisively, a phase-scrambling counterfactual: we surrogate-scramble the slow-oscillation phase to abolish coupling while exactly preserving each band's power spectrum, and compare against an amplitude-matched control that alters power but preserves coupling. A mechanistic representation must collapse its internal PAC signal under phase-scrambling but not under the power-matched control; a spectral-statistics model responds oppositely. Third, causal steering: perturbing a recovered PAC direction should shift downstream clinical/cognitive predictions coupling-consistently. Metrics quantify a PAC-beyond-power index, a scramble-vs-power-match causal asymmetry, and a mechanism-based failure predictor. Either outcome sharpens what deployed brain foundation models represent, with direct implications for their clinical and BCI reliability. The downstream implication is application-specific: if PAC is absent (only marginal power is encoded), EEG foundation models should not be trusted for PAC-driven readouts -- seizure / epileptogenic-zone monitoring, Parkinsonian beta-gamma biomarkers, working-memory load, and sleep spindle-slow-oscillation staging -- without explicit coupling features; if PAC is represented and steerable, these clinical and BCI uses gain support. We pre-register the primary layer(s) and PAC estimator (Tort modulation index, with mean-vector-length as secondary) to avoid post-hoc selection.
Experiments: Experiment 1 (H1 — PAC decodable beyond marginal band power): Tests assertion (a): cross-frequency phase-amplitude coupling (PAC) is decodable from internal representations beyond what per-band power predicts. Data (existing): public EEG with established PAC -- a working-memory/cognitive-load set (theta-gamma PAC), Sleep-EDF (slow-oscillation-spindle coupling), and a clinical cohort where PAC is a biomarker (e.g., an epilepsy corpus); ground-truth PAC per epoch via the Tort modulation index and comodulograms, plus per-band power (delta-gamma). We use >= 5,000 epochs total, split by subject (no subject crosses splits). Models (frozen, inference only): LaBraM, CBraMod, and CodeBrain (public EEG foundation models with per-token representations); preprocessing per model documented, pre-tokenization activations probed where feasible. Trainable: ridge linear probes (L2 by CV, 3 seeds). Systems compared: representation probe vs a probe on the full per-band power vector. Decisive metric first: PAC-Beyond-Power Index = test R^2 for the modulation index from the representation minus R^2 from the full band-power vector, after regressing out the power-predictable component, reported per phase-amplitude band pair. Indecision band up front: an index in [0.01, 0.05] (R^2 units) cannot decide and is reported as ambiguous coupling encoding; index >= 0.05 with CI lower bound > 0.01 is convincing relational-coupling encoding beyond marginal spectra; index <= 0.01 means only marginal power is encoded, supporting the surface-spectral hypothesis.

Experiment 2 (H2 — phase-scramble vs power-match counterfactual, decisive): Tests assertion (b): a phase-scramble that destroys coupling while preserving each band's power spectrum should specifically collapse the internal PAC signal, whereas an amplitude-matched control that changes power but preserves coupling should not; and the internal signal should reproduce the correct comodulogram specificity. Data (constructed from the Experiment 1 epochs): (a) amplitude-adjusted-Fourier-transform surrogates that abolish cross-frequency phase relations while preserving each band's power (verified: power preserved, modulation index abolished, surrogate diagnostics reported); (b) power-matched surrogates that rescale band amplitudes to change power by a comparable amount while keeping coupling intact. Model: same three frozen models; readout is the probed modulation index / recovered PAC feature. Systems compared: phase-scramble vs power-match; also the model-implied coupling map vs the ground-truth comodulogram against a shuffled-band-pair control. Decisive metric first: Scramble-vs-Power-Match Causal Asymmetry = |PAC-signal drop under phase-scramble| / |PAC-signal change under power-match|, CI over epochs. Indecision band up front: an asymmetry whose CI lies in [1.3, 2.0] cannot decide and is reported as weak coupling sensitivity; CI lower bound > 2.0, with the comodulogram-fidelity correlation beating the shuffled control, is convincing coupling encoding; CI upper bound < 1.3 (or a reversed response driven by power) is the marginal-spectral signature. This is the decisive test; a null is the headline negative result.

Experiment 3 (H3 — causal PAC steering): Tests assertion (c): steering a recovered PAC direction causally shifts downstream predictions in the coupling-consistent direction. Data: epochs with downstream labels (cognitive-load level, sleep stage, or pathology likelihood). Model: frozen; the PAC direction is the Experiment 1 probe direction (or an SAE feature aligned with coupling); no backbone training. Procedure: add matched-norm perturbations moving representations toward/away from high PAC and read the downstream prediction; controls are matched-norm random directions and a band-power direction. Decisive metric first: mechanism-selectivity = |downstream shift under PAC direction| / |shift under random direction|, CI over epochs. Indecision band up front: selectivity CI in [1.3, 2.0] cannot decide (no clean causal handle); CI lower bound > 2.0 with a coupling-consistent downstream shift is convincing causal use of PAC; CI upper bound < 1.3 means no separable causal PAC direction. A negative result, with H1-H2 nulls, supports the marginal-power conclusion and warns against trusting EEG FMs for PAC-driven diagnoses.
Risk Factors and Limitations: PAC and band power are correlated in real EEG (high-power epochs can inflate spurious PAC), making the relational-beyond-power separation statistically demanding; we mitigate with power-residualization, the phase-scramble-vs-power-match counterfactual (which holds power fixed), amplitude-adjusted surrogates, and established bias-corrected PAC estimators.

Phase-scrambling surrogates that perfectly preserve power while destroying coupling are nontrivial; we use standard amplitude-adjusted Fourier-transform surrogates and validate that per-band power is preserved and modulation index is abolished before feeding to the model, reporting surrogate-quality diagnostics.

Some EEG FMs tokenize/normalize signals (patching, spectral tokenization, per-channel normalization) that may discard or transform phase information; we document each model's preprocessing, probe pre-tokenization activations where feasible, and prioritize models retaining temporal/phase structure.

PAC ground truth is itself estimator-dependent and noisy for short epochs; we use longer epochs where possible, multiple PAC metrics (Tort modulation index, mean vector length), and report sensitivity to estimator choice.

Linear probes recovering a PAC direction do not guarantee causal use; we address this with steering plus random/band-power-direction controls, though distributed encodings may blur single-direction interventions.

A negative result (models encode marginal band power but not cross-frequency coupling) is scientifically decisive and directly clinically relevant, since it would warn against trusting EEG FMs for PAC-driven diagnoses (seizure, Parkinsonian, working-memory biomarkers); we frame either outcome as the first mechanism-defining test of whether brain foundation models represent cross-frequency phase-amplitude coupling.

Baselines and leakage: the representation probe is compared against linear and nonlinear predictors from the full band-power vector, from the raw waveform, and from shuffled representations; all metrics are reported with bootstrap CIs, and splits are strictly by subject to prevent within-subject leakage, with epoch-length and estimator sensitivity reported.
All experiments are inference-only on public pretrained models plus small probes/SAEs and public EEG datasets, keeping compute at academic scale.

Name: pseudoscalar_chirality_probe
Title: Sign Flips Under a Mirror: Testing Whether Molecular Foundation Models Represent Chirality as a Pseudoscalar Mechanism, Not Just Enantiomer Labels
Short Hypothesis: Chirality is an exactly-known geometric mechanism with a precise mathematical signature: it is a PSEUDOSCALAR quantity - invariant to rotation and translation but flipping SIGN under mirror reflection (parity) - and it is what distinguishes enantiomers, which are identical in every scalar/achiral property yet can differ drastically in binding and toxicity. We hypothesize that if a molecular foundation model represents the chirality MECHANISM rather than a memorized R/S label or surface substructure, then (a) a recoverable internal 'chirality' direction behaves as a pseudoscalar - unchanged under 3D rotation but flipping sign under mirror reflection of the geometry, (b) a mirror-reflection counterfactual that flips ONLY handedness (holding all scalar invariants - distances, angles, connectivity - fixed) flips the internal chirality signal and the model's enantioselective property prediction, whereas an achiral-preserving perturbation of matched magnitude does not, and (c) steering this pseudoscalar direction causally swaps predicted enantiomer-dependent properties. The mirror-flip counterfactual is a falsifiable, mechanism-defining test that R/S classification accuracy and substructure correlation cannot provide.
Related Work: Two lines bracket the gap. (1) Chirality-aware architectures - ChiENN (2023), tetrahedral-chirality message passing (2020), MolKGNN (2023), ChIRo (2021), ChiDeK (2026), Chi-Geometry benchmark (2025) - are motivated by the proof that standard/E(3)-invariant GNNs CANNOT represent chirality ('E(3)-equivariant models cannot learn chirality', 2024), and they BUILD handedness in by construction, judged by R/S accuracy or enantioselective-property RMSE. (2) FM-representation work hints chirality is decodable: Rem3Di (2026) constructs explicit pseudoscalar features from atomistic-FM latents to distinguish enantiomers, SMILES-heteroencoder latent arithmetic (2025) builds chirality descriptors by subtracting enantiomer latents, and the reaction-analogy GNN work (2025) shows linear structure in atom embeddings. Crucially, all of these either engineer chirality by construction, or measure downstream enantiomer-discrimination accuracy - none tests whether a general molecular foundation model's INTERNAL representation already encodes chirality with its defining pseudoscalar (parity-odd, rotation-even) symmetry, whether that signal is causally load-bearing for enantioselective predictions, or uses a mirror-reflection counterfactual to separate the mechanism from a memorized R/S label. Because R/S labels, chiral substructure, and true handedness are entangled in training data, classification accuracy cannot arbitrate this. Our pseudoscalar-symmetry probe, mirror-flip counterfactual, and causal chirality steering are the novel, mechanism-defining contribution. To position the contribution against prior art: Rem3Di-style pseudoscalar latent features and enantiomer-subtraction descriptors already show chirality is decodable, and chirality-aware architectures build handedness in, so our novelty is not the pseudoscalar construct but a benchmarked, causal audit protocol — an evaluation standard with exact mirror-paired counterfactuals, achiral double-dissociation controls, and a formal pseudoscalar-compliance (parity-odd, rotation-even) criterion — that asks whether a general FM's representation spontaneously and causally uses chirality, reported as evidence for or against rather than a complete causal proof. Geometric-reflection tests (3D models) and stereotag-propagation tests (SMILES/graph models) are kept as distinct claims, not merged. Concrete failure scenarios the audit flags: ranking the toxic enantiomer as safe, mispredicting enantioselective binding/optical activity, and shortcut R/S memorization that fails on novel scaffolds. Adopters: benchmark creators, FM developers, and safety/toxicity and medicinal-chemistry modelers.
Abstract: Chirality - molecular handedness - is one of chemistry's most consequential and exactly-known geometric mechanisms: enantiomers are mirror images identical in every achiral property yet can differ dramatically in biological activity and toxicity (the thalidomide tragedy being the canonical example). Its mathematical signature is precise: chirality is a pseudoscalar, invariant under rotation and translation but flipping sign under mirror reflection. This makes it an ideal, unambiguous probe for whether molecular foundation models learn geometric mechanism or surface statistics - especially since a theorem shows standard E(3)-invariant models cannot represent it at all. We probe pretrained 3D atomistic and molecular foundation models (e.g., atomistic MLIP backbones such as MACE, Uni-Mol, and chirality-capable encoders) plus SMILES/graph chemical FMs, asking three mechanism-defining questions. First, a pseudoscalar-symmetry probe: is a recoverable internal chirality direction invariant under 3D rotation yet sign-flipping under mirror reflection, as physics dictates? Second, and most decisively, a mirror-reflection counterfactual: we reflect a molecule's geometry to flip ONLY handedness while exactly preserving all scalar invariants, and test whether the internal chirality signal and the model's enantioselective property prediction flip, whereas an achiral perturbation of matched magnitude does not. Third, causal steering along the pseudoscalar direction should swap enantiomer-dependent predictions. Metrics quantify a pseudoscalar-fidelity index, a mirror-flip-vs-achiral causal asymmetry, and an enantioselective prediction-swap rate. Either outcome sharpens whether molecular foundation models - increasingly used in drug design where the wrong enantiomer can be toxic - represent the handedness mechanism or are blind to it. Framed as an evaluation standard rather than a one-off probe, passing the audit should predict better robustness and transfer on enantioselective endpoints (chiral binding, toxicity, optical activity), giving FM developers and safety modelers a concrete pass/fail criterion for whether a molecular FM can be trusted where the wrong enantiomer is harmful.
Experiments: Experiment 1 (H1 — chirality direction behaves as a pseudoscalar): Tests clause (a): a recoverable internal 'chirality' direction is unchanged under 3D rotation but flips sign under mirror reflection. Data: enantiomer pairs with ground-truth handedness — the Chi-Geometry synthetic benchmark (clean isolation of a single stereocenter) plus real drug-like R/S pairs; use 2,000 molecules (1,200 train / 300 val / 500 test, split by scaffold), with paired mirror-image 3D conformers generated for each — fewer than all available because we require a single well-defined chiral element. Model: Uni-Mol (3D graph, ~48M parameters, stereochemistry-aware) and ChemBERTa-2 (~46M parameters, ingests @/@@ stereo tags), frozen; a supervised probe separating R from S (and a delta-representation between a molecule and its mirror image) recovers the candidate direction, seeds 0–4; MACE-MP-0 (E(3)-invariant, provably chirality-blind) is a built-in negative control expected to yield a definitional null. Systems compared: the chirality signal under (i) many random 3D rotations and (ii) mirror reflection. Decisive metric (first): Pseudoscalar-Fidelity Index combining rotation invariance (1 − normalized variance of the signal under rotation) and mirror sign-flip consistency (fraction of test molecules whose signal reverses sign under reflection). Convincing: rotation invariance ≥ 0.9 AND sign-flip consistency ≥ 0.9, with the E(3)-invariant control showing no decodable handedness. Indecision band: sign-flip consistency in [0.4, 0.6] (chance-like) or rotation invariance in [0.5, 0.8] — no consistent parity-odd, rotation-even behavior; clause (a) fails or is inconclusive here. Negative result: sign-flip consistency ≈ 0.5 or rotation invariance < 0.5 — the direction is not a pseudoscalar (a label/statistics reading).

Experiment 2 (H2 — mirror-reflection vs achiral-perturbation counterfactual): Tests clause (b): flipping only handedness (holding all scalar invariants fixed) flips the internal chirality signal and the enantioselective property prediction, whereas an achiral-preserving perturbation of matched magnitude does not. Data: 500 chiral test molecules; each yields a matched pair — (mirror-flip) reflect the 3D geometry (for SMILES/graph models flip the @/@@ tag), holding distances, angles, connectivity, and formula fixed; (achiral control) a matched-RMSD conformational/isometric perturbation that does not change handedness — plus a double-dissociation control on achiral molecules (no stereocenter) expected to show no swap. Model/probe as Experiment 1, seeds 0–4; read-outs are the chirality probe and an enantioselective property head (predicted optical-rotation sign, chiral-column elution order, or enantiosensitive docking score). Systems compared: |signal/prediction change| under mirror-flip vs under achiral perturbation. Decisive metric (first): Mirror-Flip-vs-Achiral Causal Asymmetry = median(|Δ mirror-flip|) / median(|Δ achiral|). Convincing: asymmetry ≥ 3 and ≥ 80% of mirror-flips produce the physically correct sign-reversal/order-swap in the enantioselective read-out, with the achiral-molecule control showing none. Indecision band: asymmetry in [0.7, 2.0] — handedness flip is not privileged over an achiral perturbation; clause (b) fails here. Negative result: asymmetry ≈ 1 — the model responds to geometric change, not to the parity flip that defines enantiomers.

Experiment 3 (H3 — causal pseudoscalar steering): Tests clause (c): steering the pseudoscalar direction causally swaps predicted enantiomer-dependent properties. Data: the same 500 chiral test molecules; steer the recovered chirality direction with matched magnitude and both signs. Model/probe as above, seeds 0–4. Systems compared: chirality direction vs matched-norm random directions vs an achiral-feature direction. Decisive metrics (first): Enantioselective Prediction-Swap Rate under chirality steering, and Steering Selectivity = |effect of chirality direction| / |effect of random direction|. Convincing: swap rate ≥ 0.7 and selectivity ≥ 3, with random and achiral directions not producing swaps. Indecision band: selectivity in [0.7, 2.0] or swap rate in [0.4, 0.6] — steering is non-selective; clause (c) fails or is inconclusive here. Negative result: selectivity ≈ 1 or swap rate ≈ 0.5 — no causal handle that swaps enantioselective predictions.
Risk Factors and Limitations: Many 3D atomistic FMs are E(3)-invariant by construction and therefore provably cannot represent chirality; for these the pseudoscalar probe returns a definitional null, so the rich mechanism tests apply mainly to chirality-capable models (Rem3Di-style pseudoscalar-feature backbones, Uni-Mol with stereochemistry, stereo-aware SMILES/graph FMs). We report the invariant-model null as a decisive, separately-stated positive control and prioritize chirality-capable models for the mechanism tests.

SMILES/graph models encode chirality via discrete stereo-tags (@/@@) rather than continuous geometry, so 'mirror reflection' is operationalized as a tag flip; this tests whether the model propagates a handedness label to enantioselective predictions (still mechanism-relevant) but is a slightly different claim than geometric pseudoscalar behavior. We run both the 3D-geometry reflection (for 3D models) and the tag-flip (for SMILES models) and clearly distinguish the two claims.

R/S labels, chiral substructure, and true handedness are entangled, making the mechanism-beyond-label separation demanding; we mitigate with the mirror-flip counterfactual (which holds all scalar invariants and the substructure fixed while flipping only handedness), the achiral-molecule double-dissociation control, and the pseudoscalar-symmetry test that a label-lookup cannot pass under 3D rotations.

Enantioselective ground-truth data (optical rotation, ECD sign, chiral elution order, enantiosensitive docking) is limited and noisy; we use curated benchmarks (chiral-chromatography datasets, ECD/OR sets, Chi-Geometry) and report sensitivity to data confidence, focusing decisive tests on molecules with a single well-defined chiral element.

Reflecting a 3D geometry can push conformers off the model's data distribution; but the enantiomer is itself a valid physical molecule, so the reflected geometry is in-distribution by construction - we nonetheless verify conformer validity and match the achiral control perturbation on RMSD so any residual OOD effect is shared.

Linear probes recovering a chirality direction do not guarantee causal use; we address this with steering, the mirror-flip counterfactual, and random/achiral-direction controls, though distributed/superposed encodings may blur single-direction interventions - we use both probe directions and delta (enantiomer-difference) representations.

A negative result (models encode R/S labels or achiral substructure but do not represent chirality as a pseudoscalar, failing the mirror-flip counterfactual) is scientifically decisive and directly safety-relevant - it would warn against trusting molecular FMs for enantioselective property and toxicity prediction, precisely where the wrong enantiomer can be harmful; we frame either outcome as the first mechanism-defining test of whether molecular foundation models represent the pseudoscalar chirality mechanism.
All experiments are inference-only on public pretrained models plus small probes and public chirality/enantioselective datasets, keeping compute at academic scale.

Name: protonation_state_ph_probe
Title: Does the Model Know the pH? Testing Whether Chemistry Foundation Models Represent the Protonation-State (Henderson-Hasselbalch) Mechanism, Not Just Neutral Structure
Short Hypothesis: A molecule's charge state - and therefore its solubility, permeability, and binding - is governed by an exactly-known mechanism: the Henderson-Hasselbalch relation, which says the fraction of a molecule that is protonated flips discontinuously as pH crosses its pKa. Chemistry foundation models are typically fed a single (often neutral) structure and no pH, so whether they internally represent this pH-dependent ionization mechanism is untested. We hypothesize that if a chemistry FM represents the mechanism rather than surface neutral-structure statistics, then (a) a molecule's dominant protonation state at a given pH is decodable from internal representations beyond what its neutral structure alone predicts, (b) a pH-crossing counterfactual - moving pH across an ionizable group's pKa while holding the input structure fixed - shifts the internal charge-state/property signal as Henderson-Hasselbalch predicts, whereas an equal pH change that does NOT cross a pKa does not, and (c) the effect localizes to the ionizable site. The pH-cross-vs-no-cross counterfactual is an exact, mechanism-defining test that pKa-prediction accuracy and neutral-structure correlation cannot provide.
Related Work: Two lines bracket the gap. (1) pKa/protonation prediction models - Uni-pKa (2023/24), Starling (2025), TripKa (2026), AcepKa/PlayMolecule (2026), BCL-XpKa (2024) - BUILD the protonation ensemble and thermodynamic consistency in by construction and are judged by pKa accuracy; none asks whether a general chemistry FM already encodes the pH-dependent ionization mechanism. (2) Chemistry-model interpretability - MoleX (2024, functional-group linear decomposition), 'Unveiling Latent Knowledge via SAEs' on SMI-TED (2025), 'Circuits, Features, and Heuristics in Molecular Transformers' (2025, valence circuits), 'BERT Learns Chemistry' (2020), and attribution studies for solubility (2024) - recover features aligned with functional groups and physicochemical properties, but all validate against neutral-structure, pH-independent annotations. Crucially, no work tests whether a chemistry FM internally represents the RELATIONAL, pH-dependent Henderson-Hasselbalch mechanism (charge state flips as pH crosses pKa), whether that representation is causally load-bearing, or uses a pH-crossing counterfactual to separate mechanism from neutral-structure correlation. Because pKa and neutral structure are entangled in training data (and pH is usually absent as input), correlation and pKa-benchmark accuracy cannot arbitrate this. Our protonation-state-beyond-structure probe, pH-cross-vs-no-cross counterfactual, and causal ionization-site steering are the novel, mechanism-defining contribution, transferred into a safety-critical drug-property setting where charge state controls bioavailability. To state the contribution precisely: Henderson–Hasselbalch and pKa prediction are established, and we propose neither a new pKa model nor new chemistry, but a mechanism-level, causal interpretability audit — a falsifiable test (the pH-cross-vs-no-cross counterfactual plus ionization-site localization) of whether a frozen chemistry FM's internal representation spontaneously encodes pH-dependent ionization, reported as evidence for or against encoding rather than proof of complete causality. pKa predictors build the ionization ensemble in by construction and are scored on pKa accuracy; neutral-property interpretability probes validate against pH-independent annotations; neither tests whether a general FM already carries the pH-dependent mechanism. The strongest claim comes from the explicit pH-conditioned setting, with the structure-only microstate-swap and pH-aware control bracketing it. Who changes behavior: medicinal chemists and ADMET/property-prediction ML groups (trusting logD/solubility predictions for ionizable drugs that switch charge between gut and blood pH) and chemistry-FM developers (whether to add pH conditioning).
Abstract: The physicochemical behavior of drug-like molecules - solubility, membrane permeability, and protein binding - is dominated by their charge state, which is set by an exactly-known mechanism: the Henderson-Hasselbalch relation, in which the protonated fraction of an ionizable group flips discontinuously as environmental pH crosses the group's pKa. The same molecule can be neutral in the stomach and charged in the blood, radically changing its properties. This makes protonation an ideal, mechanism-defining probe for whether chemistry foundation models learn pH-dependent mechanism or merely encode a static neutral structure - especially since these models are usually given no pH input at all. We probe pretrained chemistry FMs (e.g., SMI-TED/FM4M, ChemBERTa-2, Uni-Mol) plus a pH-aware variant, using molecules with well-characterized ionizable groups and experimental pKa/pH-dependent property data. First, a protonation-state-beyond-structure probe: is a molecule's dominant charge state at a given pH decodable from internal representations beyond what its neutral structure predicts? Second, and most decisively, a pH-crossing counterfactual: we vary pH across an ionizable group's pKa while holding the input structure fixed and measure whether the internal charge-state and pH-dependent-property signal shifts as Henderson-Hasselbalch dictates (sigmoidal titration curve centered at pKa), versus an equal-magnitude pH change that does not cross any pKa, which should not. Third, causal steering along a recovered ionization direction and site-localization. Metrics quantify a protonation-beyond-structure index, a cross-vs-no-cross causal asymmetry, and a titration-curve fidelity score. Either outcome sharpens whether deployed chemistry models represent the ionization mechanism that controls drug behavior. A positive result would license using these FMs for pH-dependent property prediction and tell medicinal chemists which models to trust; a negative result is actionable because it names a missing, addable mechanism, pointing FM developers toward pH conditioning rather than larger neutral-structure pretraining.
Experiments: Experiment 1 (H1 — protonation state decodable beyond neutral structure): Tests clause (a): the dominant protonation state at a given pH is decodable from internal representations beyond what the neutral structure alone predicts. Data: monoprotic drug-like molecules with a single confident experimental pKa — pooled from ChEMBL/AstraZeneca pKa (~7,900 measurements) and SAMPL6–8 (~110 combined); use 1,200 molecules (700 train / 200 val / 300 test, split by Bemis–Murcko scaffold so no scaffold crosses splits), evaluated on a pH grid of 0.5 units over 0–14 — fewer than all of ChEMBL because we require a single dominant ionizable group and a reliable pKa. pH is supplied to structure-only models by feeding the pH-appropriate protonation microstate SMILES, and to pH-aware models via pH conditioning. Model: ChemBERTa-2 (SMILES transformer, ~46M parameters) and Uni-Mol (3D graph, ~48M parameters), frozen; only a logistic-regression probe is trained, seeds 0–4; Uni-pKa serves as an upper-bracket reference. Systems compared: charge-state decoding from the representation vs a neutral-structure baseline (probe on ionizable-group identity/count from the neutral graph), representation residualized against the neutral-structure features. Decisive metric (first): Protonation-Beyond-Structure Index = balanced accuracy(charge state | representation) − balanced accuracy(charge state | neutral-structure features). Convincing: Index ≥ 0.10 with 95% CI lower bound above 0.03. Indecision band: Index in [−0.02, 0.03] — within probe noise; a result here means pH-conditioned charge adds nothing beyond static structure and clause (a) fails. Negative result (Index ≤ −0.02 or in band): the model carries neutral-structure statistics, not a pH-dependent ionization code.

Experiment 2 (H2 — pH-crossing vs no-crossing counterfactual): Tests clause (b): moving pH across an ionizable group's pKa (holding the input fixed) shifts the internal charge-state/property signal as Henderson–Hasselbalch predicts, whereas an equal pH change that does not cross a pKa does not. Data: 600 monoprotic test molecules from Experiment 1; each yields a matched pair — (cross edit) pH from pKa−2 to pKa+2 (flips dominant charge); (no-cross control) an equal 4-unit pH change entirely on one side of the pKa (charge unchanged). For structure-only models the microstate SMILES is swapped only when the edit crosses the pKa; for pH-aware models only the pH token changes. Model/probe as Experiment 1, seeds 0–4; read-out is the charge-state probe and the logD/solubility head where present. Systems compared: |signal change| under cross edit vs under no-cross control. Decisive metric (first): Cross-vs-No-Cross Causal Asymmetry = median(|Δsignal cross|) / median(|Δsignal no-cross|). Convincing: asymmetry ≥ 3. Indecision band: asymmetry in [0.7, 2.0] — crossing the pKa is not privileged over an equal non-crossing pH change; clause (b) fails here. Negative result: asymmetry ≈ 1, i.e., the model responds to pH magnitude, not to the mechanism-defining pKa crossing.
