Experiment 3 (H2 — Henderson–Hasselbalch titration-curve fidelity): Tests the quantitative content of clause (b): the internal charge-state signal traces a sigmoid centred at the true pKa. Data: the same 600 molecules; sweep pH finely (0.25-unit steps) across each pKa. Model/probe as above, seeds 0–4. Systems compared: internal-signal-vs-pH fit to a Henderson–Hasselbalch sigmoid vs shuffled-pKa labels. Decisive metric (first): inflection-point error = |recovered inflection pH − true pKa| (pH units), with sigmoid fit R^2 as secondary. Convincing: median inflection error ≤ 0.5 pH units and fit R^2 ≥ 0.8. Indecision band: inflection error in (0.5, 1.5] pH units — a titration-like but mislocated response; a result here means the shape is present but not quantitatively tied to the true pKa, partial and inconclusive support for (b). Negative result: inflection error > 1.5 pH units or fit R^2 < 0.5, indistinguishable from shuffled labels — no titration mechanism represented.

Experiment 4 (H3 — ionization-site localization): Tests clause (c): the pH-crossing effect localizes to the ionizable site rather than being diffuse. Data: the same 600 molecules, restricted to the subset with per-atom/per-token representations (Uni-Mol; ChemBERTa-2 via token attribution). Model as above, seeds 0–4. Systems compared: representational change at the ionizable atom/group vs matched non-ionizable atoms under the pH-cross edit; occlusion of the ionizable group as an additional control. Decisive metric (first): Localization Fraction = share of the total pH-induced representational-change norm concentrated at the ionizable site. Convincing: Localization Fraction ≥ 0.5 (site occupies a small fraction of atoms yet carries at least half the change), well above the atom-count-proportional null. Indecision band: fraction within ±50% of the atom-count-proportional expectation — no meaningful concentration; clause (c) fails here. Negative result: fraction at or below the atom-count null, i.e., the ionization signal is diffuse and not tied to the titrating group.
Risk Factors and Limitations: pKa and neutral structure are entangled (the ionizable group is part of the structure), making the protonation-beyond-structure separation statistically demanding; we mitigate with neutral-structure residualization, the pH-crossing counterfactual (which holds structure fixed and varies only pH), and the titration-curve fidelity test that a neutral-structure model cannot pass with the correct inflection at pKa.

Most chemistry FMs take no pH input, so 'varying pH' must be operationalized either by supplying the pH-appropriate protonation microstate SMILES (which changes the input, partially confounding the structure-fixed ideal) or via pH conditioning only in pH-aware models. We run both operationalizations, clearly report the caveat, and treat the microstate-swap as changing only the ionization of the target group while matching the rest of the structure; a truly mechanism-aware model should nonetheless respond only when the swap corresponds to a real pKa-crossing.

Providing protonated microstates as input tests whether the model correctly propagates a charge-state change to properties, which is a slightly different (but still mechanism-relevant) claim than 'the model infers pH-dependence from neutral structure'; we distinguish these two claims explicitly and report both.

Experimental pKa and pH-dependent property data are noisy and assay-dependent (SAMPL, ChEMBL, Novartis); we use curated benchmark subsets, focus counterfactuals on molecules with a single dominant ionizable group and confident pKa, and report sensitivity to data confidence thresholds; multiprotic molecules are analyzed separately.

Linear probes recovering an ionization direction do not guarantee causal use; we address this with steering plus random-direction controls and site-localization, though distributed/superposed encodings may blur single-direction interventions - we use both probe directions and SAE features.

A negative result (models encode neutral structure but not the pH-dependent ionization mechanism, failing the cross-vs-no-cross counterfactual) is scientifically decisive and directly safety-relevant - it would warn against trusting chemistry FMs for pH-dependent solubility, permeability, and bioavailability predictions, especially for ionizable drugs that change charge between gut and blood pH; we frame either outcome as the first mechanism-defining test of whether chemistry FMs represent the Henderson-Hasselbalch protonation mechanism.
All experiments are inference-only on public pretrained models plus small probes/SAEs and public pKa/property datasets (SAMPL6-8, ChEMBL, Novartis), keeping compute at academic scale.

Name: cascade_flux_irreversibility_probe
Title: Which Way Does Energy Flow? Testing Whether Turbulence Foundation Models Represent the Directional, Time-Irreversible Energy Cascade, Not Just Instantaneous Field Statistics
Short Hypothesis: The defining mechanism of turbulence is the Richardson-Kolmogorov energy cascade: kinetic energy is transferred directionally across scales (net forward, large-to-small) at a rate Pi(k) whose mean is set by the dissipation rate, and this transfer breaks time-reversal symmetry (a time-reversed turbulent flow would carry energy up-scale, which is physically forbidden). A single velocity snapshot is nearly statistically identical under time reversal, so instantaneous field statistics cannot encode cascade direction. We hypothesize that if a turbulence/physics foundation model represents the cascade mechanism rather than instantaneous spatial statistics, then (a) the signed inter-scale energy flux Pi(k) is decodable from internal representations of a short trajectory beyond what single-snapshot statistics predict, (b) feeding the model a time-reversed trajectory (identical instantaneous statistics, inverted cascade direction) flips its internal flux signal and degrades its rollout as physics dictates, while a spatially-scrambled control matched on the spectrum does not, and (c) steering a recovered cascade-flux direction causally shifts small-scale energy generation. The forward-vs-time-reversed counterfactual is an exact, mechanism-defining test that field-statistics correlation cannot pass.
Related Work: Interpretability of physics/weather foundation models shows single physical QUANTITIES are encoded and steerable: 'Physics Steering' (2025) extracts steerable vorticity/diffusion/speed directions that transfer across systems; 'Uncovering Emergent Physics Representations Learned In-Context by LLMs' (2025) finds energy features whose ablation degrades forecasting; GraphCast SAE work recovers cyclones/atmospheric rivers. All recover a scalar quantity at a point/instant. Separately, a rich turbulence literature (Kolmogorov -5/3 spectrum; the coherent structure of the energy cascade, 2023; information-flux causality of inter-scale transfer, 2024; hidden scale invariance, 2023-2025) establishes the cascade as a directional, time-irreversible, scale-relational mechanism, and the emerging thermodynamics-of-turbulence view frames the cascade explicitly as an arrow of time. Crucially, no interpretability work tests whether a foundation model's INTERNAL representation encodes the directional, time-irreversible inter-scale energy flux Pi(k) that DEFINES turbulence, whether that flux representation is causally load-bearing, or uses a time-reversal counterfactual to separate cascade mechanism from instantaneous field statistics. Prior physics-interpretability answers 'is a quantity encoded'; the cascade asks 'is the directional flow of energy across scales, and its broken time-symmetry, represented'. Our directional-flux probe, forward-vs-time-reversed counterfactual, and causal flux steering are the novel, mechanism-defining contribution, distinct from conservation-law or single-quantity tests. Stated in one sentence, the novelty is the first test of whether a foundation model encodes a time-irreversible, inter-scale energy flux Pi(k) rather than a pointwise scalar quantity — a falsifiable, causal test (the forward-vs-time-reversed counterfactual plus flux steering) of spontaneous encoding, reported as evidence for or against rather than a claim of complete mechanistic causality. This is distinct from prior physics-interpretability that recovers/steers single scalars (energy, vorticity) at a point/instant, and from the turbulence-irreversibility literature that characterizes the cascade in the data but not in a model's representation. Why now: PDE foundation models are being deployed for weather and fluids, where long-horizon rollout reliability and physical-consistency hinge on whether cascade direction is represented. Downstream decisions that change: surrogate model selection, training-objective and benchmark design (adding directional/irreversibility tests), and trust in long rollouts. Audience: PDE/weather-surrogate developers, the turbulence-ML community, and interpretability researchers.
Abstract: Turbulence is defined not by any single field value but by a directional, scale-relational mechanism: the Richardson-Kolmogorov energy cascade, in which kinetic energy is transferred on average from large to small scales at a flux Pi(k), a process that breaks time-reversal symmetry and constitutes a physical arrow of time. Foundation models for physics have been shown to encode individual quantities such as energy and vorticity, but whether they represent the cascade itself remains untested. This is decisive because the cascade cannot be read off a single snapshot: a velocity field and its time-reverse are statistically almost identical, yet their cascade directions are opposite. We probe pretrained multi-physics PDE surrogates (e.g., Poseidon, Multiple-Physics-Pretraining, DPOT) on isotropic-turbulence trajectories (JHTDB DNS), where the signed inter-scale flux Pi(k) is computable exactly. First, a flux-beyond-snapshot probe: is Pi(k) decodable from internal representations of a short trajectory beyond what single-frame spectral statistics allow? Second, and most decisively, a time-reversal counterfactual: we feed the model a forward trajectory versus its time-reverse (identical instantaneous statistics, inverted energy flux) and compare against a phase-scrambled control matched on the energy spectrum; a mechanistic representation must flip its internal flux signal and mis-forecast the reversed (unphysical, up-scale-cascading) trajectory, while responding little to the spectrum-matched scramble. Third, causal steering of a recovered cascade-flux direction should shift small-scale energy generation as physics predicts. Metrics quantify a flux-beyond-snapshot index, a forward-vs-reversed asymmetry, and a steering-selectivity ratio. Either outcome sharpens whether turbulence foundation models represent the mechanism that defines turbulence. Practically, a model blind to cascade direction cannot be trusted for long extrapolative rollouts even when its single-frame statistics look correct; the test therefore becomes a physical-consistency criterion for selecting and benchmarking PDE surrogates, and a negative result argues for irreversibility-aware training objectives rather than merely larger models.
Experiments: Experiment 1 (H1 — signed inter-scale flux decodable beyond single-snapshot statistics): Tests clause (a): the signed inter-scale energy flux Pi(k) is decodable from internal representations of a short trajectory beyond what single-snapshot statistics predict. Data: Johns Hopkins Turbulence Database (JHTDB) forced isotropic turbulence (1024^3 field, ~5,000 stored time frames); sample 2,000 short trajectories of 10 consecutive frames each (1,200 train / 200 val / 600 test, split by non-overlapping time windows), plus a decaying-isotropic DNS set for cross-check — fewer than all frames because trajectories must be non-overlapping to avoid leakage. Per timestep and scale band compute ground-truth spectral flux Pi(k) via filtered subgrid energy transfer. Model: DPOT (Fourier-transformer physics FM, ~30M-parameter base variant) and Poseidon (~158M), frozen; only a ridge probe on the best layer, seeds 0–4. Systems compared: probe R^2 for signed Pi(k) from the trajectory representation vs a single-frame baseline (ridge on one frame's spectrum and structure-function statistics). Decisive metric (first): Flux-Beyond-Snapshot Index = R^2(signed Pi(k) | trajectory representation) − R^2(signed Pi(k) | single-frame statistics). Convincing: Index ≥ 0.15 with 95% CI lower bound above 0.05, and the recovered flux has the correct net-forward sign across the inertial range. Indecision band: Index in [−0.03, 0.05] — within probe noise; a result here means the model adds no directional information over an (essentially time-symmetric) snapshot and clause (a) fails. Negative result: Index ≤ −0.03 or in band — the representation is an instantaneous field statistic, blind to cascade direction.

Experiment 2 (H2 — forward vs time-reversed counterfactual): Tests clause (b): a time-reversed trajectory (identical instantaneous statistics, inverted cascade) flips the internal flux signal and degrades rollout, while a spectrum-matched scramble does not. Data: 600 test trajectories; for each build (forward), (exact time-reverse: reverse frame order and flip velocity sign), and (phase-scramble control: randomize spatial phases preserving E(k)). Model/probe as Experiment 1, seeds 0–4; read-outs are the Experiment-1 flux probe and one-step rollout error where the model forecasts. Systems compared: internal flux-sign response and rollout error across forward, reversed, and scrambled. Decisive metrics (first): (i) Flux-Sign Flip Rate = fraction of trajectories whose internal flux sign reverses under time reversal; (ii) Reversed/Forward Rollout Ratio. Convincing: Flip Rate ≥ 0.7 and Rollout Ratio ≥ 1.5, while the scramble produces a flip rate below 0.3 and a rollout ratio near 1 (effect is cascade-specific, not generic OOD). Indecision band: Flip Rate in [0.4, 0.6] or Rollout Ratio in [0.9, 1.2] — no clear directional asymmetry; clause (b) fails here. Negative result: symmetric response (Flip Rate ≈ 0.5, Rollout Ratio ≈ 1) — the model treats a physically forbidden reversed cascade like the real one.

Experiment 3 (H2 — flux magnitude dose-response): Tests the quantitative content of clause (b): the internal flux tracks the physically correct mean flux (equal to dissipation rate in the inertial range). Data: trajectories spanning a range of dissipation rates / Reynolds numbers drawn from JHTDB and DNS (300 trajectories across ~5 dissipation levels). Model/probe as above, seeds 0–4. Systems compared: internal flux read-out vs true mean Pi; shuffled labels as null. Decisive metric (first): Spearman rho and slope agreement between internal flux and true Pi. Convincing: rho ≥ 0.6, correct sign, slope within ±30% of 1.0. Indecision band: rho in [0.2, 0.4] — weak magnitude tracking; report as inconclusive on quantitative fidelity. Negative result: rho < 0.2, indistinguishable from shuffled — no dissipation-set flux magnitude represented.

Experiment 4 (H3 — causal cascade-flux steering): Tests clause (c): steering a recovered cascade-flux direction causally shifts small-scale energy generation. Data: 600 test trajectories; direction recovered as a supervised flux-probe direction and as a delta-representation between high-forward-flux and low/backward-flux states. Model/probe as above; add matched-norm perturbations along the flux direction at the best layer and roll out, seeds 0–4. Systems compared: flux direction vs matched-norm random directions vs an energy-magnitude direction. Decisive metric (first): Steering Selectivity = |change in small-scale (high-k) energy generation from flux-direction steering| / |change from random-direction steering|. Convincing: selectivity ≥ 3 with the physically consistent sign (increasing forward flux builds small-scale energy / sharpens the spectrum tail), and the energy-magnitude direction not reproducing the directional effect. Indecision band: selectivity in [0.7, 2.0] — no better than random; clause (c) fails here. Negative result: selectivity ≈ 1, indicating no dedicated causal cascade-flux direction.
Risk Factors and Limitations: The signed flux Pi(k) correlates with instantaneous spatial structure (strain/enstrophy configurations), making the flux-beyond-snapshot separation statistically demanding; we mitigate with single-snapshot residualization, the time-reversal counterfactual (which holds instantaneous statistics fixed and inverts only direction), and the spectrum-matched phase-scramble control that a cascade-specific effect would not respond to.

Feeding a time-reversed (unphysical) trajectory pushes the model off its training distribution, so the reversed-rollout error could reflect generic OOD failure rather than cascade sensitivity; we control this with the spectrum-matched scramble (also OOD but non-directional) and by testing the internal flux-sign flip on inputs, which is an intra-representation measure less confounded by output-space OOD.

Some physics FMs operate on fixed short input windows or specific resolutions that may limit access to multi-frame temporal information needed to see direction; we document each model's input protocol, use the maximal available window, and prioritize models that ingest trajectories.

Ground-truth Pi(k) depends on the filtering/decomposition choice (spectral vs physical-space filter); we use standard filtered subgrid transfer and report sensitivity to filter width and scale-band definition.

Linear probes recovering a flux direction do not guarantee causal use; we address this with steering plus random/energy-magnitude-direction controls, though distributed/superposed encodings may blur single-direction interventions.

A negative result (models encode instantaneous field statistics but not the directional, time-irreversible cascade, responding symmetrically to time reversal) is scientifically decisive and directly relevant to trusting turbulence surrogates for long rollouts and extrapolation, though it may be perceived as confirmatory of skepticism; we frame either outcome as the first mechanism-defining test of whether turbulence foundation models represent the energy cascade and its broken time-symmetry.
All experiments are inference-only on public pretrained models plus small probes and public DNS/turbulence datasets (JHTDB), keeping compute at academic scale.

Name: saha_boltzmann_abundance_probe
Title: Does the Model Know the Curve of Growth? Testing Whether Stellar Foundation Models Disentangle Abundance from Temperature via Saha-Boltzmann Line Physics
Short Hypothesis: The strength of an absorption line in a stellar spectrum is not a monotone readout of elemental abundance: it is governed by the Saha-Boltzmann excitation/ionization equilibrium (line strength depends on temperature through level populations) and by the nonlinear curve of growth (linear -> saturated -> damping regimes). We hypothesize that if a stellar foundation model represents this mechanism rather than surface line-depth statistics, its internal abundance representation will (a) be invariant to temperature-driven line-strength changes at fixed abundance, (b) follow the curve of growth (saturating with respect to equivalent width) rather than tracking raw line depth, and (c) encode the physically-mandated coupling among multiple lines of the same element that share excitation potential. An exact counterfactual - vary Teff at fixed [Fe/H] versus vary [Fe/H] at fixed Teff - makes this a mechanism-defining rather than correlation-matching test. The 'abundance representation' is defined operationally as the linear probe direction (fit on a held-out split at the best-R2 layer) decoding [Fe/H]; the primary claim is the single Teff-vs-[Fe/H] counterfactual (a), with synthetic-to-real transfer as the one confirmatory validation, and curve-of-growth and multi-line coupling as supporting analyses.
Related Work: Astronomy interpretability has grown quickly: SAEs on galaxy morphology (Euclid Q1, 2025; SFNet, 2024), attention analyses showing SpectraFM (2024) attends to chemically-informative wavelengths, disentangled chemical-tagging networks (Price-Jones/Bovy line, 2021), symbolic regression from GNNs for cosmology (2020), and interpretable anomaly/attribution methods for spectra (2021-2025). AstroCLIP (2024) and OJALA (2026) provide cross-modal / SED foundation models that decode stellar parameters. All of these either (i) attribute which wavelengths matter, (ii) recover monosemantic morphology features, or (iii) show a parameter is decodable. None tests whether a stellar foundation model internally represents the Saha-Boltzmann/curve-of-growth mechanism that determines how abundance maps to line strength, whether the model correctly disentangles the well-known abundance-Teff degeneracy at the representational level, or whether its internal abundance direction is causally load-bearing and physics-consistent. Because line strength is jointly set by abundance and temperature via an exactly-known physical law, this is a rare setting where mechanism can be cleanly separated from correlation. Our counterfactual, curve-of-growth, and multi-line-coupling tests are the novel contribution. The novelty is a mechanistic hypothesis test under exact counterfactuals, not a new model, dataset, or benchmark.
Abstract: Stellar spectra are among the most physically constrained data in science: the strength of any absorption line is set jointly by elemental abundance and by the Saha-Boltzmann excitation/ionization equilibrium through temperature-dependent level populations, and it grows with abundance along a nonlinear curve of growth (linear, saturated, and damping regimes). This makes stellar foundation models an ideal testbed for whether scientific foundation models learn mechanism or surface statistics. We ask whether stellar spectral foundation models (e.g., SpectraFM, AstroCLIP's spectrum encoder, and open transformer spectral models) internally represent this line-formation mechanism. First, we test disentanglement of the classic abundance-temperature degeneracy: using synthetic spectra where we can hold [Fe/H] fixed while varying Teff (which strongly changes Fe line strengths) and vice versa, we probe whether the model's internal 'abundance' direction is invariant to Teff-driven line-strength changes at fixed abundance and responds selectively to true abundance changes. Second, we test curve-of-growth structure: does the internal abundance representation saturate (as physics dictates) rather than track raw line depth or equivalent width linearly? Third, we test multi-line coupling: lines of the same element sharing excitation potential must vary together per Saha-Boltzmann; we test whether the model encodes this coupling and whether it correctly separates high- versus low-excitation lines' temperature sensitivity. We validate causally by ablating/steering the recovered abundance direction and by transferring from synthetic to real spectra (APOGEE/GALAH). Metrics quantify a temperature-invariance-of-abundance index, curve-of-growth agreement, and multi-line coupling fidelity. Either outcome sharpens what stellar foundation models actually represent, with implications for trusting them in low-metallicity and parameter-degenerate regimes. Concretely, the temperature-invariance index doubles as a failure flag for abundance estimates in exactly the low-metallicity and Teff-[Fe/H]-degenerate regimes where astronomy most needs reliability, supporting model auditing, calibration, and selection among stellar FMs for chemical-tagging and Galactic-archaeology users.
Experiments: Experiment 1 (H1 — Abundance–temperature disentanglement, primary counterfactual): Tests the H1(a) claim that the model's internal abundance representation is invariant to temperature-driven line-strength changes at fixed abundance. Data: a synthetic grid of stellar spectra generated with a standard radiative-transfer code (Turbospectrum/MOOG with MARCS atmospheres) spanning Teff, log g, [Fe/H], and a few element abundances, where abundance and temperature can be varied exactly independently; we generate ~5,000 spectra covering matched counterfactual pairs — (a) fix [Fe/H], vary Teff over a range producing large Fe line-strength change; (b) fix Teff, vary [Fe/H] by a matched line-strength amount — 5,000 is sufficient to sample the pairs across the grid and is cheap to synthesize. Also assemble real labeled spectra from APOGEE (~650k) and GALAH (~600k) for the later transfer test. Model: public stellar spectral foundation models — SpectraFM and the AstroCLIP spectrum encoder (plus an open transformer spectrum model if available) — frozen; trainable = per-layer linear probes decoding Teff, log g, [Fe/H] (baseline decodability, must reach R² ≥ 0.8 to license the readout); 5 folds, 3 seeds. Systems compared: change in the decoded-abundance direction under the abundance-varying pair (b) vs the temperature-varying pair (a). Decisive metric first: Temperature-Invariance-of-Abundance Index TIA = |Δabundance representation under (b)| / |Δabundance representation under (a)|. Convincing result: TIA ≫ 1 (e.g., ≥ 3) — abundance representation moves with true abundance, not with Teff-driven line strength. Undecidable band: TIA in [0.9, 1.4] — abundance readout responds to temperature-driven line strength as much as to abundance, read as a line-depth statistic (H1 unsupported); band fixed before data. Negative result: TIA ≈ 1 means no disentanglement, H1 fails and the curve-of-growth/coupling structure targeting the abundance direction is compromised.

Experiment 2 (H2 — Curve-of-growth test): Tests the H2(b) claim that the internal abundance readout follows the saturating curve of growth rather than tracking raw line depth. Data: for a fixed Fe line/element, sweep abundance across linear, saturated, and damping regimes, computing the true equivalent-width curve of growth from the synthesis (~50 abundance steps × several lines, from the Experiment-1 synthesizer). Model: frozen SpectraFM/AstroCLIP, fixed Experiment-1 abundance readout. Systems compared: internal abundance readout vs true log-abundance, contrasted with a raw-equivalent-width readout (saturates) and a raw-line-depth readout (does not). Decisive metric first: goodness-of-fit of the internal abundance readout to the true log-abundance across regimes, and whether it reproduces the saturation plateau (curvature parameter). Convincing result: internal readout tracks the saturating curve of growth (fit R² ≥ 0.8 across regimes) with a saturation plateau, unlike the linear raw-line-depth readout. Undecidable band: the internal readout matches raw line depth as well as it matches the curve of growth (ΔR² between the two fits in [−0.05, 0.05]) — cannot distinguish mechanism from line-depth statistic; band fixed before data. Negative result: internal readout linear in line depth with no saturation means it tracks surface statistics, H2 fails.

Experiment 3 (H3 — Multi-line Saha–Boltzmann coupling): Tests the H3(c) claim that the model encodes the physically-mandated coupling among multiple lines of the same element sharing excitation potential — shared abundance dependence but excitation-dependent Teff sensitivity. Data: for an element with multiple lines of differing excitation potential (e.g., clean, well-separated Fe I lines identified from the synthesis), synthesize spectra varying Teff and abundance; restrict to non-blended lines. Model: frozen models; per-line temperature sensitivity measured by masking/occluding each line region; a shared-abundance-subspace coherence score computed across same-element lines vs different-element lines (control); 3 seeds. Systems compared: per-line temperature sensitivity in the representation vs the Saha–Boltzmann-predicted sensitivity; same-element vs different-element subspace coherence; controls include shuffled-line-identity (permuting which spectral regions are treated as the element's lines) and matched-SNR / resolution / continuum-normalization variants to confirm the coupling is not a preprocessing artifact. Decisive metric first: alignment (correlation) between representational per-line Teff-sensitivity and the Saha–Boltzmann prediction, plus the shared-abundance coherence gap (same-element − different-element). Convincing result: alignment ≥ 0.6 AND same-element coherence clearly exceeds different-element coherence. Undecidable band: alignment in [0.3, 0.45] or a coherence gap within its 3-seed CI of 0 — reported as inconclusive coupling; band fixed before data. Negative result: no alignment with Saha–Boltzmann sensitivity and no shared-abundance coherence means multi-line coupling is absent, H3 fails.

Experiment 4 (H1 — Causal load-bearing (ablation/steering) and synthetic-to-real transfer): Tests that the disentangled abundance/temperature directions are causally load-bearing and survive on real data. Data: the Experiment-1 synthetic grid plus real APOGEE/GALAH spectra (pipeline labels as ground truth). Model: frozen models; ablate the recovered abundance direction and measure degradation of abundance prediction while Teff prediction is preserved (and vice versa); steer along the abundance direction and check that predicted/reconstructed spectra (where a decoder or masked head exists) move in the curve-of-growth-correct direction; controls = matched-norm random directions; 3 seeds. Systems compared: abundance-direction ablation vs Teff-direction ablation vs random-direction ablation; synthetic vs real. Decisive metric first: selective degradation ratio = (abundance-prediction error increase when abundance direction ablated) / (abundance-prediction error increase when a random direction of equal norm ablated), with Teff prediction expected preserved. Convincing result: ratio ≥ 3 with Teff prediction largely intact, and the disentanglement/curve-of-growth structure reproduces on real APOGEE/GALAH spectra. Undecidable band: ratio in [1.2, 2.0] or structure that holds on synthetic but only weakly on real — reported as inconclusive causal use / limited transfer; band fixed before data. Negative result: ratio ≈ 1 (ablation no more damaging than random) or no transfer to real spectra means the directions are entangled or synthetic-only, bounding H1.

Experiment 5 (H1 — Low-metallicity/degeneracy stress, failure prediction, and cross-model convergence): Tests where disentanglement degrades and whether the invariance index flags unreliable estimates, plus convergence across models — sharpening, not enlarging, H1. Data: metal-poor and strong abundance–Teff-degeneracy regions of the synthetic grid, plus real metal-poor stars from APOGEE/GALAH with pipeline labels. Model: frozen SpectraFM/AstroCLIP; per-layer emergence analysis and CKA between models' abundance subspaces; 3 seeds. Systems compared: TIA and abundance-prediction error across metallicity regimes; TIA as a flag for high-error stars. Decisive metric first: AUROC of the temperature-invariance index for flagging high-error stars, plus mean pairwise CKA of abundance subspaces. Convincing result: TIA-based flagging AUROC ≥ 0.75 and CKA ≥ 0.6 (convergent Saha–Boltzmann-consistent structure). Undecidable band: AUROC in [0.55, 0.65] or CKA in [0.3, 0.45] — reported as weak failure-prediction / weak convergence; band fixed before data. Negative result: TIA at chance for flagging errors and CKA at the random floor means the invariance signal is neither diagnostic nor convergent, bounding H1's practical and universality claims.
Risk Factors and Limitations: Abundance and Teff are correlated in real stellar populations, so disentanglement could be confounded; we mitigate with synthetic spectra where the two are varied exactly independently and use matched-line-strength controls.

Synthetic spectra may differ from real spectra (synthetic gap), so representations learned on real data may not fully engage the synthetic grid; we test synthetic-to-real transfer explicitly and, where possible, use models pre-trained partly on synthetic data (e.g., SpectraFM).

Linear probes recovering an abundance direction do not guarantee causal use; we address this with ablation/steering and random-direction controls, though distributed/superposed encodings may blur single-direction interventions.

Some models tokenize/normalize spectra (continuum normalization, resampling) in ways that may alter line-strength information; we document each model's preprocessing and probe pre-normalization activations where feasible.
Occlusion-based per-line sensitivity measurements can be noisy for blended lines; we restrict multi-line coupling tests to clean, well-separated lines identified from the synthesis.

A negative result (models track line-strength statistics and do not disentangle abundance from temperature per Saha-Boltzmann) is scientifically decisive and directly relevant to trusting these models in degenerate/metal-poor regimes, though it may be perceived as confirmatory of skepticism; we frame either outcome as the first mechanism-defining test of line-formation physics in stellar foundation models.
All experiments are inference-only on public pretrained models plus small probes and standard synthesis tools/public spectral surveys, keeping compute at academic scale.

Name: reading_frame_degeneracy_probe
Title: Does the Model Read in Frame? Causally Testing Whether Genomic Foundation Models Internally Represent the Triplet Reading Frame and Codon-Degeneracy Structure of the Genetic Code
Short Hypothesis: The genetic code is an exactly-known discrete mechanism: nucleotides are read in non-overlapping triplets anchored by a reading frame, and 61 sense codons map many-to-one onto 20 amino acids (degeneracy). We hypothesize that genomic foundation models trained on raw nucleotides internally represent this mechanism rather than mere k-mer statistics, meaning (a) their internal representations are frame-aware (encode a codon's position modulo 3 relative to the true reading frame), (b) synonymous codons are organized by their shared amino-acid identity (degeneracy geometry), and (c) this frame structure is causally load-bearing: a single-nucleotide frameshift insertion catastrophically and specifically reorganizes downstream codon-level representations and predictions, whereas a length-matched in-frame (3-nucleotide) insertion does not. Frameshift-vs-in-frame is an exact counterfactual matched on length and local composition, making this a rare mechanism-defining rather than correlation-matching test. The primary novelty is the causal frame claim (c) in raw-nucleotide models; the degeneracy geometry (b) is a supporting secondary analysis and frame-feature steering is exploratory.
Related Work: Interpretability of genomic FMs has surged: Interpreting Evo 2 (2025) and Decode-gLM (2025) use SAEs to recover coding-sequence, tRNA/rRNA, and viral features; SAE studies on small gene LMs and Nucleotide Transformer recover transcription-factor motifs; nucleotide-dependency analysis (2024) reveals functional elements; cdsFM (2024) reports models 'recapitulate the overall structure of the genetic code'; Genomic Tokenizer (2025) builds codon/frame biology into tokenization by construction. Crucially, all of these are descriptive annotation-matching or build codon structure in by design. cdsFM shows the map is learnable when codons are tokenized, but does not test nucleotide-level models, nor whether the reading FRAME (position mod 3, the anchoring mechanism) is internally represented and causally used, nor whether degeneracy (synonymous equivalence) is geometrically encoded independent of local composition. No prior work uses the exact frameshift-vs-in-frame counterfactual to causally arbitrate whether a nucleotide-level FM represents the triplet-reading mechanism versus k-mer statistics. This causal, exact-counterfactual, degeneracy-geometry test is our novel contribution. The frameshift-vs-in-frame counterfactual is strictly stronger than annotation-probe work because it is matched on length and local composition, so a differential response cannot be attributed to k-mer content - isolating the reading mechanism itself; cdsFM/Genomic Tokenizer either tokenize codons or build frame in by design and so cannot test whether a nucleotide-level model represents frame.
Abstract: The genetic code is one of biology's few exactly-known, discrete mechanisms: DNA is read in non-overlapping triplets anchored by a reading frame, and 61 sense codons map many-to-one onto 20 amino acids. This makes it an ideal, unambiguous probe for whether genomic foundation models learn mechanism or merely nucleotide-level statistics. We ask three mechanism-defining questions of nucleotide-level genomic FMs (Nucleotide Transformer, DNABERT-2, and Evo 2). First, are internal representations frame-aware: can we linearly decode a nucleotide's position modulo 3 relative to the true reading frame, beyond what local composition permits, and is a distinct feature dedicated to frame? Second, is codon degeneracy geometrically encoded: do synonymous codons cluster by their shared amino acid while remaining separable at the codon level, controlling for GC-content and dinucleotide statistics? Third, and most decisively, is frame structure causally load-bearing? We construct an exact counterfactual: inserting a single nucleotide (a frameshift) versus inserting a length-matched triplet (in-frame) within a coding sequence. A model that represents the reading mechanism should show catastrophic, specific downstream reorganization of codon-level representations and amino-acid predictions after a frameshift but near-invariance after an in-frame insertion; a k-mer statistical model should respond similarly to both. We further steer the recovered frame feature and test whether it induces frameshift-like downstream effects. Metrics quantify a frame-decodability-beyond-composition index, a degeneracy-clustering score, and a frameshift-vs-in-frame causal asymmetry. Either outcome sharpens what genomic foundation models actually represent, with direct implications for variant-effect and indel interpretation. If nucleotide FMs fail this exact test, indel/frameshift-robustness benchmarks should gate their use in coding-region variant-effect prediction, splice/coding annotation, and pathogenicity scoring; if they pass, it validates a mechanistic inductive bias and can inform model choice.
Experiments: Experiment 1 (H1 — Frame-awareness probe beyond local composition): Tests the H1(a) claim that genomic foundation models encode a nucleotide's position modulo 3 relative to the true reading frame. Data: well-annotated coding sequences (CDS) from RefSeq/Ensembl across 5 species with known frames and start/stop codons (millions of CDS exist); we use 5,000 CDS (~5M nucleotides), stratified by species and length — 5,000 gives ample per-frame-class examples while keeping activation extraction feasible; each nucleotide carries its ground-truth position mod 3. Model: Nucleotide Transformer, DNABERT-2, and Evo 2 at a feasible size, all frozen; trainable = per-layer linear probes predicting position mod 3; 5 folds, 3 seeds. Systems compared: model-activation probe vs two strict baselines — a local one-hot/k-mer feature probe (frame must exceed local composition) and a randomly-initialized same-architecture model (confirms the structure is learned during pretraining). Additional baselines: a hand-crafted 3-periodicity detector (if it matches the learned probe, frame reduces to codon periodicity), amino-acid-preserving frame-breaking perturbations, and noncoding-region negatives. Decisive metric first: Frame-Decodability-Beyond-Composition Index = probe accuracy(model) − probe accuracy(local-composition baseline). Convincing result: index ≥ 0.15 with absolute model accuracy ≥ 0.9, and the random-init model near the composition baseline. Undecidable band: index in [0.03, 0.08] — frame decodability barely exceeds composition, reported as inconclusive; band fixed before data. Negative result: index ≈ 0 (or random-init as good as pretrained) means frame is not represented beyond k-mer statistics, H1 fails.

Experiment 2 (H2 — Degeneracy geometry of synonymous codons): Tests the H2(b) claim that synonymous codons are organized by shared amino-acid identity. Data: codon occurrences from the 5,000 CDS; codon-level representation = mean-pool of the triplet or codon-token embedding. Model: frozen NT/DNABERT-2/Evo 2, fixed activations. Systems compared: codon geometry colored by amino acid vs a GC/dinucleotide-regressed-out version (partial geometry), and vs the true codon-table degeneracy pattern (4-/2-/6-fold boxes). Decisive metric first: silhouette/clustering score of codons grouped by amino acid, plus a nested test (amino acid decodable AND codon identity still separable within amino acid). Convincing result: silhouette significantly positive after regressing out GC/dinucleotide content, and the learned degeneracy pattern mirrors the true code's fold structure. Undecidable band: partial silhouette in [0.0, 0.05] — clustering attributable to composition not degeneracy, reported as unsupported; band fixed before data. Negative result: no synonymous clustering beyond composition means degeneracy geometry is absent, H2 fails.

Experiment 3 (H3 — Frameshift-vs-in-frame causal counterfactual, primary test): Tests the decisive H3(c) claim that a single-nucleotide frameshift catastrophically and specifically reorganizes downstream codon representations while a length-matched in-frame (3-nt) insertion does not. Data: within each of 2,000 CDS from the Experiment-1 test split, at matched interior positions, construct paired edits — (a) insert 1 nucleotide (frameshift), (b) insert 3 nucleotides (in-frame) — with insertions matched on local nucleotide composition; this exact counterfactual is matched on length and local composition. Model: frozen models; measure change in downstream codon-level representations and per-position amino-acid/codon (masked-token) predictions after the insertion; 3 seeds. Systems compared: frameshift vs in-frame edits, as a function of distance downstream. Decisive metric first: Frameshift-vs-In-frame Causal Asymmetry = downstream-representation-change(frameshift) / downstream-representation-change(in-frame). Convincing result: asymmetry ≫ 1 (e.g., ≥ 3), rising with downstream distance, for the single-nucleotide models. Undecidable band: asymmetry in [0.9, 1.4] — frameshift and in-frame edits perturb the model equally, read as k-mer behavior (H3 unsupported); band fixed before data. Negative result: asymmetry ≈ 1 means the model does not represent the reading frame causally, H3 fails and (per the hypothesis) the model is a k-mer statistic.

Experiment 4 (H3 — Amino-acid consistency of frameshift effects and frame-feature steering): Tests that the frameshift's downstream effect is the biologically-correct shifted-frame reinterpretation, and that steering an internal frame feature reproduces it. Data: the 2,000 paired-edit CDS from Experiment 3, plus stop/start anchoring stimuli (premature in-frame stop insertion vs a synonymous same-length non-stop change). Model: frozen models; for coding-aware readouts, translate model-preferred codons or use Evo 2's coding-sequence feature; frame-feature steering uses the recovered frame direction / SAE frame feature at a chosen position, controls = matched-norm random and shuffled-frame-label directions; 3 seeds. Systems compared: (i) induced downstream reinterpretation vs the ground-truth +1/+2 shifted reading; (ii) frame-direction steering vs random/shuffled controls; (iii) premature-stop insertion vs synonymous control. Decisive metric first: agreement between induced downstream codon reinterpretation and the true shifted-frame amino-acid sequence, and steering mechanism-selectivity = |effect_frame direction| / |effect_random direction|. Convincing result: downstream agreement well above chance AND selectivity ≥ 3, with premature-stop causing a larger loss-of-coding reorganization than the synonymous control. Undecidable band: agreement near chance or selectivity in [1.2, 2.0] — reported as inconclusive causal frame use; band fixed before data. Negative result: no shifted-frame agreement and null steering means frame is not the causal variable even if Experiment-3 asymmetry appeared, so H3's mechanism reading is unsupported.

Experiment 5 (H1/H2 — Layer/emergence, cross-model convergence, and statistics-to-mechanism brackets): Locates frame/degeneracy structure and brackets it, without enlarging the claim. Data: the Experiment-1 CDS set. Model: frozen NT/DNABERT-2/Evo 2, per-layer analysis; brackets = a codon-tokenized model where frame is built in (cdsFM/EnCodon, upper) and a model trained on frame-scrambled sequences (lower); CKA between the three models' frame subspaces; 3 seeds. Note: BPE-tokenized models (DNABERT-2) are handled by mapping token spans to nucleotide positions, with single-nucleotide Evo 2 prioritized for the cleanest test. Systems compared: per-layer frame accuracy and degeneracy silhouette across depth; nucleotide-model decodability vs the codon-tokenized upper and scrambled lower brackets. Decisive metric first: layer of peak frame-awareness, mean pairwise CKA of frame subspaces, and where nucleotide-model frame accuracy falls between the brackets. Convincing result: a reproducible emergence layer, CKA ≥ 0.6, and frame accuracy clearly above the scrambled lower bracket. Undecidable band: CKA in [0.3, 0.45] or accuracy within noise of the scrambled bracket — reported as weakly convergent / no learned frame advantage; band fixed before data. Negative result: nucleotide-model frame structure at the scrambled bracket means frame is not learned, bounding H1/H2.
Risk Factors and Limitations: Frame position modulo 3 correlates with local codon composition in real CDS, so frame decodability could partly reflect composition; we mitigate with strict local-composition baselines, GC/dinucleotide controls, and the exact frameshift-vs-in-frame counterfactual which is matched on length and local composition.

Some models (e.g., BPE-tokenized DNABERT-2) do not tokenize per-nucleotide or per-codon, complicating position-mod-3 alignment; we handle this by mapping token spans to nucleotide positions and report per-model tokenization caveats, prioritizing single-nucleotide models (Evo 2) for the cleanest test.

Steering the frame feature in a nonlinear model may push activations off-manifold and yield uninterpretable outputs; we bound perturbation magnitude, report sensitivity, and use random/shuffled-label controls, relying primarily on the input-space frameshift counterfactual as causal evidence.
Distributed/superposed encodings may mean no single clean 'frame' feature exists; we use both linear probe directions and SAE features and report aggregate-direction results.

A negative result (models respond similarly to frameshift and in-frame insertions, i.e., k-mer statistics dominate) is scientifically decisive and directly relevant to trusting these models for indel/variant-effect prediction, though it may be perceived as confirmatory of skepticism; we frame either outcome as the first exact-mechanism causal test of the reading frame.
All experiments are inference-only on public pretrained models plus small probes/SAEs and public genome annotations, keeping compute at academic scale.

Name: convergence_vs_ancestry_probe
Title: Similarity Is Not Ancestry: Do Genomic Foundation Models Encode True Common Descent or Just Sequence Resemblance? A Convergent-Evolution Counterfactual
Short Hypothesis: The scientifically-correct mechanism of biological relatedness is common descent (a phylogenetic tree of shared-derived characters), which is NOT the same as raw sequence/phenotypic similarity: convergent evolution, long-branch attraction, and horizontal gene transfer are exactly the cases where similarity misleads about ancestry. Recent work shows genomic foundation models encode a 'tree of life' whose geodesic distances correlate with phylogenetic distance, but correlation cannot separate genuine ancestry-encoding from mere sequence-similarity clustering. We hypothesize that if a genomic FM's internal representation encodes true common descent (mechanism) rather than similarity (correlation), then on discordant cases where similarity and true phylogeny disagree, the model's internal geometry will track the true tree, not the misleading similarity; if it merely clusters by resemblance, it will place convergent/HGT sequences with their look-alikes rather than their true relatives.
Related Work: The Evo 2 blog 'Finding the Tree of Life in Evo 2' (2025) shows phylogeny is encoded as a curved manifold whose geodesic distances correlate with phylogenetic distance, and that embeddings capture codon statistics. 'Investigating Representation Universality: Genealogical Representations' (2024) finds tree-like cone subspaces in LLMs and confirms causal relevance via patching. The geometry-of-hierarchy line (Park et al. 2024) formalizes hierarchical concepts as orthogonality, and vision-model work (SAE ImageNet-hierarchy, DCNN semantic relatedness) shows taxonomic structure emerges from recognition training. Crucially, systematics itself (Hierarchies, classifications, cladograms and phylogeny 2023; Wiley & Lieberman) stresses that nested-set taxonomic similarity and generative phylogeny (common descent via synapomorphy) are conceptually distinct, and that convergent evolution/homoplasy is precisely where they diverge. No interpretability work tests whether a genomic FM encodes the mechanism (common descent) versus the correlate (sequence similarity). Because prior evidence relies on correlation with phylogenetic distance on concordant data — where similarity and ancestry agree — it cannot arbitrate this. Our discordant-case counterfactual (convergence, long-branch attraction, HGT) is the mechanism-defining test that distinguishes ancestry from resemblance, and is the novel contribution. We state the contribution as a benchmark and problem definition first: a reusable 'similarity-vs-ancestry' discordance benchmark (convergence / long-branch-attraction / HGT triples with adjudicated true-relative vs look-alike labels and explicit inclusion criteria) on which any future DNA foundation model can be scored, rather than a theory claim about a single model. The novelty of the setting (curated discordant cases where similarity and phylogeny disagree) is separate from the novelty of the inference (ancestry vs resemblance); we claim both but attribute the decisive leverage to the discordant cases, since correlation on concordant data cannot arbitrate.
Abstract: Biological relatedness has a precise scientific mechanism — common descent, a bifurcating tree of shared-derived characters — which is deliberately distinct from raw similarity: convergent evolution, long-branch attraction, and horizontal gene transfer make unrelated lineages resemble each other and true relatives look distant. Genomic foundation models have recently been shown to encode a 'tree of life' whose internal geodesic distances correlate with phylogenetic distance, prompting claims that they represent evolutionary relationships. But correlation on concordant data cannot distinguish encoding true ancestry (mechanism) from encoding sequence resemblance (a mere correlate). We propose the first mechanism-defining test using discordant cases where similarity and true phylogeny disagree. We curate three classes of ground-truth discordance from the systematics literature: (1) molecular convergence / homoplasy (independently evolved identical sequence traits in distant lineages), (2) long-branch-attraction pairs (rapidly-evolving lineages that similarity-based methods erroneously group), and (3) horizontally-transferred genes whose gene tree contradicts the species tree. For each, similarity places a query with its look-alike; true phylogeny places it with its actual relative. We test whether the internal representations of genomic FMs (Evo 2, Nucleotide Transformer, DNABERT-2) place the query with its true relative or its look-alike, using a discordance-resolution index, and whether a recoverable 'ancestry subspace' resists similarity confounds. We validate causally by patching the ancestry subspace into similarity-driven decisions. Either outcome sharpens whether these models learn evolutionary mechanism or resemblance, with direct implications for their use in phylogenomics and variant interpretation. Concretely, the outcome changes downstream practice in ortholog search, phylogenetic inference, and variant interpretation, and sets an evaluation norm for genomic-FM builders: if models track resemblance and fail on convergence/LBA/HGT, embedding-based homology and phylogenomic pipelines should not be trusted on discordant loci and must fall back to alignment / maximum-likelihood-tree methods; if a residual, causally-steerable ancestry subspace survives, embeddings can instead be used to flag discordance. The benchmark is released for reuse so later models are directly comparable.
Experiments: Experiment 1 (H1 — discordance resolution: true relative vs look-alike): Tests the core claim that on cases where sequence similarity and true phylogeny disagree, a genomic foundation model's internal geometry follows true common descent rather than resemblance. Data (existing, curated into triples): documented discordant cases from the systematics literature and databases -- convergent molecular evolution (echolocating-mammal Prestin/convergent substitutions, C4 photosynthesis genes, antifreeze glycoproteins), classic long-branch-attraction cases with densely-sampled resolved trees, and horizontal-gene-transfer genes with well-supported donor lineages (HGT databases plus manually validated cases). Each case gives a triple (query Q, true-relative T by common descent, look-alike L by sequence similarity) with similarity(Q,L) > similarity(Q,T). Such well-supported discordant triples number in the low hundreds; we use up to 200 triples and report per-category counts, accepting modest n with paired bootstrap statistics. As a calibration control we first replicate the known result that embedding distance correlates with patristic distance on ~500 non-discordant taxa (Spearman rho) to select best layers. Models (frozen, inference only): Nucleotide Transformer (500M and 2.5B checkpoints), DNABERT-2 (117M), and Evo 2 at a feasible size; mean-pooled per-sequence embeddings per layer; input length standardized, per-model tokenization caveats reported. Systems compared: model embedding vs an explicit k-mer/alignment-identity similarity baseline (scores ~0 by construction) and a maximum-likelihood phylogenetic gold standard (scores ~1). Decisive metric first: Discordance-Resolution Index = fraction of triples with d(Q,T) < d(Q,L), paired-bootstrap CI. Indecision band up front: an index whose CI lies in [0.45, 0.60] cannot decide and is reported as no reliable ancestry preference; index with CI lower bound > 0.60 is convincing ancestry-over-similarity encoding; index with CI upper bound < 0.45 means the model follows the look-alike (similarity representation). A negative result (index <= 0.45) is the decisive finding that these models encode resemblance, not descent.

Experiment 2 (H2 — ancestry signal beyond raw resemblance): Tests whether any descent signal survives removal of the raw sequence-composition similarity that embeddings are known to carry, and whether the failure scales with homoplasy severity as a genuine mechanism (not noise) would. Data: the same up-to-200 discordant triples plus the concordant calibration set. Model: frozen backbones from Experiment 1; the only trainable component is a linear probe predicting patristic distance (ridge, L2 by CV), trained on concordant taxa in one clade and tested on held-out clades (cross-clade transfer) and on discordant triples, 3 seeds. Procedure: (i) regress out a k-mer-frequency similarity component from the representation and recompute the Discordance-Resolution Index on the residual; (ii) rank triples by homoplasy/branch-length asymmetry and fit index vs severity. Systems compared: full-embedding vs residualized-embedding vs k-mer baseline. Decisive metric first: residual Discordance-Resolution Index (same units as H1) and the Spearman slope of resolution-failure vs homoplasy severity. Indecision band up front: residual index CI in [0.45, 0.60] cannot decide (reported as ancestry signal indistinguishable from resemblance once composition is removed); CI lower bound > 0.60 is convincing surviving ancestry encoding; CI upper bound < 0.45 means the apparent signal was resemblance. For the dose-response, a severity slope with CI spanning 0 is indecisive; a clearly negative slope (more homoplasy -> more failure) is the mechanistically-expected pattern. Negative results here reinforce the similarity-only conclusion.

Experiment 3 (H3 — causal ancestry-subspace intervention): Tests whether the ancestry structure is causally used: steering the recovered ancestry subspace toward the true relative should flip similarity-driven-wrong decisions, whereas control directions should not. Data: the subset of discordant triples the model gets wrong under H1 (places Q with L). Model: frozen backbones; the ancestry direction is the probe subspace from Experiment 2 (no backbone training). Procedure: patch/steer Q's ancestry-subspace component toward T at matched norm and read whether a nearest-relative ranking flips to T; controls are matched-norm random directions and a k-mer-composition direction. Decisive metric first: mechanism-selectivity = fraction of correct flips under ancestry steering / fraction under matched random steering, bootstrap CI. Indecision band up front: selectivity CI in [1.3, 2.0] cannot decide and is reported as no clean causal handle; CI lower bound > 2.0 with an absolute ancestry-flip rate > 0.5 is convincing causal ancestry encoding; CI upper bound < 1.3 (ancestry steering no better than random) means no causal ancestry direction exists. A negative result is consistent with distributed/absent ancestry encoding and, combined with H1-H2 nulls, supports the similarity-representation conclusion.
Risk Factors and Limitations: Ground-truth discordant cases are limited in number and some 'true' phylogenies are themselves debated; we restrict to well-supported, densely-sampled cases and report sensitivity to case-confidence thresholds, accepting modest sample sizes with appropriate statistics.

Molecular convergence at the whole-sequence level is rarer than at single-site level; we include both single-gene convergent cases and site-level convergence aggregated over informative positions, and document which regime each model can access given its context window.

Some FMs tokenize/normalize sequences (BPE tokenization in DNABERT-2, context limits in others) which may prevent access to whole-gene or genome-scale phylogenetic signal; we standardize input lengths, prioritize the model best suited to each case, and report per-model tokenization caveats.

Removing the similarity confound via k-mer residualization is imperfect and may over- or under-correct; we report results both with and without residualization and treat the residual test as a conservative lower bound on ancestry encoding.

The ancestry subspace recovered by a probe may reflect training-data phylogenetic labeling correlated with similarity; cross-clade transfer and the causal patching test mitigate this but distributed encodings may blur single-subspace interventions.

A negative result (models track resemblance and fail on convergence/LBA/HGT) is scientifically decisive and directly relevant to trusting FMs for phylogenomics and variant interpretation, though it may be perceived as confirmatory of skepticism; we frame either outcome as the first mechanism-defining test separating common descent from sequence similarity.

Confound controls: we match or adjust triples for sequence length, GC content, gene-family size, and overall taxonomic distance, and report the Discordance-Resolution Index stratified by each, so a positive result cannot be explained by these covariates rather than by ancestry.
All experiments are inference-only on public pretrained models plus small probes, standard phylogenetic gold-standard tools, and public curated datasets, keeping compute at academic scale.

Name: le_chatelier_shift_probe
Title: Does the Model Shift the Right Way? Testing Whether Reaction Foundation Models Represent Le Chatelier Equilibrium Shifts, Not Just Static Reaction Identity
Short Hypothesis: Chemical equilibrium has an exactly-known, directional, relational mechanism: Le Chatelier's principle plus the law of mass action say that when an equilibrium is stressed (add/remove a species, change pressure/volume, change temperature for an exo/endothermic reaction), the equilibrium shifts in a specific, sign-determined direction to counteract the stress, with a magnitude set by the reaction quotient relative to K. We hypothesize that if a reaction/thermodynamics foundation model represents this mechanism rather than static reaction identity, then (a) the SIGNED shift direction under a given stress is decodable from internal representations beyond what the reaction's identity/stoichiometry alone predicts, (b) a stress-direction counterfactual - adding versus removing the same species, or the same temperature change for an exothermic versus endothermic reaction - flips the internal shift signal as thermodynamics dictates, whereas a stress that leaves the equilibrium unchanged (e.g., adding an inert species at constant volume, or a pressure change for a reaction with equal moles on both sides) does not, and (c) steering a recovered 'shift-direction' axis causally moves predicted product/reactant balance in the Le-Chatelier-consistent direction. The add-vs-remove and exo-vs-endo counterfactuals are exact, mechanism-defining tests that static reaction-identity correlation cannot pass.
Related Work: Two lines bracket the gap. (1) Reaction/thermodynamics ML - equilibrium-constant predictors, reaction-thermodynamics models, and chemistry foundation models (SMI-TED/FM4M, ChemBERTa, reaction transformers) - predict K, dG, or products but are judged by regression/accuracy, not by whether they internalize the directional Le Chatelier response to a stress. (2) Chemistry-model interpretability - SAEs on chemistry LMs ('Unveiling Latent Knowledge', 2025) recovering static substructure/physicochemical/pharmacological features, attribution for solubility (2024), design-choice/latent-space studies (2025), and the SchNet reaction-analogy work (2025) showing constant static 'reaction vectors' (alcohol->carbonyl = '-H2') - all recover static, non-relational structure. Physics-model steering (Physics Steering 2025; emergent energy features 2025) recovers and steers single scalar quantities, not a directional equilibrium-shift response. Crucially, no work tests whether a model internally represents the RELATIONAL, directional Le Chatelier mechanism - that stressing an equilibrium produces a sign-determined shift - whether that shift representation is causally load-bearing, or uses an add-vs-remove / exo-vs-endo counterfactual to separate the mechanism from static reaction identity. The reaction-analogy work is the closest, but it encodes a fixed transformation, not the response of an equilibrium to a perturbation. Our shift-direction-beyond-identity probe, stress-direction counterfactual, and causal shift-axis steering are the novel, mechanism-defining contribution. Against the three families: K/dG regressors are scored on accuracy, SAE and feature cataloguing recover static substructure and constant reaction vectors, and scalar steering moves single quantities, none representing the sign-determined response of an equilibrium to a stress.
Abstract: Chemical equilibrium is governed by one of chemistry's most fundamental and exactly-known relational mechanisms: Le Chatelier's principle and the law of mass action, which dictate that stressing an equilibrium - by adding or removing a species, changing pressure/volume, or changing temperature - shifts it in a specific, sign-determined direction to counteract the stress. The direction is not a property of the reaction alone but of the reaction-and-stress together: the same reaction shifts toward products when a reactant is added and toward reactants when it is removed. This makes Le Chatelier an ideal, mechanism-defining probe for whether reaction foundation models learn equilibrium mechanism or merely static reaction identity. We probe pretrained reaction/thermodynamics and chemistry foundation models on curated and synthetic equilibrium systems where the equilibrium constant and the true shift direction under each stress are exactly known. First, a shift-direction-beyond-identity probe: is the signed equilibrium-shift direction under a given stress decodable from internal representations beyond what the reaction's identity and stoichiometry predict? Second, and most decisively, a stress-direction counterfactual: adding versus removing the same species (opposite shifts) and the same temperature change applied to an exothermic versus endothermic reaction (opposite shifts) should flip the internal shift signal, while an equilibrium-neutral stress (inert-species addition, or pressure change for equal-mole reactions) should not. Third, causal steering of a recovered shift-direction axis. Metrics quantify a shift-beyond-identity index, a stress-direction causal asymmetry, and a mass-action dose-response test. Either outcome sharpens whether reaction models represent the equilibrium mechanism that underlies reaction design and process chemistry. The novel object is a signed latent shift-direction axis with counterfactual sign-flips and invariances, a test of a relational perturbation-response mechanism rather than another equilibrium-constant predictor; it is at once a new probe and a small benchmark of matched-stress cases, and it moves model evaluation from accuracy-on-K to mechanism-fidelity. Reaction-prediction, catalysis, process-chemistry, and FM-interpretability researchers would use it for condition recommendation and yield optimization under perturbations, where a model that stores only static reaction identity cannot say which way conditions push the equilibrium.
Experiments: Experiment 1 (H1 -- signed shift direction is decodable beyond static reaction identity): Tests clause (a): the SIGNED shift direction under a given stress is decodable from internal representations beyond what reaction identity/stoichiometry alone predicts. Data: (i) a constructed set of 2,000 synthetic gas/solution equilibria with specified stoichiometry, K, and reaction-enthalpy sign, so the shift direction under each add/remove/pressure/temperature stress is analytically known; and (ii) ~200 curated real equilibria (acid-base, esterification/hydrolysis, Haber-type, solubility) with literature K and dH signs. We encode each (reaction, current-composition, stress) case in each model's native input format. Synthetic data is generated because no public dataset pairs reactions with signed shift labels across matched stresses; real cases provide a transfer check. Model: a masked chemistry FM (SMI-TED / FM4M, ~10-100M parameters), a reaction transformer, and (where available) a reaction-thermodynamics/equilibrium-constant predictor, public weights, frozen; only linear probes trained. Probes: logistic (signed shift direction), L2 via 5-fold CV, 5 seeds with reaction-family-grouped splits; report mean +/- SD. Systems compared: (i) a static-identity baseline predicting shift direction from reaction identity/stoichiometry alone (which cannot resolve add-vs-remove); (ii) Shift-Beyond-Identity Index = signed-shift accuracy from the representation minus the static-identity accuracy, after residualizing the identity-predictable component. Decisive metric first: Shift-Beyond-Identity Index (accuracy points). Convincing: Index >= 10 points (95% bootstrap CI over held-out families excluding 0, >=4/5 seeds). Refute: Index <= 2 points. Indeterminate band 2-10 points (stated before the data): unresolved -- some stress-conditioned signal but not enough to claim the mechanism; reported as such. A negative result means the model carries only static reaction identity, contradicting clause (a). Note: models that ingest no stress/composition are, by construction, an informative lower bracket that cannot exceed the baseline; we report per model how stress is supplied.

Experiment 2 (H2 -- add-vs-remove and exo-vs-endo stress-direction counterfactual): Tests clause (b), the decisive counterfactual. Data: from the synthetic set (reused) we form matched stress pairs holding the reaction fixed -- add a reactant vs remove the same reactant (opposite shift), and the same temperature increase applied to an exothermic vs an endothermic reaction (opposite shift); ~1,000 pairs per stress type. Model: the frozen chemistry/reaction-thermodynamics FMs that ingest reaction conditions/composition (prioritized); condition-agnostic models reported as the lower bracket. Systems compared: one stress direction vs its opposite; shuffled-stress control. Decisive metric first: fraction of pairs whose internal shift signal flips sign correctly across add/remove and across exo/endo. Convincing: correct sign-flip fraction >= 0.8 across both counterfactuals with the shuffled-stress control near 0.5. Refute: sign-flip fraction <= 0.6 (stress-agnostic signal). Indeterminate band 0.6-0.8 (declared up front): partial, reported as qualified. Matched stress magnitude makes any generic off-distribution effect shared. A negative result means the internal signal does not respond to stress direction as thermodynamics dictates, contradicting clause (b).

Experiment 3 (H2 -- equilibrium-neutral double dissociation and mass-action dose-response): Strengthens clause (b) with the neutral-stress control and the magnitude law, both of which a static or stress-agnostic model fails. Data: from the synthetic set (reused), equilibrium-neutral stresses that do NOT shift equilibrium (inert species added at constant volume; pressure change for equal-moles-of-gas reactions) paired with genuine stresses; plus a dose ladder varying stress magnitude with the mass-action-predicted shift (reaction quotient vs K) as ground truth. Model: frozen FMs with the shift probe. Systems compared: genuine vs equilibrium-neutral stress; increasing stress magnitude. Decisive metric first: (i) genuine-vs-neutral shift-signal magnitude ratio, and (ii) Spearman correlation between internal shift-signal magnitude and the mass-action-predicted shift. Convincing: ratio >= 3 (neutral stresses near-zero signal) AND dose-response Spearman >= 0.5 with correct saturation, shuffled-magnitude control near 0. Refute: ratio in [0.7, 1.5] OR Spearman <= 0.2. Indeterminate band: ratio 1.5-3 or Spearman 0.2-0.5 (declared before the data) -- partial, reported as qualified. A negative result means the model cannot separate real from neutral stresses or track magnitude, weakening clause (b).

Experiment 4 (H3 -- steering a shift-direction axis moves predicted balance the Le-Chatelier way): Tests clause (c). Data: add-stress-vs-remove-stress case pairs (reused) to recover the axis. Model: frozen FMs; only the direction is fitted, recovered as a supervised probe direction and as an add-minus-remove delta, steered at matched L2 norm. Systems compared: (i) shift-direction axis; (ii) 20 matched-norm random directions; (iii) a static-reaction-identity direction. Decisive metric first: mechanism-selectivity = |predicted product-reactant balance shift under shift-axis steering| / |mean shift under random directions|, with correct Le-Chatelier sign. Convincing: selectivity >= 3, correct sign, and the identity direction producing no consistent shift, across probe and delta recovery. Refute: selectivity <= 1.5. Indeterminate band 1.5-3 (declared up front): partial causal traction, reported without a strong claim. A negative result means the axis is not causally wired to the predicted balance, contradicting clause (c).

Experiment 5 (H1-H3 -- layer emergence, cross-model convergence, and mechanism brackets): Tests robustness of clauses (a)-(c). Data: synthetic and curated real equilibria (reused). Model: the chemistry and reaction-thermodynamics FMs, frozen; probes/directions as above. Systems compared: (i) per-layer Shift-Beyond-Identity Index and steering selectivity; (ii) CKA between recovered shift-direction subspaces; (iii) upper bracket = an explicit mass-action/equilibrium solver that computes shifts by construction, lower bracket = a static reaction-identity classifier with no stress access; plus synthetic-vs-real agreement. Decisive metric first: fraction of the identity-to-mechanism bracket each model closes. Convincing: >=50% closure for at least one model AND CKA >= 0.5 AND synthetic-real sign agreement >= 0.8. Refute: all models within noise of the static-identity lower bracket. Indeterminate band: 20-50% closure or CKA 0.3-0.5 (declared up front) -- partial/model-specific. A negative result means no model exceeds static identity. All runs are inference-only on public FMs plus small probes and synthetic/public equilibrium data, feasible on a single GPU.
Risk Factors and Limitations: Reaction identity and shift behavior are entangled in real data, making the shift-beyond-identity separation statistically demanding; we mitigate with identity-residualization, the add-vs-remove and exo-vs-endo counterfactuals (which hold the reaction fixed and vary only the stress), the equilibrium-neutral double-dissociation control, and mass-action dose-response tests a static model cannot pass.

Most chemistry FMs take a single molecule or reaction as input and no explicit stress/composition, so 'applying a stress' must be operationalized via the model's input format (e.g., altered composition tokens, temperature/pressure conditioning where available, or reaction-condition inputs for reaction-thermodynamics models); we prioritize models that ingest reaction conditions or composition, clearly report per-model how stress is supplied, and treat condition-agnostic models as an informative lower bracket that by construction cannot represent shifts.

Synthetic equilibria give exact control but may differ from what models saw in training, risking off-distribution behavior; we cross-validate with curated real equilibria (acid-base, esterification, Haber) and report sensitivity to synthetic-vs-real agreement.

Real equilibrium constants and enthalpy signs are condition-dependent and noisy; we use well-characterized reactions, restrict decisive tests to cases with confident K and dH signs, and report sensitivity to thermodynamic-data confidence.

Linear probes recovering a shift-direction axis do not guarantee causal use; we address this with steering plus random/identity-direction controls, though distributed/superposed encodings may blur single-direction interventions - we use both probe directions and delta-representations.

A negative result (models encode static reaction identity but not the directional Le Chatelier shift, failing the stress-direction counterfactual) is scientifically decisive and directly relevant to trusting reaction models for reaction design, yield optimization, and process chemistry - where predicting how conditions shift equilibrium is central; we frame either outcome as the first mechanism-defining test of whether reaction foundation models represent Le Chatelier equilibrium shifts.
All experiments are inference-only on public pretrained models plus small probes and public/synthetic equilibrium datasets, keeping compute at academic scale.

Name: dimensional_homogeneity_probe
Title: Does the Model Know Its Units? Probing Dimensional Homogeneity and Buckingham-Pi Structure in Physics Foundation Models
Short Hypothesis: Dimensional analysis is the most universal, theory-independent constraint in physics: physical laws are dimensionally homogeneous, and the Buckingham Pi theorem says a system's behavior depends only on dimensionless groups, invariant under rescaling of base units. We hypothesize that if physics foundation models represent genuine physical mechanism rather than surface numerical statistics, their internal representations will (a) organize variables along axes corresponding to physical dimensions (length, time, mass), (b) be approximately invariant to unit-rescaling transformations that leave the dimensionless Pi groups fixed, and (c) causally use dimensionless-group structure when forecasting. A model that merely fits numbers will lack this scale-covariant, dimensionally-homogeneous internal organization. No prior interpretability work tests unit/dimension structure, only individual quantities like energy. We frame (a)-(c) as three separable, individually-falsifiable hypotheses - linear dimensional decodability, representation-level Pi-invariance, and causal reliance on dimensional consistency - and a positive probe supports 'latent dimensional structure', not full physical understanding.
Related Work: Prior interpretability work shows physics foundation models linearly encode and causally steer individual physical *quantities* (Physics Steering 2025; Uncovering Emergent Physics Representations 2025 on energy; From Neurons to Neutrons 2024 recovering the semi-empirical mass formula; the GraphCast weather-model SAE study 2025; Interpreting Physics in Video World Models 2026). Separately, an entire mathematical literature formalizes dimensional analysis, dimensional homogeneity, and the Buckingham Pi theorem (Formalizing dimensional analysis in Lean 2025; Dimensioned Algebra 2021; Quantities, Dimensions and Dimensional Analysis 2014), and NUMCoT (2024) shows LLMs struggle with unit conversions at the token level. Crucially, no interpretability study asks whether a physics foundation model's *internal representation* respects the dimensional/unit structure and scale-covariance (Buckingham Pi) that underlies all physical law. Existing work tests whether a single quantity is encoded and matters; we test whether the deeper, relational, symmetry-level constraint of dimensional homogeneity is internalized. This scale-covariance / Pi-group test is the novel contribution, complementing (not extending) the quantity-encoding line of work. The novelty is an interpretability finding about pretrained physics FMs, not Buckingham-Pi itself; it is distinguished from trivial input normalization by probing internal activations (pre-normalization where possible), and from dimensionless-learning models (which build nondimensionalization in by construction) that serve here as an upper-bracket baseline.
Abstract: Dimensional analysis is the closest thing physics has to a universal, theory-agnostic law: every valid physical equation is dimensionally homogeneous, and the Buckingham Pi theorem guarantees that a system's dimensionless behavior is invariant under any consistent rescaling of the base units of length, time, and mass. This makes it an ideal, mechanism-defining probe for whether physics foundation models learn physics or merely fit numbers. We investigate whether pretrained multi-physics surrogates and time-series/PDE foundation models internally represent dimensional and unit structure. We introduce three tests.
