First, a dimensional-axis probe: we test whether internal representations linearly encode the physical dimension (length/time/mass exponents) of variables and quantities, organizing them along interpretable dimensional axes. Second, a scale-covariance test: we apply unit-rescaling transformations to inputs that leave all dimensionless Pi groups fixed (e.g., simultaneously rescaling length and time so a Reynolds or Froude number is unchanged) and measure whether internal representations and predictions remain invariant, versus rescalings that change the Pi groups, which should change them. Third, a causal dimensional-homogeneity test: we steer representations along dimensionally-inconsistent directions and check that forecasts degrade more than for dimensionally-consistent perturbations of equal magnitude. Metrics quantify dimensional-probe accuracy, a Pi-invariance index (representation change under fixed-Pi vs Pi-changing rescalings), and a homogeneity-selectivity ratio. This yields the first test of whether physics foundation models internalize the scale-covariant, dimensionally-homogeneous structure at the heart of physical law, with direct implications for their extrapolation reliability across scales. Practically, the answer decides whether practitioners in SciML and surrogate modeling can trust a physics FM across unit systems and scales or must keep applying explicit nondimensionalization and unit-robust evaluation - a live concern in simulation-to-real transfer, where an unnoticed change of scale (e.g., across Reynolds regimes) produces expensive extrapolation errors. We frame the contribution as a practical diagnostic, not only a conceptual probe.
Experiments: Experiment 1 (H1 — Dimensional-axis probe): Tests the H1(a) claim that physics foundation models organize variables along axes corresponding to base physical dimensions (length L, time T, mass M). Data: evaluation trajectories from PDE/dynamical benchmarks whose governing dimensionless groups are analytically known — pipe/channel flow (Reynolds), shallow-water (Froude), pendulum/oscillators (dimensionless amplitude, damping), reaction-diffusion (Péclet, Damköhler); we draw 150 trajectories per system (600 total) from PDEBench and generated ODE integrations, enough to cover each dimensionless-group range while keeping extraction to a few GPU-hours. Each field variable carries its ground-truth (L,T,M) exponent vector. Model: 2–3 pretrained physics/time-series foundation models with public weights (a multi-physics PDE surrogate — Poseidon or MPP/DPOT — plus a numerical time-series foundation model), frozen; trainable = per-layer linear probes mapping per-variable activations to the (L,T,M) exponent vector, with a dimension-classification head; 5 folds, 3 seeds. Systems compared: probe on model activations vs probe on raw numerical inputs, plus preprocessing controls (standardized-input and, as an upper bracket, an explicitly nondimensionalized model) and a random-dimension-label control, so probe success cannot be a normalization artifact and structure is shown to be model-contributed. Decisive metric first: probe R² for the exponent vector and dimension-classification accuracy on held-out variables. Convincing result: classification accuracy ≥ 0.85 and a PCA/CCA where variables cluster by dimension, exceeding the raw-input baseline by a clear margin. Undecidable band: accuracy in [0.5, 0.65] (chance depends on class count) — weak dimensional structure, reported as partially encoded and not used as a homogeneity axis in Experiment 4; band fixed before data. Negative result: accuracy near the raw-input baseline means dimensions are not organized as internal axes, H1 fails and the causal test is moot.

Experiment 2 (H2 — Pi-invariance / representation scale-covariance): Tests the H2(b) claim that representations are approximately invariant to unit rescalings that leave the dimensionless Pi groups fixed, yet sensitive to rescalings that change a Pi group. Data: the 600 Experiment-1 trajectories; for each, construct (a) fixed-Pi rescalings (multiply all lengths by λ_L, times by λ_T so every governing dimensionless group is exactly unchanged) and (b) Pi-changing rescalings (shift one variable so e.g. Reynolds changes by a controlled amount), λ swept over a small range around 1. Model: frozen models; no training beyond reusing Experiment-1 readouts; 3 seeds. Systems compared: internal representation change under fixed-Pi vs matched-magnitude Pi-changing rescalings. Decisive metric first: Pi-Invariance Index PII = (representation change under Pi-changing) / (representation change under matched-magnitude fixed-Pi). Convincing result: PII ≥ 3 (nearly invariant to fixed-Pi, sensitive to Pi-changing) in at least one model. Undecidable band: PII in [1.2, 2.0] — partial scale-covariance, reported as inconclusive; band fixed before data. Negative result: PII ≈ 1 (responds to both equally) means the model is a number-fitter lacking scale-covariant structure, H2 fails. Note (matched to Risk): rescalings use small λ and are compared against Pi-changing rescalings of equal input-space magnitude so generic OOD failure cannot masquerade as Pi-sensitivity.

Experiment 3 (H2 — Prediction-level scale-covariance and cross-scale extrapolation): Tests the H2(b) claim at the output level — a fixed-Pi-rescaled input should forecast the correctly rescaled trajectory. Data: the 600 trajectories with their fixed-Pi rescalings across a range of λ. Model: frozen models, forecasting only; 3 seeds. Systems compared: predicted rescaled trajectory vs ground-truth rescaled trajectory, as a function of λ. Decisive metric first: normalized forecast error between the model's rescaled-input prediction and the true rescaled trajectory, versus λ. Convincing result: error stays below the model's own in-distribution forecast error out to a rescaling factor of at least 2× in each direction, showing genuine covariance. Undecidable band: rescaled-input error within [1×, 1.5×] the in-distribution error only for |log λ| < 0.2 — covariance holds only infinitesimally, reported as weak; band fixed before data. Negative result: error grows immediately with any λ ≠ 1 means predictions are not scale-covariant, H2 fails at the output level.

Experiment 4 (H3 — Causal dimensional-homogeneity intervention): Tests the H3(c) claim that the model causally expects dimensional homogeneity — perturbing along dimensionally-consistent directions harms forecasts less than dimensionally-inconsistent perturbations of equal magnitude. Data: the 600 trajectories; using the Experiment-1 dimensional axes, build matched-magnitude activation perturbations that are (a) dimensionally consistent (perturb a variable along its own dimension's directions) vs (b) dimensionally inconsistent (inject a length-typed component into a time-typed quantity). Model: frozen models; both rolled out; controls = matched-norm random directions and shuffled-dimension-label directions; 3 seeds. Systems compared: consistent vs inconsistent perturbations. Decisive metric first: Homogeneity-Selectivity Ratio HSR = downstream forecast error(inconsistent) / downstream forecast error(consistent). Convincing result: HSR ≥ 1.5 with the shuffled-label control near 1. Undecidable band: HSR in [0.9, 1.3] — no differential sensitivity, read as the model not enforcing homogeneity (H3 unsupported); band fixed before data. Negative result: HSR ≈ 1 means dimensional consistency is not causally used, H3 fails even if H1/H2 decodability held.

Experiment 5 (H1/H2 — Cross-system, cross-model universality and construction brackets): Tests whether dimensional structure transfers and is convergent, and brackets it. Data: Experiment-1 activations; a probe trained on flow systems is tested on diffusion systems (transfer). Model: frozen foundation models; brackets run identically — a from-scratch single-system surrogate (expected weak Pi-invariance, lower) and, where feasible, a model trained on nondimensionalized inputs (expected strong Pi-invariance by construction, upper). Systems compared: transfer probe accuracy, CKA between models' dimensional subspaces, and PII across the brackets. Decisive metric first: cross-system transfer accuracy and mean pairwise CKA of dimensional subspaces. Convincing result: transfer accuracy well above chance and CKA ≥ 0.6, with foundation-model PII above the from-scratch bracket, indicating convergent dimensional structure. Undecidable band: CKA in [0.3, 0.45] or transfer within noise of chance — reported as non-transferable/weakly convergent; band fixed before data. Negative result: no transfer and foundation-model PII at the from-scratch bracket means dimensional structure is idiosyncratic and not conferred by broad pretraining, bounding H1/H2.
Risk Factors and Limitations: Fixed-Pi rescalings may push inputs outside the model's training distribution, confounding invariance measurement with generic OOD failure; we mitigate by using small rescaling factors, reporting sensitivity to lambda, and comparing against Pi-changing rescalings of matched input-space magnitude.

Some benchmark models normalize/standardize inputs internally, which may trivially remove or destroy dimensional signal; we document each model's preprocessing and, where possible, probe pre-normalization activations.

Linear probes recovering a dimensional axis do not guarantee causal use; we address this with the causal homogeneity test and random/shuffled-label controls, though distributed encodings may blur single-direction interventions.
Constructing exactly-fixed-Pi transformations requires knowing the full set of governing dimensionless groups; we restrict to well-characterized benchmark systems where these are analytically known.

A negative result (models are number-fitters lacking scale-covariant structure) is scientifically decisive and extrapolation-relevant, though possibly perceived as confirmatory of skepticism; we frame either outcome as the first mechanism-level test of dimensional homogeneity in foundation models.
All experiments are inference-only on pretrained public models plus small linear probes and controlled input transformations, keeping compute at academic scale.

Name: lagrangian_pv_conservation_probe
Title: Conserved Along the Flow? Testing Whether Weather Foundation Models Represent Potential Vorticity as a Lagrangian Material Invariant, Not Just a Snapshot Field
Short Hypothesis: Potential vorticity (PV) is defined by an exactly-known relational mechanism: it is a material Lagrangian invariant, exactly conserved FOLLOWING an air parcel in adiabatic/frictionless flow, and modified only by diabatic/frictional processes in a specific, quantifiable way. A single snapshot of PV is directionless about conservation; the invariant only exists along trajectories. We hypothesize that if a weather foundation model represents this mechanism rather than storing PV as an instantaneous field, then (a) the model's internal PV signal is conserved along its OWN predicted parcel trajectories in adiabatic regions, (b) a diabatic-vs-adiabatic counterfactual makes the internal PV drift specifically where latent heating/friction act (and stay conserved elsewhere), and (c) steering a recovered 'diabatic-PV-source' direction causally injects PV anomalies in the physically-correct sense. The along-trajectory conservation and diabatic-source counterfactual are exact, mechanism-defining tests that snapshot-field decodability cannot pass.
Related Work: Weather-model interpretability recovers single instantaneous features and steers them: SAEs on GraphCast (2025) find tropical cyclones, atmospheric rivers, sea-ice; GraphDOP work (2025) shows a unified world model inferring non-local fields (jet streams) and applies FSOI data-assimilation diagnostics; Physics Steering (2025) steers vorticity/diffusion directions; 'Uncovering Emergent Physics Representations' (2025) finds steerable energy features. All recover a quantity at a point/instant. Separately, atmospheric dynamics establishes PV as a MATERIAL Lagrangian invariant (Haynes-McIntyre 1990 impermeability/conservation theorems; Lagrangian PV-tracer conservation tests 1994; PV-tracer diabatic-attribution technique 2015/2019; Wernli-Gray 2024 review of diabatic PV modification), exactly conserved along trajectories except for quantifiable diabatic/frictional sources. Crucially, no interpretability work tests whether a weather foundation model's INTERNAL representation encodes PV as a trajectory-conserved invariant with its diabatic-source structure, whether that is causally load-bearing, or uses a diabatic-vs-adiabatic counterfactual to separate the Lagrangian-conservation mechanism from a mere snapshot field. Prior work answers 'is a quantity encoded'; the material-invariant question asks 'is it conserved following the flow, and modified only by the right processes'. Our along-trajectory conservation probe, diabatic-source counterfactual, and causal PV-source steering are the novel, mechanism-defining contribution, distinct from spatial-balance or total-integral conservation tests.
Abstract: Data-driven weather foundation models now rival physical solvers, and interpretability studies show they encode recognizable instantaneous fields such as cyclones, vorticity, and energy. But atmospheric dynamics is defined by relational invariants, chief among them potential vorticity (PV): a material Lagrangian quantity that is exactly conserved following an air parcel in adiabatic, frictionless flow, and altered only by diabatic heating and friction in a precise, attributable way. A single snapshot cannot express this conservation mechanism, which lives along trajectories, making PV an ideal mechanism-defining probe. We ask whether pretrained weather foundation models (GraphCast and Pangu-Weather) internally represent PV as a trajectory-conserved invariant rather than an instantaneous field. Using ERA5 and the model's own rollouts, we first probe whether PV is decodable from internal representations. Then, most decisively, we test along-trajectory conservation: following the model's predicted parcel trajectories, does the internal PV signal remain constant in adiabatic regions and drift only where diabatic processes act? A diabatic-vs-adiabatic counterfactual perturbs latent heating in a target region and tests whether the internal PV drift appears specifically there, with the physically-correct sign, while remote adiabatic parcels stay conserved; a spatially-scrambled control of matched magnitude should not. Finally, causal steering of a recovered diabatic-PV-source direction should inject PV anomalies in the correct sense. Metrics quantify along-trajectory conservation, a diabatic-vs-adiabatic drift asymmetry, and steering selectivity. Either outcome sharpens whether operational weather models represent the material invariant behind extratropical dynamics. The novelty is a test of Lagrangian invariance in representations, not a claim that PV theory is new, and not merely whether PV is decodable at a point but whether the representation preserves PV under the model's OWN flow map and drifts only where diabatic processes lawfully act; that lawful diabatic-source localization is the key differentiator from snapshot probes, SAEs, and steering on GraphCast and Pangu. Weather-FM builders, dynamical meteorologists, and forecast-verification researchers would use it to validate trust in long-rollout cyclone and Rossby-wave forecasts and to diagnose failure modes; the along-trajectory template applies to any materially conserved quantity, and a negative result motivates physics-aware training objectives.
Experiments: Experiment 1 (H1 -- the internal PV signal is conserved along the model's own predicted parcel trajectories in adiabatic regions): Tests clause (a). Data: ERA5 (existing, used as is; hourly 1940-present). We use 6-hourly winds, temperature, geopotential, and humidity for ~200 extratropical rollout cases sampled across seasons and regions (2000-2020), computing ground-truth Ertel PV on isentropic surfaces at each step, parcel trajectories integrated from the wind field, and diabatic tendencies (latent heating from moisture/precipitation, boundary-layer friction) so adiabatic vs diabatic parcels are labeled. Model: GraphCast (~37M parameters) and Pangu-Weather (~256M parameters), public weights, frozen; only linear probes trained. Probes: ridge regression to decode PV (and its constituents, absolute vorticity and static stability) from per-grid activations, L2 via 5-fold CV, 5 seeds with case-grouped splits; report mean +/- SD. Systems compared: (i) a snapshot-field baseline (PV predictable from the instantaneous field); (ii) along the model's own rollout, the drift of probed PV FOLLOWING a parcel (Lagrangian) vs the Eulerian fixed-point variance; (iii) the true Lagrangian PV (approximately constant). Decisive metric first: Lagrangian-to-Eulerian drift ratio = along-trajectory coefficient-of-variation of probed PV in adiabatic parcels divided by the Eulerian PV variability over the same segment. Convincing: ratio <= 0.5 with a 95% bootstrap CI (over cases) upper bound < 0.7, i.e. probed PV is substantially more conserved following the flow than a fixed-point view would predict, and above the reanalysis numerical-conservation floor reported as reference. Refute: ratio >= 0.9 (no better than Eulerian; PV stored as a snapshot). Indeterminate band 0.5-0.9 (stated before the data): unresolved -- partial Lagrangian conservation, reported without claiming the mechanism. A negative result means the internal PV does not conserve following the flow, contradicting clause (a).

Experiment 2 (H2 -- diabatic lawful drift along trajectories): Tests part of clause (b): where diabatic processes act, the probed PV changes along trajectories with the physically-correct sign and magnitude. Data: the same ~200 rollout cases (reused), restricted to diabatic parcels (latent-heating cores, boundary-layer friction), with the true diabatic PV source from the PV-tracer diabatic-attribution framework (PV generated below, destroyed above a heating maximum). Model: frozen GraphCast/Pangu with the Experiment-1 PV probe. Systems compared: along-trajectory probed-PV change vs the true diabatic PV source; shuffled-region control. Decisive metric first: Spearman correlation between along-trajectory probed-PV change and the true diabatic PV source, with sign-agreement fraction. Convincing: Spearman >= 0.5 AND sign agreement >= 0.7, shuffled control near 0. Refute: Spearman <= 0.2 or sign agreement <= 0.55. Indeterminate band: Spearman 0.2-0.5 or sign agreement 0.55-0.7 (declared up front) -- partial lawful drift, reported as qualified. A negative result means the model does not track diabatic PV modification, weakening clause (b).

Experiment 3 (H2 -- diabatic-vs-adiabatic counterfactual): Tests the decisive part of clause (b): a diabatic perturbation makes internal PV drift specifically where latent heating acts while remote adiabatic parcels stay conserved. Data: ~30 moist warm-conveyor-belt cyclone cases (subset of the rollout cases, reused). For each we perturb the initial state to enhance/remove latent heating in a target region, holding remote adiabatic regions fixed, and compare to a spatially-scrambled control perturbation of matched magnitude placed where it should not generate PV. Model: frozen GraphCast/Pangu, inference-only rollouts, PV probe reused. Systems compared: diabatic-region perturbation vs matched scrambled control. Decisive metric first: Diabatic-vs-Adiabatic Drift Asymmetry = |probed-PV drift in the perturbed diabatic region| / |drift under the matched control|. Convincing: median asymmetry >= 3 over the 30 cases with the correct PV dipole sign in >=70% and bootstrap-CI lower bound > 1.5, while remote adiabatic parcels retain along-trajectory conservation (Experiment-1 ratio unchanged). Refute: asymmetry in [0.7, 1.5]. Indeterminate band 1.5-3 (declared before the data): partial support, reported as qualified. Matched magnitude makes any generic off-distribution effect shared. A negative result means the internal PV drift is not diabatically localized, contradicting clause (b).

Experiment 4 (H3 -- steering a diabatic-PV-source direction injects the physically-correct PV dipole): Tests clause (c). Data: diabatic-vs-adiabatic parcel-state pairs (reused) to recover the direction. Model: frozen GraphCast/Pangu; only the direction is fitted, recovered as a supervised probe direction and as a diabatic-minus-adiabatic delta, steered at matched L2 norm at a target region during rollout. Systems compared: (i) diabatic-source direction; (ii) 20 matched-norm random directions; (iii) an adiabatic-advection direction. Decisive metric first: mechanism-selectivity = |PV-readout/rollout dipole response under diabatic-source steering| / |mean response under random directions|, with correct dipole sign. Convincing: selectivity >= 3, correct sign, and the advection direction failing to reproduce the dipole, across probe and delta recovery. Refute: selectivity <= 1.5. Indeterminate band 1.5-3 (declared up front): partial causal traction, reported without a strong claim. A negative result means the direction is not causally wired to PV generation, contradicting clause (c).

Experiment 5 (H1-H3 -- layer emergence, cross-model convergence, and PV brackets): Tests robustness of clauses (a)-(c). Data: the ERA5 rollout cases (reused). Model: GraphCast and Pangu, frozen; probes/directions as above. Systems compared: (i) per-block Lagrangian-to-Eulerian drift ratio and steering selectivity; (ii) CKA between recovered PV-conservation subspaces across the two models; (iii) upper bracket = a PV-tracer diagnostic that conserves PV by construction, lower bracket = a snapshot-PV regressor with no trajectory information. Decisive metric first: fraction of the snapshot-to-Lagrangian bracket each model closes. Convincing: >=50% closure for at least one model AND CKA >= 0.5. Refute: all models within noise of the snapshot lower bracket. Indeterminate band: 20-50% closure or CKA 0.3-0.5 (declared up front) -- partial/model-specific, no convergence claim. A negative result means weather FMs store PV as a snapshot rather than a Lagrangian invariant. All runs are inference-only on public FMs plus small probes and public ERA5 data with standard PV/trajectory diagnostics, feasible on a single GPU.
Risk Factors and Limitations: PV along trajectories correlates with instantaneous field structure, making the along-trajectory-conservation-beyond-snapshot separation demanding; we mitigate by comparing Lagrangian (following-flow) drift against Eulerian variance, using the diabatic-vs-adiabatic counterfactual (which holds magnitude fixed and varies only whether diabatic processes act), and the spatially-scrambled control.

Parcel trajectories must be computed from the model's own wind field and are subject to integration error, especially at long lead times; we use short trajectory segments, standard trajectory-integration schemes, and report sensitivity to integration accuracy.

Perturbing latent heating in the initial state may push inputs off the model's training distribution, confounding the diabatic drift with generic OOD failure; we mitigate with physically-plausible perturbation magnitudes, compare against a matched-magnitude scrambled control (so any generic OOD effect is shared), and report sensitivity to perturbation strength.
GraphCast operates on an icosahedral mesh with grid-locked features; we control for grid position, aggregate along isentropic-surface parcels, and prioritize invariant scalar channels for probing.

PV is only approximately conserved numerically even in reanalysis (dynamical-core non-conservation is comparable to physical processes, per the PV-tracer literature); we restrict adiabatic conservation tests to regions and lead times where numerical PV conservation is well-controlled and report the reanalysis conservation floor as a reference.

Linear probes recovering a PV/diabatic-source direction do not guarantee causal use; we address this with steering plus random/advection-direction controls, though distributed encodings may blur single-direction interventions.

A negative result (models store PV as a snapshot field but do not conserve it following the flow, failing the along-trajectory and diabatic-source tests) is scientifically decisive and directly relevant to trusting weather foundation models for extratropical cyclone and Rossby-wave dynamics where PV thinking is central, and for long rollouts; we frame either outcome as the first mechanism-defining test of whether weather foundation models represent PV as a Lagrangian material invariant.
All experiments are inference-only on public pretrained models plus small probes and public ERA5 data with standard PV/trajectory diagnostics, keeping compute at academic scale.

Name: space_group_absence_probe
Title: Forbidden Reflections: Testing Whether Crystal Foundation Models Represent Space-Group Symmetry Operations and Their Systematic-Absence Selection Rules, Not Just Atomic Coordinate Statistics
Short Hypothesis: Crystal structure is governed by an exactly-known discrete-group mechanism: the crystallographic space group, whose symmetry operations (screw axes, glide planes, centering) impose exact selection rules on diffraction — systematic absences (certain reflections have identically zero intensity) — and fix atomic multiplicities/degeneracies via Wyckoff positions. These are relational consequences of the group operations, not readable from any single atom's coordinates. We hypothesize that if a crystal foundation model fed only raw atomic positions (no symmetry labels) represents the space-group mechanism rather than coordinate statistics, then (a) space-group symmetry class and systematic-absence structure are decodable from internal representations beyond what local coordinate/composition features predict, (b) a symmetry-breaking counterfactual — a tiny displacement that lifts a systematic absence (turns a forbidden reflection allowed) at nearly-fixed geometry — shifts the internal symmetry signal, whereas a symmetry-preserving displacement of matched magnitude does not, and (c) steering a recovered symmetry-operation direction causally reshapes symmetry-dependent predictions. The absence-lifting vs symmetry-preserving counterfactual is an exact, mechanism-defining test that coordinate-magnitude correlation cannot pass.
Related Work: Two lines bracket the gap. (1) Symmetry is BUILT IN by construction: space-group-equivariant generative models (SGEquiDiff 2025, Space Group Conditional Flow Matching 2025, DiffCSP++ 2024) and equivariant property predictors constrain outputs to obey the group by design; they never ask whether a symmetry-agnostic model internally discovers it. (2) Space group is PREDICTED as a supervised label from XRD patterns (Suzuki 2020; MSDN 2020; contrastive powder-XRD 2025) or from composition (Cosy 2024) — these are classifiers, not tests of what a coordinate-based foundation model internally encodes. Interpretability of crystal models (CGCNN interpretability 2018 extracting site energies; Site-Net attention 2022; 'Comparing latent features of uMLIPs' 2025; my own periodic-law and convex-hull probes) recovers pointwise/energetic or generic latent structure. 'On the Symmetries of Deep Learning Models and their Internal Representations' (2022) and 'Interpreting Equivariant Representations' (2024) analyze architectural (weight-space) symmetry, not whether a model represents the DATA's crystallographic space group. Crucially, no work tests whether a general crystal FM's internal representation encodes the space-group OPERATIONS and their exact systematic-absence selection rules, whether that representation is causally load-bearing, or uses an absence-lifting counterfactual to separate the symmetry mechanism from coordinate statistics. That relational, causal, selection-rule-grounded test is our novel contribution. In three-family terms: equivariant models build symmetry in by construction, supervised classifiers predict the space-group label, and interpretability recovers pointwise or energetic structure, none testing whether a symmetry-agnostic model internally discovers the group operations and their systematic-absence selection rules.
Abstract: The atomic arrangement of every crystal is organized by an exactly-known discrete-group mechanism: its crystallographic space group. The group's symmetry operations — screw axes, glide planes, and lattice centering — have precise, testable consequences: they force systematic absences (specific diffraction reflections are identically zero) and fix atomic multiplicities through Wyckoff positions. These are relational properties of the whole structure, invisible in any single atom's coordinates, making space-group symmetry an ideal mechanism-defining probe for whether crystal foundation models learn crystallographic mechanism or merely coordinate statistics — especially models fed only raw positions with no symmetry labels. We probe pretrained crystal foundation models (universal MLIP backbones such as MACE-MP-0 and a crystal representation FM such as CLOUD/CGCNN) on Materials Project structures with known space groups and computable structure factors. First, a symmetry-beyond-coordinates probe: are the space-group class and systematic-absence pattern decodable from internal representations beyond what local coordinate and composition features predict? Second, and most decisively, an absence-lifting counterfactual: we apply a tiny atomic displacement that breaks a symmetry operation and turns a systematically-absent (forbidden) reflection allowed, holding geometry nearly fixed, versus a symmetry-preserving displacement of matched magnitude; a mechanism-representing model must shift its internal symmetry signal for the absence-lifting edit but not the preserving one, while a coordinate-statistics model responds to displacement magnitude regardless. Third, causal steering of a recovered symmetry-operation direction. Metrics quantify a symmetry-beyond-coordinates index, an absence-lifting causal asymmetry, and a Wyckoff-multiplicity fidelity test. Either outcome sharpens whether deployed crystal models represent the symmetry that governs materials properties. The novelty is the causal, selection-rule-grounded test of representation, not the crystallographic facts, and specifically what prior symmetry-latent probing does not do: fixed-geometry absence lifting and operation-level causal steering rather than space-group classification accuracy. Systematic absences are a stronger phenomenon than classification because they are exact, relational selection rules a coordinate-statistics model cannot fake. The concrete downstream use is model validation for symmetry-dependent property prediction (ferroelectricity, piezoelectricity, optical activity) and safer deployment of universal MLIPs in symmetry-aware materials screening; a negative result tells practitioners to supply explicit symmetry inputs rather than trust coordinate-based emergence.
Experiments: Experiment 1 (H1 -- space-group class and systematic-absence structure are decodable beyond local coordinate/composition features): Tests clause (a). Data: Materials Project (existing, used as is; ~150,000 relaxed inorganic structures). We draw a subset of ~30,000 structures balanced across crystal systems / the 230 space groups where possible, each with its space group, Wyckoff assignments, and computed structure factors / systematic-absence pattern (from space-group extinction rules via spglib/pymatgen). Model: a universal MLIP (MACE-MP-0 or SevenNet, foundation-scale, ~1-10M parameters) and a crystal representation FM (CGCNN / CLOUD), all ingesting raw atomic coordinates and species with NO explicit space-group input, public weights, frozen; only linear probes trained. Probes: logistic (crystal system, point group, space group; absence-pattern multi-label F1), L2 via 5-fold CV, 5 seeds with composition-grouped splits (no shared composition prototype across splits); report mean +/- SD. We probe invariant scalar channels first for equivariant MLIPs and report per-channel. Systems compared: (i) a local-coordinate/composition baseline (nearest-neighbor distances, angles, element counts) predicting the same labels; (ii) Symmetry-Beyond-Coordinates Index = model-representation decoding score (absence-pattern F1 / space-group accuracy) minus the local-feature baseline, after residualizing the coordinate-predictable component. Decisive metric first: Symmetry-Beyond-Coordinates Index. Convincing: Index >= 0.10 (F1 or accuracy) with 95% bootstrap CI over held-out compositions excluding 0, in >=4/5 seeds. Refute: Index <= 0.02. Indeterminate band 0.02-0.10 (stated before the data): unresolved -- some relational symmetry signal beyond coordinates but not enough to claim the mechanism; reported as such. A negative result means the representation carries only coordinate statistics, contradicting clause (a).

Experiment 2 (H2 -- absence-lifting vs symmetry-preserving counterfactual): Tests clause (b), the decisive counterfactual. Data: from the Experiment-1 subset (reused) we select ~500 structures with a symmetry operation producing a systematic absence (e.g., a 2_1 screw axis forcing 0k0, odd k, absent). For each we construct two equal-RMSD atomic-displacement edits: an absence-lifting edit that breaks the operation so a forbidden reflection acquires nonzero structure factor (verified by recomputing structure factors; space group lowered), and a symmetry-preserving control edit of matched RMSD that keeps the operation and the reflection absent. Model: the frozen crystal FMs; the Experiment-1 probe reused as the internal symmetry readout (plus a symmetry-dependent property head where available). Systems compared: absence-lifting vs matched symmetry-preserving edit, per structure. Decisive metric first: Absence-Lifting Causal Asymmetry = |symmetry-signal change under the absence-lifting edit| / |change under the matched symmetry-preserving edit|. Convincing: median asymmetry >= 3 over the ~500 structures with the signal moving toward lower symmetry under absence lifting in >=70% of cases and bootstrap-CI lower bound > 1.5. Refute: asymmetry in [0.7, 1.5] (responds to raw displacement, not the symmetry change). Indeterminate band 1.5-3 (declared up front): partial support, reported as qualified. Matched RMSD makes any generic off-distribution effect shared. A negative result means the model does not track the symmetry operation behind the absence, contradicting clause (b).

Experiment 3 (H2 -- Wyckoff-multiplicity fidelity): Strengthens clause (b) by testing whether the representation encodes symmetry-equivalent (same-Wyckoff-orbit) atoms as a coupled, degenerate set. Data: structures with high-multiplicity special positions and general positions (reused subset). Model: frozen crystal FMs exposing per-atom representations (prioritized; pooled-only models use a coarser whole-structure fallback with the caveat reported). Systems compared: perturbing one atom of a symmetry-equivalent orbit vs a general-position atom, and the induced response pattern against the Wyckoff-predicted equivalence structure; shuffled-orbit control. Decisive metric first: correlation between the model's induced response pattern and the Wyckoff-predicted equivalence structure. Convincing: correlation >= 0.5 with the shuffled-orbit control near 0. Refute: correlation <= 0.15. Indeterminate band 0.15-0.5 (declared before the data): partial multiplicity encoding, reported as qualified. A negative result means the model does not respect Wyckoff degeneracy, weakening clause (b).

Experiment 4 (H3 -- steering a symmetry-operation direction reshapes symmetry-dependent predictions): Tests clause (c). Data: high-symmetry structures and their symmetry-broken counterparts (reused) to recover the direction. Model: frozen crystal FMs; only the direction is fitted, recovered as a supervised symmetry-class probe direction and as a high-symmetry-minus-broken delta, steered at matched L2 norm on invariant channels. Systems compared: (i) symmetry direction; (ii) 20 matched-norm random directions; (iii) a coordinate-magnitude direction. Decisive metric first: mechanism-selectivity = |symmetry-dependent readout change under symmetry steering| / |mean change under random directions|. A decisive sub-test: steer toward/away from centrosymmetry and check whether centrosymmetry-gated property predictions (piezoelectric/optical activity, which require non-centrosymmetry) turn on/off accordingly. Convincing: selectivity >= 3, correct sign, centrosymmetry gate flips as predicted, and the coordinate direction failing to reproduce it, across probe and delta recovery. Refute: selectivity <= 1.5 or no centrosymmetry-gate response. Indeterminate band 1.5-3 (declared up front): partial causal traction, reported without a strong claim. A negative result means the direction is not causally wired to symmetry-dependent predictions, contradicting clause (c).

Experiment 5 (H1-H3 -- layer emergence, cross-model convergence, and symmetry brackets): Tests robustness of clauses (a)-(c). Data: the Materials Project subset (reused). Model: MACE-MP-0/SevenNet and CGCNN/CLOUD, frozen; probes/directions as above. Systems compared: (i) per-layer Symmetry-Beyond-Coordinates Index and steering selectivity; (ii) CKA between recovered symmetry subspaces across models; (iii) upper bracket = a space-group-equivariant model (SGEquiDiff/DiffCSP++ representations) that encodes the group by construction, lower bracket = a coordinate-only classifier with no relational access. Decisive metric first: fraction of the coordinate-to-symmetry bracket each model closes. Convincing: >=50% closure for at least one model AND CKA >= 0.5. Refute: all models within noise of the coordinate-only lower bracket. Indeterminate band: 20-50% closure or CKA 0.3-0.5 (declared up front) -- partial/model-specific, no universality claim. A negative result means coordinate-based crystal FMs do not exceed coordinate statistics. All runs are inference-only on public FMs plus small probes and public Materials Project data with standard structure-factor/symmetry tools, feasible on a single GPU.
Risk Factors and Limitations: Space-group class correlates with local coordinate statistics (high-symmetry structures have characteristic bond geometries), making the symmetry-beyond-coordinates separation statistically demanding; we mitigate with coordinate-residualization, the absence-lifting counterfactual (which holds RMSD fixed and varies only the symmetry operation), the symmetry-preserving control edit, and the Wyckoff-multiplicity double dissociation.

The absence-lifting and symmetry-preserving edits are synthetic distortions; unrealistic displacements may push structures off the model's training distribution, confounding the symmetry response with generic out-of-distribution failure. We mitigate with small displacements, verify the intended absence change via recomputed structure factors, and compare edits of matched RMSD so any generic OOD effect is shared, reporting sensitivity to displacement magnitude.

Equivariant MLIP features are tensorial; probing must respect invariant vs equivariant channels. We focus probes on invariant scalar channels first and report per-channel results, and note that a strongly equivariant model may encode symmetry implicitly in a way that requires careful readout.

Some crystal FMs pool to a single structure embedding, limiting per-atom Wyckoff analysis; we prioritize models exposing per-atom representations for the multiplicity test and report pooling caveats, using whole-structure probes as a coarser fallback.

Ground-truth space-group and Wyckoff assignments from Materials Project can have tolerance-dependent ambiguity for near-symmetric structures; we use standard symmetry-finder tolerances, restrict decisive tests to unambiguous cases, and report sensitivity to the symmetry tolerance.

Linear probes recovering a symmetry direction do not guarantee causal use; we address this with steering plus random/coordinate-direction controls, though distributed/superposed encodings may blur single-direction interventions — we use both probe directions and delta-representations.

A negative result (models encode coordinate statistics but not the space-group symmetry mechanism, failing the absence-lifting counterfactual) is scientifically decisive and directly relevant to trusting crystal foundation models for symmetry-dependent properties (ferroelectricity, piezoelectricity, optical activity, all gated by point-group/centrosymmetry) and for symmetry-aware materials discovery; we frame either outcome as the first mechanism-defining test of whether coordinate-based crystal FMs represent crystallographic space-group operations and their systematic-absence selection rules.
All experiments are inference-only on public pretrained models plus small probes and public Materials Project data with standard structure-factor/symmetry tools, keeping compute at academic scale.

Name: foldon_pathway_ordering_probe
Title: Does the Model Know the Order of Folding? Testing Whether Protein Language Models Represent the Kinetic Foldon Pathway, Not Just the Thermodynamic Native Structure
Short Hypothesis: Protein folding has two distinct mechanisms: the thermodynamic native structure (which contacts exist at equilibrium) and the kinetic folding PATHWAY (the ordered, time-sequenced assembly of cooperative foldon units, early vs late). These are separable: two residues equally important to the native fold can form at very different folding stages, and foldon ORDER is a relational, temporal property invisible to native-contact statistics. We hypothesize that if a protein language model (PLM) represents the kinetic pathway rather than only the native structure, then (a) a residue's folding stage / foldon-order (early-to-late) is decodable from internal representations beyond what native-structure importance predicts, (b) representational coupling between residues is stronger for those that co-fold in the same foldon (kinetic co-assembly) than for distance-matched residues that are native-contacting but fold at different stages, and (c) steering a recovered folding-order axis causally shifts predictions in a stage-consistent way. The same-native-contact/different-fold-stage counterfactual is a mechanism-defining test that native-structure correlation cannot pass.
Related Work: Existing PLM interpretability recovers features aligned with the THERMODYNAMIC native structure: BERTology-Meets-Biology (2020) shows attention captures contact maps and binding sites; InterPLM (2024) and 'Interpreting and Steering PLMs' (2025) recover SAE features for binding sites, motifs, and structural domains; 'Insights Into the Inner Workings' (2023) finds heads correlating with active sites. All validate against static, equilibrium annotations. Separately, decades of biochemistry establish the KINETIC folding pathway as a distinct mechanism: proteins fold via ordered, cooperative foldon units in a defined stepwise pathway (Englander & Mayne 'The nature of protein folding pathways' 2014; 'The case for defined protein folding pathways' 2017), and folding kinetics/order are encoded in sequence and can evolve independently of thermodynamic stability (RNases H ancestral-folding study 2016 shows kinetics and thermodynamics tuned independently; philosophy-of-folding review 2023 stresses thermodynamic vs kinetic explanations are separable). Native-state hydrogen-exchange gives residue-resolved folding-stage/foldon ground truth. Crucially, no interpretability work tests whether a PLM internally represents the kinetic folding ORDER (foldon pathway) as opposed to the native structure, whether that representation is causally load-bearing, or uses a same-native-contact/different-fold-stage counterfactual to separate the two mechanisms. Because native importance and folding stage are correlated (both track structural centrality), native-annotation matching cannot arbitrate this. Our folding-stage-beyond-native probe, foldon-co-assembly coupling test, and folding-order counterfactual are the novel, mechanism-defining contribution.
Abstract: Protein language models (PLMs) are known to encode the thermodynamic native structure of proteins — which residues contact, where binding sites and secondary-structure elements sit. But how a protein reaches that structure is governed by a distinct kinetic mechanism: the folding pathway, in which cooperative units called foldons assemble in a defined temporal order, early foldons forming before late ones. These two mechanisms are separable — folding order can evolve independently of native stability, and a residue's folding stage is a relational, temporal property that native-contact statistics do not reveal — making the kinetic pathway an ideal mechanism-defining probe for whether PLMs learn folding mechanism or merely equilibrium structure. We probe ESM-2 using proteins with residue-resolved folding-stage ground truth from native-state hydrogen-exchange and defined foldon pathways. First, a folding-stage-beyond-native probe: is a residue's foldon-order (early-to-late folding stage) decodable from internal representations beyond what native-structure importance (contacts, solvent accessibility, conservation) predicts? Second, a foldon-co-assembly coupling test: is representational coupling stronger between residues that fold together in the same foldon than between distance-matched native-contacting residues that fold at different stages? Third, and most decisively, a folding-order counterfactual: comparing mutations/perturbations that alter the kinetic pathway (change foldon order or stability) versus native-preserving controls, we test whether the internal folding-order signal responds to kinetic changes specifically. We validate causally by steering a recovered folding-order axis. Metrics quantify a stage-beyond-native index, a co-assembly coupling ratio, and a kinetic-vs-native causal asymmetry. Either outcome sharpens whether PLMs, used for stability and design, represent how proteins fold or only what they fold into. The novelty locus is explicit: a new question (kinetic pathway vs thermodynamic structure), a new ground-truth alignment (residue-resolved native-state-hydrogen-exchange foldon labels we will curate and release as a benchmark), and a new discriminative counterfactual (same-native-contact/different-fold-stage), not a new probing method and not a claim that steering alone establishes mechanism. The stakes are concrete: whether to use PLMs for mutation prioritization that affects folding rate and pathway, with direct relevance to aggregation risk, cotranslational and fold-switching design, and stability-vs-kinetics engineering. A null result is equally informative, bounding what evolutionary sequence statistics encode, and the released labels and code unlock pathway-aware pretraining and kinetic annotation transfer.
Experiments: Experiment 1 (H1 -- a residue's folding stage/foldon-order is decodable beyond native-structure importance): Tests clause (a). Data: proteins with residue-resolved kinetic ground truth (existing, used as is): native-state hydrogen-exchange (HX) datasets giving per-residue protection/opening free energies and foldon assignments (cytochrome c, RNase H, and other proteins with published foldon pathways), plus Phi-value datasets giving per-residue transition-state involvement. Because such residue-resolved kinetic data exists for only a modest set of well-studied proteins, we pool ALL available foldon-mapped proteins (~15-20 proteins, ~2,000-4,000 residues total) and report statistics accounting for small protein-level n. Per residue we record foldon/folding-stage order and native-structure features (native contacts, relative solvent accessibility, secondary structure, conservation). Model: ESM-2 150M and 650M (3B as compute allows), public weights, frozen; only linear probes trained. Probes: ridge (continuous stage) and logistic (early-vs-late), L2 via 5-fold CV, 5 seeds with leave-whole-protein-out splits (no residues from a protein shared across splits) to bar leakage; report mean +/- SD. Systems compared: (i) a native-structure baseline predicting folding stage from native-structure features alone; (ii) Stage-Beyond-Native Index = probe R^2 (and early-vs-late accuracy) from the representation minus the native-structure baseline, after residualizing the native-structure-predictable component. Decisive metric first: Stage-Beyond-Native Index. Convincing: Index >= 0.10 R^2 with a 95% bootstrap CI (over held-out proteins) excluding 0, in >=4/5 seeds. Refute: Index <= 0.02 (CI includes 0). Indeterminate band 0.02-0.10 R^2 (stated before the data; especially likely given small protein-level n): unresolved -- reported as underpowered rather than as support or refutation. A negative result means folding stage is explained by native-structure centrality, contradicting clause (a).

Experiment 2 (H2 -- foldon co-assembly coupling): Tests clause (b), the decisive test: co-folding (same-foldon) residues are internally coupled beyond spatial proximity. Data: residue pairs from the foldon-mapped proteins (reused); same-foldon pairs vs distance-matched, native-contacting control pairs from DIFFERENT foldons, matched on 3D distance and native-contact status so the only difference is kinetic co-assembly. Pairs (thousands) give more statistical power than the protein count. Model: frozen ESM-2; coupling measured by how a masked/mutated perturbation at residue i propagates to residue j (and conditional representational dependence). Systems compared: same-foldon pairs vs distance-matched different-foldon native-contacting pairs. Decisive metric first: Co-Assembly Coupling Ratio = coupling(same-foldon) / coupling(distance-matched different-foldon). Convincing: median ratio >= 3 with a 95% bootstrap CI (over pairs, clustered by protein) lower bound > 1.5. Refute: ratio in [0.7, 1.5] (coupling tracks only distance/contact). Indeterminate band 1.5-3 (declared up front): partial support, reported as qualified. A negative result means coupling tracks native contact rather than co-assembly, contradicting clause (b).

Experiment 3 (H2 -- folding-order mutation counterfactual): Strengthens clause (b) with input-space causal-adjacent evidence. Data: mutations with known kinetic effects (existing, from HX/Phi-analysis): pathway-altering mutations shown to shift foldon order/stability with minimal native-structure change, vs native-preserving/kinetics-neutral control mutations matched on native-structure and conservation change; tens of such mutation pairs across the foldon-mapped proteins. Model: frozen ESM-2, folding-order probe from Experiment 1 reused. Systems compared: pathway-altering vs kinetics-neutral mutation at the affected foldon. Decisive metric first: Kinetic-vs-Native Causal Asymmetry = |folding-order-signal change under the pathway-altering mutation| / |change under the kinetics-neutral control|. Convincing: median asymmetry >= 3 with bootstrap-CI lower bound > 1.5. Refute: asymmetry in [0.7, 1.5]. Indeterminate band 1.5-3 (declared before the data): partial, reported as qualified. Matched native/conservation change makes generic off-manifold effects shared. A negative result means the model does not respond specifically to kinetic changes, weakening clause (b).

Experiment 4 (H2 -- kinetics-vs-thermodynamics double dissociation): Strengthens clause (b) by showing the folding-order signal tracks the kinetic axis, not stability. Data: proteins/series where folding kinetics and thermodynamic stability vary independently (e.g., the RNase H ancestral series; existing). Model: frozen ESM-2 with the folding-order signal. Systems compared: partial correlation of the internal folding-order signal with folding order controlling for stability, and with stability controlling for order. Decisive metric first: the difference (partial-correlation with kinetics) minus (partial-correlation with stability). Convincing: kinetics partial-correlation >= 0.4 AND exceeds the stability partial-correlation by >= 0.3 (a double dissociation). Refute: the two partial correlations within 0.1 of each other (no dissociation). Indeterminate band: gap 0.1-0.3 (declared up front) -- partial dissociation, reported as qualified. A negative result means the signal is not distinctly kinetic, weakening clause (b).

Experiment 5 (H3 -- steering a folding-order axis shifts predictions stage-consistently): Tests clause (c). Data: early-folding vs late-folding residue sets (reused) to recover the axis. Model: frozen ESM-2; only the direction is fitted, recovered as a supervised probe direction and as an early-minus-late delta, steered at matched L2 norm at target residues. Systems compared: (i) folding-order direction; (ii) 20 matched-norm random directions; (iii) a native-structure-importance direction. Decisive metric first: mechanism-selectivity = |masked-prediction/variant-effect readout shift under folding-order steering| / |mean shift under random directions|, with stage-consistent sign. Convincing: selectivity >= 3, correct sign, and the native-structure direction failing to reproduce it, across probe and delta recovery. Refute: selectivity <= 1.5. Indeterminate band 1.5-3 (declared up front): partial causal traction, reported without a strong claim. A negative result means the axis is not causally wired to stage-consistent predictions, contradicting clause (c).

Experiment 6 (H1-H3 -- layer/scale, cross-model analysis, and pathway brackets): Tests robustness of clauses (a)-(c) across depth and model scale. Data: the foldon/Phi-value datasets (reused). Model: ESM-2 150M/650M/3B and (as a comparison) AF2 single-sequence Evoformer representations, frozen; probes/directions as above. Systems compared: (i) Stage-Beyond-Native Index and steering selectivity across layers and from 150M to 3B; (ii) CKA between recovered folding-order subspaces (ESM-2 vs AF2); (iii) upper bracket = an explicit foldon-pathway/HX-derived folding-order model, lower bracket = a native-structure-only predictor with no temporal information. Decisive metric first: fraction of the native-to-kinetic bracket each model closes, and its trend with scale. Convincing: >=50% closure for at least one model AND CKA >= 0.5 between models carrying the signal. Refute: all models within noise of the native-structure lower bracket at all scales. Indeterminate band: 20-50% closure or CKA 0.3-0.5 (declared up front) -- partial/model-specific. A negative result means PLMs represent native structure but not the kinetic pathway. All runs are inference-only on public models plus small probes and public HX/Phi-value/structure datasets, feasible on a single GPU.
Risk Factors and Limitations: Folding stage correlates with native-structure centrality (buried, highly-connected residues often fold early), making the stage-beyond-native separation statistically demanding; we mitigate with native-structure residualization, the distance-matched different-foldon control pairs, the folding-order counterfactual, and the kinetics-vs-thermodynamics double dissociation.

Residue-resolved kinetic ground truth (native-state HX foldon assignments, Φ-values) exists for only a modest set of well-studied proteins, limiting sample size; we pool across all available foldon-mapped proteins (cytochrome c, RNase H, and others) and report statistics accounting for small n, treating the co-assembly and counterfactual tests as the diagnostic core.

Foldon assignments and HX-derived folding order are themselves experimental inferences with uncertainty and some debate (defined-pathway vs energy-landscape views); we restrict decisive tests to well-established foldon pathways, report sensitivity to foldon-assignment confidence, and frame results relative to the specific ground-truth used.

PLMs are trained on evolutionary sequences that reflect native structure, and it is genuinely plausible they encode no kinetic-pathway information; a null result is expected under skepticism. We treat this as scientifically decisive (PLMs represent thermodynamic structure but not the kinetic folding pathway) and include AF2 and an explicit foldon model as brackets.

Linear probes recovering a folding-order axis do not guarantee causal use; we address this with steering, the counterfactual, and random/native-direction controls, though distributed/superposed encodings may blur single-direction interventions — we use both probe directions and delta-representations.

In-silico perturbations may push representations off-manifold; we bound perturbation magnitude, use single mild mutations and masking, and report sensitivity, relying on the input-space mutation counterfactual as primary causal-adjacent evidence.

A negative result is directly relevant to trusting PLMs for folding-kinetics-dependent tasks (misfolding, aggregation, folding-rate and pathway design), where the native structure alone is insufficient; we frame either outcome as the first mechanism-defining test of whether PLMs represent the kinetic foldon folding pathway distinct from the thermodynamic native structure.
All experiments are inference-only on public pretrained models (ESM-2, optionally AF2 single-sequence) plus small probes and public HX/Φ-value/structure datasets, keeping compute at academic scale.

Name: ps_traveltime_distance_probe
Title: Timing, Not Loudness: Do Seismic Foundation Models Represent the P–S Travel-Time Distance Mechanism, or Just Waveform Amplitude Statistics?
Short Hypothesis: Earthquake distance is fixed by an exactly-known relational mechanism: the arrival-time difference between the fast P-wave and the slower S-wave grows linearly with hypocentral distance (delta_t ≈ distance × (1/v_S − 1/v_P)), and magnitude follows a saturating log-amplitude-corrected-for-distance law—not raw amplitude. Seismic foundation models are trained on waveforms where distance and amplitude are correlated (nearer, larger). We hypothesize that if these models represent the seismological mechanism rather than amplitude/morphology statistics, then (a) distance is decodable from internal representations beyond what waveform amplitude predicts, (b) a P–S-gap counterfactual that stretches only the inter-arrival time (at fixed amplitude and morphology) will shift the internal distance estimate as physics dictates, while a whole-trace time-shift control (which leaves the gap unchanged) will not, and (c) steering a recovered 'P–S gap' direction causally shifts distance predictions. The gap-vs-shift counterfactual is an exact, mechanism-defining test that amplitude-based correlation cannot pass.
Related Work: Interpretability of seismic models is entirely post-hoc XAI attribution confirming LOCAL, descriptive alignment: Grad-CAM/SHAP show PhaseNet attends to P/S arrivals and that vertical vs horizontal components drive P vs S picks (2025); Integrated Gradients traces feature-importance drift in earthquake forecasting (2026) and pre-rupture deformation (2025); RNN hidden-state visualization for volcano-seismic events (2022). Seismic foundation models with public weights now exist (SeisLM 2024, SeisCLIP 2023, Seismic Foundation Model 2023, SeisMoLLM 2025) and decode distance/magnitude as downstream tasks. Crucially, all interpretability work is correlational attribution ('the model looks at the P and S arrivals'); none tests whether the model's INTERNAL representation encodes the RELATIONAL travel-time law—that the P–S time gap, not amplitude, determines distance—nor uses a gap-vs-shift counterfactual to separate this mechanism from amplitude/morphology correlation. Because distance and amplitude are correlated in catalogs, ordinary attribution and benchmark accuracy cannot arbitrate this. Our P–S-gap counterfactual, distance-beyond-amplitude probe, and causal gap-steering are the novel, mechanism-defining contribution, moving beyond 'the model sees the arrivals' to 'the model represents that the arrival SEPARATION sets the distance.' To be explicit about the contribution: the P–S travel-time law is textbook seismology and we propose no new locator; the novelty is a mechanism-level interpretability audit — a falsifiable, causal test (the gap-vs-shift counterfactual plus gap-direction steering) of whether a frozen seismic FM's internal representation spontaneously encodes the relational travel-time law, reported as evidence for or against encoding rather than a claim of complete mechanistic causality. Unlike PhaseNet/XAI attribution (which shows only that the model looks at the arrivals) and downstream distance/magnitude benchmarks (confounded by the distance–amplitude correlation), neither can arbitrate mechanism vs amplitude shortcut. The audience is operational seismology and earthquake-early-warning developers (who need to know whether a locator fails on atypical events where the amplitude–distance correlation breaks), seismic-FM builders (model selection and auditing), and ML interpretability.
Abstract: Seismic foundation models now estimate earthquake distance and magnitude from raw waveforms, and interpretability studies confirm they attend to P- and S-wave arrivals. But attending to the arrivals is not the same as representing the mechanism that makes them informative: hypocentral distance is set by the travel-time difference between the fast P-wave and slower S-wave, a relation that grows linearly with distance and is independent of how loud the signal is, while magnitude requires correcting amplitude for that distance. Because nearer earthquakes are also larger and louder, distance and amplitude are correlated in training data, so benchmark accuracy and attribution maps cannot tell whether a model uses the P–S timing mechanism or an amplitude shortcut. We propose the first mechanism-defining test. Using pretrained seismic foundation models (SeisLM, SeisCLIP, Seismic Foundation Model) evaluated on public labeled waveform datasets (STEAD, DiTing) with known source distances, we ask three questions. First, a distance-beyond-amplitude probe: is distance decodable from internal representations beyond what waveform amplitude/energy predicts? Second, and most decisively, a P–S-gap counterfactual: we resample the segment between the P and S arrivals to stretch or compress only the inter-arrival time at fixed amplitude and waveform morphology, which by physics must change the inferred distance, and compare against a whole-trace time-shift control that leaves the gap unchanged; a mechanistic representation must move its distance estimate for the gap edit but not the shift, while an amplitude-statistics model does the opposite. Third, causal gap-direction steering. Metrics quantify a distance-beyond-amplitude index, a gap-vs-shift causal asymmetry, and a magnitude-distance-correction fidelity test. Either outcome sharpens whether deployed seismic models locate earthquakes for the right physical reason. If confirmed, the audit becomes a selection and auditing criterion for early-warning models; if refuted, it identifies a missing physical mechanism that FM training or physics-informed regularization must supply — a decision that raw benchmark accuracy cannot inform.
Experiments: Experiment 1 (H1 — distance decodable beyond waveform amplitude): Tests hypothesis clause (a): hypocentral distance is recoverable from internal representations beyond what raw waveform amplitude/energy predicts. Data: STEAD (~1.2M labeled three-component waveforms with P and S picks, hypocentral distance, magnitude) and DiTing (~2.7M); use a 40,000-trace subset (24k train / 4k val / 12k test, split by seismic event so no event crosses splits), keeping only SNR>10 dB traces with analyst-confirmed P and S picks and stratifying uniformly over 0–200 km — fewer than the full catalog because the confident-pick, SNR, and distance-balancing filters (which deliberately weaken the natural distance–amplitude correlation) are essential to the test. Model: SeisLM (transformer waveform encoder, ~30M parameters) and the Seismic Foundation Model (SFM, masked-autoencoder ViT, ~100M parameters); backbone frozen, only a ridge-regression linear probe (L2 chosen by 5-fold CV) trained on the best layer, seeds 0–4. Systems compared: probe R^2 for distance from the frozen representation vs an amplitude baseline (ridge on log peak amplitude, RMS energy, and 8 envelope-shape features), with the representation residualized against those amplitude features before re-decoding. Decisive metric (first): Distance-Beyond-Amplitude Index = test R^2(distance | representation) − R^2(distance | amplitude features). Convincing: Index ≥ 0.15 with 95% CI lower bound above 0.05, and the residual distance direction correlates more with a delta_t (P–S gap) probe than with an amplitude probe. Indecision band: Index in [−0.03, 0.05] — within probe noise of zero; a result here means distance adds nothing beyond amplitude and clause (a) is unsupported (amplitude-shortcut reading). Negative result (Index ≤ −0.03 or inside the band): the representation is an amplitude statistic, not a distance code, which already undercuts the mechanism hypothesis.

Experiment 2 (H2 — P–S-gap vs whole-trace-shift counterfactual): Tests clause (b): stretching only the inter-arrival gap shifts the internal distance estimate, while a whole-trace time-shift (which leaves the gap unchanged) does not. Data: 3,000 high-SNR confident-pick traces drawn from the Experiment-1 test events; each yields a matched pair — (gap edit) resample only the P-to-S segment to change delta_t by a controlled factor with tapered splice joins, preserving amplitude scale and the P and S packet morphology; (shift control) translate the whole trace by an equal number of samples, leaving delta_t fixed. Model/probe as Experiment 1 (frozen backbones, seeds 0–4); read-out is the Experiment-1 distance probe and the model's distance head where present. Systems compared: |change in distance estimate| under gap edit vs under shift control, on the same traces. Decisive metric (first): Gap-vs-Shift Causal Asymmetry = median(|Δdistance gap edit|) / median(|Δdistance shift control|). Convincing: asymmetry ≥ 3 and the gap-edit Δdistance has the correct (positive) sign. Indecision band: asymmetry in [0.7, 2.0] — the timing gap is not privileged over a generic shift; a result here means the model is insensitive to the mechanism-defining inter-arrival timing and clause (b) fails. Negative result: asymmetry ≈ 1, i.e., displacement moves the estimate as much as the physically meaningful gap, indicating a morphology/statistics reading rather than the travel-time mechanism.

Experiment 3 (H2 — physics dose-response of the linear travel-time law): Tests the quantitative content of clause (b): that the induced distance change follows delta_t = distance × (1/v_S − 1/v_P). Data: the same 3,000 test traces; sweep the gap-stretch factor across 7 levels spanning ±30% of delta_t. Model/probe as above, seeds 0–4. Systems compared: model-induced Δdistance vs the physically predicted Δdistance from the regional v_P, v_S; shuffled-stretch-factor labels as a null control. Decisive metric (first): slope agreement = fitted slope(model Δdistance vs predicted Δdistance), plus Spearman rho of the same relation. Convincing: rho ≥ 0.6, correct sign, and fitted slope within ±30% of 1.0 (predicted). Indecision band: rho in [0.2, 0.4] or slope outside ±30% but same sign — a weak, physically-loose response; a result here means the model tracks gap direction but not the law's magnitude, partial support for (b) that should be reported as inconclusive on quantitative fidelity. Negative result: rho < 0.2 or wrong sign, indistinguishable from the shuffled control — no travel-time law is represented.

Experiment 4 (H3 — causal P–S-gap-direction steering): Tests clause (c): steering a recovered 'P–S gap' direction causally shifts distance predictions. Data: the same 3,000-trace test set; the gap direction is recovered two ways — a supervised delta_t probe direction, and the mean delta-representation between short-gap and long-gap traces at matched amplitude. Model/probe as above; add matched-norm perturbations along the gap direction to the frozen best-layer activations and read the distance head, seeds 0–4. Systems compared: gap direction vs matched-norm random directions vs an amplitude-probe direction. Decisive metric (first): Steering Selectivity = |Δdistance from gap-direction steering| / |Δdistance from random-direction steering|. Convincing: selectivity ≥ 3, Δdistance in the gap-consistent sign, and amplitude-direction steering not reproducing it. Indecision band: selectivity in [0.7, 2.0] — the gap direction is no more causal than a random one; a result here means the recovered direction is correlational, not a causal handle, and clause (c) is unsupported. Negative result: selectivity ≈ 1, indicating no dedicated causal distance-via-timing direction.
Risk Factors and Limitations: Distance and amplitude are strongly correlated in real catalogs, making the distance-beyond-amplitude separation statistically demanding; we mitigate with amplitude-residualization, the gap-vs-shift counterfactual (which holds amplitude and morphology fixed while varying only the timing gap), and the physics dose-response test that an amplitude model cannot reproduce with the correct slope.

The gap-edit counterfactual is a synthetic waveform manipulation; time-stretching the inter-arrival segment may introduce spectral artifacts or push traces off the model's data distribution, confounding the gap-edit response with generic OOD failure. We mitigate with small stretch factors, tapered splice joins, spectral-artifact diagnostics, and by comparing against the whole-trace shift control of matched sample-count perturbation; we report sensitivity to stretch magnitude.

Some foundation models ingest time-frequency spectra (e.g., SeisCLIP) or normalize/tokenize waveforms in ways that may discard absolute timing or amplitude; we document each model's preprocessing, probe pre-normalization activations where feasible, and prioritize models that retain raw temporal structure (SeisLM) for the cleanest timing test.

Arrival picks (P and S) in STEAD/DiTing are pipeline estimates with error, adding noise to the gap edit and to delta_t labels; we restrict counterfactuals to high-SNR traces with confident picks and report sensitivity to pick-quality thresholds.

Linear probes recovering a gap/distance direction do not guarantee causal use; we address this with steering plus random/amplitude-direction controls, though distributed/superposed encodings may blur single-direction interventions.

A negative result (models estimate distance from amplitude/morphology statistics and fail the gap-vs-shift counterfactual) is scientifically decisive and directly relevant to trusting seismic foundation models for earthquake location and early warning—especially for atypical events where the amplitude–distance correlation breaks—though it may be perceived as confirmatory of skepticism; we frame either outcome as the first mechanism-defining test of whether seismic FMs represent the P–S travel-time distance law.
All experiments are inference-only on public pretrained models plus small probes and public labeled waveform datasets (STEAD, DiTing), keeping compute at academic scale.

Name: radiative_feedback_pattern_probe
Title: Where the Warming Is, Not Just How Warm: Testing Whether Weather Foundation Models Represent the Pattern-Dependent Radiative Feedback Mechanism, Not Just Global-Mean Temperature
Short Hypothesis: Earth's radiative response to warming is governed by an exactly-known relational mechanism: the top-of-atmosphere (TOA) radiation anomaly is not a function of global-mean surface temperature alone but of the SPATIAL PATTERN of warming (the 'pattern effect'), because local feedbacks (Planck, lapse-rate, cloud, water-vapor) differ by region - e.g., warming concentrated in tropical stratocumulus decks produces a far more negative radiative feedback than the same global-mean warming spread elsewhere. A single scalar mean temperature is degenerate about feedback strength. We hypothesize that if a machine-learning weather/climate emulator represents the radiative-feedback mechanism rather than a mean-temperature-to-radiation shortcut, then (a) the TOA radiation anomaly is decodable from internal representations beyond what global-mean surface temperature predicts, along an axis carrying warming-pattern information, (b) a pattern-holding counterfactual - rearranging the spatial pattern of a surface-temperature anomaly while holding its global mean fixed - shifts the internal radiation/feedback signal as physics dictates, whereas a pattern-preserving amplitude change moves it along the Planck line, and (c) steering a recovered 'pattern-effect' direction causally shifts predicted TOA radiation in the feedback-consistent direction. The same-mean/different-pattern counterfactual is an exact, mechanism-defining test that mean-temperature correlation cannot pass.
Related Work: Two lines bracket the gap. (1) ML for radiative feedbacks: 'CNNs Trained on Internal Variability Predict Forced Response of TOA Radiation by Learning the Pattern Effect' (2025) shows a CNN can predict TOA radiation from surface-temperature MAPS and, via XAI saliency, draws skill from physically-meaningful regions; 'Examining Fast Radiative Feedbacks Using ML Weather Emulators' (2026) shows historically-trained emulators reproduce fast CO2 radiative responses at the OUTPUT level; causal-emulation work (Bayesian filtering 2025; forced-response limitations 2025) studies forced responses externally. (2) Weather-model interpretability: SAE studies on GraphCast (2025) recover single instantaneous features (cyclones, atmospheric rivers, sea-ice) and steer them; GraphDOP work (2025) shows a unified world-model representation; the ocean-role study (2026) correlates OUTPUT errors with SST. Crucially, all of these operate at the input-output / saliency level or recover single instantaneous fields - none tests whether a foundation model's INTERNAL representation encodes the RELATIONAL pattern-effect mechanism (that radiative feedback depends on WHERE warming occurs, not just the global mean), whether that representation is causally load-bearing, or uses a same-mean/different-pattern counterfactual to separate the radiative-feedback mechanism from a mean-temperature shortcut. The CNN pattern-effect paper uses saliency to show WHICH regions matter for a prediction; it does not test whether the internal representation encodes feedback as a pattern-dependent quantity distinct from the mean, nor perform causal pattern-holding interventions. Our pattern-effect-beyond-mean probe, same-mean/different-pattern counterfactual, and causal pattern-effect steering are the novel, mechanism-defining contribution, in a safety-critical climate-sensitivity setting.
Abstract: Machine-learning weather and climate emulators are increasingly used to study Earth's response to greenhouse-gas forcing, and interpretability studies have shown they encode recognizable physical fields. But the quantity that ultimately sets climate sensitivity - the top-of-atmosphere (TOA) radiative feedback - is governed by a relational mechanism that a single number cannot express: the 'pattern effect'. The TOA radiation anomaly depends not on global-mean surface temperature alone but on the spatial PATTERN of warming, because local Planck, lapse-rate, cloud, and water-vapor feedbacks differ sharply by region; the same global-mean warming can imply strongly or weakly stabilizing feedback depending on where it is concentrated. This makes the pattern effect an ideal, mechanism-defining probe for whether emulators learn the feedback mechanism or a mean-temperature shortcut. We probe pretrained weather/climate foundation models (GraphCast, Pangu-Weather, and a fast-feedback-capable emulator) on reanalysis and climate-model data where surface-temperature fields, TOA radiation, and diagnosed feedbacks are known. First, a feedback-beyond-mean probe: is the TOA radiation anomaly decodable from internal representations beyond what global-mean surface temperature predicts, along an axis carrying warming-pattern information? Second, and most decisively, a same-mean/different-pattern counterfactual: we rearrange the spatial pattern of a surface-temperature anomaly holding its global mean fixed (which physics says changes the radiative feedback), versus a pattern-preserving amplitude change (which moves along the Planck line), and test whether the internal radiation/feedback signal responds to the pattern - a mean-shortcut model responds only to amplitude. Third, causal steering of a recovered pattern-effect direction. Metrics quantify a feedback-beyond-mean index, a pattern-vs-amplitude causal asymmetry, and a regional-feedback fidelity test. Either outcome sharpens whether emulators represent the mechanism behind climate sensitivity. The claim is an internal-representation hypothesis, not a new climate finding and not a new feedback mechanism: it asks whether a hidden layer encodes feedback as pattern-dependent beyond the global mean, and it is at once a new probe and a new causal pattern-holding intervention, distinct from prior output-level Green's-function and SST-pattern evaluation. Its significance is model-verification rather than societal-impact overreach: emulator builders, climate-model evaluators, and interpretability researchers would add the same-mean/different-pattern counterfactual to validation suites that today check only outputs, catching the mean-temperature shortcut precisely where it breaks for novel warming patterns.
Experiments: Experiment 1 (H1 -- TOA radiation is decodable beyond global-mean surface temperature, along a pattern-carrying axis): Tests clause (a). Data (existing, used as is): ERA5 surface-temperature fields paired with CERES top-of-atmosphere (TOA) radiation (2000-2022), plus CMIP6 amip-piForcing and abrupt-4xCO2 members and the Green's-function / patterned-SST experiments that provide regional radiative-feedback kernels; per state we record the global-mean surface-temperature anomaly, the warming-pattern field, the TOA radiation anomaly, and the pattern-implied feedback. We use ~10,000 monthly states across reanalysis and CMIP members. Model: GraphCast (~37M) and Pangu-Weather (~256M), plus a fast-feedback-capable emulator (ACE-class), public weights, frozen; only linear probes trained. Because the pattern effect appears in the FAST radiative feedback on weekly timescales, we probe fast-feedback-relevant fields and prioritize the emulator that exposes/can be probed for TOA-relevant output, reporting per-model what is measurable; we probe pre-normalization activations where preprocessing would remove absolute-anomaly information. Probes: ridge, L2 via 5-fold CV, 5 seeds with time-blocked splits; report mean +/- SD. Systems compared: (i) a mean-temperature baseline predicting TOA radiation from global-mean surface temperature (the Planck/shortcut predictor); (ii) Feedback-Beyond-Mean Index = probe R^2 for TOA radiation from the representation minus the global-mean R^2, after residualizing the global-mean-predictable component; (iii) alignment of the recovered radiation direction with a pattern probe vs a mean probe. Decisive metric first: Feedback-Beyond-Mean Index. Convincing: Index >= 0.10 R^2 (95% bootstrap CI over held-out time blocks excluding 0, >=4/5 seeds) with the recovered direction correlating more strongly with the pattern probe than the mean probe.
