Refute: Index <= 0.02. Indeterminate band 0.02-0.10 R^2 (stated before the data): unresolved -- some pattern-dependent signal but not enough to claim the mechanism; reported as such. A negative result means TOA radiation is explained by global-mean temperature alone, contradicting clause (a).

Experiment 2 (H2 -- same-mean/different-pattern vs pattern-preserving-amplitude counterfactual): Tests clause (b), the decisive counterfactual. Data: ~40 base states from which we build two matched surface-temperature-anomaly edits each: a pattern edit that rearranges the spatial anomaly (e.g., moving warming out of tropical stratocumulus/east-Pacific low-cloud decks) while holding the GLOBAL MEAN exactly fixed (changing feedback by the pattern effect), and an amplitude control edit that scales the anomaly (changing the mean) with the PATTERN fixed (moving radiation along the Planck line). Patterns are drawn from CMIP pattern-effect experiments to stay physically plausible; the global mean is verified fixed. Model: the frozen emulators, inference-only; probe from Experiment 1 as the internal radiation readout. Systems compared: same-mean pattern edit vs pattern-preserving amplitude edit. Decisive metric first: Pattern-vs-Amplitude Causal Asymmetry = |radiation-signal change under the same-mean pattern edit| / |radiation-signal change per unit anomaly magnitude under the amplitude edit, matched on total anomaly magnitude|. Convincing: median asymmetry >= 3 over the 40 states with the pattern edit moving radiation in the feedback-consistent sign in >=70% and bootstrap-CI lower bound > 1.5. Refute: asymmetry in [0.7, 1.5] (negligible response to pattern at fixed mean -- a shortcut). Indeterminate band 1.5-3 (declared up front): partial support, reported as qualified. Matched magnitude makes any generic off-distribution effect shared. A negative result means feedback does not depend on where warming is, contradicting clause (b).

Experiment 3 (H2 -- regional-feedback fidelity against Green's-function ground truth): Strengthens clause (b) by testing that localized warming produces region-specific feedback, not a uniform response. Data: localized warming patches placed in different regions at fixed global mean (constructed from the base states, reused), with region-specific Green's-function/kernel feedbacks as ground truth (strongly negative for tropical low-cloud regions, weaker elsewhere). Model: frozen emulators with the radiation probe. Systems compared: model-induced regional radiation change vs ground-truth regional feedback; shuffled-region control. Decisive metric first: Spearman correlation between the model's regional radiation response and the ground-truth regional feedback, with sign agreement. Convincing: Spearman >= 0.5 AND sign agreement >= 0.7, shuffled control near 0. Refute: Spearman <= 0.2 or sign agreement <= 0.55 (pattern-agnostic uniform response). Indeterminate band: Spearman 0.2-0.5 or sign agreement 0.55-0.7 (declared before the data) -- partial regional fidelity, reported as qualified. A negative result means the model does not resolve regional feedback differences, weakening clause (b).

Experiment 4 (H3 -- steering a pattern-effect direction shifts predicted TOA radiation the feedback-consistent way, without moving the mean): Tests clause (c). Data: high-feedback vs low-feedback patterns at matched global mean (reused) to recover the direction. Model: frozen emulators; only the direction is fitted, recovered as a supervised probe direction and as a high-minus-low-feedback delta, steered at matched L2 norm. Systems compared: (i) pattern-effect direction; (ii) 20 matched-norm random directions; (iii) a global-mean-temperature direction. Decisive metric first: mechanism-selectivity = |TOA-radiation readout change under pattern-effect steering| / |mean change under random directions|; cross-talk = |global-mean shift under pattern-effect steering| / |mean shift under the mean direction|. Convincing: selectivity >= 3, correct feedback sign, cross-talk <= 0.2 (radiation moves, global mean barely does), across probe and delta recovery. Refute: selectivity <= 1.5 or cross-talk >= 0.6. Indeterminate band: selectivity 1.5-3 or cross-talk 0.2-0.6 (declared up front) -- entangled/partial control, reported without a clean causal claim. A negative result means the pattern-effect axis is not independently steerable, contradicting clause (c).

Experiment 5 (H1-H3 -- layer emergence, cross-model convergence, and feedback brackets): Tests robustness of clauses (a)-(c). Data: the reanalysis/CMIP states (reused). Model: GraphCast, Pangu, and the fast-feedback emulator, frozen; probes/directions as above. Systems compared: (i) per-layer Feedback-Beyond-Mean Index and steering selectivity; (ii) CKA between recovered pattern-effect subspaces across emulators; (iii) upper bracket = a Green's-function/radiative-kernel model that computes feedback from the pattern by construction, lower bracket = a global-mean-temperature-to-radiation regressor with no pattern access. Decisive metric first: fraction of the mean-shortcut-to-pattern-effect bracket each model closes. Convincing: >=50% closure for at least one model AND CKA >= 0.5. Refute: all models within noise of the mean-only lower bracket. Indeterminate band: 20-50% closure or CKA 0.3-0.5 (declared up front) -- partial/model-specific, no convergence claim. A negative result means emulators predict radiation from global-mean temperature. All runs are inference-only on public FMs plus small probes and public reanalysis (ERA5/CERES) and CMIP pattern-effect data, feasible on a single GPU.
Risk Factors and Limitations: Global-mean surface temperature and warming pattern are correlated in ordinary data, making the feedback-beyond-mean separation statistically demanding; we mitigate with mean-residualization, the same-mean/different-pattern counterfactual (which holds the global mean fixed and varies only the pattern), the regional-feedback fidelity test using Green's-function ground truth, and the amplitude-control edit.

The pattern-rearrangement counterfactual is a synthetic edit; physically-implausible warming patterns may push inputs off the model's training distribution, confounding the pattern response with generic out-of-distribution failure. We mitigate with physically-plausible patterns (drawn from CMIP pattern-effect experiments), verify the global mean is held fixed, compare against amplitude edits of matched magnitude (so any generic OOD effect is shared), and report sensitivity to pattern-edit magnitude.

Many medium-range weather emulators (GraphCast, Pangu) may not directly output TOA radiation and have short rollout horizons, while the pattern effect is usually a decadal/forced concept; we focus on the FAST radiative feedback that is present on weekly timescales (per the 2026 fast-feedback study, historically-trained emulators reproduce it), prioritize emulators that expose or can be probed for radiation-relevant fields, and report per-model what is measurable, treating the fast-feedback-capable emulator as the primary testbed.

Ground-truth regional feedbacks (Green's functions/kernels) are themselves model-derived and uncertain; we use consensus Green's-function experiments and radiative kernels, restrict decisive tests to regions with robust feedback estimates, and report sensitivity to the feedback reference.

Emulators normalize/tokenize inputs, which may remove absolute-anomaly information relevant to radiation; we document each model's preprocessing, probe pre-normalization activations where feasible, and prioritize models retaining the surface-temperature field.

Linear probes recovering a pattern-effect direction do not guarantee causal use; we address this with steering, cross-talk controls, and random/mean-direction controls, though distributed/superposed encodings may blur single-direction interventions - we use both probe directions and delta-representations.

A negative result (models predict radiation from global-mean temperature and fail the same-mean/different-pattern counterfactual) is scientifically decisive and directly relevant to trusting ML emulators for climate-sensitivity and pattern-effect studies - precisely where the mean-temperature shortcut breaks for novel warming patterns; we frame either outcome as the first mechanism-defining test of whether weather/climate foundation models represent the pattern-dependent radiative feedback mechanism.
All experiments are inference-only on public pretrained models plus small probes and public reanalysis (ERA5/CERES) and CMIP pattern-effect data, keeping compute at academic scale.

Name: convex_hull_competition_probe
Title: Stable Relative to What? Testing Whether Crystal Foundation Models Represent the Relational Convex-Hull Competition of Thermodynamic Stability, Not Just Pointwise Formation Energy
Short Hypothesis: Thermodynamic stability is not a pointwise property of a compound but a relational, competitive one: a phase is stable only if no combination of competing phases at the same composition has lower energy (its energy above the convex hull). We hypothesize that crystal foundation models—now routinely conditioned on 'distance to hull' to generate 'stable' materials—internally encode pointwise formation energy (a correlational proxy) rather than the relational competition that actually defines stability. A mechanistic representation must change a compound's internal stability signal when its competing neighbors in composition space change, even though the compound itself is untouched; a pointwise representation will not. This competitor-context counterfactual is a clean, mechanism-defining test that correlation with hull distance on the standard database cannot provide.
Related Work: Crystal foundation models are explicitly built around convex-hull stability: Matra-Genoa (2026) and UniMat diffusion (2023) condition generation on distance-to-hull; CLOUD (2025) is a physics-informed crystal FM; Matbench Discovery (2025) shows the decision-critical boundary is 0 eV/atom above the hull, where accurate regressors incur high false-positive rates. The 'seven-facet polyhedron' work (2026) shows the formation-energy hull has a compact, interpretable relational structure, and Sun et al. (2016) quantified the thermodynamic scale of metastability. Interpretability of materials models (CGCNN interpretability 2018; 'Comparing latent features of uMLIPs' 2025; 'Beyond Converging Representations' 2025; 'Occupancies vs Embeddings' 2025) recovers site-energy contributions, cross-model feature alignment, and DFT-like internal structure—but all examine POINTWISE energetics or generic latent geometry. None tests whether a crystal FM's internal representation encodes the RELATIONAL, COMPETITIVE convex-hull mechanism that distinguishes formation energy from actual stability, nor whether that internal signal is causally sensitive to the competitor context. Because hull distance and formation energy are highly correlated on the standard database, correlation-based benchmarks cannot separate the two; our competitor-context counterfactual is the novel, mechanism-defining contribution. We state plainly that the contribution is a mechanistic-interpretability test -- a competitor-context counterfactual plus causal steering -- not a new stability benchmark, and not a claim that the convex-hull phenomenon is itself new. It is distinct from prior output-level hull benchmarks (Matbench Discovery) and formation-energy-misprediction studies, which score pointwise accuracy; we instead ask what the internal representation encodes. Only the hull-conditioned generative model natively ingests competitor context, so we treat it as the primary testbed and report per model class how context is injected, avoiding overstated generality.
Abstract: Machine-learning models of crystals are now used to discover 'stable' inorganic materials, and stability is defined by the convex hull of formation energies: a compound is stable only if no linear combination of competing phases at the same composition has lower energy. Stability is therefore intrinsically relational—a compound's fate depends on its competitors—yet it is nearly perfectly correlated with pointwise formation energy on the standard Materials Project database, so ordinary benchmarks cannot tell whether models learn the relational competition or merely a pointwise energy proxy. We propose the first mechanism-defining test. Using public crystal foundation models (a generative model conditioned on hull distance such as Matra-Genoa/UniMat, a crystal representation FM such as CLOUD, and a universal MLIP such as MACE-MP-0), we ask whether their internal representations encode the convex-hull competition structure. First, a relational-beyond-pointwise probe: can we linearly decode a compound's energy-above-hull from its representation beyond what its own formation energy predicts, and is a distinct direction dedicated to 'competitive margin'? Second, and most decisively, a competitor-context counterfactual: we present the same target compound in two composition-space contexts that differ only in which competing phases exist (constructed from Materials Project phase diagrams), such that the target is on-hull in one context and above-hull in the other. A mechanistic representation must shift its internal stability signal and its generation/classification decision accordingly; a pointwise representation will not. We validate causally by steering the recovered competition direction. Metrics quantify a relational-beyond-pointwise index, a competitor-context sensitivity ratio, and a hull-boundary failure predictor. Either outcome sharpens what deployed materials-discovery models actually represent. Downstream, this changes how generative and ranking models for materials discovery are validated: if the representation is purely pointwise (the null), hull-conditioned generative pipelines and stability rankings should be trusted only with explicit relative-to-competitors re-scoring and near-hull calibration, since the model cannot itself reason about the competition that defines stability; if a causally load-bearing competition direction exists, embeddings can support relational stability screening. The intended users are materials-ML practitioners and generative-discovery / benchmark builders; we downplay broader societal claims and pre-register the relational-beyond-pointwise index and competitor-context sensitivity ratio and their statistical tests before analysis.
Experiments: Experiment 1 (H1 — relational stability beyond pointwise formation energy): Tests whether a crystal foundation model encodes energy-above-hull (the relational, competitive quantity) beyond the compound's own formation energy (the pointwise proxy). Data (existing): Materials Project (public; >150,000 compounds with DFT formation energy, energy-above-hull E_hull, phase diagrams, and decomposition/competing phases). We use a stratified sample of 20,000 compounds spanning E_hull from 0 to 0.2 eV/atom, oversampling the near-hull region, split 70/15/15 train/val/test by chemical system (no system crosses splits). Model (frozen, inference only): a hull-conditioned generative crystal model (public diffusion checkpoint), a crystal representation model (CLOUD), and the universal MLIP MACE-MP-0 (~4-5M params); pooled per-structure activations per layer. Trainable part: ridge linear probes only (L2 by CV, 3 seeds). Systems compared: probe from model representation vs a formation-energy-only regressor. Decisive metric first: Relational-Beyond-Pointwise Index = test R^2 for E_hull from the representation minus R^2 from formation energy alone, after regressing out the formation-energy-predictable component of the representation. Indecision band up front: an index in [0.01, 0.05] (R^2 units) cannot decide and is reported as ambiguous relational encoding; index >= 0.05 with bootstrap CI lower bound > 0.01 is convincing competitive-margin encoding beyond pointwise energy; index <= 0.01 means the model carries only pointwise energetics. Negative result here supports the core hypothesis that these models are pointwise, not relational.

Experiment 2 (H2 — competitor-context counterfactual, decisive): Tests the defining prediction: changing a compound's competing neighbors while leaving the compound itself untouched must change a mechanistic model's internal stability signal, but not a pointwise one; and the change must be local to the compound's hull facet. Data (constructed from existing): for ~300 curated target compositions, build two contexts from real Materials Project phase diagrams -- (a) target ON the hull (stable), and (b) an added real lower-lying competing phase so the SAME target is ABOVE the hull -- plus a control edit that alters distant phases not touching the target's facet (facet-change computed exactly from the phase diagram). Real competing phases are used where available; any synthetic competitor is flagged. Model: the hull-conditioned generative model is the cleanest testbed (it explicitly ingests distance-to-hull); for CLOUD and MACE-MP-0 the competing set is supplied as a co-embedded reference and the internal readout measured relative to the constructed local hull. Frozen weights; readout via the Experiment 1 probe. Systems compared: context-(a) vs context-(b) shift, and true-facet-change edits vs distant-phase control edits. Decisive metric first: Competitor-Context Sensitivity Ratio = |internal-stability shift between (a) and (b)| / |shift under the distant-phase control edit|, with CI over targets. Indecision band up front: a ratio whose CI lies in [1.3, 2.0] cannot decide and is reported as weak relational sensitivity; CI lower bound > 2.0, together with the facet-locality control showing shifts scale with true facet change, is convincing relational encoding; CI upper bound < 1.3 (the model ignores competitor context) is the pointwise signature. This is the decisive test; a null here is the headline negative result.

Experiment 3 (H3 — causal competition-direction steering): Tests whether the recovered competitive-margin direction is causally load-bearing -- steering it should flip an on-hull compound to predicted-unstable without changing its formation-energy readout. Data: on-hull test compounds from Experiment 1. Model: frozen; the competition direction is the supervised probe (and, where feasible, a sparse-autoencoder feature) separating high/low E_hull at fixed formation energy. Procedure: add matched-norm perturbations along the competition direction; controls are matched-norm random directions and the formation-energy direction. Decisive metric first: mechanism-selectivity = |stability-decision change under competition direction| / |change under random direction|, plus the fraction of on-hull compounds flipped to unstable while the formation-energy readout stays within noise. Indecision band up front: selectivity CI in [1.3, 2.0] cannot decide (no clean causal direction); CI lower bound > 2.0 with a flip fraction > 0.5 is convincing causal use of a relational direction; CI upper bound < 1.3 means no separable causal competition direction exists. A negative result, with H1-H2 nulls, supports the pointwise conclusion.

Experiment 4 (H4 — hull-boundary failure prediction): Tests whether the relational-representation strength explains where the model misclassifies stability near E_hull = 0, the regime where crystal models are documented to fail. Data: Materials Project test compounds within 0.05 eV/atom of the hull, labeled stable vs metastable. Model: frozen backbones; predictor is the per-compound competitor-context sensitivity or residual-E_hull probe confidence, logistic link only (3 seeds). Systems compared: internal-signal predictor vs output-confidence and formation-energy-only baselines. Decisive metric first: AUROC for flagging near-boundary misclassifications from the internal relational signal. Indecision band up front: AUROC in [0.60, 0.70] cannot decide and is reported as a weak link; AUROC >= 0.70 with CI lower bound > 0.60 and beating both baselines is convincing that relational encoding governs boundary reliability; AUROC <= 0.60 (near the 0.50 chance line) means it does not, weakening the mechanistic reading even if the counterfactual is positive.
Risk Factors and Limitations: Formation energy and E_hull are strongly correlated on the standard database, making the relational-beyond-pointwise separation statistically demanding; we mitigate with residualization, the competitor-context counterfactual (which holds the target fixed), and facet-locality controls.

Providing 'competitor context' is architecture-dependent: representation FMs and MLIPs do not natively take a phase-diagram context, so context must be injected via co-embedded reference sets or by evaluating the internal readout relative to a constructed local hull; we report per-model how context is supplied and treat the hull-conditioned generative model as the cleanest testbed since it explicitly ingests distance-to-hull.

Constructing counterfactual contexts requires curated phase diagrams and, ideally, hypothetical competing phases; we use Materials Project phase diagrams and real competing phases where possible, and clearly flag any synthetic competitors.

Linear probes recovering a competition direction do not guarantee causal use; we address this with steering and random/formation-energy-direction controls, though distributed encodings may blur single-direction interventions.
Some models pool to a single structure embedding, limiting fine-grained analysis; we prioritize models exposing usable per-structure representations and report pooling caveats.

A negative result (models encode pointwise formation energy but not the relational competition) is scientifically decisive and directly relevant to trusting hull-conditioned generative discovery pipelines, though it may be perceived as confirmatory of skepticism; we frame either outcome as the first mechanism-defining test of whether crystal FMs represent the convex-hull competition that defines stability.

Input-set and leakage controls: because changing the competing-phase set changes the model input, we add null edits that alter the input set without moving the target's hull facet, nearest-neighbor chemical edits, and a no-context control, and require the competitor-context shift to exceed all of these; splits are by chemical system with no system crossing splits, and composition / system identity is held fixed across the two contexts.
All experiments are inference-only on public pretrained models plus small probes/SAEs and public Materials Project data, keeping compute at academic scale.

Name: nernst_overpotential_decomposition_probe
Title: Voltage Is Not Charge: Testing Whether Battery Foundation Models Decompose Terminal Voltage into Thermodynamic Nernst OCV and Kinetic Overpotential, Not Just Raw Voltage Statistics
Short Hypothesis: A battery's terminal voltage is set by an exactly-known decomposition: V = OCV(SOC) - overpotential(current), where the open-circuit voltage is a purely thermodynamic, current-independent function of state-of-charge (Nernst equation) and the overpotential is a kinetic, current-dependent loss (Butler-Volmer / diffusion). These are physically independent contributions: the same terminal voltage can correspond to very different SOCs depending on the load current, which is exactly why SOC estimation fails under high current. We hypothesize that if a battery/time-series foundation model represents this mechanism rather than raw voltage statistics, then (a) SOC (the thermodynamic OCV component) is decodable from internal representations beyond what instantaneous terminal voltage predicts, along an axis distinct from overpotential, (b) a current-holding vs SOC-holding counterfactual moves the two internal signals independently, and (c) steering a recovered 'overpotential' direction reshapes the voltage-current relationship without changing the SOC readout. The load-current counterfactual is a falsifiable, mechanism-defining test that terminal-voltage correlation cannot pass.
Related Work: Two lines bracket the gap. (1) Physics-informed and electrochemical battery models - ECINN (2024, embedding Nernst/Butler-Volmer/diffusion equations), single-particle-model + Nernst SOC estimators (2020), and equivalent-circuit models - BUILD the OCV/overpotential decomposition in by construction; they are judged by SOC estimation error, not by what a general model internally represents. (2) Data-driven battery foundation/time-series models (BatteryML, transformer SOC/SOH estimators, general TSFMs like Chronos/TimesFM applied to battery telemetry) predict SOC/state directly from voltage-current-temperature sequences; interpretability of such models is limited to feature-attribution over input channels. Interpretability of scientific foundation models (Physics Steering 2025, showing steerable physical-concept directions; From Neurons to Neutrons 2024) recovers and steers single physical quantities, but none tests whether a battery model internally SEPARATES the thermodynamic Nernst OCV(SOC) from the kinetic overpotential(current), whether that decomposition is causally load-bearing, or uses a load-current counterfactual to arbitrate mechanism vs voltage statistics. Because terminal voltage, SOC, and current are entangled in ordinary discharge data, correlation-based SOC benchmarks cannot separate the two contributions. Our OCV-beyond-voltage probe, current-holding counterfactual, and causal overpotential steering are the novel, mechanism-defining contribution, in a safety-critical setting where confusing kinetic voltage sag with true depletion causes dangerous SOC misestimation. To sharpen the claim: the Nernst OCV / kinetic-overpotential decomposition is textbook electrochemistry (approximate under temperature, hysteresis, and aging) and we propose no new estimator; the novelty is mechanistic interpretability of a spontaneous OCV/overpotential factorization in models that do NOT impose it — data-driven battery and general time-series FMs (Chronos/TimesFM) — via a load-current double dissociation and causal steering, reported as evidence that representations contain separable information consistent with the mechanism rather than a claim of complete mechanistic causality. The surprising setting is a model trained only for forecasting or degradation, not SOC, spontaneously separating thermodynamic from kinetic voltage. Concrete failure scenarios where confusing kinetic sag with depletion is dangerous: EV hard acceleration, drone peak draw, and cold-temperature discharge. What changes: model selection, high-load calibration, deployment constraints, and whether to add physics-based regularizers — for BMS/battery-ML developers, benchmark designers, and the broader question of validating scientific time-series FMs in safety-critical systems.
Abstract: Battery management systems increasingly use machine-learning models to estimate state-of-charge (SOC) from voltage, current, and temperature telemetry, and errors are most dangerous precisely under high load, where the terminal voltage sags for kinetic reasons even though the battery is not actually depleted. The physics is exactly known: terminal voltage decomposes into a thermodynamic open-circuit voltage that depends only on SOC (the Nernst equation) and a kinetic overpotential that depends on current (Butler-Volmer and diffusion losses). These are independent contributions - the same voltage can mean very different SOCs at different currents - making batteries an ideal, mechanism-defining testbed for whether foundation models learn the electrochemical mechanism or merely voltage statistics. We probe pretrained battery/time-series foundation models on public cycling datasets (e.g., NASA, Oxford, CALCE, and BatteryML benchmarks) where SOC, current, and OCV are known or computable. First, an OCV-beyond-voltage probe: is SOC (the thermodynamic component) decodable from internal representations beyond what instantaneous terminal voltage predicts, along an axis distinct from overpotential? Second, and most decisively, a current-holding counterfactual: we change the load current at fixed SOC (which changes overpotential, not OCV) versus change SOC at fixed current (which changes OCV, not overpotential), and test whether the two internal signals move independently - a mechanistic representation separates them, a voltage-statistics representation collapses them. Third, causal steering of a recovered overpotential direction should reshape the voltage-current response without shifting the SOC readout. Metrics quantify an OCV-beyond-voltage index, a thermodynamic-kinetic disentanglement ratio, and a SOC-error failure predictor. Either outcome sharpens whether deployed battery models estimate charge for the right physical reason. Standard SOC benchmarks average over load and miss this failure mode; the audit supplies a targeted diagnostic that would change model selection and high-load calibration for battery-management systems, and more broadly demonstrates a template for validating whether scientific time-series foundation models factorize thermodynamic from kinetic contributions before safety-critical deployment.
Experiments: Experiment 1 (H1 — SOC decodable beyond terminal voltage, distinct from overpotential): Tests clause (a): SOC (the thermodynamic OCV component) is decodable from internal representations beyond what instantaneous terminal voltage predicts, along an axis distinct from overpotential. Data: public cycling datasets — NASA PCoE, Oxford Battery Degradation (8 cells), CALCE, and BatteryML benchmark cells — providing time series of terminal voltage, load current, temperature, and coulomb-counted SOC; compute ground-truth OCV(SOC) from low-rate/pseudo-OCV data and per-timestep overpotential = terminal voltage − OCV(SOC). Use ~200,000 timesteps from cells with reliable SOC labels (split by cell so no cell crosses splits) — fewer than all telemetry because decisive tests require cells with trustworthy pseudo-OCV/relaxation labels. Model: a BatteryML transformer SOC/SOH estimator (~few-M parameters, per-timestep representations) and a general time-series FM (Chronos, ~200M parameters, or TimesFM ~200M) applied to the telemetry, frozen; ridge probes on the best layer, seeds 0–4. Systems compared: probe R^2 for SOC from the representation vs an instantaneous-terminal-voltage baseline, representation residualized against voltage; plus the angle between recovered SOC/OCV and overpotential directions. Decisive metric (first): OCV-Beyond-Voltage Index = R^2(SOC | representation) − R^2(SOC | terminal voltage). Convincing: Index ≥ 0.15 (95% CI lower bound above 0.05) and SOC–overpotential axis angle ≥ 60 degrees. Indecision band: Index in [−0.03, 0.05] or angle in [30, 45] degrees — SOC barely separable from voltage; clause (a) fails or is inconclusive here. Negative result: Index ≤ −0.03 or angle < 30 degrees — SOC collapses onto terminal voltage, the dangerous voltage-statistics reading.

Experiment 2 (H2 — current-holding vs SOC-holding double-dissociation counterfactual): Tests clause (b): a current-holding vs SOC-holding counterfactual moves the two internal signals independently. Data: matched edits — (overpotential edit) change load current at fixed SOC (changes overpotential/terminal voltage, not OCV); (OCV edit) change SOC at fixed current (changes OCV, not overpotential) — built from controlled real telemetry segments plus synthetic sequences from a calibrated equivalent-circuit/single-particle model for exact independent manipulation (≥5,000 matched pairs; results reported separately for real vs synthetic and cross-validated). Model/probe as Experiment 1, seeds 0–4; read-outs are the SOC and overpotential probes. Systems compared: movement of each internal signal under each edit. Decisive metrics (first): Overpotential-Edit Ratio = |Δoverpotential signal| / |ΔSOC signal| under the current edit; OCV-Edit Ratio = |ΔSOC signal| / |Δoverpotential signal| under the SOC edit. Convincing: both ratios ≥ 3 (each edit moves its own physical axis — a double dissociation). Indecision band: either ratio in [0.7, 2.0] — the axes are not cleanly separable; clause (b) fails or is inconclusive here. Negative result: ratios ≈ 1, or SOC moving whenever voltage moves — the model reads current-induced voltage sag as depletion, the mechanism failure of interest.

Experiment 3 (H2 — overpotential dose-response to current): Tests the quantitative content of clause (b): the internal overpotential signal grows with current in the physically correct direction while SOC stays constant. Data: the same test cells; sweep load current across a range at fixed SOC. Model/probe as above, seeds 0–4. Systems compared: induced overpotential-signal change vs the Butler–Volmer/ohmic prediction; SOC-readout stability across the sweep; shuffled-current labels as null. Decisive metrics (first): Spearman rho and sign agreement between induced overpotential change and predicted overpotential; and SOC drift (max |ΔSOC readout| across the sweep, in SOC %). Convincing: rho ≥ 0.6 with correct sign and SOC drift ≤ 3 SOC %. Indecision band: rho in [0.2, 0.4] or SOC drift in (3, 8] SOC % — weak or leaky decomposition; inconclusive on (b). Negative result: rho < 0.2 or SOC drift > 8 SOC % — no current-dependent overpotential law, or SOC contaminated by current.

Experiment 4 (H3 — causal overpotential-direction steering): Tests clause (c): steering a recovered 'overpotential' direction reshapes the voltage-current relationship without changing the SOC readout. Data: the same test cells; direction recovered as a supervised overpotential-probe direction and a delta-representation between high-current and low-current states at matched SOC. Model/probe as above; add matched-norm perturbations along the overpotential direction at the best layer and re-read the predicted voltage-current response and SOC, seeds 0–4. Systems compared: overpotential direction vs a matched SOC/OCV direction vs matched-norm random directions. Decisive metrics (first): Steering Selectivity = |voltage-sag change from overpotential steering| / |change from random steering|; Cross-talk = |SOC shift from overpotential steering| in SOC %. Convincing: selectivity ≥ 3 with cross-talk ≤ 3 SOC % (voltage response reshapes, SOC essentially fixed), while the SOC/OCV direction shifts SOC without changing overpotential. Indecision band: selectivity in [0.7, 2.0] or cross-talk in (3, 8] SOC % — non-selective or entangled steering; clause (c) fails or is inconclusive here. Negative result: selectivity ≈ 1 — no dedicated causal overpotential direction.
Risk Factors and Limitations: SOC, terminal voltage, and current are entangled in ordinary discharge data, making the OCV-beyond-voltage separation statistically demanding; we mitigate with voltage-residualization, the current-holding double-dissociation counterfactual (which holds one physical quantity fixed while varying the other), synthetic equivalent-circuit sequences giving exact independent control, and physics dose-response tests a voltage-only model cannot reproduce.

Ground-truth OCV(SOC) and overpotential require accurate coulomb-counted SOC and low-rate OCV curves, which drift with aging and temperature and are noisy; we use well-characterized benchmark cells with pseudo-OCV/relaxation data, restrict decisive tests to cells with reliable SOC labels, and report sensitivity to OCV-curve and aging assumptions.

The current-holding counterfactual on real telemetry is constrained by what operating points exist in the data; we supplement with synthetic sequences from a calibrated equivalent-circuit/single-particle model for exact independent manipulation, clearly reporting which results are synthetic vs real and treating cross-validation between them as key.

Some battery/time-series foundation models take fixed input windows, normalize channels, or output only a scalar SOC, limiting fine-grained decomposition analysis; we document each model's preprocessing, prioritize models exposing per-timestep representations, probe pre-normalization activations where feasible, and treat scalar-only models as an informative lower bracket.

Linear probes recovering OCV/overpotential directions do not guarantee causal use; we address this with steering, cross-talk controls, and random-direction controls, though distributed/superposed encodings may blur single-direction interventions - we use both probe directions and delta-representations.

A negative result (models encode voltage statistics and collapse the thermodynamic-kinetic decomposition, failing the current-holding counterfactual) is scientifically decisive and directly safety-relevant - it would warn that deployed battery models may misread kinetic voltage sag as true depletion, causing dangerous SOC misestimation under high load and low temperature; we frame either outcome as the first mechanism-defining test of whether battery foundation models decompose terminal voltage into Nernst OCV and kinetic overpotential.

All experiments are inference-only on public pretrained models plus small probes and public battery cycling datasets (NASA, Oxford, CALCE, BatteryML) with standard equivalent-circuit simulation, keeping compute at academic scale.

Name: amoc_density_buoyancy_probe
Title: Density, Not Just Temperature: Testing Whether Ocean Foundation Models Represent the Buoyancy-Driven AMOC Mechanism via a Temperature-Salinity Compensation Counterfactual
Short Hypothesis: The Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation (AMOC) is driven by an exactly-known relational mechanism: overturning strength scales (via thermal wind) with the meridional DENSITY gradient set at high latitudes by surface buoyancy loss, where density depends nonlinearly on BOTH temperature and salinity through the equation of state — warming and freshening both REDUCE density and both weaken overturning. This means the same sea-surface temperature (SST) field can imply strengthening or weakening AMOC depending on salinity. We hypothesize that if ocean/climate foundation models represent the buoyancy mechanism rather than SST statistics, then (a) the AMOC-relevant density gradient is decodable from internal representations beyond what temperature alone predicts, (b) a temperature-salinity compensation counterfactual that changes T and S together so surface DENSITY is unchanged shifts the internal overturning signal little, whereas a matched edit that changes density (equal T change, no compensating S change) shifts it strongly, and (c) steering a recovered density-gradient direction causally shifts predicted overturning. The density-compensated-vs-uncompensated counterfactual is an exact, mechanism-defining test that SST-based correlation cannot pass.
Related Work: Interpretability of Earth-system foundation models has surged: SAE studies on GraphCast (2025) recover interpretable features (tropical cyclones, atmospheric rivers, sea-ice) and steer them; GraphDOP work (2025) shows unified observation-driven world-model representations and applies data-assimilation diagnostics (FSOI); an ocean-atmosphere emulator-error study (2026) correlates GraphCast forecast errors with SST to infer implicit ocean information. All of these recover single features or global input-output error correlations — none tests whether a model's internal representation encodes the RELATIONAL, density-driven buoyancy mechanism that governs the AMOC, nor uses a temperature-salinity compensation counterfactual to separate density from temperature. Physical oceanography establishes the mechanism precisely: AMOC strength scales with the meridional density gradient via near-geostrophic/thermal-wind balance and is controlled by high-latitude surface buoyancy loss and the nonlinear equation of state (AMOC reviews 2015/2019; 'What Causes the AMOC to Weaken in CMIP5?' 2019 uses thermal wind to attribute weakening to density changes; 'Controls on AMOC strength' 2024 links buoyancy forcing and stratification to overturning). Because SST and density are correlated in ordinary ocean data, correlation-based benchmarks and SST-error diagnostics cannot arbitrate whether a model uses temperature statistics or the density mechanism. Our density-beyond-temperature probe, TS-compensation counterfactual, and causal density-gradient steering are the novel, mechanism-defining contribution, transferred into the safety-critical setting of AMOC tipping-point prediction. To be exact: the buoyancy/thermal-wind theory of the AMOC is established and we propose no new AMOC theory or forecaster; the contribution is a mechanism-level, causal interpretability probe — a falsifiable test (the T–S compensation counterfactual plus density-gradient steering) of whether an ocean surrogate's internal representation spontaneously encodes the density (not just temperature) mechanism, reported as evidence for or against encoding. Because few deployed ocean FMs expose internal states, we scope the primary claim to accessible ocean/climate emulators, using a modest academic-scale reanalysis-trained surrogate as the main testbed and testing deployed models only where internals are available. Prior AMOC-from-T/S work forecasts AMOC; it does not test internal density representation. What changes in practice: mechanistic validation and model selection for AMOC/tipping-point emulators, and calibration of climate-risk estimates — audiences being climate scientists, operational forecasting groups, and AI-for-science interpretability.
Abstract: The Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation (AMOC) is a climate tipping element, and machine-learning ocean/Earth-system foundation models are increasingly used to emulate and forecast ocean state. AMOC dynamics are governed by an exactly-known relational mechanism: overturning strength scales with the meridional density gradient, which is set at high latitudes by surface buoyancy loss, and density depends nonlinearly on both temperature and salinity through the equation of state. Crucially, warming and freshening both reduce density and both weaken overturning, so the same sea-surface-temperature field can accompany strengthening or weakening AMOC depending on salinity. This makes the AMOC an ideal, mechanism-defining testbed for whether ocean foundation models learn the buoyancy mechanism or merely temperature statistics. We probe pretrained ocean/climate foundation models (and observation-driven Earth-system emulators exposing internal states) on reanalysis data (ORAS5/GLORYS, plus CMIP output) where temperature, salinity, density, and the AMOC streamfunction are known. First, a density-beyond-temperature probe: is the AMOC-relevant meridional density gradient decodable from internal representations beyond what temperature alone predicts, along an axis distinct from SST? Second, and most decisively, a temperature-salinity compensation counterfactual: we perturb surface T and S together so that density is unchanged (density-compensated) versus perturbing T without compensating S (density-changing) with matched temperature magnitude; a mechanistic representation must move its overturning signal for the density-changing edit but not the compensated one, while a temperature-statistics model responds to both equally. Third, causal density-gradient steering. Metrics quantify a density-beyond-temperature index, a compensated-vs-uncompensated causal asymmetry, and a buoyancy dose-response test. Either outcome sharpens whether deployed ocean models represent the mechanism behind a major climate tipping point. This matters for climate-risk practice: a surrogate that tracks SST but not density would silently fail exactly under freshening-driven AMOC weakening — the tipping regime of greatest concern — so the audit becomes a mechanistic-validation and model-selection criterion for emulators used in climate-risk assessment, beyond what SST-error diagnostics reveal.
Experiments: Experiment 1 (H1 — density gradient decodable beyond temperature): Tests clause (a): the AMOC-relevant meridional density gradient (and AMOC index) is decodable from internal representations beyond what temperature alone predicts. Data: ORAS5 and GLORYS12 ocean reanalyses (3D temperature, salinity, potential density; monthly fields ~1958–present) and a set of CMIP6 members spanning AMOC strengths; use 480 monthly North Atlantic snapshots per product (split by decade into train/val/test so no year crosses splits) with ground-truth density from the equation of state, the meridional density gradient, and an AMOC index (streamfunction max at 26N) — fewer than the full archive because we focus on the subpolar/deep-water-formation region where salinity modulates density. Model: a public ocean emulator with accessible internal states where available; as the primary testbed, a modest academic-scale multi-variable ocean surrogate (~10M-parameter transformer) pretrained on reanalysis, frozen, with ridge probes on the best layer, seeds 0–4. Systems compared: probe R^2 for density gradient (and AMOC index) from the representation vs a temperature-only baseline, representation residualized against temperature; plus the angle between recovered temperature and density directions. Decisive metric (first): Density-Beyond-Temperature Index = R^2(density gradient | representation) − R^2(density gradient | temperature). Convincing: Index ≥ 0.15 (95% CI lower bound above 0.05) and temperature–density axis angle ≥ 60 degrees. Indecision band: Index in [−0.03, 0.05] or angle in [30, 45] degrees — density barely separable from temperature; clause (a) fails or is inconclusive here. Negative result: Index ≤ −0.03 or angle < 30 degrees — the model encodes temperature statistics and ignores the salinity contribution to density.

Experiment 2 (H2 — temperature–salinity compensation counterfactual): Tests clause (b): a T–S edit that leaves surface density unchanged shifts the internal overturning signal little, whereas an equal T change with no compensating S change shifts it strongly. Data: 500 subpolar North Atlantic test snapshots; for each build (compensated) change surface T by delta_T and S by the delta_S that leaves potential density unchanged via the equation-of-state expansion coefficients; (uncompensated) the same delta_T with no S change (density changes). Density (un)changed is verified by the equation of state before feeding the model. Model/probe as Experiment 1, seeds 0–4; read-out is the density-gradient/AMOC probe (and forecast AMOC-relevant fields where the emulator rolls out). Systems compared: |overturning-signal change| under uncompensated vs compensated edits, as a function of delta_T. Decisive metric (first): Compensated-vs-Uncompensated Causal Asymmetry = median(|Δsignal uncompensated|) / median(|Δsignal compensated|). Convincing: asymmetry ≥ 3. Indecision band: asymmetry in [0.7, 2.0] — the model responds to temperature regardless of density compensation; clause (b) fails here. Negative result: asymmetry ≈ 1, i.e., a temperature-statistics reading blind to whether salinity compensates the buoyancy change.

Experiment 3 (H2 — buoyancy dose-response with correct sign): Tests the quantitative content of clause (b): the internal AMOC signal responds monotonically and with the physically correct sign to density-changing buoyancy forcing. Data: the same 500 snapshots; sweep density-changing perturbations across a range — both freshwater-hosing-like (salinity) and warming-like (temperature) — that alter high-latitude density. Model/probe as above, seeds 0–4. Systems compared: induced AMOC-signal change vs the thermal-wind prediction (increasing high-latitude density strengthens overturning; decreasing it weakens overturning); shuffled-perturbation labels as null. Decisive metric (first): Spearman rho and sign agreement between induced AMOC change and predicted change, computed separately for salinity- and temperature-driven perturbations. Convincing: rho ≥ 0.6 with correct sign for BOTH perturbation types (the model integrates T and S into density, not just T). Indecision band: rho in [0.2, 0.4], or correct sign for temperature but not salinity — partial, temperature-leaning response; inconclusive on (b). Negative result: rho < 0.2 or wrong sign — no density-driven buoyancy law represented.

Experiment 4 (H3 — causal density-gradient steering): Tests clause (c): steering a recovered density-gradient direction causally shifts predicted overturning. Data: 500 test snapshots; direction recovered as a supervised density-gradient probe direction and a delta-representation between high- and low-gradient states. Model/probe as above; add matched-norm perturbations along the density direction at the best layer and read the AMOC output, seeds 0–4. Systems compared: density-gradient direction vs matched-norm random directions vs a pure SST direction. Decisive metrics (first): Steering Selectivity = |ΔAMOC from density-direction steering| / |ΔAMOC from random-direction steering|; Cross-talk with the SST direction. Convincing: selectivity ≥ 3 with the buoyancy-consistent sign and the SST direction not reproducing it. Indecision band: selectivity in [0.7, 2.0] — no better than random; clause (c) fails here. Negative result: selectivity ≈ 1 — no dedicated causal density-gradient direction.
Risk Factors and Limitations: Temperature and density are strongly correlated in ocean data (temperature dominates density variance in many regions), making the density-beyond-temperature separation statistically demanding; we mitigate with temperature-residualization, the TS-compensation counterfactual (which holds density fixed while varying temperature), the buoyancy dose-response test that a temperature-only model cannot reproduce with correct sign in salinity-dominated regimes, and by focusing decisive tests on the subpolar North Atlantic where salinity strongly modulates density.

The compensation counterfactual is a synthetic surface edit; unrealistic T-S combinations may push inputs off the model's data distribution, confounding the density-changing response with generic out-of-distribution failure. We mitigate with small physically-plausible perturbations, verify density is (un)changed via the equation of state before feeding to the model, report OOD diagnostics, and compare compensated vs uncompensated edits of matched temperature magnitude so any OOD effect is shared.

Many ocean/Earth-system foundation models are proprietary or lack accessible internal states; we prioritize models with public weights and usable representations and, as a fallback, pretrain a modest multi-variable ocean surrogate on reanalysis (academic-scale) to serve as the primary testbed, reporting this scope clearly.

The AMOC streamfunction is a deep, integrated quantity while foundation models may emphasize surface fields; the internal 'overturning signal' may be weak or only surface-proxied. We probe both the density gradient (a more directly represented quantity) and any AMOC-index readout, and treat the density-gradient result as the primary mechanism evidence.

Reanalysis salinity (especially subpolar/estuarine) has known biases, adding label noise; we use consensus regions, multiple reanalysis products, and CMIP output for controlled T-S variation, reporting sensitivity to product choice.

Linear probes recovering a density direction do not guarantee causal use; we address this with steering plus random/SST-direction controls, though distributed/superposed encodings may blur single-direction interventions — we use both probe directions and delta-representations.

A negative result (models encode temperature statistics but not the density-driven buoyancy mechanism, failing the compensation counterfactual) is scientifically decisive and directly safety-relevant — it would warn against trusting ocean foundation models for AMOC weakening/tipping-point prediction, precisely where freshening breaks the temperature-density correlation; we frame either outcome as the first mechanism-defining test of whether ocean foundation models represent the buoyancy-driven AMOC mechanism.
All experiments are inference-only on public pretrained models (or one modest academic-scale surrogate) plus small probes and public reanalysis/CMIP data, keeping compute at academic scale.

Name: activity_cliff_geometry_probe
Title: Smooth Where It Should Jump: Do Chemistry Foundation Models Internally Represent Activity Cliffs as Pharmacophore-Localized Discontinuities, or Just Smooth Structural Similarity?
Short Hypothesis: Activity cliffs — pairs of near-identical molecules with large potency differences — are exactly where molecular property models fail. We hypothesize this failure has a mechanistic signature: chemistry foundation models embed structurally-similar molecules close together regardless of whether a tiny change flips potency, so their internal representation is locally SMOOTH across cliffs (structure-driven) rather than DISCONTINUOUS at the potency-flipping substructure (mechanism-driven). If instead a model represents the underlying pharmacophore mechanism, then (a) cliff-forming matched transformations should produce a larger, localized representational jump than potency-neutral (non-cliff) matched transformations of comparable structural magnitude, and (b) that jump should causally localize to the pharmacophore-relevant substructure via activation patching. The exact matched-molecular-pair cliff-vs-non-cliff counterfactual makes this a mechanism-defining test of WHY cliffs are hard, not another cliff predictor.
Related Work: A large body of work treats activity cliffs (ACs) as a prediction problem: MoleculeACE (Exposing the Limitations, 2022) shows all ML methods struggle at ACs and descriptor methods beat deep models; ACNet, ACES-GNN, ACANet, ACtriplet, and SCAGE (Nature Comm 2025) build AC-aware predictors or explanation-supervised GNNs. Separately, interpretability of chemistry models (Unveiling Latent Knowledge via SAEs 2025; MoleX 2024; concept-whitening GNNs) recovers concept features aligned with functional groups and pharmacological classes, and roughness/RePRA analyses (ROGI-XD 2023; RePRA 2023) show pretrained representations do NOT produce smoother QSPR surfaces. Crucially, none of these asks the mechanism-defining question: is the AC failure caused by the model's internal representation being locally smooth across cliffs (blind to the discontinuity), and does the representational change at a cliff causally localize to the pharmacophore substructure that actually flips potency? Prior AC work measures output error or trains cliff-aware losses; prior interpretability work matches features to marginal annotations. Our exact cliff-vs-matched-non-cliff counterfactual, representational-smoothness geometry, and causal pharmacophore-localization patching are the novel contribution, explaining WHY cliffs are hard at the representational level rather than engineering around them. Concretely, this refines the prevailing 'similarity-preservation / representation-collapse' reading of the MoleculeACE result (van Tilborg et al., 2022) -- which documents that all ML models, including pretrained ones, fail at cliffs but leaves the internal cause unspecified -- by defining a testable mechanistic object, the cliff-induced representational discontinuity, and asking whether it exists and causally localizes. The novelty is the object of study and the causal method (matched counterfactual + activation patching), not the activity-cliff phenomenon itself. Beyond explanation, the deliverable is a reusable matched cliff-vs-non-cliff counterfactual suite and a smoothness-diagnostic protocol for selecting and validating chemistry foundation models on cliff-heavy lead-optimization campaigns.
Abstract: Activity cliffs — pairs of molecules differing by a minor structural change yet showing large potency differences — are the single most reliable failure mode of molecular property models, but why they are hard remains a black box. We propose a mechanism-defining test of whether chemistry foundation models represent the pharmacophore mechanism behind cliffs or merely encode structural similarity. Our central hypothesis is that these models embed structurally-similar molecules close together regardless of potency, making their internal representation locally SMOOTH across a cliff — blind to the very discontinuity that defines it — which would mechanistically explain the observed failures. We test this with an exact counterfactual built from matched molecular pairs (MMPs): cliff pairs (same transformation, large potency jump) versus matched non-cliff pairs (comparable structural transformation, negligible potency change) against the same targets, drawn from MoleculeACE and ChEMBL. First, we measure the internal representational distance induced by each transformation across layers in models such as ChemBERTa/MoleculeSTM, SMI-TED (FM4M), and Uni-Mol, testing whether cliff transformations produce larger, sharper representational jumps than matched non-cliff transformations — or whether both are equally smooth (the failure signature). Second, using sparse autoencoders and linear probes we test whether a dedicated feature/direction tracks potency independent of structure. Third, via activation patching we test whether the cliff-induced representational change causally localizes to the pharmacophore-relevant substructure (e.g., the atom whose modification creates a steric clash or breaks a hydrogen bond), versus being diffuse. Metrics quantify a cliff-vs-non-cliff jump ratio, a potency-beyond-structure decoding index, and a pharmacophore-localization score. Either outcome sharpens why deployed chemistry models fail precisely where drug discovery needs them most. The 'so what' is concrete: if representations are locally smooth (the failure signature), practitioners should distrust foundation-model potency predictions across cliffs and route lead-optimization decisions through local counterfactual and uncertainty checks; if instead a pharmacophore-localized discontinuity is found, model-selection and interpretability assumptions can exploit it and SAR analysis can trust the internal geometry. The test targets medicinal chemists doing structure-activity analysis, chemistry-foundation-model builders, and activity-cliff benchmark authors.
Experiments: Experiment 1 (H1 — cliff-vs-non-cliff representational jump): Tests the core claim that a chemistry foundation model's internal geometry is locally smooth across activity cliffs — i.e. a tiny structural edit that flips potency (a cliff) moves the representation no more than a comparable edit that leaves potency unchanged (a non-cliff). Data (existing, adapted): MoleculeACE (public; 30 ChEMBL targets, ~48,000 molecules with curated pIC50). From it we build, per target, cliff pairs (ECFP4 Tanimoto >= 0.9, |dpIC50| >= 2.0) and non-cliff pairs (Tanimoto >= 0.9, |dpIC50| <= 0.5), each a single matched-molecular-pair transformation, and match the two sets on transformation magnitude (heavy atoms changed within +/-1, ECFP4 distance within +/-0.02) so only the potency consequence differs. MoleculeACE yields ~10^3-10^4 candidate cliff pairs; we cap at 200 matched pairs/target (limited by the scarcer cliff side), ~4,000-6,000 pairs total, enough for per-model bootstrap CIs. Models (all frozen, inference only): ChemBERTa-2 (~46M params, MLM checkpoint), Uni-Mol (~48M, 3D graph), plus an ECFP4 2048-bit fingerprint as a purely-structural lower bound; representations taken at every layer, seeds only affect the later probes (0,1,2). Systems compared: each deep model vs ECFP, per layer. Decisive metric first: Cliff-vs-Non-cliff Jump Ratio = median cosine distance over cliff pairs / median over matched non-cliff pairs, with 95% bootstrap CI over pairs, best layer per model. Indecision band, stated up front: a ratio whose CI falls within [1.1, 1.5] cannot decide, and we then report the smoothness question unresolved for that model and defer to the H3 patching test; CI lower bound > 1.5 is a mechanism-aware jump; CI upper bound < 1.1 (expected for ECFP by construction) is the hypothesized smooth-failure signature. Convincing support: deep models sit at <= 1.1 like ECFP. Negative result (deep models >= 1.5) would refute the smoothness claim and show these models already jump at cliffs.

Experiment 2 (H2 — potency encoded beyond structure): Tests whether the representation carries potency information above raw structural similarity, the encoding that a mechanism-aware model must have and a purely smooth one lacks. Data: the same matched cliff pairs from Experiment 1 (MoleculeACE, 30 targets). Model: same frozen ChemBERTa-2 and Uni-Mol; the only trainable part is a ridge linear probe (L2 chosen by 5-fold CV on the training targets), trained on 20 targets and tested on the 10 held-out targets, 3 seeds. Systems compared: model-representation probe vs a fingerprint-distance-only predictor. Decisive metric first: Potency-Beyond-Structure Index = within-pair accuracy of predicting which molecule of a matched cliff pair is more potent from the representation, minus the accuracy from ECFP distance alone. Indecision band up front: an index in [0.03, 0.10] (accuracy points) cannot decide and is reported as weak/ambiguous potency encoding; index >= 0.10 with bootstrap CI lower bound > 0.03 is convincing evidence of potency-beyond-structure; index <= 0.03 means the model adds nothing beyond structure, consistent with the smooth-failure hypothesis. Negative result here strengthens the core claim.

Experiment 3 (H3 — causal pharmacophore localization via patching): Tests hypothesis assertion (b): that any cliff-induced representational jump is causally carried by the pharmacophore-relevant substructure, not diffused across the molecule. Data (adapted): single-transformation MMP cliffs from Experiment 1 for which the changed atom/group is unambiguous (we keep only pairs with exactly one MMP transformation; ~30-40% of cliffs qualify, ~1,500-2,000 pairs). Model: Uni-Mol and ChemBERTa-2 (frozen), which expose per-atom/per-token activations. Method: for each cliff pair, patch the low-potency molecule's activations with the high-potency molecule's at (i) the pharmacophore substructure only vs (ii) matched-size off-target substructures, and read the change in a frozen potency-probe output (probe from Experiment 2). Systems compared: pharmacophore patch vs off-target patch. Decisive metric first: Pharmacophore-Localization Score = |delta prediction from pharmacophore patch| / |delta from matched off-target patch|, bootstrap CI over pairs. Indecision band up front: a score whose CI lies in [1.3, 2.0] cannot decide and is reported as partial/uncertain localization; CI lower bound > 2.0 is convincing causal localization to the pharmacophore; CI upper bound < 1.3 means the effect is spatially diffuse (no localized mechanism), consistent with the smoothness hypothesis. A negative result (score ~1) supports the core claim that cliffs are not represented as pharmacophore-localized discontinuities.

Experiment 4 (SECONDARY — trim if space is limited; H4 — smoothness predicts the documented cliff failure): H1-H3 already establish the core mechanistic claim, so this is a secondary correlational tie-in that tests the framing claim that this representational signature explains WHERE the model's potency predictions actually fail. Data: MoleculeACE cliff pairs (30 targets) with the benchmark's reported per-molecule potency errors from a standard fine-tuned regressor head. Model: frozen backbones from Experiment 1; the per-pair jump ratio and localization score are the predictors, no new training beyond a logistic link (3 seeds). Systems compared: internal-signal predictor vs an output-confidence baseline (predicted-variance / ensemble disagreement). Decisive metric first: AUROC for flagging the high-error cliff pairs (top-quartile absolute error) from the internal smoothness signal. Indecision band up front: AUROC in [0.60, 0.70] cannot decide and is reported as a weak link; AUROC >= 0.70 with CI lower bound > 0.60 and beating the confidence baseline is convincing that the representational signature explains the failure; AUROC <= 0.60 (near the 0.50 chance line) means the signature does not track failures, weakening the mechanistic-signature claim even if Experiments 1-3 are positive. This experiment is what ties the internal geometry to the real-world cliff failure the hypothesis is about.
Risk Factors and Limitations: Matching cliff and non-cliff pairs on structural-transformation magnitude is imperfect; residual structural differences could confound the jump ratio. We mitigate with tight fingerprint-distance and atoms-changed matching and report sensitivity to the matching threshold.

Pharmacophore-relevant substructure assignment from MMP transformations may be ambiguous for pairs with multiple simultaneous changes; we restrict causal-patching to single-transformation MMP-cliffs and, where available, use docking/known SAR to confirm the responsible group.

Some FMs pool to a single molecule embedding, limiting token/atom-level patching; we prioritize models with per-atom/per-token activations (Uni-Mol, ChemBERTa) for the localization test and use whole-molecule patching as a coarser fallback.
Potency labels (pIC50) are assay-dependent and noisy across ChEMBL sources; we use MoleculeACE's curated targets and report robustness to potency-difference thresholds defining a cliff.

A finding that models are locally smooth across cliffs (ratio ≈ 1) is a negative result about mechanism, but it is precisely the mechanistic explanation for the well-documented AC failure mode and is decision-relevant for trusting these models in lead optimization; we frame either outcome as explaining WHY cliffs are hard at the representational level.

Alternative-explanation controls: because representational distance could track generic prediction difficulty, assay noise, or scaffold change rather than the cliff mechanism, we add difficulty-matched non-cliff pairs, assay-source-stratified subsets, and scaffold-hop vs within-scaffold splits, and require the cliff-vs-non-cliff jump to survive all three.

Patching sanity checks: for H3 we add random-substructure patches, same-size chemically-unrelated patches, and label-shuffled controls, and require the pharmacophore-localization score to exceed all of them; H2 probes use scaffold- and target-disjoint splits to rule out leakage and are reported both within- and across-target.
All experiments are inference-only on public pretrained models plus small probes/SAEs and public benchmark data (MoleculeACE, ChEMBL), keeping compute at academic scale.

Name: spin_state_exchange_probe
Title: Does the Model Know About Spin? Testing Whether Atomistic Foundation Models Represent the Exchange/Hund's-Rule Mechanism of Spin-State Energetics, or Only Nuclear Geometry
Short Hypothesis: A defining, exactly-known quantum-chemical mechanism is that molecular energy and reactivity depend on electronic spin state through exchange interactions (Hund's rule, singlet-triplet gaps, high-/low-spin splitting) — a dependence that is invisible to nuclear geometry alone. We hypothesize that (a) most universal machine-learning interatomic potentials (MLIPs), which take only nuclei/charge as input, are structurally blind to spin state and therefore collapse distinct spin isomers to a single representation, whereas (b) spin-aware atomistic/quantum-chemistry foundation models that do receive spin information internally encode the exchange-driven spin-state ordering as a recoverable, causally load-bearing direction that reproduces the correct sign and magnitude of singlet-triplet and high-/low-spin gaps. A spin-flip counterfactual at fixed geometry is an exact, mechanism-defining test that geometry-only correlation cannot pass.
Related Work: Prior interpretability of atomistic models shows embeddings encode DFT-derived quantities: 'Occupancies vs Embeddings' (2025) recovers atomic occupancies from GNN embeddings; Schutt et al. (2018) extract atom-wise energies, partial charges, and periodic-table-like element embeddings; GNN-LRP work (2024-2025) decomposes NNP energies into physically-meaningful many-body terms; 'Comparing latent features of uMLIPs' (2025) and 'Beyond Converging Representations' (2025) characterize and align MLIP latent geometry. Separately, an entire ML-DFT literature (differentiable Kohn-Sham XC functionals, DM21, Skala) learns the exchange-correlation functional, whose whole purpose is to capture the exchange energy that governs spin-state ordering. Crucially, all atomistic-interpretability work probes geometry- or density-derived pointwise quantities; none tests whether a foundation model internally represents the SPIN-STATE / EXCHANGE mechanism — the dependence of energy on spin multiplicity at fixed nuclear geometry — nor uses a spin-flip counterfactual to arbitrate whether the model captures this mechanism or is blind to it. Because most MLIPs cannot even ingest spin state, this is a rare setting where a mechanism (exchange-driven spin energetics) is provably separable from the geometry correlate. Our spin-degeneracy counterfactual, exchange-direction probe, and causal spin-state steering are the novel, mechanism-defining contribution. The novelty locus in one sentence: mechanistic interpretability of spin-aware atomistic foundation models under fixed-geometry spin-flip counterfactuals -- distinct from prior spin-aware / magnetic MLIP work that adds spin as an input or target without asking whether exchange energetics are internally represented. The spin-blindness result for geometry-only MLIPs is a theorem-like setup, not a discovery; the contribution is the probe methodology together with a curated, public fixed-geometry spin-state counterfactual suite (singlet/triplet and high-/low-spin pairs with reference gaps) that could become a standard release-time check for open-shell chemistry.
Abstract: The energy and reactivity of molecules and materials depend not only on where the nuclei sit but on the electronic spin state: exchange interactions and Hund's rule set singlet-triplet gaps in carbenes and O2, and high-spin/low-spin splittings in transition-metal complexes, all at fixed nuclear geometry. This makes spin-state energetics an ideal, exactly-known mechanism for testing whether atomistic foundation models learn quantum-chemical mechanism or merely a geometry-to-energy correlate. We first show that a large class of universal machine-learning interatomic potentials (MLIPs) is structurally blind to spin state — taking only nuclear positions and total charge as input, they must assign identical energies and representations to distinct spin isomers of the same geometry, a decisive negative result for their use on open-shell chemistry. We then ask, for spin-aware atomistic/quantum-chemistry foundation models that do receive spin multiplicity (or are trained across spin states), whether they internally represent the exchange mechanism. Using curated spin-state pairs (singlet/triplet carbenes and O2, high-/low-spin Fe(II)/Co(III) complexes) with reference CASPT2/DFT energies, we probe whether an 'exchange/spin-state' direction is recoverable and reproduces the correct sign and magnitude of the spin gap beyond what geometry predicts. Most decisively, a spin-flip counterfactual holds geometry fixed and flips only the spin label: a mechanistic representation must shift its energy readout and internal state by the correct spin gap, while a geometry-only model cannot. We validate causally by steering the recovered spin direction. Metrics quantify a spin-blindness index, a spin-gap-beyond-geometry index, and a spin-flip causal asymmetry. Either outcome sharpens whether atomistic foundation models can be trusted on the open-shell, spin-dependent chemistry that dominates catalysis and radical reactions. The downstream decision is concrete for MLIP developers and users: geometry-only universal MLIPs must not be applied to spin-crossover, open-shell catalysis, bond dissociation, or magnetic materials, where a wrong spin ordering flips the qualitative conclusion (e.g., predicting a low-spin ground state for a spin-crossover complex, or the wrong triplet/singlet carbene reactivity); spin-aware models are trustworthy for these only if they reproduce exchange trends, not merely gate on the spin label. The lesson generalizes to mechanism-faithfulness of scientific foundation models beyond chemistry.
Experiments: Experiment 1 (SETUP / sanity baseline — a theorem-like check, not a discovery; H1 — spin-blindness of geometry-only MLIPs): It frames the main test by verifying assertion (a): universal MLIPs that ingest only nuclei/charge are structurally blind to spin state and collapse distinct spin isomers to one representation. Data (existing): spin-state pairs at fixed geometry with reliable references -- singlet/triplet methylene and substituted carbenes, singlet/triplet O2, and octahedral transition-metal complexes with high-/low-spin states (Fe(II), Co(III), Mn) from published CASPT2/DMRG/DFT spin-gap benchmarks (TMC/SSE datasets); we use up to 300 spin pairs. Models (frozen, inference only): geometry-only MLIPs MACE-MP-0, CHGNet, SevenNet, and Orb; per-structure energies and representations. Systems compared: energy and representation of spin isomer A vs B at identical geometry. Decisive metric first: Spin-Blindness Index = fraction of spin pairs with |energy(A) - energy(B)| exactly 0 AND representation distance exactly 0. Indecision band up front: for these input-invariant models the outcome is analytic, so any index in (0, 1) would flag an unexpected implicit spin channel to be investigated; an index of 1.0 is the decisive confirmation that this deployed model class cannot represent spin-state energetics at all; an index below 1.0 would mean some spin information leaks in (e.g., via charge), which we would then characterize. This is a definitional negative result, separately reported, that motivates restricting the richer tests to spin-aware models.

Experiment 2 (H2 — spin-gap-beyond-geometry and spin-flip counterfactual, decisive): Tests assertion (b): spin-aware models internally encode the exchange-driven spin-state ordering with the correct sign and magnitude, recoverable beyond geometry, and responsive to a spin-flip at fixed geometry. Data: the Experiment 1 spin pairs plus, for dose-response, ligand-field-strength and carbene-substituent series that tune the gap. Models (frozen, inference only): spin-aware atomistic models that ingest spin multiplicity (SpookyNet, a spin-conditioned MACE/AIMNet2 variant, or any spin-aware foundation MLIP with public weights); trainable part is ridge linear probes only (3 seeds). Procedure: (i) regress out the geometry-predictable component (using a geometry-only MLIP's energy/features) and re-decode the reference spin gap from the residual; (ii) at FIXED geometry flip only the spin multiplicity input and read the energy/representation change against the reference gap; (iii) across the tuning series test the trend. Systems compared: spin-aware model vs geometry-only features; spin-flip edit vs a matched control geometry perturbation of comparable energy scale. Decisive metric first: Spin-Flip Causal Asymmetry = |shift under spin-flip| / |shift under matched geometry-control edit|, plus the correlation between the model's spin-flip energy response and the reference gap (and fraction with correct sign). Indecision band up front: an asymmetry whose CI lies in [1.3, 2.0], or a gap-correlation CI in [0.2, 0.5], cannot decide and is reported as spin-sensitive-but-not-faithful; asymmetry CI lower bound > 2.0 WITH gap-correlation CI lower bound > 0.5, correct sign in > 80% of pairs, and a monotonic dose-response is convincing exchange encoding; asymmetry CI upper bound < 1.3 (~0 response) is the spin-insensitive signature. This decisive test separates genuine exchange encoding from a trivial spin-label lookup (which would fail the transfer/dose-response).

Experiment 3 (OPTIONAL strengthening — framed as representation-sensitivity / manipulation rather than a strong causal claim; H3 — causal spin-state steering): Tests assertion (b)'s causal-load-bearing clause: a recovered spin-state/exchange direction, when steered, shifts the energy prediction in the spin-gap-consistent direction. Data: the spin pairs and tuning series from Experiment 2. Model: frozen spin-aware model; the spin direction is a supervised probe (or SAE feature) separating spin isomers, no backbone training. Procedure: steer along the spin direction at matched magnitude and read the energy prediction; controls are matched-norm random directions. Decisive metric first: mechanism-selectivity = |energy shift under spin direction| / |shift under random direction|, CI over systems. Indecision band up front: selectivity CI in [1.3, 2.0] cannot decide (no clean causal direction); CI lower bound > 2.0 with a spin-gap-consistent shift is convincing causal exchange encoding; CI upper bound < 1.3 means no separable causal spin direction. A negative result -- spin-aware models gating on the label without a steerable exchange direction, and geometry-only models blind -- is the decisive combined finding about atomistic FMs on open-shell chemistry.
Risk Factors and Limitations: Many public MLIPs are geometry-only and thus spin-blind by construction; the spin-blindness result is definitional for those models, so the richer mechanism tests apply only to spin-aware models, of which fewer public foundation-scale weights exist. We prioritize the strongest available spin-aware model and treat the geometry-only blindness as a decisive, separately-reported finding.

Spin-aware models may simply gate energy on the spin label without internally representing exchange; we mitigate by requiring correct sign AND magnitude AND monotonic ligand-field/substituent trends (dose-response), which a trivial label-lookup would not reproduce across unseen systems, and by cross-system transfer tests.

Reference spin gaps (CASPT2/DMRG) are themselves method-dependent and can disagree, especially for transition metals; we use consensus benchmark subsets, report sensitivity to the reference method, and emphasize sign and trend agreement over exact magnitude.

Spin and geometry can be correlated in equilibrium structures (different spin states relax to different geometries); the spin-flip counterfactual controls this by holding geometry fixed, but off-equilibrium single-point energies may fall outside training distribution — we bound this and report OOD diagnostics.

Linear probes recovering a spin direction do not guarantee causal use; we address this with steering plus random-direction controls, though distributed encodings may blur single-direction interventions.

A negative result (spin-aware models gate on the label but do not reproduce exchange trends, and geometry-only models are blind) is scientifically decisive and directly relevant to trusting atomistic foundation models on catalysis, radicals, and magnetism, though it may be perceived as confirmatory of skepticism; we frame either outcome as the first mechanism-defining test of spin-state exchange energetics in atomistic foundation models.
All experiments are inference-only on public pretrained models plus small probes/SAEs and public spin-state benchmark datasets, keeping compute at academic scale.

Name: periodic_law_probe
Title: Do Foundation-Model Interatomic Potentials Internally Recover the Periodic Law? A Causal Test of Chemical-Trend Representations and Their Link to Out-of-Distribution Failure
