Short Hypothesis: Universal machine-learning interatomic potentials (MLIPs) trained on broad materials/molecular data internally organize element embeddings and per-atom feature spaces along the same low-dimensional axes as the periodic law (period, group, electronegativity, atomic radius, valence). We hypothesize that (a) these axes are recoverable and causally load-bearing (perturbing them along a 'chemical trend' direction shifts predictions in the physically-correct direction), and (b) an element's or environment's distance from the model's learned periodic manifold quantitatively predicts where the model extrapolates unreliably. If true, this gives a mechanism-grounded, physics-interpretable failure detector; if false, it shows foundation MLIPs rely on non-transferable memorized statistics. The single centerpiece claim is causal (part a): periodic-trend directions are load-bearing in pretrained foundation MLIPs; recoverability and the manifold-distance failure detector are the supporting hypotheses.
Related Work: Schutt et al. (2018) showed atomistic NN element embeddings partially recover periodic-table ordering, and 'From Neurons to Neutrons' (2024) found helical embeddings encoding nuclear physics. GNN-LRP work decomposes MLIP energies into physically-consistent n-body terms; 'Beyond Converging Representations' (2025) shows scientific foundation models align and collapse to low-information representations far from training data. These works either (i) match learned features to known chemistry descriptively, or (ii) study alignment/convergence globally. None causally tests whether the periodic-law structure inside modern *universal foundation MLIPs* (MACE-MP-0, Orb, SevenNet, CHGNet, EquiformerV2 trained on Materials Project/OMat) is load-bearing, nor connects the geometry of that internal chemical manifold to concrete out-of-distribution (OOD) failure prediction. Our causal-intervention plus failure-prediction framing is the novel contribution, moving beyond descriptive trend-matching to a predictive, mechanism-grounded diagnostic. Concretely, the delta over Schutt et al. (descriptive embedding ordering) and recent OOD-embedding work is three-fold: causal steering along recovered trend directions, discrete same-group embedding swaps, and evaluation on foundation MLIPs; we release the probe/steering suite and a held-out rare-chemistry split as a public benchmark. We claim recovery of partial, transferable periodic trends, not a new theory of chemistry.
Abstract: The periodic law compresses the chemistry of the elements into a handful of transferable trends. We ask whether modern universal machine-learning interatomic potentials (MLIPs), now used as chemistry/materials foundation models, internally rediscover these trends and, crucially, whether that internal structure is causally responsible for their predictions and predictive of their failures. Prior interpretability work has descriptively noted periodic-table-like structure in atomistic embeddings, but has not tested whether such structure is load-bearing or whether its geometry governs out-of-distribution reliability. We probe several pretrained foundation MLIPs (e.g., MACE-MP-0, CHGNet, Orb, SevenNet) at both the element-embedding and per-atom-feature level. We first recover, via linear probes and manifold learning, directions encoding period, group, electronegativity, covalent radius, and valence, quantifying how faithfully the learned chemical manifold matches the true periodic table. We then perform causal interventions: steering an atom's internal representation along a recovered 'electronegativity' or 'radius' direction should shift predicted energies, forces, and charges in the physically-correct, quantitatively-scaled direction; scrambling the direction should not. Finally, we test whether an atom's or structure's distance from the learned periodic manifold predicts per-structure error on held-out and deliberately OOD systems (rare elements, unusual oxidation states, exotic coordination), yielding a physics-interpretable, calibration-free failure detector. The result is a causal, mechanism-grounded account of whether foundation MLIPs learn the periodic law or memorize training statistics, with direct implications for their safe deployment in materials discovery. Operationally, a model-native manifold-distance score would let practitioners abstain or route to DFT before trusting an MLIP on unseen chemistry (screening, active learning, model selection); we benchmark it against element rarity, training-set density, composition-only, kNN, and deep-ensemble baselines and report calibration, so any advantage is attributable to periodic geometry rather than data density.
Experiments: Experiment 1 (H1 — Recovering the periodic manifold from embeddings and atom features): Tests the H1 claim that universal MLIPs organize element embeddings and per-atom features along periodic-law axes (period, group, Pauling electronegativity, covalent radius, valence-electron count, first ionization energy). Data: 5,000 structures sampled from the Materials Project (~150k materials exist) and QM9 (134k molecules exist), stratified to cover all 89 elements up to Bi plus a rare-element tail; 5,000 is chosen so every element appears ≥30 times for stable per-element statistics while keeping activation extraction to a few GPU-hours — more structures repeat element contexts without adding periodic coverage. Ground-truth periodic descriptors are tabulated constants (Mendeleev/pymatgen). Model: four pretrained foundation MLIPs with public weights — MACE-MP-0, CHGNet, Orb, SevenNet — all frozen, inference only; trainable = ridge linear probes and partial-least-squares maps on the invariant scalar channels of element embeddings and per-atom features, per layer; 5 CV folds, 3 seeds. Systems compared: probe on model features vs probe on a random-permutation of the same features (destroying element identity) as a floor. Decisive metric first: held-out probe R² for each descriptor, averaged over folds. Convincing result: R² ≥ 0.8 for group/period/electronegativity in at least one layer of each model, and a 2-D PCA that visibly reproduces periodic-table row/column topology. Undecidable band: R² in [0.4, 0.6] for a descriptor — present but weak structure; such a descriptor is not used as a steering axis in Experiment 2 and is reported as partially encoded; band fixed before data. Negative result: R² < 0.4 across descriptors and models means the periodic law is not linearly recoverable, H1 fails, and the causal/failure tests targeting recovered directions are moot.

Experiment 2 (H2 — Causal steering along chemical-trend directions): Tests the H2(a) claim that recovered periodic axes are causally load-bearing — perturbing a per-atom representation along an electronegativity or covalent-radius direction shifts energy/force/charge predictions in the physically-correct direction. Data: 500 structures from the Experiment-1 test split spanning diverse coordination environments (500 keeps the α-sweep × seed × structure grid affordable; each structure yields many atoms, so this is ample). Model: the four frozen MLIPs with the fixed Experiment-1 unit directions; steering adds ±α·(unit direction) to a target atom's invariant channels at the best-R² layer, α swept over {0.25,0.5,1,2}× the per-channel activation std; 3 seeds. Systems compared: true-direction steering vs matched-norm random/scrambled-direction control. Decisive metric first: mechanism-selectivity index M = |Δoutput along true direction| / |Δoutput along random direction|, plus sign-consistency (fraction of atoms whose predicted change has the physically-expected sign) and monotonicity of Δoutput in α. Convincing result: M ≥ 3 with sign-consistency ≥ 0.8 and monotone dose-response in at least one model. Undecidable band: M in [1.2, 2.0] or sign-consistency in [0.55, 0.65] — weak causal use, reported as inconclusive for that model/axis; band fixed before data. Negative result: M ≈ 1 or chance sign-consistency means recovered axes are decodable but not causal, so H2(a) fails even where H1 held.

Experiment 3 (H2 — Trend-swap counterfactual by element-embedding substitution): Tests H2(a) with a discrete, interpretable intervention — replacing a target element's embedding with a same-group neighbor's (e.g., Na→K, Cl→Br) should move predictions along the true periodic trend. Data: 40 same-group substitution pairs across groups 1, 2, 13–17 applied to 300 host structures where the substituted site is chemically sensible (300 hosts × 40 pairs is tractable; hosts drawn from the Experiment-1 set). Ground-truth trend deltas from experimental/DFT tables (ionization energy, covalent radius). Model: four frozen MLIPs; embedding table entry swapped, no retraining; 3 seeds over host sampling. Systems compared: predicted property delta under true-neighbor swap vs under a random-element swap of matched embedding-norm. Decisive metric first: Spearman ρ between predicted deltas and true periodic-trend deltas across substitutions. Convincing result: ρ ≥ 0.6 for true-neighbor swaps and near-zero for random swaps. Undecidable band: ρ in [0.3, 0.45] — directionally suggestive but not decisive, reported as partial support; band fixed in advance. Negative result: ρ ≈ 0 means embedding geometry does not carry usable trend structure, reinforcing an H2 failure.

Experiment 4 (H3 — Manifold-distance predicts extrapolation failure): Tests the H3(b) claim that an atom's/structure's distance from the learned periodic manifold predicts where force/energy error is large. Data: (a) held-out in-distribution MP/QM9 structures with existing DFT labels, 2,000 structures; (b) deliberately OOD sets with published DFT references — rare-element compounds, unusual oxidation states, exotic coordination, high-pressure phases — 1,000 structures assembled from existing benchmark subsets (e.g., MPtrj tails, Matbench rare splits); we reuse existing DFT labels only, no new DFT, to stay in academic budget. Model: four frozen MLIPs; manifold distance = reconstruction residual from the Experiment-1 low-dimensional chemical subspace and Mahalanobis distance in probe space; no training beyond the fitted subspace. Systems compared: manifold distance vs generic baselines — embedding norm, deep-ensemble variance, feature-space kNN distance, element rarity, training-set density, and a composition-only baseline; we also report calibration (reliability curves, expected calibration error). Decisive metric first: AUROC for flagging the top-decile-error structures, and Spearman ρ between distance and per-structure force MAE. Convincing result: manifold-distance AUROC ≥ 0.75 AND exceeds every baseline's AUROC by ≥ 0.05. Undecidable band: AUROC within 0.03 of the best baseline — no physics-specific advantage, reported as "not distinguishable from generic OOD detection"; band fixed before data. Negative result: manifold distance at chance (AUROC ≤ 0.55) or below baselines means periodic geometry is not a failure detector and H3 fails.

Experiment 5 (H1 — Cross-model convergence of the periodic subspace): Tests whether the recovered periodic structure is a convergent property (strengthening H1's generality, not enlarging it). Data: the Experiment-1 activations for all four models on the shared 5,000 structures. Model: four frozen MLIPs; no training beyond CKA/Procrustes alignment of the fitted chemical subspaces. Systems compared: linear CKA between each model pair's periodic subspace vs CKA between a model's periodic subspace and a random subspace of equal dimension. Decisive metric first: mean pairwise CKA of periodic subspaces. Convincing result: CKA ≥ 0.6 across pairs, well above the random-subspace floor. Undecidable band: CKA in [0.3, 0.45] — partial alignment, reported as weakly convergent; band fixed before data. Negative result: CKA near the random floor means each model encodes an idiosyncratic representation, so convergence is not supported (does not by itself refute per-model H1).

Experiment 6 (H1/H2 — Scale and training-breadth ablation): Tests whether periodic-manifold faithfulness and its causal load-bearing-ness grow with model scale/data breadth. Data: the Experiment-1/2 splits. Model: frozen MLIP variants that differ only in scale or training set where public — MACE-MP-0 size variants and MP-trained vs OMat-trained checkpoints; probes/steering re-run identically; 3 seeds. Systems compared: Experiment-1 probe R² and Experiment-2 selectivity M across the ordered variants. Decisive metric first: sign and magnitude of the R²-vs-scale and M-vs-scale slopes. Convincing result: monotone positive slopes reproducible across seeds, indicating scale/breadth increases periodic faithfulness and causal use. Undecidable band: |slope| within its 3-seed standard error — reported as no scale effect. Negative result: flat or negative slopes mean broader training does not buy more periodic-law structure, an informative bound on H1/H2 rather than a contradiction.
Risk Factors and Limitations: Probe recovery of a direction does not guarantee causal use; we mitigate with steering interventions and random-direction controls, but distributed/superposed encodings may weaken clean single-direction effects.
Steering in a nonlinear equivariant network may push representations off-manifold, producing uninterpretable outputs; we bound alpha to stay near the data manifold and report sensitivity to alpha.
Equivariance constraints mean per-atom features are tensorial; probing must respect invariant vs equivariant channels, adding methodological care (we focus probes on invariant scalar channels first).

Manifold-distance may correlate with error simply through data density rather than genuine periodic-law geometry; we control against generic OOD detectors (kNN, ensemble variance) to isolate the physics-grounded signal.

A negative result (models memorize statistics rather than encode transferable periodic trends) is scientifically informative but may be perceived as less exciting; we frame either outcome as a decisive, deployment-relevant finding.
Ground-truth OOD errors require DFT reference labels; we rely on existing labeled benchmark subsets and published DFT to keep costs within an academic budget.

Failure-mode analysis is pre-specified: we report when periodic geometry fails to predict error and attribute residual error to covariate shift, DFT-label noise, or representation/layer choice, so a null detector result is diagnostic rather than ambiguous.

Name: universality_class_collapse_probe
Title: Same Exponents, Different Stuff: Do Physics Foundation Models Represent Universality Classes, or Just Microscopic Detail?
Short Hypothesis: Universality is the defining, exactly-known mechanism of critical phenomena: near a continuous phase transition, microscopically-different systems collapse onto the SAME critical exponents, determined only by symmetry and spatial dimensionality, not microscopic details. We hypothesize that if a physics/scientific foundation model represents this mechanism rather than surface configuration statistics, its internal representation near criticality will (a) organize systems by universality class (collapsing microscopically-distinct systems of the same class together while separating same-looking systems of different classes), (b) encode a recoverable 'reduced temperature / distance-to-criticality' direction that reproduces finite-size scaling collapse, and (c) causally track class membership. A same-class-different-microscopics vs different-class-similar-microscopics counterfactual is an exact, mechanism-defining test that correlation with raw configurations cannot pass.
Related Work: A large literature draws an ANALOGY between deep networks and the renormalization group (Scale-invariant feature extraction and RG flow 2018; Towards quantifying information flows 2022; Interpreting Deep Learning via RG 2022; RG for DNNs: Universality of learning 2025), and studies criticality signatures IN networks (Universal Scaling Laws of Absorbing Phase Transitions in DNNs 2023; Critical Phase Transition in LLMs 2024; Internal Representations in SNNs and criticality 2024). These treat the NETWORK itself as a critical/RG system, or map data-derived RG flows. None tests whether a model TRAINED ON PHYSICAL SYSTEM DATA internally represents the physics concept of universality classes — that critical exponents depend only on symmetry and dimensionality, not microscopic details — nor uses a same-class/different-class counterfactual to separate this mechanism from raw-configuration correlation. Statistical-physics work (Potts/percolation hyperuniversality 2025; lower-bound-on-nu conjecture 2025; quantum critical exponent extraction 2026) rigorously defines universality classes and exponents as ground truth. Our contribution is the first mechanism-defining test of whether a scientific foundation model encodes universality-class structure, its causal load-bearingness, and its finite-size-scaling faithfulness — distinct from the network-as-RG analogy line. We separate the novelty claims: the primary contribution is the representation-level test of universality-class structure under a same-class / different-microscopics counterfactual; the multi-system-pretraining-and-transfer setting and the causal steering result are secondary and reported as such, not conflated. This is distinct from prior CNN critical-exponent-extraction work (single-system exponent regression) because it requires class collapse across microscopically-distinct systems and transfer to a held-out system. If we pretrain our own model we call it a 'multisystem scientific model,' not a 'foundation model,' unless breadth and scale are documented.
Abstract: The single deepest organizing principle of critical phenomena is universality: near a continuous phase transition, systems that differ completely at the microscopic level — different lattices, interactions, and degrees of freedom — exhibit identical critical exponents, determined only by symmetry and spatial dimensionality. Two systems that look nothing alike can belong to the same universality class, while two that look almost identical can belong to different ones. This makes universality an ideal, exactly-known mechanism for testing whether foundation models that ingest physical system data learn the underlying mechanism or merely surface configuration statistics. We probe scientific foundation models applied to spin/lattice systems (either public multi-physics/statistical-mechanics surrogates, or a modest transformer/CNN foundation model pretrained across many statistical-mechanics systems), evaluated on Monte-Carlo configurations from the 2D Ising, 3-state Potts, XY, and site/bond percolation models whose universality classes and critical exponents are exactly known. First, a class-organization probe: near criticality, are microscopically-distinct systems of the same class collapsed together in the representation, and same-looking systems of different classes separated, beyond raw-configuration similarity? Second, a finite-size-scaling test: does a recovered 'reduced-temperature' direction reproduce the data-collapse scaling function with the correct critical exponents? Third, and most decisively, a universality-class counterfactual: pairs matched to be same-class-but-different-microscopics versus different-class-but-similar-microscopics; a mechanistic representation groups by class, a configuration-statistics one groups by appearance. We validate causally by steering the class direction. Metrics quantify a class-beyond-configuration index, scaling-collapse fidelity, and a same-class/different-class separation ratio. Either outcome sharpens what these models represent. Under raw-configuration correlation alone it is impossible to collapse microscopically-distinct same-class systems together while separating similar-looking different-class systems and to reproduce finite-size-scaling collapse only with the correct class exponents; that is the falsifiable prediction. The downstream consequence is for scientific-FM evaluation and use: if class structure is encoded and transfers, such models can support cross-system extrapolation, better critical-point estimation, and simulator replacement / active learning on unseen lattice models; if they group by appearance (the null), cross-system extrapolation from these models is untrustworthy and this becomes an evaluation standard rather than a curiosity.
Experiments: Experiment 1 (H1 — organization by universality class beyond configuration statistics, decisive): Tests assertion (a): near criticality the representation organizes systems by universality class -- collapsing microscopically-distinct systems of the same class while separating same-looking systems of different classes -- beyond raw-configuration similarity. Data (constructed): Monte-Carlo configuration ensembles (Metropolis/Wolff/Swendsen-Wang) for models with exactly-known classes -- 2D Ising, 2D q=3 Potts, 2D XY (BKT), 2D site and bond percolation, and dilute/next-nearest-neighbor Ising variants (same 2D-Ising class, different microscopics) -- swept through each transition at several lattice sizes L, labeled by class, reduced temperature t, and known exponents (nu, beta, gamma); >= 50,000 configurations, split so held-out systems exist. Model (frozen for analysis): either a public scientific foundation model with per-configuration representations, or, as a documented academic-scale fallback, a modest CNN/transformer pretrained self-supervised (masked reconstruction / temperature regression) across MULTIPLE systems and never told class labels (one pretraining run, seeds 0,1,2); analysis is inference-only plus linear probes. Systems compared: (i) representation probe vs raw-configuration/order-parameter features for class decoding; and (ii) the counterfactual pairs -- same-class/different-microscopics (nearest-neighbor vs dilute/NNN 2D Ising at their critical points) vs different-class/similar-appearance (q=2 vs q=3 Potts at criticality). Decisive metrics first: Class-Beyond-Configuration Index = class-decoding accuracy from the representation minus what raw-configuration/order-parameter features achieve (after residualizing configuration features); and Same-Class/Different-Class Separation Ratio = representational distance(same-class pair) / representational distance(different-class-but-similar-appearance pair). Indecision bands up front: a Class-Beyond-Configuration Index in [0.03, 0.10] cannot decide (ambiguous class encoding); index >= 0.10 with CI lower bound > 0.03 is convincing class-beyond-appearance encoding; index <= 0.03 is the appearance-only signature. For the ratio, mechanism predicts < 1: a ratio whose CI lies in [0.67, 0.90] cannot decide; CI upper bound < 0.67 (same class collapses together despite different microscopics) is convincing universality encoding; CI lower bound > 0.90 (groups by appearance, not class) is the configuration-statistics signature. These together are the decisive test; a null is the headline negative result.

Experiment 2 (H2 — finite-size-scaling faithfulness): Tests assertion (b): a recoverable reduced-temperature / distance-to-criticality direction reproduces finite-size-scaling collapse with the CORRECT class exponents and fails with the wrong ones. Data: the Experiment 1 ensembles across multiple L and t for the clean second-order classes (Ising, Potts, percolation); XY/BKT treated as a separate carefully-analyzed case, not a decisive counterfactual. Model: frozen backbone; a reduced-temperature direction recovered by a linear probe across L and t, no backbone training. Procedure: test whether model-implied observables obey M*L^(beta/nu) = f(t*L^(1/nu)) with the true known exponents, and whether the collapse degrades when wrong-class exponents are imposed. Systems compared: collapse under correct vs wrong-class exponents. Decisive metric first: scaling-collapse quality = ratio of collapse residual with wrong-class exponents to residual with correct-class exponents (larger means the correct exponents collapse the data selectively), CI over bootstrap resamples of configurations. Indecision band up front: a ratio whose CI lies in [1.0, 1.5] cannot decide and is reported as no selective collapse (exponents not faithfully encoded); CI lower bound > 1.5 is convincing that the internal signal collapses only under its true class's exponents; CI upper bound < 1.0 or ~1.0 means the representation does not encode the correct scaling. A negative result here, even with a positive H1, would mean class structure is present but not quantitatively faithful.

Experiment 3 (H3 — causal class steering and generalization): Tests assertion (c): a recovered class-membership direction is causally load-bearing, and class structure generalizes to a held-out system, distinguishing an encoded mechanism from per-system memorization. Data: configurations at criticality for two classes, plus a system held out of pretraining but in a known class (a 2D Ising variant, or 3D Ising if feasible). Model: frozen; the class direction is a supervised probe or a delta-representation between two classes at criticality, no backbone training. Procedure: steer a configuration's representation with matched magnitude toward another class and read the class/exponent readout (or masked-reconstruction statistics); controls are matched-norm random directions and a raw-configuration direction; separately, test class decoding on the held-out system. Decisive metric first: mechanism-selectivity = |class-readout change under class direction| / |change under random direction|, CI over configurations; plus held-out-system class-decoding accuracy above the raw-configuration baseline. Indecision band up front: selectivity CI in [1.3, 2.0] cannot decide (no clean causal class direction); CI lower bound > 2.0 with class-consistent steering, and held-out class-decoding beating the configuration baseline by > 0.10 accuracy, is convincing causal, generalizing class encoding; selectivity CI upper bound < 1.3, or held-out decoding at the configuration baseline, means class membership is memorized per system rather than encoded as a mechanism. A negative result supports the configuration-statistics conclusion.
Risk Factors and Limitations: Universality-class membership correlates with visible configuration features near criticality (e.g., cluster geometry), making the class-beyond-configuration separation statistically demanding; we mitigate with raw-configuration residualization, the matched same-class/different-microscopics counterfactual, and the finite-size-scaling test which a configuration-statistics model cannot pass with correct exponents.

Public scientific foundation models trained on statistical-mechanics configurations may be scarce; we fall back on pretraining a modest multi-system CNN/transformer surrogate ourselves, which is academic-scale (small lattices, standard Monte-Carlo data) but is not a 'large' foundation model — we report this scope clearly and treat cross-system generalization as the foundation-model-relevant test.

Distinguishing BKT (XY) scaling from second-order transitions requires care (essential singularity, no simple power-law nu); we treat XY as a separate, carefully-analyzed case and focus decisive counterfactuals on clean second-order classes (Ising, Potts, percolation).

Finite-size effects and limited lattice sizes blur exponents; we use standard finite-size scaling with multiple L and report exponent-estimation uncertainty, relying on relative collapse quality (correct vs wrong-class exponents) rather than absolute precision.

Linear probes recovering a class direction do not guarantee causal use; we address this with steering plus random/configuration-direction controls, though distributed/superposed encodings may blur single-direction interventions.

A negative result (models encode configuration statistics and group by appearance, not universality class) is scientifically decisive and directly relevant to trusting such models for cross-system extrapolation and critical-point prediction, though it may be perceived as confirmatory of skepticism; we frame either outcome as the first mechanism-defining test of whether scientific foundation models represent universality classes.

Baselines and pair balancing: we add a supervised phase classifier, order-parameter-only features, random features, and simple clustering on handcrafted observables as reference points, and specify how same-class/different-microscopics and different-class/similar-appearance pairs are matched and balanced (equal counts per class and lattice size); ablations sweep pretraining-data breadth, architecture, representation layer, and probe type.
All experiments are inference-only on the model plus small probes and standard Monte-Carlo simulations (or one modest self-supervised pretraining run), keeping compute at academic scale.

Name: developmental_arrow_directionality_probe
Title: Which Way Is Forward? Testing Whether Single-Cell Foundation Models Represent the Irreversible Arrow of Differentiation, Not Just Cell-State Identity
Short Hypothesis: Differentiation has a defining, directional, quasi-irreversible mechanism: cells flow along lineages from high-potency progenitors to low-potency differentiated states, with transcriptional potency (entropy) decreasing monotonically and the reverse transition physically disfavored. Crucially, a static expression snapshot is directionless - RNA-velocity and trajectory tools must inject direction from splicing/metabolic-labeling signals the model never sees. We hypothesize that if a single-cell foundation model (scFM) represents the developmental-arrow mechanism rather than merely cell-state identity, then (a) the signed developmental direction between two adjacent states along a known lineage is decodable from internal representations beyond what marginal cell-state similarity predicts, (b) its internal 'developmental progression' axis reproduces the monotonic, irreversible decrease of transcriptional potency/entropy (a dose-response), and (c) an in-silico transition that moves a cell in the forward (differentiation) direction is treated differently from the equal-magnitude reverse (dedifferentiation) transition. The forward-vs-reverse asymmetry is a mechanism-defining test that identity-clustering and pseudotime-correlation cannot pass.
Related Work: RNA-velocity and trajectory-inference tools (Velocyto, scVelo, CellRank, dynamo, LatentVelo, VelvetVAE) all establish that snapshot expression is directionless: they must obtain the arrow of differentiation from EXTERNAL spliced/unspliced ratios or metabolic labeling, and Hodge-decomposition/dynamical-systems treatments formalize the directional (curl-free/gradient) structure of the velocity field. scFM interpretability instead recovers static concepts: SAE/transcoder studies (scFeatureLens 2024, Concept-SAE 2025, transcoder circuits 2025) find features matching cell types, tissues, and cell-cycle phase, and a systematic evaluation (2026) shows scGPT/Geneformer attention captures co-expression, not causal regulation. Causal single-cell VAEs (sVAE+, SAMS-VAE) learn intervention structure but are bespoke, not tests of pretrained scFMs. Crucially, no work tests whether a pretrained scFM's INTERNAL representation encodes the temporal DIRECTIONALITY and quasi-irreversibility of differentiation (the developmental arrow) from snapshot input alone, whether that direction is causally load-bearing, or uses a forward-vs-reverse transition asymmetry to separate the arrow mechanism from static cell-state identity. Because adjacent developmental states are also the most similar in expression, identity-based clustering and raw pseudotime correlation cannot arbitrate this; the signed-direction-beyond-identity probe, potency dose-response, and forward-vs-reverse counterfactual are the novel, mechanism-defining contribution.
Abstract: Single-cell foundation models (scFMs) are increasingly used to annotate cell states and infer developmental trajectories, and their internal features are known to encode cell-type identity. But differentiation is defined not by identity alone but by a directional, quasi-irreversible mechanism: cells flow from high-potency progenitors to low-potency differentiated fates, transcriptional potency decreases along the way, and the reverse transition is physically disfavored. A static expression snapshot is directionless - this is precisely why RNA-velocity tools must inject the arrow from splicing signals the model never receives - making developmental directionality an ideal, mechanism-defining probe for whether scFMs internalize developmental priors or merely cluster cell states. We probe pretrained scFMs (scGPT, Geneformer, cell2sentence) on well-characterized developmental atlases with ground-truth lineage order and pseudotime/velocity (pancreatic endocrinogenesis, hematopoiesis, dentate gyrus neurogenesis). First, a direction-beyond-identity probe: is the signed developmental direction between two adjacent lineage states decodable from internal representations beyond what marginal cell-state similarity predicts? Second, a potency dose-response: does a recovered 'developmental progression' axis reproduce the monotonic decrease of transcriptional entropy/potency, rather than tracking arbitrary cell-type labels? Third, and most decisively, a forward-vs-reverse counterfactual: an in-silico gene-program shift that moves a cell in the differentiation direction versus the equal-magnitude dedifferentiation direction should be treated asymmetrically by a mechanism-representing model. We validate causally by steering a recovered direction axis. Metrics quantify a direction-beyond-identity index, a potency-monotonicity score, and a forward-vs-reverse asymmetry. Either outcome sharpens whether deployed scFMs understand which way development runs - critical for reprogramming, regeneration, and cancer. The novel claim is specifically about directionality and quasi-irreversibility, the forward-vs-reverse asymmetry, potency monotonicity, and a reversible-cell-cycle double dissociation, not the mere existence of a maturity axis, and it is tested from snapshot embeddings without the velocity cues trajectory tools require. The downstream decision it settles is whether scFMs can be trusted for directional perturbation design and lineage reasoning in reprogramming, regeneration, and cancer dedifferentiation, or only for static annotation. A negative result is equally consequential: it would invalidate a common mechanistic reading of scFM embeddings.
Experiments: Experiment 1 (H1 -- signed developmental direction is decodable beyond cell-state similarity): Tests clause (a): the signed direction between two adjacent states along a known lineage is decodable from internal representations beyond what marginal cell-state similarity predicts. Data: three developmental atlases with established lineage order and RNA-velocity/metabolic-labeling ground truth, used as is: pancreatic endocrinogenesis (Bastidas-Ponce 2019, ~36,000 cells), mouse hematopoiesis, and dentate-gyrus neurogenesis (Hochgerner 2018, ~18,000 cells), all scVelo/CellRank-processed; per cell we record branch, ground-truth pseudotime, velocity-derived direction, and potency (CytoTRACE / expression entropy). We form ~5,000 adjacent-cell pairs per atlas along lineages plus a matched control set of unrelated-cell-type pairs. Model: scGPT (~51M parameters), Geneformer (~10-40M), cell2sentence (GPT-2-based, ~124M), public weights, frozen; only linear probes trained. Probes: logistic (signed earlier-vs-later order), L2 via 5-fold CV, 5 seeds with donor/batch-grouped splits; report mean +/- SD. Systems compared: (i) a static identity/similarity baseline predicting order from raw-expression cell-state similarity; (ii) Direction-Beyond-Identity Index = signed-order accuracy from the representation minus the similarity-baseline accuracy, after residualizing the identity-predictable component; reported separately along-lineage vs across-unrelated-types. Decisive metric first: Direction-Beyond-Identity Index (percentage points of accuracy). Convincing: Index >= 10 points along-lineage (95% bootstrap CI over held-out donors excluding 0, >=4/5 seeds) with the across-unrelated control near 0. Refute: Index <= 2 points (no directional information beyond similarity). Indeterminate band 2-10 points (stated before the data): unresolved -- weak directional signal, reported without treating clause (a) as established. A negative result means order is explained by cell-state similarity, contradicting clause (a).

Experiment 2 (H1 -- potency dose-response along the lineage): Further tests clause (a) by checking the recovered progression axis reproduces the monotonic, signed decrease of transcriptional potency, the specific directional structure similarity cannot supply. Data: the same three atlases (reused) with per-cell CytoTRACE/entropy potency. Model: frozen scFMs; we recover a 'developmental progression' direction as a supervised probe direction and as a progenitor-minus-differentiated delta. Systems compared: internal progression signal vs ground-truth potency along the lineage; shuffled-order-label control. Decisive metric first: Spearman correlation between the internal progression signal and ground-truth potency, plus a monotonicity fraction (share of consecutive lineage steps with the correct sign). Convincing: |Spearman| >= 0.5 AND monotonicity >= 0.75, with the shuffled control near 0. Refute: |Spearman| <= 0.2 or monotonicity <= 0.55 (non-monotonic / identity-tracking). Indeterminate band: Spearman 0.2-0.5 or monotonicity 0.55-0.75 (declared up front) -- partial gradient, reported as qualified. A negative result means the axis does not reproduce the potency gradient, weakening clause (a).

Experiment 3 (H2 -- forward vs reverse in-silico transition asymmetry): Tests clause (b), the decisive counterfactual: a forward (differentiation) edit is treated differently from an equal-magnitude reverse (dedifferentiation) edit. Data: along each lineage we build ~2,000 forward edits (shift expression toward the next, more-differentiated real neighbor by up/down-regulating lineage-driver genes) and matched-magnitude reverse edits (toward the previous progenitor neighbor), using real neighboring-state profiles as targets; plus a non-developmental cell-cycle axis (cyclic, reversible) as a double-dissociation control. Model: frozen scFMs, including a generative/masked head where available (scGPT) for plausibility. Systems compared: forward vs reverse edit (matched magnitude), and developmental vs cell-cycle axis. Decisive metric first: Forward-vs-Reverse Asymmetry = |model response to the forward edit| / |model response to the reverse edit| (response = change in internal progression signal and in masked-gene/next-state prediction). Convincing: median asymmetry >= 3 along developmental lineages with the reverse edit flagged as more anomalous/implausible in >=70% of cases, AND the cell-cycle control asymmetry within [0.7, 1.5] (vanishes) -- a double dissociation. Refute: developmental asymmetry in [0.7, 1.5] (forward and reverse treated symmetrically). Indeterminate band 1.5-3 (declared before the data): partial arrow, reported as qualified. Matched magnitude makes any generic off-distribution effect shared. A negative result means the model treats differentiation and dedifferentiation symmetrically, contradicting clause (b).

Experiment 4 (H2 -- branch-point directional specificity): Strengthens clause (b) at lineage bifurcations. Data: known branch points in the three atlases (reused; e.g., endocrine alpha/beta split), each with a pre-commitment progenitor and two fates. Model: frozen scFMs with the progression axis from Experiment 2. Systems compared: internal ordering of progenitor vs both fates, against a similarity-collapse baseline. Decisive metric first: fraction of branch points where the internal direction orders the progenitor before BOTH fates without collapsing them. Convincing: >= 0.8 of branch points ordered correctly, exceeding the similarity baseline by >= 0.2. Refute: <= 0.55 (chance-like / collapsed). Indeterminate band 0.55-0.8 (declared up front): partial, reported as qualified. A negative result means the model collapses divergent fates by similarity, weakening clause (b).

Experiment 5 (H3 -- steering the progression axis produces a signed, asymmetric downstream shift): Tests clause (c). Data: progenitor-vs-differentiated pairs (reused) to recover the axis; cells along lineages as steering targets. Model: frozen scFMs; only the direction is fitted. We steer the recovered developmental-progression axis at matched L2 norm in the forward vs reverse sense. Systems compared: (i) progression axis; (ii) 20 matched-norm random directions; (iii) a static identity-difference direction. Decisive metric first: mechanism-selectivity = |downstream cell-state/potency readout shift under progression steering| / |mean shift under random directions|, together with sign consistency (forward steering lowers potency, reverse raises it). Convincing: selectivity >= 3 with correct signed, asymmetric effect, and the identity-difference direction failing to reproduce it, across probe and delta recovery. Refute: selectivity <= 1.5 or no sign asymmetry. Indeterminate band 1.5-3 (declared before the data): partial causal traction, reported without a strong claim; superposed encoding is the leading alternative. A negative result means the axis is not causally wired to differentiation, contradicting clause (c).

Experiment 6 (H1-H3 -- layer emergence, cross-model convergence, and arrow brackets): Tests robustness of clauses (a)-(c) across depth and models. Data: the three atlases (reused). Model: scGPT, Geneformer, cell2sentence, frozen; probes/directions as above. Systems compared: (i) per-layer Direction-Beyond-Identity Index and steering selectivity; (ii) CKA between recovered progression subspaces across models; (iii) upper bracket = an RNA-velocity/CellRank directional model that encodes the arrow by construction, lower bracket = a static-identity classifier with no directional access. Decisive metric first: fraction of the identity-to-arrow bracket each model closes. Convincing: >=50% closure for at least one model AND cross-model CKA >= 0.5. Refute: all models within noise of the static-identity lower bracket. Indeterminate band: 20-50% closure or CKA 0.3-0.5 (declared up front) -- partial/model-specific, no universality claim. A negative result means no scFM exceeds identity clustering. All runs are inference-only on public models plus small probes and public velocity-annotated atlases, feasible on a single GPU.
Risk Factors and Limitations: Adjacent developmental states are the most similar in expression, so directional signal is entangled with cell-state identity, making the direction-beyond-identity separation statistically demanding; we mitigate with identity/similarity residualization, the forward-vs-reverse counterfactual (which holds edit magnitude fixed and varies only direction), and the cell-cycle (reversible) double-dissociation control.

Ground-truth developmental direction itself comes from RNA velocity/metabolic labeling, which is noisy and can be unreliable in some regions; we use datasets where velocity/pseudotime is well-validated (pancreas, hematopoiesis, dentate gyrus), cross-check with independent potency (CytoTRACE) and known lineage biology, and report sensitivity to ground-truth confidence.

The forward/reverse in-silico edits are synthetic and may push profiles off the model's data distribution, confounding the asymmetry with generic out-of-distribution behavior; we mitigate by matching forward and reverse edit magnitudes (so any generic OOD effect is shared), using real neighboring-state profiles as edit targets where possible, and reporting edit-magnitude sensitivity.

scFMs use different tokenizations (rank-based for Geneformer, value-binned for scGPT, sentence for cell2sentence) and may pool to a single cell embedding, limiting fine-grained edits; we document each model's input scheme, prioritize models exposing usable per-cell representations, and report per-model caveats.

Linear probes recovering a progression direction do not guarantee causal use; we address this with steering plus random/identity-direction controls, though distributed/superposed encodings may blur single-direction interventions - we use both probe directions and delta-representations.

A negative result (scFMs cluster cell states but do not represent the directional, irreversible arrow of differentiation, treating forward and reverse transitions symmetrically) is scientifically decisive and directly relevant to trusting scFMs for trajectory inference, reprogramming, regeneration, and cancer dedifferentiation - precisely the settings where getting the arrow backwards is catastrophic; we frame either outcome as the first mechanism-defining test of whether single-cell foundation models represent the developmental arrow.
All experiments are inference-only on public pretrained models plus small probes and public developmental atlases with velocity/pseudotime ground truth, keeping compute at academic scale.

Name: spatial_tme_relational_probe
Title: Does the Foundation Model See the Neighborhood? Testing Whether Pathology Models Encode Spatial-Relational Tumor-Microenvironment Mechanisms, Not Just Local Morphology
Short Hypothesis: The prognostic and biological mechanism of cancer is not local cell identity alone but the spatial-relational organization of the tumor microenvironment (TME): immune infiltration into tumor nests, spatial exclusion of lymphocytes, tumor-stroma boundary geometry. We hypothesize that pathology foundation models trained on large tissue-patch collections internally encode these relational (neighborhood-context) structures, distinct from and beyond their well-documented local cell-type concepts, and that this relational structure (a) is decodable, (b) is causally load-bearing for prognostic prediction, and (c) matches spatial biology as measured by spatial transcriptomics. If instead the models encode only a bag of local morphologies, patch-context ablations and spatial-relation probes will show no structure beyond local cell counts. We test this at a specified representation level - slide-level neighborhood-attention aggregators and their patch embeddings - and frame the contribution primarily as a controlled evaluation framework (a relational-beyond-local benchmark with matched permutation, causal context-ablation, and spatial-omics validation), not as a new biological mechanism.
Related Work: A wave of pathology interpretability work (PICASSO/Kim et al. 2026; CytoSAE 2025; Mammo-SAE 2025; 'Learning biologically relevant features via SAEs' 2024; ICFL microscopy 2024) uses sparse autoencoders/dictionary learning to recover monosemantic features that match LOCAL morphological annotations — cell types, calcifications, tissue classes. Concept-MIL and ConceptCLIP link patch concepts to diagnosis; representational-similarity and robustness-index papers characterize global embedding geometry and center confounds. Critically, all validate features against MARGINAL, local annotations (what a patch contains), not against the SPATIAL-RELATIONAL organization among cells/regions that constitutes the actual cancer-biology mechanism (immune infiltration, exclusion, boundary structure) known to drive prognosis. No prior work tests whether pathology FMs encode neighborhood-context relational structure, whether that structure is causally used, or whether it aligns with spatial-transcriptomics ground truth. Our relational, causal, spatial-omics-grounded test is the novel contribution, moving beyond 'the model recognizes cell X' to 'the model represents that immune cells are excluded from the tumor nest.' Concretely, what recent neighborhood/spatial-transcriptomics pathology models lack is a control isolating relational signal from local composition: none reports a relational-beyond-local index paired with a composition-matched neighborhood-permutation null and a causal context-ablation, which is the specific gap we fill.
Abstract: Interpretability studies of pathology foundation models have shown they encode local morphological concepts such as cell types and tissue classes. But the mechanism that actually governs cancer behavior and prognosis is relational and spatial: whether cytotoxic lymphocytes infiltrate a tumor nest or are excluded from it, the geometry of the tumor-stroma boundary, and immune-desert versus inflamed ecologies. We ask whether pathology foundation models internally represent this spatial-relational tumor-microenvironment (TME) structure, beyond a bag of local morphologies, and whether that structure is causally load-bearing and biologically faithful. Using public whole-slide datasets with paired or co-registered spatial transcriptomics (e.g., 10x Xenium/Visium colorectal and lung cohorts) and immunohistochemistry, we extract patch- and neighborhood-level representations from several public pathology FMs (UNI2, Virchow2, Prov-GigaPath, CONCH). First, we build relational probes that predict TME relationships defined from cell segmentation and spatial statistics — infiltration score, immune-tumor colocalization/exclusion, boundary curvature — and test whether these are decodable beyond local cell-count baselines. Second, we run causal context-ablation experiments: we swap or scramble a patch's spatial neighbors and measure whether relational features and prognostic predictions change as predicted by TME biology (e.g., breaking infiltration should shift an immune-inflamed feature toward immune-desert). Third, we validate against spatial transcriptomics by testing whether relational features align with measured immune-signaling gene programs (T-cell cytotoxicity, IFN-gamma) at the same tissue location. Metrics quantify a relational-beyond-local index, context-ablation causal selectivity, and transcriptomic alignment. The result informs concrete decisions - biomarker validation, model selection, and deployment auditing - and, if relational structure is absent, motivates redesigning aggregators or supervision rather than only re-benchmarking. We frame this as a representation/mechanism study, not a direct diagnostic advance, and pre-specify leakage-safe splits by patient, slide, center, and stain. Either outcome sharpens what these clinically-deployed models actually 'see.'
Experiments: Experiment 1 (H1 — Relational structure decodable beyond local cell counts): Tests the H1(a) claim that pathology foundation models encode spatial-relational TME structure distinct from local cell identity. Data: public whole-slide-image cohorts (TCGA colorectal COAD/READ and lung LUAD, ~1,000 slides available) with cell segmentation/classification via HoVer-Net, plus co-located spatial transcriptomics (10x Xenium/Visium colorectal and lung); we use 400 slides tiled into ~20,000 neighborhood windows — 400 slides span centers and phenotypes while keeping SAE/probe fitting tractable; all splits are leakage-safe by patient, slide, center, and stain source, and we pre-specify that RBLI > 0.1 counts as support, [0.05, 0.1] as partial support, and <= 0.05 as failure for each descriptor. Ground-truth relational descriptors per window: immune-infiltration score (lymphocyte fraction within tumor nests), immune–tumor spatial exclusion (cross-type Ripley's K), tumor–stroma boundary length/curvature, and inflamed/excluded/desert label. Model: UNI2, Virchow2, Prov-GigaPath, CONCH, all frozen; trainable = ridge probes on patch/neighborhood embeddings and per-model SAEs (dictionary 4,096, L1 1e-3) for candidate relational features; 5 folds, 3 seeds. Systems compared: probe on model representations vs a strict LOCAL baseline given only the same window's cell-type counts/densities (no arrangement). Decisive metric first: Relational-Beyond-Local Index RBLI = probe R²(model) − probe R²(local-count baseline), per relational descriptor. Convincing result: RBLI > 0.1 for infiltration/exclusion/boundary in at least one model, significant over folds. Undecidable band: RBLI in [0.0, 0.05] — no reliable structure beyond bag-of-cells, reported as local-only for that descriptor; band fixed before data. Negative result: RBLI ≤ 0 across models means only local morphology is encoded, H1 fails and the causal/biology tests targeting relational features are moot.

Experiment 2 (H1 — Neighborhood-permutation control): Tests that the Experiment-1 relational signal is genuinely spatial by destroying arrangement while preserving composition. Data: the 20,000 windows; for grid/aggregator models, permute neighbor patches within a window (preserving cell-type counts); where pixel re-embedding is cheap, spatially scramble cells and re-render. Model: same frozen models and fixed Experiment-1 features. Systems compared: relational-feature prediction on true vs scrambled windows, and local-morphology-feature prediction on the same. Decisive metric first: relational-feature drop under scrambling = R²(true) − R²(scrambled), contrasted with the (expected near-zero) drop for local features. Convincing result: relational features collapse under scrambling (drop > 0.1) while local features stay stable (drop < 0.03). Undecidable band: relational drop in [0.03, 0.08] — weak spatial dependence, reported as inconclusive; band fixed before data. Negative result: relational features unchanged by scrambling means the Experiment-1 signal was not truly relational (it rode on composition), undercutting H1.

Experiment 3 (H2 — Causal context-ablation on relational feature and prognosis): Tests the H2(b) claim that relational structure is causally load-bearing — swapping a tumor patch's neighborhood context shifts the 'inflamed' feature and the downstream prediction in the biologically-correct direction. Data: 2,000 tumor windows from Experiment 1 with clear phenotype labels. Model: frozen patch-context / neighborhood-attention models; intervention replaces a tumor patch's true immune-rich neighbors with immune-poor neighbors (and vice versa) at the embedding level; control swaps with neighbors matched on stain/center but same TME phenotype (should not shift); 3 seeds. Systems compared: relation-breaking swap vs matched-phenotype control. Decisive metric first: context-ablation causal selectivity = |shift_relation-breaking| / |shift_matched-control| for the inflamed feature and for the subtype/prognostic head. Convincing result: selectivity ≥ 3 with shifts in the biologically-correct direction. Undecidable band: selectivity in [1.2, 2.0] — weak causal use, reported as inconclusive; band fixed before data. Negative result: selectivity ≈ 1 means the relational feature is decodable but not causal for prediction, H2 fails.

Experiment 4 (H3 — Spatial-transcriptomics faithfulness): Tests the H3(c) claim that recovered relational features match spatial biology beyond local composition. Data: co-registered spatial-transcriptomics spots (Xenium/Visium) at Experiment-1 windows, using immune-signaling gene programs (T-cell cytotoxicity, IFN-γ response, exhaustion) as ground truth; restricted to high-quality-registration datasets. Model: frozen models, fixed relational features. Systems compared: relational feature vs measured gene program, controlling for local cell composition. Decisive metric first: partial Spearman ρ between the relational feature and the gene program, partialling out local cell-type composition. Convincing result: partial ρ ≥ 0.3 retained after the composition control, in ≥2 programs. Undecidable band: partial ρ in [0.1, 0.2] — weak residual signal, reported as inconclusive; band fixed before data. Negative result: partial ρ ≈ 0 after control means the feature adds nothing over local composition in explaining spatial biology, H3 fails.

Experiment 5 (H2 — Prognostic load-bearing and center-confound control): Tests the clinically-relevant half of H2(b) — that prognostic signal rides on relational features — while ruling out center/stain artifacts. Data: TCGA cohorts with survival (COAD/READ, LUAD; ~800 slides with outcome). Model: frozen models; feature-group ablation removes relational vs local feature groups from a Cox/discrete-time survival head fit on top of frozen features; center/stain confound controlled via the Robustness-Index approach (hold out centers, report stratified performance); 3 seeds. Systems compared: survival performance with vs without relational features, and across held-out centers. Decisive metric first: drop in concordance index (C-index) when relational features are ablated, and its stability across centers. Convincing result: relational-feature ablation drops C-index by ≥ 0.03 and the drop persists across held-out centers (not a center artifact). Undecidable band: C-index drop in [0.0, 0.015] or a drop that vanishes under center stratification — reported as no robust prognostic contribution; band fixed before data. Negative result: no C-index drop, or drop explained by center confound, means relational structure is not prognostically load-bearing, bounding H2.
Risk Factors and Limitations: Grid-based FMs process patches independently, so 'context' must come from the slide-level aggregator; models with weak or absent spatial context may show no relational structure by construction — we report per-model and use neighborhood-attention aggregators where available.

Re-rendering scrambled tissue for causal ablation is nontrivial; for patch-grid models we operate at the neighbor-patch level (permute/swap embeddings), which is feasible, while pixel-level scrambling is used only where re-embedding is cheap.

Co-registration between H&E and spatial transcriptomics is imperfect, adding noise to the transcriptomic-faithfulness test; we use datasets with high-quality registration and report registration-error sensitivity.

Local cell counts and spatial relations are correlated in real tissue, making the relational-beyond-local separation statistically demanding; we mitigate with matched controls and partial-correlation analyses but residual confounding may attenuate effects.
Center/stain confounds strongly organize pathology embeddings (per the Robustness-Index literature); relational signal could be confounded and we explicitly control for it.

A negative result (models encode only local morphology, no relational TME structure) is scientifically decisive and clinically important, though possibly perceived as confirmatory of skepticism; we frame either outcome as a sharpening of what deployed pathology FMs represent.
All experiments are inference-only on public pretrained models plus small probes/SAEs and public data, keeping compute at academic scale.

Name: hill_cooperativity_shape_probe
Title: Steepness Is Not Potency: Testing Whether Drug-Response Foundation Models Represent the Cooperative Hill Dose-Response Mechanism, Not Just Where the Curve Sits
Short Hypothesis: The dose-response of a drug is governed by an exactly-known relational mechanism, the Hill equation: response is a sigmoidal function of dose whose LOCATION is set by potency (IC50/EC50) but whose STEEPNESS is set by the Hill coefficient nH, which encodes cooperativity/multi-site binding (nH=1 is non-cooperative Michaelis-Menten-like; nH>1 is positively cooperative, ultrasensitive; nH<1 is negatively cooperative). Potency and cooperativity are physically independent axes: two drugs with identical IC50 can have completely different curve shapes and therefore different therapeutic windows and safety margins. We hypothesize that if drug-response foundation models represent this mechanism rather than a scalar potency proxy, then (a) the Hill coefficient (curve shape/cooperativity) is decodable from internal representations along an axis distinct from potency, (b) a shape-vs-potency counterfactual - changing nH at fixed IC50 versus changing IC50 at fixed nH - moves the two internal signals separately, and (c) steering a recovered 'cooperativity' direction causally reshapes predicted dose-response steepness without shifting its location. The shape-holding counterfactual is an exact, mechanism-defining test that dose-response prediction accuracy and potency correlation cannot provide.
Related Work: The Hill equation is the century-old, exactly-known model of dose-response and cooperativity (A hundred years of the Hill equation 2013; Hill coefficients, dose-response curves and allosteric mechanisms 2009; multiphasic dose-response fitting 2015 shows ~28% of curves need beyond-Hill shape), and it explicitly separates potency (IC50) from cooperativity (nH). Drug-response and pharmacology ML - DrugCell, cell-viability foundation models, and molecular-property FMs - predict dose-response or IC50 from drug/cell features, and interpretability of chemistry/toxicity models (Interpreting NN Toxicity Prediction by Extracting Learned Chemical Features 2024; SAE studies on chemistry FMs; MoleX) recovers substructure/functional-group features validated against POINTWISE, potency-like annotations. Physics/scientific-model interpretability (From Neurons to Neutrons 2024; Physics Steering 2025) recovers and steers single scalar quantities, and 'What Has a Foundation Model Found?' (2025) shows models often learn task-specific heuristics rather than the underlying world model. Crucially, no interpretability work tests whether a drug-response FM internally represents the RELATIONAL Hill mechanism - specifically that curve STEEPNESS/cooperativity (nH) is a distinct axis from potency (IC50) - whether that shape representation is causally load-bearing, or uses a shape-holding counterfactual to separate cooperativity from potency. Because nH and IC50 are entangled and both correlate with overall efficacy in screening data, correlation-based benchmarks and pointwise-feature interpretability cannot arbitrate this. Our cooperativity-beyond-potency probe, shape-vs-potency counterfactual, and causal steepness steering are the novel, mechanism-defining contribution, and they land in a safety-critical setting because curve steepness (Hill coefficient) directly governs therapeutic window and toxicity margins. Precisely, the novelty is representation-level — whether a pretrained drug-response model encodes Hill curve shape (cooperativity, nH) as a latent factor independent of potency (IC50), demonstrated via an internal double dissociation and causal steering — not the Hill separation itself (textbook) nor a new IC50 predictor; we report evidence for or against separable encoding rather than complete mechanistic causality. IC50-prediction and curve-fitting work and pointwise chemistry interpretability cannot test this because nH and IC50 are entangled and both correlate with efficacy. So what: models that ignore steepness can mis-rank safety margins even when IC50 is accurate, so pharmacology-ML groups should evaluate nH (not just IC50) and prefer curve-predicting over scalar-only models — the audience being drug-response ML developers, benchmark designers, and safety/toxicity modelers.
Abstract: A drug's dose-response curve is described by an exactly-known relational mechanism, the Hill equation: response rises sigmoidally with dose, its location fixed by potency (IC50) and its steepness fixed by the Hill coefficient, which encodes cooperativity and multi-site binding. These are physically independent axes - two drugs with identical potency can have radically different curve shapes, and the shape (steepness) determines the therapeutic window and safety margin. This makes the Hill equation an ideal, mechanism-defining probe for whether drug-response foundation models learn the underlying pharmacological mechanism or merely a scalar potency proxy. We probe pretrained drug-response and molecular-property foundation models on large cell-viability screens (GDSC, PRISM, NCI-60) whose curves are fitted to Hill parameters. First, a cooperativity-beyond-potency probe: is the Hill coefficient (curve steepness) decodable from internal representations along an axis distinct from potency? Second, and most decisively, a shape-vs-potency counterfactual: using controlled synthetic and matched real curves we change the Hill coefficient at fixed IC50 (reshape without relocating) versus change IC50 at fixed Hill (relocate without reshaping), and test whether the two internal signals move independently - a mechanistic representation separates them, a potency-proxy representation collapses shape onto location. Third, causal steepness steering: perturbing a recovered cooperativity direction should reshape the predicted curve's steepness without shifting its midpoint. Metrics quantify a cooperativity-beyond-potency index, a shape-potency disentanglement ratio, and a Hill-fidelity dose-response test. Either outcome sharpens whether deployed drug-response models represent the curve-shape mechanism that governs drug safety. The concrete consequence is that a potency-proxy model can rank two drugs with identical IC50 but different therapeutic windows identically; the audit therefore supplies a curve-shape evaluation criterion for model selection and benchmarking in drug-response ML, and a negative result argues for shape-aware training targets rather than potency-only objectives.
Experiments: Experiment 1 (H1 — Hill coefficient decodable along an axis distinct from potency): Tests clause (a): the Hill coefficient nH (curve shape/cooperativity) is decodable from internal representations along an axis distinct from potency. Data: fitted dose-response curves from GDSC1/2, PRISM Repurposing, and NCI-60 (together several hundred thousand drug–cell curves with fitted IC50, nH, Emax and raw points); use 30,000 well-sampled high-confidence curves (18k train / 3k val / 9k test, split by drug so no drug crosses splits) plus synthetic Hill curves for exact control — fewer than the full screens because we require ≥6 dose points and a confident single-Hill fit. Model: a transformer dose-response predictor trained on GDSC (DrugCell-style) and ChemBERTa-2 (~46M parameters) on the drug SMILES, frozen; only ridge probes on the best layer, seeds 0–4. Systems compared: probe R^2 for nH from the representation vs a baseline predicting nH from IC50 and Emax and simple raw-curve features, representation residualized against potency; also the angle between the recovered potency and cooperativity probe directions. Decisive metric (first): Cooperativity-Beyond-Potency Index = R^2(nH | representation) − R^2(nH | potency+Emax features). Convincing: Index ≥ 0.15 (95% CI lower bound above 0.05) and potency–cooperativity axis angle ≥ 60 degrees (near-orthogonal). Indecision band: Index in [−0.03, 0.05] or axis angle in [30, 45] degrees — shape barely separable from potency; clause (a) fails or is inconclusive here. Negative result: Index ≤ −0.03 or angle < 30 degrees — shape collapses onto potency, a scalar-potency-proxy representation.

Experiment 2 (H2 — shape-vs-potency double-dissociation counterfactual): Tests clause (b): changing nH at fixed IC50 versus changing IC50 at fixed nH moves the two internal signals separately. Data: matched curve pairs — (reshape) change nH holding IC50 fixed; (relocate) change IC50 holding nH fixed — built from 4,000 synthetic Hill curves (exact control) plus real drug–cell pairs from the Experiment-1 test set selected to differ in one parameter at a time. Model/probe as Experiment 1, seeds 0–4; read-outs are the potency and cooperativity probes. Systems compared: movement of each internal signal under each edit. Decisive metrics (first): Reshape Ratio = |Δcooperativity signal| / |Δpotency signal| under the reshape edit; Relocate Ratio = |Δpotency signal| / |Δcooperativity signal| under the relocate edit. Convincing: both ratios ≥ 3 (each edit moves its own axis — a double dissociation). Indecision band: either ratio in [0.7, 2.0] — the two axes are not cleanly separable; clause (b) fails or is inconclusive here. Negative result: ratios ≈ 1 or shape moving whenever location moves — shape is collapsed onto location.

Experiment 3 (H2 — Hill-shape fidelity / ultrasensitivity): Tests the quantitative content of clause (b): the model's predicted curve follows a Hill sigmoid with the correct steepness. Data: the same 9,000 test curves; sweep dose finely and fit the model's predicted response to a Hill equation. Model/probe as above, seeds 0–4. Systems compared: model-implied nH vs true nH; shuffled-nH labels as null; a check that nH>1 curves come out sharper than nH=1. Decisive metric (first): Spearman rho and slope between model-implied nH and true nH. Convincing: rho ≥ 0.6, correct sign, slope within ±30% of 1.0, and ultrasensitive (nH>1) curves reproduced as sharper. Indecision band: rho in [0.2, 0.4] — weak steepness tracking; inconclusive on quantitative fidelity. Negative result: rho < 0.2 or a single canonical steepness for all drugs — no cooperativity mechanism represented.

Experiment 4 (H3 — causal cooperativity steering): Tests clause (c): steering a recovered 'cooperativity' direction reshapes predicted steepness without shifting its location. Data: 9,000 test curves; direction recovered as a supervised nH-probe direction, an SAE feature separating steep from shallow curves, and a delta-representation between high-nH and low-nH cases at matched IC50. Model/probe as above; add matched-norm perturbations along the cooperativity direction at the best layer and re-read the predicted curve, seeds 0–4. Systems compared: cooperativity direction vs a matched potency direction vs matched-norm random directions. Decisive metrics (first): Steering Selectivity = |steepness change from cooperativity steering| / |steepness change from random steering|; Cross-talk = |IC50 shift from cooperativity steering| in log-dose units. Convincing: selectivity ≥ 3 with cross-talk ≤ 0.1 log-dose units (steepness changes, midpoint essentially fixed), while the potency direction shifts IC50 without changing steepness. Indecision band: selectivity in [0.7, 2.0] or cross-talk in (0.1, 0.3] log-dose — steering is non-selective or entangled; clause (c) fails or is inconclusive here. Negative result: selectivity ≈ 1 — no dedicated causal cooperativity direction.
Risk Factors and Limitations: nH and IC50 are entangled in screening data (both correlate with overall efficacy and with drug/target class), making the cooperativity-beyond-potency separation statistically demanding; we mitigate with potency-residualization, the shape-vs-potency double-dissociation counterfactual (which holds one parameter fixed while varying the other), and synthetic Hill curves giving exact independent control.

Fitted Hill coefficients from screening data are noisy, especially for curves with few doses or shallow responses, adding label noise to nH; we restrict primary analyses to well-sampled, high-confidence fits, use synthetic curves for the decisive counterfactual, and report sensitivity to fit-quality thresholds; multiphasic curves are analyzed separately.

Some drug-response FMs take only drug and cell-line identity (not a curve) as input and output a single scalar (e.g., IC50), so 'representing curve shape' may be architecturally out of scope for them; we prioritize models that predict full dose-response curves or ingest dose, clearly report per-model scope, and treat scalar-only models as an informative lower bracket that by construction cannot represent nH.

Operationalizing the shape/potency edits depends on the model's input format (curve-in vs identity-in); for identity-in models we test whether the internal representation nonetheless encodes nH as a distinct axis and use synthetic-curve models where a curve can be manipulated directly, reporting the caveat.

Linear probes recovering a cooperativity direction do not guarantee causal use; we address this with steering, cross-talk controls, and random-direction controls, though distributed/superposed encodings may blur single-direction interventions - we use both probe directions and SAE features.

A negative result (models encode a scalar potency proxy and collapse curve shape onto location, failing the shape-vs-potency counterfactual) is scientifically decisive and directly safety-relevant - it would warn that deployed drug-response models miss the cooperativity/steepness information that determines therapeutic window and toxicity margin, especially for ultrasensitive or multiphasic drugs; we frame either outcome as the first mechanism-defining test of whether drug-response foundation models represent the Hill cooperative dose-response mechanism.
All experiments are inference-only on public pretrained models plus small probes/SAEs and public dose-response datasets (GDSC, PRISM, NCI-60), keeping compute at academic scale.

Name: contralateral_symmetry_probe
Title: Compared to the Other Side? Testing Whether Radiology Foundation Models Represent the Bilateral-Symmetry Comparison Mechanism, Not Just Local Texture
Short Hypothesis: A large, clinically dominant class of radiological findings is defined RELATIONALLY by bilateral asymmetry: the body is approximately bilaterally symmetric, so radiologists call a region abnormal when it DIFFERS from its contralateral counterpart (one whiter lung, one denser breast, one effusion-filled hemithorax), and the identical local texture appearing symmetrically on both sides is often a normal variant or systemic. We hypothesize that if radiology foundation models represent this contralateral-comparison mechanism rather than absolute local texture, then (a) a region's abnormality signal is decodable from internal representations beyond what its local patch texture alone predicts, (b) a symmetry counterfactual - implanting the same abnormal-looking texture bilaterally (symmetric, should suppress asymmetry-defined pathology) versus unilaterally (asymmetric, pathology) - shifts the internal finding signal accordingly, whereas a texture-only model responds identically, and (c) the effect causally depends on the contralateral region. The bilateral-vs-unilateral implant is an exact, mechanism-defining counterfactual that texture-based correlation and concept-alignment interpretability cannot provide.
Related Work: Radiology-imaging interpretability is dominated by (i) shortcut/spurious-feature detection and mitigation (Detecting Shortcuts in Chest X-Rays 2023; 'Shortcuts Causing Bias in Radiology AI' 2023; RoentMod counterfactual editing 2025; Reveal2Revise medical-AI-safety 2025; Weight-Space Correlation feature-utilization 2025), (ii) concept dissection and alignment (Mammo-CLIP Dissect 2025; Mammo-SAE 2025; expert-labeled CNN units 2018), and (iii) representation-quality/robustness critiques (ViT semantic-meaningfulness 2025; pathology representational-similarity 2025) and anatomy-aware SSL (AFiRe 2025, RayDINO 2024, EXACT 2026). All of these test whether features are spurious, whether units align with named concepts, or whether representations are robust - i.e. LOCAL, per-region annotation-matching or shortcut auditing. None tests whether the model internally performs the RELATIONAL contralateral (bilateral-symmetry) COMPARISON that formally defines a major class of radiological findings, whether that comparison is causally load-bearing, or uses a bilateral-vs-unilateral implant counterfactual to separate the symmetry mechanism from absolute texture. Because abnormal texture and abnormal asymmetry co-occur in real scans, correlation and concept-alignment cannot arbitrate this. Our relational-beyond-local probe, symmetric-vs-asymmetric implant counterfactual, and causal contralateral-ablation are the novel, mechanism-defining contribution, moving beyond 'the model sees the opacity' to 'the model represents that this side differs from the other.' To be precise about the delta: this is not a new symmetry-aware architecture (Siamese/contralateral CXR and mammography models already exist and build the comparison in) but a mechanism-level audit of whether frozen, general pretrained FMs spontaneously instantiate the contralateral comparison — a falsifiable, causal test (the bilateral-vs-unilateral implant plus contralateral ablation) reported as evidence for or against contralateral comparison in representations, not definitive clinical mechanistic causality. Shortcut-detection, concept-alignment, and robustness work test local per-region features, not the relational comparison. Because bilateral asymmetry drives a large fraction of clinically important findings (effusion, pneumothorax, asymmetric density), a model that reads absolute texture would produce false positives on symmetric normal variants and false negatives when contralateral context matters. Who would use it: FM developers, radiology benchmark designers, and clinical-AI safety auditors.
Abstract: Radiologists diagnose a large fraction of findings not by absolute local appearance but by comparison: the body is approximately bilaterally symmetric, so a whiter lung, a denser breast, or a fluid-filled hemithorax is flagged because it differs from the opposite side, while the same texture appearing on both sides is often a normal variant. This relational bilateral-symmetry mechanism is exactly known and clinically central, making it an ideal probe for whether radiology foundation models learn mechanism or merely local texture. We test whether models such as RayDINO, a multi-anatomy X-ray encoder, and Mammo-CLIP internally represent the contralateral-comparison mechanism, using public chest X-ray (MIMIC-CXR, CheXpert) and mammography data with lateralized finding labels. First, a relational-beyond-local probe: is a region's abnormality decodable from internal representations beyond what its local patch texture alone predicts, and does the recovered signal track left-right difference? Second, and most decisively, a symmetry counterfactual: using anatomically realistic image editing we implant the same abnormal-looking texture either bilaterally (symmetric, which for asymmetry-defined findings should suppress the pathology signal) or unilaterally (asymmetric, pathology), and measure whether the internal finding signal responds to the asymmetry rather than the raw texture; a texture-only model responds identically to both. Third, causal contralateral ablation: masking or replacing the opposite side should shift the finding signal for a mechanism-representing model but not a local one. Metrics quantify a relational-beyond-local index, a bilateral-vs-unilateral causal asymmetry, and a contralateral-dependence ratio. Either outcome sharpens whether deployed radiology models diagnose for the right relational reason. If deployed models lack the comparison, evaluation practice should add lateralized and symmetric-variant test cases and model selection should favor per-region/contralateral-aware encoders; the audit thus becomes a benchmarking and model-selection tool for clinical-AI developers rather than an interpretability curiosity.
Experiments: Experiment 1 (H1 — abnormality decodable beyond local patch texture): Tests clause (a): a region's abnormality signal is decodable from internal representations beyond what its local patch texture alone predicts. Data: MIMIC-CXR (~377k chest radiographs) and CheXpert (~224k) for asymmetry-defined findings (pleural effusion, pneumothorax, unilateral consolidation, asymmetric opacity), plus CBIS-DDSM (~10k mammograms) for breast asymmetry/density; use 5,000 chest images (3,000 train / 500 val / 1,500 test, split by patient) with laterality-annotatable findings — fewer than the full sets because we require reliable laterality and near-symmetric anatomy.
