Model: RayDINO (chest X-ray ViT SSL encoder, ~300M parameters, per-patch tokens) and patch-level Mammo-CLIP, frozen; only a logistic probe on the best layer, seeds 0–4. Systems compared: pathology decoding from the region representation vs a strict local-texture baseline (probe seeing only the target patch, no contralateral context), representation residualized against the local-patch features; absolute-texture-defined findings (e.g., calcifications) serve as a built-in double-dissociation control expected to show near-zero relational signal. Decisive metric (first): Relational-Beyond-Local Index = balanced accuracy(pathology | region representation) − balanced accuracy(pathology | local patch). Convincing: Index ≥ 0.10 (95% CI lower bound above 0.03) for asymmetry-defined findings and ≤ 0.03 for texture-defined controls. Indecision band: Index in [−0.02, 0.03] — within probe noise; a result here means no contralateral information beyond local texture and clause (a) fails. Negative result: Index ≤ −0.02 or in band for asymmetry-defined findings — the model reads absolute local texture, not the bilateral comparison.

Experiment 2 (H2 — bilateral vs unilateral implant counterfactual): Tests clause (b): implanting the same abnormal-looking texture bilaterally (symmetric, should suppress asymmetry-defined pathology) versus unilaterally (asymmetric, pathology) shifts the internal finding signal, whereas a texture-only model responds identically. Data: 1,000 near-symmetric test images (lung fields/breast parenchyma) from Experiment 1; using anatomically realistic editing (RoentMod-style insertion for chest X-ray; controlled contralateral copy for symmetric implants) build matched pairs — (unilateral) implant on one side; (bilateral) the same texture on both sides — matched on total implanted texture and edit realism. Model/probe as Experiment 1, seeds 0–4; read-out is the pathology probe and classification head. Systems compared: |finding-signal change| under unilateral vs under bilateral implant, per finding type. Decisive metric (first): Bilateral-vs-Unilateral Causal Asymmetry = median(|Δsignal unilateral|) / median(|Δsignal bilateral|). Convincing: asymmetry ≥ 3 (unilateral raises the finding, bilateral suppresses it). Indecision band: asymmetry in [0.7, 2.0] — both edits raise the signal comparably; clause (b) fails here (texture-counting reading). Negative result: asymmetry ≈ 1, i.e., the model counts implanted texture regardless of symmetry, not the contralateral comparison.

Experiment 3 (H3 — contralateral-region ablation): Tests clause (c): the finding effect causally depends on the contralateral region. Data: 1,000 test images with a genuine unilateral finding; mask/replace the healthy contralateral region with a matched normal patch and measure the change in the finding signal on the untouched pathological side. Model/probe as above, seeds 0–4. Systems compared: contralateral ablation vs a matched-size, matched-distance ipsilateral non-diagnostic ablation (control). Decisive metric (first): Contralateral-Dependence Ratio = |Δfinding signal under contralateral ablation| / |Δfinding signal under ipsilateral-control ablation|. Convincing: ratio ≥ 3 — removing the reference side materially changes the judgment while an equal ipsilateral removal does not. Indecision band: ratio in [0.7, 2.0] — the contralateral side is no more load-bearing than an ipsilateral region; clause (c) fails here. Negative result: ratio ≈ 1, i.e., the judgment is unaffected by removing the reference side — a local-texture model.
Risk Factors and Limitations: Abnormal texture and abnormal asymmetry co-occur in real scans, making the relational-beyond-local separation statistically demanding; we mitigate with local-patch residualization, the bilateral-vs-unilateral implant counterfactual (which holds implanted texture fixed and varies only symmetry), the absolute-texture-defined-finding double-dissociation control, and matched ipsilateral-ablation controls.

The implant and ablation counterfactuals are synthetic edits; anatomically unrealistic implants (especially bilateral copies) could push images off the model's data distribution, confounding the effect with generic OOD failure. We mitigate with validated realistic editing (RoentMod-style for chest X-ray, careful contralateral mirroring/copy for controlled texture), report realism/artifact diagnostics, and compare unilateral vs bilateral edits of matched realism so any OOD effect is shared.

Bilateral symmetry is only approximate (cardiac silhouette, gastric bubble, handedness), so a truly symmetric implant is not perfectly normal; we restrict primary tests to anatomically near-symmetric regions (lung fields, breast parenchyma) and report sensitivity, and we use radiologist-adjudicated laterality labels where available.

Some findings ARE defined by absolute texture (calcifications, specific nodules) rather than asymmetry; we explicitly separate asymmetry-defined from texture-defined findings and use the latter as a negative control rather than expecting a relational signal.

Foundation models that pool to a single global embedding limit per-region/contralateral analysis; we prioritize models exposing per-patch spatial representations (RayDINO, ViT patch tokens, patch-level Mammo-CLIP) and report pooling caveats.

Linear probes recovering an asymmetry direction do not guarantee causal use; we address this with steering, contralateral ablation, and random/texture-direction controls, though distributed/superposed encodings may blur single-direction interventions.

A negative result (models diagnose from absolute local texture and respond identically to symmetric vs asymmetric implants, failing the contralateral-ablation test) is scientifically decisive and directly safety-relevant - it would warn that deployed radiology models miss the relational comparison radiologists rely on, risking false positives on symmetric normal variants and false negatives when contralateral context matters; we frame either outcome as the first mechanism-defining test of whether radiology foundation models represent the bilateral-symmetry comparison mechanism.

All experiments are inference-only on public pretrained models plus small probes and public radiology datasets (MIMIC-CXR, CheXpert, CBIS-DDSM/VinDr-Mammo) with validated counterfactual editing tools, keeping compute at academic scale.

Name: sabatier_volcano_probe
Title: Too Weak or Too Strong? Testing Whether Catalysis Foundation Models Internally Represent the Sabatier Volcano, Not Just Monotone Binding Energy
Short Hypothesis: Catalytic activity follows the Sabatier principle: it is a NON-MONOTONE, relational function of intermediate binding energy — optimal at an intermediate value, with activity limited by poor reactant activation when binding is too weak and by poor product desorption when binding is too strong. Models trained to predict pointwise adsorption energies (e.g., on OC20) are never required to learn this two-sided, rate-determining-step structure. We hypothesize that if a catalysis foundation model internally represents the mechanism, its representation will (a) encode the volcano's two-sided distance-to-peak, (b) distinguish weak-binding-limited from strong-binding-limited catalysts even when their binding-energy deviation magnitudes are equal, and (c) causally track the switch in rate-determining step across the peak; a pointwise/monotone representation collapses the two limiting regimes. The opposite-side-of-the-peak counterfactual is an exact, mechanism-defining test that monotone binding-energy prediction cannot pass.
Related Work: Post-hoc XAI on shallow catalysis ML (SHAP/LIME/symbolic regression on adsorption-energy predictors; 'Explainable Data-driven Modeling of Adsorption Energy' 2024; HEA scaling-relation studies 2023; 'Beyond Scaling Relations' 2019; AutoML feature-deletion 2024) recovers descriptors and MONOTONE linear scaling relations, and volcano-plot ML (Meyer et al. 2018; Sharma et al. 2024 'Mapping and Reshaping the Activity Volcano') USES models to construct volcanoes downstream. Interpretability of atomistic foundation models ('Comparing latent features of uMLIPs' 2025; 'Beyond Converging Representations' 2025; CGCNN interpretability 2018) recovers pointwise site energies and characterizes latent geometry. Crucially, all of these either (i) attribute features to a monotone adsorption-energy target, or (ii) apply the model's energy predictions to build a volcano externally. None tests whether the model's INTERNAL representation encodes the Sabatier principle itself — the non-monotone, two-sided, rate-determining-step structure that defines catalytic activity — nor uses an opposite-side-of-the-peak counterfactual to separate weak- from strong-binding limitation. Because these models are trained on pointwise adsorption energies, whether they internalize the relational volcano mechanism is untested; that is our novel, mechanism-defining contribution. We reframe the novelty around a precisely defined mechanistic property -- internal separation of the rate-determining-step regime (weak-binding-limited vs strong-binding-limited) at matched |deviation| from the peak -- which is provably not a monotone transform of the scalar adsorption-energy label the model was trained on, and therefore not trivially recoverable. This is a mechanistic-interpretability test, not a new activity predictor; the new task is inferring the limiting regime from representation under matched-energy confounds. Causal steering is secondary and reported only for models with an activity-relatable head.
Abstract: The central organizing principle of heterogeneous catalysis is the Sabatier principle: catalytic activity is a non-monotone function of how strongly a surface binds key intermediates, peaking at an intermediate binding strength. Below the peak, activity is limited by weak reactant activation; above it, by poor product desorption. This yields the iconic volcano plot — a relational, two-sided mechanism in which the rate-determining step switches across the summit. Catalysis foundation models are trained to predict pointwise adsorption energies (e.g., on the Open Catalyst dataset), a target that never requires learning this two-sided structure, so whether they internalize the Sabatier mechanism is unknown. We probe pretrained catalysis foundation models (e.g., GemNet-OC, EquiformerV2, and universal MLIPs on OC20/OC22 systems) at the representation level. First, a two-sided volcano probe: we test whether the model's internal representation encodes signed distance-to-peak and, critically, on which SIDE of the peak a catalyst lies, beyond what its scalar binding energy alone predicts. Second, and most decisively, an opposite-side counterfactual: we pair a too-weak-binding catalyst with a too-strong-binding one whose binding-energy deviation from the peak has equal magnitude but opposite sign, so their activities are similar but their limiting mechanisms opposite; a Sabatier-aware representation must separate them into weak- versus strong-limited regimes, while a monotone representation collapses them. Third, causal steering across the peak tests whether the internal rate-determining-step signal flips as predicted. Metrics quantify a volcano-side-beyond-energy index, an opposite-side separation ratio, and a rate-determining-step flip asymmetry. Either outcome sharpens whether deployed catalyst-discovery models represent the mechanism they are used to optimize. The downstream decision is whether foundation-model embeddings can be used for mechanistic screening (ranking near-peak catalysts and diagnosing the limiting step), not just adsorption-energy prediction: if the representation is monotone and collapses the two regimes (the null), volcano plots and near-peak rankings built from these models are unreliable and need external microkinetic re-scoring; if the two-sided structure is encoded, embeddings support mechanistic catalyst screening. Users are OC20/OC22 benchmark users, catalysis-ML practitioners, and experimental/theoretical catalyst designers. We pre-register the volcano-side-beyond-energy index as the primary falsifiable endpoint.
Experiments: Experiment 1 (H1 — two-sided volcano side encoded beyond scalar binding energy): Tests assertion (a): the representation encodes the volcano's two-sided distance-to-peak (which SIDE, at fixed magnitude) beyond the scalar binding energy. Data (existing): well-characterized reactions with established descriptors and DFT/experimental volcano data -- hydrogen evolution (H* binding), oxygen reduction (O*/OH* binding), CO oxidation, and ammonia synthesis (N* binding) -- across transition-metal surfaces and alloys from the Open Catalyst dataset (OC20/OC22); for each catalyst-reaction pair we record key-intermediate binding energy, known volcano peak, signed distance-to-peak, limiting-step side, and a proxy activity (thermodynamic limiting potential / microkinetic turnover). We use several thousand catalyst-reaction pairs across the four reactions. Models (frozen, inference only): an OC20 adsorption-energy predictor (GemNet-OC and/or EquiformerV2) and the universal MLIP MACE-MP-0 on the same surfaces; pooled per-structure activations per layer. Trainable: linear probes only (3 seeds). Systems compared: representation probe vs a scalar-binding-energy predictor. Decisive metric first: Volcano-Side-Beyond-Energy Index = signed-distance-to-peak sign-classification accuracy from the representation minus the accuracy from scalar binding energy alone, at matched |deviation| (so magnitude is controlled). Indecision band up front: an index in [0.03, 0.10] (accuracy points) cannot decide and is reported as ambiguous two-sided encoding; index >= 0.10 with CI lower bound > 0.03 is convincing Sabatier-side encoding; index <= 0.03 means the representation is monotone in binding energy (sign collapses), supporting the pointwise hypothesis.

Experiment 2 (H2 — opposite-side counterfactual, decisive): Tests assertion (b): the model internally distinguishes weak-binding-limited from strong-binding-limited catalysts even when their binding-energy deviations are equal in magnitude. Data (constructed from existing): matched catalyst pairs -- one too-weak, one too-strong -- with equal-magnitude, opposite-sign deviations from the peak (similar proxy activity, opposite limiting mechanism), plus same-side control pairs matched on |deviation|, drawn from the OC20 systems above. Model: same frozen models. Systems compared: opposite-side pairs vs same-side control pairs. Decisive metric first: Opposite-Side Separation Ratio = representational distance(opposite-side pair) / representational distance(same-side, same-|deviation| pair), CI over pairs, reported across reactions and as a function of |deviation|. Indecision band up front: a ratio whose CI lies in [1.1, 1.5] cannot decide and is reported as weak two-sided structure; CI lower bound > 1.5 is convincing that opposite limiting regimes are internally distinguished; CI upper bound < 1.1 (only magnitude matters, sign collapses) is the monotone/pointwise signature. This is the decisive test; a null is the headline negative result about volcano representation.

Experiment 3 (H3 — causal across-peak steering of the rate-determining step): Tests assertion (c): the model causally tracks the switch in rate-determining step across the peak -- steering a signed distance-to-peak direction should move predicted activity non-monotonically. Data: catalysts at, below, and above the peak from Experiment 1, for models with an activity-relatable head (reported per model). Model: frozen; the signed direction is a supervised probe (or SAE feature) separating the two sides, no backbone training. Procedure: steer at matched magnitude toward the strong- or weak-binding side and read predicted activity -- moving a peak catalyst either way should DECREASE activity, moving a too-strong catalyst toward the peak should INCREASE it. Controls: matched-norm random directions and a pure binding-energy-magnitude direction. Decisive metric first: Rate-Determining-Step Flip Asymmetry = fraction of steers producing the volcano-predicted (non-monotone) activity change, and mechanism-selectivity = |volcano-consistent effect| / |random-direction effect|, CIs over catalysts. Indecision band up front: selectivity CI in [1.3, 2.0], or flip fraction CI spanning 0.5, cannot decide (no clean causal two-sided handle); selectivity CI lower bound > 2.0 with flip fraction > 0.6 is convincing causal two-sided encoding; selectivity CI upper bound < 1.3 means the direction is not causally two-sided. A negative result, with H1-H2 nulls, supports the monotone conclusion and warns against trusting these models to rank near-peak catalysts.
Risk Factors and Limitations: Binding energy and volcano side are correlated across a catalyst set (side is the sign of the deviation), so the beyond-energy separation is statistically demanding; we mitigate with the opposite-side counterfactual that matches |deviation| exactly and controls that regress out binding-energy magnitude.

The 'true' volcano peak and limiting-step side depend on the chosen descriptor and microkinetic assumptions; we restrict to well-established reactions (HER, ORR, CO oxidation, NH3 synthesis) with consensus descriptors and report sensitivity to peak-location and activity-proxy choices.

Adsorption-energy foundation models may not natively output an 'activity' quantity; we derive proxy activity externally (thermodynamic limiting potential / microkinetic turnover) for ground truth and probe whether the internal representation nonetheless organizes by the two-sided structure. This is a strength (mechanism need not be in the training target) but limits the causal-steering readout to models with an activity-relatable head; we report per-model.

Steering in nonlinear equivariant networks can push representations off-manifold; we bound perturbation magnitude, report sensitivity, and use matched-norm and binding-energy-direction controls, relying primarily on the input-space opposite-side counterfactual as causal-adjacent evidence.

Linear probes recovering a volcano-side direction do not guarantee causal use; distributed/superposed encodings may blur single-direction interventions — we use both probe directions and SAE features and report aggregate-direction results.

A negative result (models encode monotone binding energy but collapse the two limiting regimes) is scientifically decisive and directly relevant to trusting catalysis foundation models used to build volcano plots and rank candidates, though it may be perceived as confirmatory of skepticism; we frame either outcome as the first mechanism-defining test of whether catalysis foundation models represent the Sabatier principle.

Label-recovery and negative controls: we match pairs on signed adsorption energy, absolute deviation, and reaction family so the probe cannot merely re-read the training label, and add negative controls using monotone synthetic tasks and scrambled peak assignments that a genuine two-sided signal must fail to fit; probes are tested for cross-reaction and cross-model generalization.

All experiments are inference-only on public pretrained models plus small probes/SAEs and public catalysis datasets (OC20/OC22) and DFT/experimental volcano references, keeping compute at academic scale.
